# INTRODUCTION

<center>IX</center>

Regarding the Guild of the Physicians, Apothecaries, and Haberdashers <note>The "Arte dei Medici, Speziali e Merciai" was one of the seven major guilds of Florence, representing not only doctors and pharmacists but also merchants of spices, dyes, and luxury goods.</note> of Florence, the following codices have come down to us and are collected in the State Archives of Florence.

### I.

Codex marked no. 1, which we will indicate with the letter *A*. Parchment, consisting of 47 leaves, measuring 25 x 34 cm, bound in wooden boards, well-written and well-preserved. It uses two leaves from Gospel books as flyleaves <note>It was common practice to reuse older, obsolete religious manuscripts as protective endpapers for new bindings.</note>. It is composed of six quires of six leaves each; these are followed by three quires of four leaves, in the second of which a leaf was cut between folio 43 and folio 44, though no interruption in the text appears as a result. From a formal point of view, it is not finished in all its parts. Up to folio 35, the titles and the initial letters of the rubrics <note>term: rubrics (from the Latin 'rubrica' for red ochre; these are the headings or instructional sections written in red ink to distinguish them from the main text)</note> are elegantly executed; from folio 36 to 40 verso, while the initial letters of the rubrics are carefully sketched, the titles are only noted in the margin in black ink and were never rewritten in red in the lines specifically left blank between the rubrics; titles are missing for rubrics 1, 12, 13, 20, and 21. From folio 40 verso to the end, the titles are entirely missing, and the initial letters of the rubrics are barely sketched in the margin of the text.

Codex *A* contains:

a) the statutes of the Guild of the Physicians, Apothecaries, and Haberdashers. It consists of three books: the first, without a title, includes 10 rubrics—

Nor is the observation valid that clause *r* of rubric XXVI is a later reform than the drafting of the text—as the introductory formula "it has been added" <note>original: *additum est*</note> demonstrates to us—because the aforementioned clause does not appear as a marginal note or an addition, but is entirely one with and forms an integral part of the text, and was added at the end of the rubric in the space of four lines purposely left blank.

(*note: original Latin: "minum dari ultra mensem februarii"* <note>meaning "not to be given beyond the month of February"</note>). Other <term>rubrics</term> <note>headings or sections in a legal document</note> are clearly composed of <term>clauses</term> <note>distinct articles or paragraphs within a rubric</note> that date back to different times. Clause *c* of rubric XI, which represents an exception to the general principle established in *b* and *c* of the same rubric, is certainly a later addition that was subsequently incorporated into the text. Rubric XVIIII, which mandates the <term>consuls</term> <note>elected leaders of the guild</note> and the <term>chamberlain</term> <note>the official in charge of the guild's treasury and administration</note> to construct two pairs of scales by January for measuring saffron—with the aim of avoiding the abuse of purchasing it *with large and unsuitable scales, about which the consuls of this craft have hitherto had many complaints* <note>original Latin: "cum bilanciis crossis et indecentibus, de quibus consules huius artis multas actenus habuerunt querelas"</note>—is certainly later than rubric XIII, *g*. In that earlier section, the consuls are ordered *to have for the said craft two pairs of scales for weighing crocus or saffron, with which scales everyone is bound... to weigh saffron* <note>original Latin: "habere pro dicta arte duo paria bilanciarum ad ponderandum crocum sive zafferanum, cum quibus bilanciis tenentur omnes.... crocum ponderare"</note>. The entirety of rubric XVI is nothing more than an expansion, with more detailed case studies, of clause *m* of rubric XIIII. Later than rubric XVI, *how the seller is bound to sift the pepper* <note>original Latin: "qualiter venditor teneatur cribellare piperem"</note>, is clause *b* of rubric LXII, which perhaps belonged to a group of rubrics added later at the end of the original statute. Rubric XXVIII was certainly composed at a later date than clause *a* of rubric XXVII, because otherwise we could not explain the repetition of the same statutory provision at such a short distance.

Equally, we could not explain the contradiction between clause *a* of rubric II, which begins *and the said chamberlain shall be bound to keep.... a boy of 15 years* <note>original Latin: "et teneatur dictus camerarius tenere.... unum puerum .XV. annorum"</note>, and clause *g* of the same rubric, *and that the said chamberlain shall not be bound to have the boy himself* <note>original Latin: "et quod dictus camerarius ipsum puerum habere non teneatur"</note>, if we did not consider that *g* was added later, as the opening formula *it has been added* <note>original Latin: "additum est"</note> alerts us. Clause *c* of rubric XXXVIIII does nothing but add a group of other feast days to be celebrated to clause *a*, and is therefore certainly later than the latter.

The opening words of the statute of the <term>physicians, apothecaries, and haberdashers</term> <note>the three distinct professional groups united under this single guild</note>, *the new constitution begins* <note>original Latin: "incipit novum constitutum"</note>, lead us to believe that there was an *old constitution* <note>original Latin: "vetus constitutum"</note>. The ancient statute was intended to regulate the relations between the first two groups of which the guild was originally composed, namely the physicians and apothecaries <note>The "Arte dei Medici e Speziali" was one of the seven major guilds of Florence; "speziali" refers to those who dealt in spices and medicines.</note>. Until February 1297 (1) the guild is simply indicated as the Guild of Physicians and Apothecaries, while the designation "Guild of Physicians, Apothecaries, and Haberdashers" <note>original: "merciai"</note> appears for the first time in our statute of 1314. Therefore, it is not difficult to suppose that the title *new* <note>original: "novum"</note> truly serves to indicate the fusion and equality among the three members achieved precisely in the year 1314.

The chronological elements of the statute for the saddlers' <note>original: "sellai"</note> branch bring us back to May 1314 (section I, a: *in the present month of May... until the end of the month of December next coming, in the current years of the Lord one thousand three hundred and fourteen, in the thirteenth indiction*) (2). The final section, *concerning the leasing of shops already leased by another craftsman* <note>original: "de conducendis apothecis per alium artificem conductis"</note> (c. 40<sup>t</sup>), was added on June 29, 1314 (3). This second statute must therefore be dated between May and June of 1314. Likewise, the confirmation by the *approvers on behalf of the commune of Florence* <note>original: "approbatores pro communi Florentie"</note> for the two preceding statutes is dated June 29, 1314.

Both the *new constitution* <note>original: "novum constitutum"</note> and the saddlers' statute are the work of a single hand. Section XXVIII of the saddlers' statute and the confirmation of 1314 were written by the notary Pietro di Ricco Bacherelli, *public Florentine notary of the said approvers, currently scribe*.

The reforms were compiled by the revisors of 1314 (4), and like the two previous statutes, were confirmed by the arbiters cor-

XIII

rectors of the Florentine guilds <note>The "Arti" were the powerful professional and trade associations of medieval Florence</note> on April 1, 1315 (folio 42, verso). Both the corrections and the confirmation of 1315 were written by the notary Michele di Soldo da Gangalandi.

The statute for the painters' branch is not dated. However, based on its position in the volume, it cannot be placed earlier than April 1, 1315—the day of the confirmation by the notary Michele di Soldo da Gangalandi—nor later than June 18, 1316, which is the most recent date found in the codex. And since the marginal addition to rubric I *b*, which bears the date of November 18, was written by the same hand that wrote the painters' statute, it is not difficult to trace the statute itself back to November 1315. The painters' statute was written by a different hand than the preceding one.

Codex A, as it has come down to us, was intended for practical use. This is evidenced by the interlinear <gloss>notes written between the lines of the main text</gloss> and marginal additions <margin>notes in the margins</margin> that were added to the statutes over time.

The revisions can be reduced to four distinct phases. The first, securely dated June 29, 1314, was carried out by the hand of the notary Pietro di Ricco Bacherelli and appears in the statutes of the guild of doctors, apothecaries, and haberdashers <note>The "medici, speziali e merciai" was the major guild to which painters were originally subordinate</note> (rubric XXXVIIII, *c*), and of the saddlers' branch (rubric VIIII *a*, XXIII). The second is to be attributed to the notary Michele di Soldo da Gangalandi, who authenticated the confirmation of the revisors of the Commune of Florence on April 1, 1315 (statutes of the doctors, apothecaries, and haberdashers XVI *a*, XXIIII *a*, XXXII *a*; saddlers' statutes, rubric XVIII, XXII, XXIII). The third is due to the same hand that wrote the painters' statute (statutes of the doctors, apothecaries, and haberdashers, rubric I *b*, II *d*, IIII *a*, VIIII *a*, XIIIII *l*, XXIII, XXIIII *a*, XXXVII *c*, XXXXVIII; saddlers' statute, rubric VIIII *a*, XXIII, XXVI). The fourth, also securely dated, is from June 18, 1316, and was executed by the hand of the notary Bene di Bencivenni da Rufina (statutes of the doctors, apothecaries, and haberdashers, rubric I *d*, I *n*, II *g*, IIII *b*, XXIIII *a*, XXV; reform of 1314, rubric I, II, III, V, VI, VII; painters' statute, rubric I *c*, *d*, II, IIII, VIII, XIIII).

## II.

Codex marked no. 3, which we will indicate with the letter *B*. A parchment codex <note>original: "Cod. membr."</note>, measuring 27x36 cm, consisting of 279 numbered folios <note>original: "cc. num." refers to 'carte', the individual leaves of the book</note>, bound in leather with two clasps and metal studs. Well preserved.

It contains the statute in Latin from 1349, comprising 92 rubrics <note>term: rubric (a titled section or chapter of a legal document, traditionally written in red ink)</note>. The table of contents <note>original: "rubricario"</note> spans folios 2-3. The statute is divided into two books without titles and without the original indication of the number of rubrics <note>(1)</note>. The first book deals with the organization of the guild <note>term: "arte" (the professional guild or trade corporation)</note>, and contains rubrics 1-16 (folios 4-17 verso); the second deals with the administration of justice, the general policing of the guild, the membership register <note>term: "matricola"</note>, etc., and contains rubrics 17-92 (folios 17 verso-55 verso). The confirmation dated September 10, 1349, follows.

The text of the statute is followed by additions and reforms, also in Latin, except for those of 1376 (rubric III), 1385, 1412, 1436 (rubrics X-XIV, XXI-XXIV), 1454, 1461 (rubrics I-X), 1463, 1468, 1483 (rubrics I-IX, XI-XX), 1491 (rubrics I-VI), 1517, 1524, 1556, 1558, which are in the vernacular <note>original: "volgare" (the everyday Italian language as opposed to formal Latin)</note>. These additions begin in 1351 and continue until 1769—contrary to the provision in rubric VIII, which stated that the statutes were to remain unchanged until November 1352. The last actual revision carried out by the "correctors" <note>term: "correttori" (officials appointed to revise or amend statutes)</note> is dated June 10, 1634. From that year until 1769, we find simple notations of payments made to the *Monte* <note>term: "Monte" (a public bank or treasury)</note> by the reform councils <note>original: "riformagioni"</note> for the three-year approval of the statutes. These vary in importance: sometimes they are very brief, other times they span several pages; some deal with a single subject, while others revise all or a very large part of the statutory material. With very few exceptions, they are always dated. They contain opening and closing formulas including the names of the revisers charged with the reform of the guild statutes, the name—

<meta>This page continues the introduction's technical description of the manuscript's physical structure and the methods used by medieval and early modern scribes to update the legal statutes.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION

and the signatures of the <term>notaries</term><note>In this context, notaries were legal officials responsible for authenticating documents and recording official acts of the city-state or guild.</note> who physically carried out and then authenticated the work of the revision. The later reforms—of which we have a brief subject index inserted between folios 277 and 278, written by a hand from the end of the 1600s—refer directly to the statute. They cite the specific rubric <note>a titled section or chapter of the law</note>, the leaf, the page, and the line, indicating the passages to be deleted, those to be added, and the precise location where the correction must be made.

Many corrections were physically executed within the body of the statute as the reading progressed, performed by the notary in the presence of the officials appointed by the <term>commune</term><note>The local city government</note> for the reform of the statutes of the <term>guilds</term><note>original: "arti"; the professional associations that governed trade and industry.</note> (1). At other times, the notary took brief notes in the margin next to the relevant statutory provisions and later drafted the correction itself more comfortably, adding the date, the name of at least one of the reformers, and his own authentication (2). Much more often, however, certain later reforms were transcribed into the margins of the statutory provisions to which they refer, so that anyone consulting the <term>codex</term><note>The bound manuscript volume</note> would have them immediately before their eyes and would not be forced to track them down by leafing through the many pages of additions.

In other instances, later reforms are referenced alongside the text of the statute to which they relate, with an indication of the leaf number in the codex. For example, on folio VII, the notary notes next to ***twelve other honest men*** <note>original Latin: "duodecim alios probos"</note>: <margin>***it must be 20, as in the addition written by Ser Maso Nelli on folio 78*** <note>original Latin: "debet esse .XX. ut in additamentum scriptum per ser Masum Nelli a. c. 78"</note></margin>; and on folio VIIII: <margin>***note certain things against this in the addition written by Ser Francesco Cioli*** <note>original Latin: "nota quedam contra hec in additamento scripto per ser Francischum Cioli"</note></margin>; on folio XV verso, the same notary annotated: <margin>***they can also choose others in another form as held in chapter 45 below*** <note>original Latin: "possunt etiam eligere alios alia forma prout habetur in cap. 45 infra"</note></margin>; on folio XVIII: <margin>***concerning this there is another ordinance written by Ser Francesco Cioli and another speaking of the provider*** <note>original Latin: "circa hoc est aliud ordinamentum scriptum per ser Francischum Cioli et aliud loquens de provisore"</note></margin>; on folio LXVIII: <margin>***this addition has been cancelled by the cancellation written by Ser Maso Nelli at leaf 79, etc.*** <note>original Latin: "capsata est hec additio per capsationem scriptam per ser Masum Nelli ad cartam 79, ecc."</note></margin>

# INTRODUCTION

The codex shows extensive traces of the use made of it even in recent times. The longer sections <note>original: "rubriche," referring to the titled chapters or headings traditionally written in red ink</note> are divided into paragraphs, many of which have a title in the margin; indexes, arrows, annotations, and cross-references between various parts of the statute and between the statute and later additions—the work of notaries from the second half of the 14th century onwards—were intended to facilitate the practical work of oversight and consultation.

*B* possesses all the characteristics of an original text. The 92 chapters of the statute are written by a single hand. As for the reforms following 1349, the handwriting varies from year to year.

### III.

Codex marked no. 2, which we will indicate with the letter *C*. Parchment <note>original: "Membr." for membranaceo</note> measuring 26 by 37 cm, bound in half-leather, consisting of 247 numbered folios <note>original: "cc. num." for carte numerate</note>, plus two unnumbered ones. Each page is dry-ruled with wide side margins and contains 30 lines.

It contains the same statute as *B*, from 1349, but in the vernacular <note>original: "volgare," meaning the local Italian dialect rather than Latin</note>. The order of the material is identical to that of *B*. Codex *C* contains only 91 chapters, not 92. The difference is due to the fact that *C* lacks chapter LXXI <note>71</note> of *B*, which was struck out before the Latin statute of 1349 was translated into the vernacular, and chapter LXXXX <note>90</note>: *concerning the prohibition of buying or keeping foreign goods for sale* <note>original Latin: "de non emendo vel retinendo laboreria forestieria ad vendendum"</note>, which was canceled in 1351. The omission of these two chapters in *C* would bring their number to 90. However, in *B*, chapter XXVII <note>27</note> was not numbered, though it appears in the table of contents under the title *how the seller is required to sift the pepper* <note>original Latin: "qualiter venditor teneatur cribellare piperem"</note>, and this chapter has been numbered in codex *C*.

A very large number of chapters lack a title; sometimes it is sketched in the margin in small script with black ink, using many heavy abbreviations. Even the initial letters of the chapters which, judging by the blank space, were meant to be executed in large, beautiful red characters, are instead merely hinted at in the margin of the text.

# INTRODUCTION
XVIII

Alongside the headings, there are rare references, from a later period, to Codex *B*, which is indicated by the name "Great Statute" or "Latin Statute." <note>original: "statuto grande" or "statuto latino". These terms distinguish the primary Latin legal text from the vernacular translations.</note>

Up to folio 191 (1435), the codex <term>Codex: a manuscript book</term> is written entirely by one hand from the 15th century; from folio 191 onwards, several different hands appear. There are 201 reforms <term>Reforms: official amendments or updates to the existing statutes</term>, ranging from folio 56 verso to folio 243 (1351 — April 26, 1558). Up to this last date, they substantially agree with those of Codex *B*. The corrections are made as in *B*, referencing the heading, the leaf, the page, the line, and the words of the statute text; but these references do not match in *C*. This is because whoever executed the vernacular translation <term>Volgarizzamento: the process of translating Latin texts into the common "vulgar" Italian tongue</term> from *B* translated literally word-for-word, sometimes even inaccurately, and did not care at all to check if there was a correspondence between the pages of the statute text in *C* and those of the later reforms, nor did they worry about the practical use for which the text was intended. Perhaps for this reason *C*—at least in its oldest part, that is, up to the reforms of the first half of the 1500s—was used less than *B*, as evidenced by the scarce references, the absolute lack of marginal annotations, and the truly excellent state of preservation of the codex itself. From the second half of the 1500s onwards, *C* shows very frequent traces of use, certainly more extensive than that of *B*. The reforms in *C* are reproduced in full from *B*, except from the year 1436 (folio 191 verso) to 1517 (folio 205 verso), during which period *C* reproduces in brief and sometimes only barely mentioned reforms that we instead find full and detailed in *B*; it also completely neglects the simple confirmations of the correcting arbitrators which are instead reported in *B* year by year. The reforms in *C* offer us a more reduced formula compared to *B*; the signatures, the notary's validations, and the *notary's mark* <note>original: "signum notarii". A unique symbol drawn by a notary to authenticate a document.</note> are missing, for which things the reader is expressly and constantly referred back to *B*.

*C* is not always the exact and faithful vernacular translation of *B*. Some additions, which in *B* are transcribed by the notaries in the margin of the statutory provisions to which they refer and which are found

# INTRODUCTION

Conversely, other passages that form part of the statutory provisions according to the redaction given to us in Codex *B*, and which were expunged in later reforms in both *B* and *C*, would be sought in vain in the text of the statute as it is given to us by Codex *C* (1). There does not seem to have been a rigid criterion in accepting or rejecting additions or deletions from the vernacular text that we find in *B*; except perhaps this: that the translator did not wish to present us merely with a complete and exact <term>vernacularization</term><note>The process of translating Latin legal or scholarly texts into the common "vulgar" tongue (Italian) for wider accessibility.</note> of the statute contained in *B*, but rather to offer us, as far as he was able, a text that—setting aside whatever had already fallen into disuse or been annulled—approached as closely as possible the current statutory law and that alone.

(1) For example: the passage <note>original: "et intaglantes quascumque res qui intaglantes forent, seu erunt matriculati ecc."</note> *and those carving any things who were carvers, or shall be matriculated etc.* is added in the margin of sheet XXV verso of *B* by the hand of the notary Azzolino Contuccini on December 7, 1351; we later find this among the reforms of 1351, and in *C* it forms an integral part of the text of the statute (rubric XXIII, *g*). The two passages <note>original: "laboraverint, fecerint seu fieri fecerint"</note> *they shall have worked, made, or caused to be made*, which were part of the text of *B* as it was drafted in 1349, but which were deleted in the reform of December 7, 1351 (rubric II, *a* and *b*), do not appear in *C* at all. The interlinear addition <note>original: "scarsellas"</note> *purses* on sheet XXV of *B*, attributed to the same Azzolino, is accepted into the text of the statute of *C* (rubric XXIII, *g*). The addition <note>original: "et omnes et singuli barbitonsores etc."</note> *and all and singular barbers etc.* from the reform of December 21, 1384, transcribed in *B* by the notary Tino di ser Ottaviani in the interline of rubric XXIII, is inserted in *C* (rubric XXIII, *e*). The two very long passages <note>original: "et quod nullus"</note> *and that no one* and the other <note>original: "salvo et riservato"</note> *saving and reserved* which appear in the text of the statute of *B* at sheets XLIIII and XLVI, and which (as appears from a marginal note by the notary Azzolino Contuccini) were expunged by the correctors on December 7, 1351, do not appear in *C* (cf. rubric L, *a*). The two clauses <note>original: "santientes e insuper etiam"</note> *decreeing and moreover also* which appear in *B* at sheet 27 and which were deleted in the revision of December 26, 1356 (rubric VI, *a* and *b*) do not appear in the text of *C* (cf. rubric XVII, *r, t*). Of the two marginal notes on sheet 57 verso of *B* (rubric LXXVI) executed on the same day and by the same hand, one is inserted into text *C*, the other is not. There is no lack of actual reading errors: e.g., <note>original: "solvendo"</note> *paying* in *B* which the translator read as <note>original: "solummodo"</note> *only* and translated as *only* (rubric LIII, *e*).

## IV.

Codex marked no. 4, which we will indicate with the letter *E*. Paper, measuring 22 x 32 cm, bound in leather, consisting of 98 numbered leaves <note>The original uses "cc." for "carte," referring to the double-sided leaves of the manuscript.</note>, plus 24 blank ones. Well preserved. It includes:

a) *Summary of the Statute of the Apothecaries' Guild* <note>original: "summarium statuti artis aromatariorum"</note>, containing 18 general principles of the guild's statutory law in brief form;

b) an extract in the vernacular <note>The "volgare" or common Italian tongue, as opposed to formal Latin.</note> of the 1349 statute, recast and completed with later reforms, comprising 71 rubrics (leaves 1-65r);

Codex *E* shows traces here and there of the use made of it: sub-headings of clauses, indexes, and cross-references from rubric to rubric were intended in practice to facilitate consultation; leaves 28-32 have been reinforced because they were worn out from too much use. Codex marked no. 5 (Strozzi Papers no. 649; class II, dist. I, no. 55). We will indicate it as *D*. Bound in parchment, consisting of 41 numbered folios, plus 17 unnumbered blank folios, measuring 22 $\times$ 30 cm. # INTRODUCTION
XXII

*E* certainly derives from *D* (1). Many additions that appear in the margins or at the end of sections in manuscript *D* are integrated directly into the body of the statutes in *E*; sections or passages that were deleted in *D* during the revision process do not appear in *E* at all; nor is *E* lacking in material errors and oversights resulting from a poor reading of *D*. The same handwriting and certain linguistic peculiarities found in *D* are also found in *E* (2). The same apparent discrepancy in the order of the sections between *D* and *E* is explained by a note on folio 30 verso and folio 37 verso of *D*. Although *D* shows traces of corrections and additions, it is not the final version. For example, next to the section *regarding going to the burial* <note>original: "d'andare alla sepultura"</note> on folio 20, there is the marginal note *needs to be re-corrected* <note>original: "àssi a ricorreggere"</note>.

These sub-groups held the right of representation, their own officials, and their own administration, over which the major guild exercised a right of control and supervision, and with whom it shared certain revenues.

As for the statute of 1349, of which we possess two versions, we have preferred to publish the vernacular text <note>the "volgare," or everyday Italian, rather than formal Latin</note>. While this is a reproduction of the Latin text of 1349, it offers the greatest interest to scholars of philology and linguistics, being one of the earliest examples of statutory legislation written in the vernacular. We have nevertheless sought to remain as close as possible to the text of *B* <note>referring to Codex B, one of the primary manuscript sources</note>. Thus, we have not failed to note, instance by instance, the passages that appear in *B* as marginal notes while in *C* <note>Codex C</note> they are inserted into the main text; the corrections in *B* which were ignored in *C*; or corrections in *C* of which there is no trace in the Latin original. We believed it appropriate to reproduce in *C*, among the additions, those headings or clauses that were annulled or reformed after 1349 and which were physically erased in *B*. However, we have deliberately ignored those marginal annotations of a recent era in *B* and *C*, written next to the headings for exclusively practical purposes, which we find later among the reforms in their proper chronological place. We have drawn the reforms up to 1435 from Codex *C*. From 1436 to 1517, we have published them from *B*, which offers them in a broader and more complete form than *C*, and because it contains the year-by-year confirmations that are entirely missing in *C*. # INTRODUCTION

### VIII.

And now a few words on the method we have followed in this publication.

We have distinguished the statutes from the reforms and the actual additions. These latter are published following the statutes in their proper chronological order, which is the same order in which they are found in the original codices <note>A codex is a handwritten book, the precursor to the modern printed book.</note>.

For the convenience of scholars, we have thought it appropriate to place the table of contents <term>rubricario: a list of headings or "rubrics" used to navigate legal documents</term> before each statute, both when it is found in the original codex and when it was possible for us to assemble it from the titles of the relevant sections. The numbering is our own, for which we have preferred Roman numerals.

The statute of the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers of 1314 and the reform of 1314 contained in Codex *A* are presented in print using two types of fonts: *roman* and *italic*. The *roman* font used for the statute and the reform of 1314 indicates everything that was accepted into the statute of 1349; the *italic* indicates what was dropped in the new edition. The opposite criteria was adopted for the publication of the vernacular <note>The "volgare" or common Italian language, as opposed to formal Latin.</note> statute of 1349, in which the *italic* indicates what was preserved from the statute and reform of 1314, and the *roman* indicates all statutory material codified after 1314.

> <note>original: "Capitula supra in volumine huius libri..."</note> The chapters contained and written above in the volume of this book of statutes of the said Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, Grocers, Belt-makers, and Shield-makers, with their additions and corrections which have not been quashed or canceled and which do not detract from the present approval and confirmation, they [the officials] have approved and confirmed, and they willed and commanded that they remain and exist in their due state, strength, and vigor.
>
> (S.N. <note>Signum Notarii: The notary's personal mark or sign</note>) I, Francesco, son of the late Ser Giovanni Ciai of Pulicciano, Florentine citizen, by imperial authority ordinary judge and public notary, and messenger, notary, and scribe of the said approved officials appointed for the Commune of Florence, have written and published all the aforesaid acts performed before me by mandate of the said officials, and therefore I have signed my name.

# INTRODUCTION

-> — XXVII — <-

and of which we find no traces in codex *A* (1). This inversion in the meaning of the characters was chosen because we wished to avoid a prevalence of italics, which tend to strain the reader's eye.

Since in both *A* and *C* <note>Codex A and Codex C refer to the specific historical manuscript volumes being compared in this edition</note> we very frequently find excessively long rubrics <note>term: rubric; from the Latin 'rubrica' (red ochre), these are the titles or introductory headings of legal sections, traditionally written in red ink</note>, and references to a specific provision contained within a rubric would prove difficult for the reader, we have decided to divide them into clauses <note>term: commi; the numbered or lettered sub-sections of a legal article</note>, marking them with small letters of the alphabet. Because these letters have been added by us, we print them in italics. This division is not entirely arbitrary. The need to divide the rubrics had already been felt by the correcting arbitrators and the notaries who used the statutes in practice. In codex *A*, where we begin these clauses, we sometimes find enlarged initial capital letters in red, sometimes a red mark in the shape of a capital *C* <note>original: "a guisa di un C maiuscolo"; likely referring to a pilcrow or paragraph mark</note>, or a hand drawn <note>term: manicule; a small hand drawn in the margin to point out important text</note> or another sign to alert the reader; in codex *B* and more rarely in *C* we even find sub-titles for the clauses in Latin or in the vernacular <note>original: "volgare"; the local Italian dialect as opposed to formal Latin</note>. Even within the statute itself there are sometimes hints of these subdivisions; for example, in rubric LIII, *c* of codex *C*, when speaking of a penalty, it is said: *as stated above in the other point*. Although the division in codex *B* is not original and the sub-titles were written by a hand that is sometimes very recent, we thought it best to take into account these elements offered by the text. Alongside the italic letters marking the clauses, we have reproduced in brackets [ ] said titles when they are provided by the codex. The additions and reforms to the statutes have also been divided by us into rubrics, having Roman numerals, and into clauses distinguished by small letters of the alphabet printed in italics.

---

(1) I have attempted to make the correspondence between the subject matter of the statute of 1314 and that of 1349 visible at a glance, even in the table of rubrics <note>original: "rubricario"; a list or index of the headings in the legal code</note> placed before the two statutes. In each of the tables, the corresponding rubric of the other statute is indicated by an Arabic numeral placed in brackets [ ] after the title of the same rubric.

# INTRODUCTION

Each page contains the text accompanied by the strictly essential illustrative notes; these are followed, separated from the text and notes by a small line, by the interlinear and marginal additions. These additions are linked to the main text using lowercase letters in upright type, and are followed, where necessary, by notes with a numbering system distinct from that of the main text. The notes to the text are in upright type; the notes to the additions, also in upright type, are underlined.

All abbreviations have been expanded according to the standards of the <term>Italian Historical Institute</term> <note>The Istituto Storico Italiano per il Medio Evo, which established national standards for editing medieval documents</note>, except for a few that occur very frequently, which can be reduced to the following:
*s* = *soldo* or *soldi* <note>A silver coin or unit of account</note>; *d.* or *den.* = *denaro* or *denari* <note>The penny or smallest unit of currency</note>; *f. p.* = *small florins* <note>original: "florenorum parvorum" or "fiorini piccoli"</note>.

The spelling has been modernized. Before *p* and *b*, when the text does not offer a different spelling, we have always expanded the abbreviations by introducing the letter *m*. In both the Latin statutes and the vernacular one, the letters *c* and *g* often occur in a palatal function <note>indicating a "soft" sound like 'ch' or 'j'</note>, for example: *vernicare* (to varnish), *ingallare* (to treat with gallnut), *accaio* (steel), *mercaio* (haberdasher), *gengavo* (ginger), *dicotto* (eighteen), *guoco* (game), etc. In these cases, we have thought it best for the accuracy of pronunciation to insert the letter *i*, placing it between brackets [ ]. In all other matters, we have adhered to the rules established by the Italian Historical Institute.

In the citations, we have used very few abbreviations so as not to unnecessarily fatigue the reader. The <term>rubrics</term> <note>The titled headings or chapters of the statutes</note> of the statutes are referenced with Roman numerals, and the clauses with lowercase italic letters; for the sake of simplicity, we have avoided citing the book numbers as well, because the rubrics—following the custom of <term>Codices</term> <note>Handwritten manuscript volumes</note> *B* and *C*—have progressive numbering from the first to the last.

The reforms and additions to the statutes are cited by the year in which they were approved, followed by the rubric in Roman numerals and the clause in small italic letters.

# STATUTE OF 1314 BOOK I, CHAPTER 1

### Here begins the new constitution of the guild and college of doctors, apothecaries,
### and grocers of the city of Florence.

In the name of God, amen. To the honor, praise, and reverence of Almighty God, and of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, [his] mother, [and of the bles]sed (1) John the Baptist, *patron and defender of the commune of Florence*, [and of al]l the Saints of God, and of the holy Roman Church, and of the supreme pontiff, and of the lords Podestà <note>The Podestà was a high-ranking foreign official brought in to manage the city's justice system</note> and Captain of the *said commune*, and of the lords Priors of the Guilds, and of the Gonfalonier of Justice of the *same* city, and to the honor and good standing of the lords Consuls and *of the entire guild of doctors, apothecaries, and grocers of the city of Florence, the following is the new constitution of the aforementioned guild and college.*

->[BOOK I]<-

## I. Concerning the election of the lords consuls and their prohibition from office.

a. And by "Gate of Saint Mary" shall be understood the districts of Oltrarno, San Piero Scheraggio, and Borgo. And those so elected they shall place...

## II. Concerning the election of the chamberlain and his office.

*a. At the beginning of the month of January, the consuls of this guild, along with twelve good men of the said guild to be chosen at their will, shall be bound to elect two good and law-abiding men of the said guild, truly Guelphs <note>Members of the political faction supporting the Pope, a requirement for holding office in many Italian cities at this time</note>, of twenty-five years of age or older, and they shall be sent to a secret scrutiny <note>A secret ballot</note> among the said twelve good men only. And whoever has the most votes shall be the chamberlain of the said guild. And he shall be elected one time in the Old Forum and the next time at the Gate of Saint Mary. And his office shall last for six months. And he shall provide a suitable surety <note>A financial guarantee or bond</note> of three hundred pounds in small florins for the good and legal exercise of his office, and for standing before the syndicate <note>An auditing committee</note> and obeying the sentences of the syndics who shall audit him.*

### III. Concerning the election of the notary.

a. *In the month of January, the consuls are bound, as quickly as they are able, to elect for the said guild one good, sufficient, and expert notary, a true Guelph <note>A member of the political faction supporting the Pope; this was a requirement for holding public or guild office in Florence</note>, for the purpose of writing all the acts of the court of the consuls and performing other duties which pertain to the said notary.*

b. *Which notary shall stay and remain, and ought to stay and remain, in the shop <note>original: "apotheca," here meaning the guild's headquarters or office</note> of the said guild, specifically and generally on all juridical days and all other days necessary to the aforementioned guild, for the exercise of his office, and to hear, recognize, and receive all civil and criminal questions and controversies, and to process them until the sentence, by both ordinary and extraordinary means.*

c. *Once the proofs have been made, the consuls shall deliver the sentence according to the form of the statutes.*

d. *And the said notary shall be compensated for his writings according to the manner written below: from every new master swearing into the guild, twelve small Florentine pennies; from every complaint, four pennies; from every seizure of goods <note>original: "preda"</note>, four pennies; from every precept and requisition, three pennies from the plaintiff; from every witness examined by him, two soldi; from every summary entry <note>term: "imbreviatura" - a short-hand legal draft made by a notary in his register</note> of the audit <note>term: "sindicatus" - the formal review of an official's conduct at the end of their term</note>, two soldi, and if it is completed, five soldi; for sentences and other various writings, he shall be satisfied according to the customary manner. And his office shall last for one year <insert>2</insert>.*

# I, IIII STATUTE OF 1314

### IIII. On the election of the councilors.

*a. During the month of January, the consuls <note>the chief magistrates of the guild</note> are bound to elect twelve (1) good and lawful councilors, who are true Guelphs <note>original: "guelfos"; supporters of the Papacy, a necessary political affiliation for public office in 14th-century Florence</note>, from the men (a) of the said guild. This shall be done in such a way that there is only one person from any single shop or warehouse. Six of these shall be from the Gate of Saint Mary, and six from the Old Market.*

*b. These twelve councilors, in the presence of the consuls or four of them, have the power to provide, confirm, establish, and ordain whatever they wish and believe to be useful for the aforementioned guild regarding proposals made to them by the Prior of the consuls—or another consul if the Prior is absent—concerning any facts or business of the said guild, in whatever way they wish, provided that at least four of the said consuls and the majority of the said councilors (b) are present.*

*c. And whatever shall be ordained by two-thirds of those councilors present, using the voting boxes and ballots <note>original: "pissides et ballottas"; a secret voting system using small containers and balls</note>, shall be valid and binding as if it had been done by the entire aforementioned community. And what is said above regarding the voting boxes and ballots shall take place in all councils which the said consuls might hold regarding any deed or matter.*

*d. Excepting that they may not ordain, propose, harangue, decree, or hold an accounting that the consuls be absolved before the end of their term of audit <note>term: "sindicatus"; the period at the end of an official's term where their actions were reviewed for legality</note>, or that the salary of masters newly coming to this guild, or any fine or tax imposed or to be imposed on anyone, be diminished or reduced in any way.*

*e. The said councilors are also bound to come to the councils of the said guild whenever they are called by a messenger or by other means. And if those summoned do not come, five shillings shall be taken immediately from those not attending—*

## V. Concerning the election of the eighteen "Good Men" who must perform the tax assessment.

*a. The consuls of this guild are bound in the month of June, if it is deemed expedient with the guild chamberlain, to elect in three turns eighteen "Good Men" <note>term: boni homines (respected citizens chosen for their integrity)</note>, who are true Guelphs <note>Members of the political faction supporting the Pope, a requirement for public life in 14th-century Florence</note>; namely, six from the Gate of Saint Mary, six from the Old Market, and six from between the district of Oltrarno and the Bishop’s Gate.*

*b. Six of these—specifically one from the Bishop’s Gate, one from the district of Oltrarno, two from the Old Market, and two from the Gate of Saint Mary—shall stay and remain secretly in a hidden place, and they are bound to impose and perform the assessment <note>term: imposita (a direct tax or levy imposed on guild members)</note> upon the men of said guild in the city and countryside of Florence; namely, upon each person, what is just and fitting. And once that assessment is made, they must bring it back sealed before the notary of this guild. And afterwards, in a similar manner and form, another six of them must perform the assessment. And afterwards the remaining six, in the said manner and form, shall perform their assessment and bring it back sealed, as has been said.*

*c. Once these assessments have been brought back, the notary of the said guild is bound to unseal the said assessments in the presence of the consuls, councilors, and the guild chamberlain, and he shall take a third from each assessment and make one body out of the said three thirds <note>This describes a "weighted average" system to ensure fairness and prevent bias in taxation</note>. This body of text shall be written in the acts of the guild, and it shall be understood to be the assessment of the men and persons of the said guild. Which assessment, as stated, once written, the consuls shall cause to be read and announced in a public assembly along with all other debts of the guild; and they shall command all debtors and those owing the assessment, or anything else, that they pay the assessment and whatever they are bound to pay to the guild chamberlain within ten days from the day of the command, under penalty of an additional quarter.*

*d. And if anyone living in the city or countryside of Florence has not paid within the said time of ten days, an additional quarter shall be taken from him without any reduction, in the name of a penalty.*

# STATUTE OF 1314
I, v

*e. And if anyone, once the said ten-day deadline has passed, has not immediately paid the principal sum and the aforementioned penalty, they shall be distrained <note>original: "pignorentur" - the legal seizure of property to settle a debt</note> and their goods seized at their own expense. They shall be compelled both in property and in person until full satisfaction is made, by the chamberlain of the guild and the syndic <note>a legal representative or official</note> appointed to litigate against them, to pay or obey the consuls; this applies also to those refusing to swear the oath to the guild, and likewise at the expense of the aforesaid guild, as is contained in another chapter.*

*f. Furthermore, the aforementioned tax-assessors <note>original: "impositores"</note> may in no way hold onto an old tax assessment when they are creating a new one.*

*g. Likewise, they may in no way set assessments for themselves, or for their partners, or their shops; instead, the consuls then in office, together with six good and capable men of the said guild, shall be bound to assess and create the tax for the said eighteen tax-assessors and their partners and companies and each one of them, according to what shall seem just to them, having considered the quality of each of the aforesaid partners. This is provided that the assessment for the said eighteen men is made before the assessment made by those same eighteen men for the other members of the guild is published.*

*h. And that these tax-assessors must be drawn from every branch <note>original: "membro"</note> of the said guild as it happens, namely: **doctors**, **apothecaries**, **mercers** <note>dealers in fine fabrics</note>, **grocers**, **purse-makers**, and **cap-makers**. And that all debts looming over the said guild and all expenses to be incurred by the guild or any branch of the guild for any matter, and all sums of money to be levied upon the same guild or any branch of the guild, must be assessed and paid in common by all craftsmen of the said guild.*

*i. And that no one from the aforesaid guild may, dare, or presume to speak, propose, harangue, or hold an argument against the aforesaid rules or any part of them, under penalty of twenty-five pounds in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccoli, the local currency of account</note>, to be taken from anyone acting to the contrary, as often as it occurs.*

*l. Moreover, the said tax-assessors shall take care to find, and shall solicitously inquire about, all apothecaries who keep or do not keep a doctor in their shops with whom they have entered into a partnership; they shall make an assessment for such an apothecary and doctor as partners by reason of the apothecary art, and for the said doctor individually by reason of the medical art, according to what shall seem just to them. And let this chapter be precise and final <note>original: "precisum et trunchum"</note>, and it must be strictly observed under penalty of ten pounds in small florins for each of the said consuls, to be taken from them by the syndics who shall audit them.*

*m. And that the new consuls shall secretly find out if the old consuls, or any one of them, has not paid his assessment. And if they find anyone has not paid, they shall immediately compel him in property and in person to pay the assessment and the established penalty for the deed, under penalty of double the amount, for each consul.*

### VI. Concerning the election of arbitrators.

a. The consuls <note>The chief executive officers of the guild</note> of this craft shall be bound, during the month of November and with the council of this craft, to elect, appoint, and nominate six good and capable arbitrators—true Guelphs <note>Members of the political faction supporting the Pope; this was a common requirement for holding office in 14th-century Florence to ensure political loyalty</note>—from among the men of this craft, namely: *three from the Old Market and three from the Gate of Saint Mary.* And in this same manner, the election of these arbitrators shall and must take place every two years.

b. Those so elected in the said month may, shall be bound to, and must correct this constitution and the chapters contained within it, and change them in whole or in part and issue new chapters. And whatever shall be done by them, or by the majority of them, shall be as valid in that respect as if it had been done by the entire aforesaid craft.

c. And the said arbitrators shall receive from the guild chamberlain <note>The treasurer</note> *three pounds in small florins* <note>original: "libras tres f. p." (florenorum parvorum)</note> *for a certain meal.* And they shall swear to keep secret those things which they have done *until the upcoming Kalends of January* <note>January 1st</note>.

### VII. Concerning the election of syndics to audit the consuls and other former officials.

a. The consuls, with the council of the said craft, shall be bound at the beginning of the month of January to elect *three good men of this craft, true Guelphs, as syndics <note>Officials appointed to audit and review the conduct of outgoing officers</note>, who must and shall be bound to audit all officials of the said craft within fifteen days of them having laid down their offices.*

b. These syndics shall be bound and must swear to perform the said office and to exercise it well and legally, and to convict or acquit those officials as they see fit according to the law within the said term, under penalty of *ten pounds in small florins for each of them.*

c. And their office shall last for one year; and they shall be subject to a prohibition <note>original: "devetum"; a mandatory waiting period before being eligible for re-election to the same office</note> for one year from the day they lay down their office.

d. This term of *fifteen days* may in no way be extended for the said syndics by any officials of the said craft or others of the said craft, under penalty of *ten pounds in small florins* for anyone extending the term or accepting the extension. And concerning the aforesaid matters, no council may be held, no proposal made, nor anything else decreed; and if such is done, it shall be void by law.

### VIII. Concerning the compelling of craftsmen of the said craft from the countryside to appoint a representative.

In the month of January of each year, the consuls of this craft shall be bound to compel each and every man of this craft dwelling in the countryside <note>original: "comitatu"; the rural territory surrounding the city</note>...

### IX. On electing a Syndic and Procurator for the Guild.

a. Since some—indeed many—of the said Guild and those publicly practicing the craft refuse to obey the aforementioned Consuls of the Guild, belittling their sentences, commands, and their very office to the grave damage and prejudice of the mentioned college, we decree and ordain that the Consuls of the said Guild, in the current years of our Lord 1309, the eighth indiction, in a public assembly of the Guild, shall be bound together with those present—and those present with them—to elect, depute, and name Ser Giovanni Bongie <insert>Ser Salvi Dini</insert> (a), notary of the said Guild, as the syndic and for the syndic of the aforesaid Guild. They grant him full, general, and special mandate with free administration for all and singular cases and business of the said Guild, and for those which might be brought against the Guild, whether civil or criminal.

b. This syndic—in whatever way, however, and by whatever words he is found to be appointed, and however his mandate is written or made—shall be held and considered by virtue of the present statute as legitimate, sufficient, and specifically appointed for all the aforesaid matters and others he may carry out for the said Guild. He must be admitted, judged, and received as legitimate and sufficient by anyone administering the law.

c. This syndic, however appointed, shall have full, pure, wide, and ample office and <term>authority</term><note>original: "baliam" (balia), referring to emergency or plenary power granted to officials in Florentine law.</note>; and he shall be bound and obligated to compel all those he finds practicing the said craft who have not yet sworn the oath to do so.

### X. On the election of the messenger.

*In the month of January, the Consuls are bound to elect, for their benefit and that of the said guild <insert>utility</insert> <note>The word "utility" is missing in the original manuscript and is added here based on comparisons with other historical copies</note>, one good and capable messenger <term>Messenger (nuntius): an official responsible for delivering summons, notices, and enforcing guild orders</term>, for the making of requests, commands, and all other individual tasks that pertain to the office of the messenger. This messenger is bound to do everything that shall be enjoined upon him by the Consuls of the said guild. And he shall remain and stay to exercise his said office continually, every day. And he shall have from the Chamberlain of the said guild for his salary, for every month in which he has continually remained to exercise the said office, forty shillings of small Florentine pennies, and not otherwise. And he shall provide a suitable surety <term>Surety (fideiussio): a financial guarantee or bond provided by a third party to ensure the official performs his duties honestly</term> of ten pounds of small Florentine pennies for the legal exercise of his office. And the said messenger shall have, for every new member <note>original: "novitio"</note> whom he brings in, twelve pennies for every pound of the payment which the member makes for his entry fee <note>original: "intratura"</note> to the guild.*

### [Book II]

## Here begins the second book of the constitution of the said guild.

### XI. Concerning the office and jurisdiction of the Lords Consuls and the rendering of accounts.

a. The consuls of this guild are bound, *in order to reduce the expenses of the said guild, to sublet half of the shop <note>original: "apothece"; here referring to the guild's headquarters or office space</note> in which the court of the aforementioned guild is accustomed to reside (1), and to remain, stay, and convene in the other half* every Friday, from the morning until the hour of Terce <note>approximately 9:00 AM</note> and from Nones <note>approximately 3:00 PM</note> until Vespers <note>sunset</note>, except for feast days and those exceptions noted in the present statute. In place of a Friday that falls on a feast day, the aforementioned consuls must convene on the preceding Thursday in the manner described above, or on another day of the week, so that in any case *one day of every week they remain to administer justice, as has been said, namely from morning until Terce, and from Nones until Vespers (2)*.

*b. And if on the said Fridays a council should be held by the Commune of Florence regarding the leaders of the guilds, four of the said consuls must go and two must remain, to provide law and justice to anyone seeking it, up to the point of a final sentence.* However, in the final sentence, and in all other difficult and serious business to be dispatched by the said consuls, at least four must be present. And whatever is done by the said four consuls shall be as valid as if it had been done by all the consuls of the said guild.

c. Truly, if any traveling foreigner <note>original: "viator foresterius"; a non-citizen or merchant passing through Florence</note> should ask for justice to be rendered to him, then the provost of the said consuls may proceed with one of his colleagues to compel, command commissions, and perform seizures <note>original: "stagimenta"; the legal seizing of goods to ensure payment or appearance in court</note> on any day at the guild shop with the notary of the aforementioned guild, and proceed in *those* specific cases as they wish.

d. If, however, any of the aforesaid consuls does not come at the competent hour determined above, and has not stayed at the said shop on the said *Fridays or Thursdays, or at least one day of every week for the rendering of justice*, the chamberlain <term>camerarius: the guild's financial officer or treasurer</term> of this guild is bound to immediately fine him five soldi in small florins <note>original: "f. p." for parvorum; the local silver-based currency of Florence</note>, unless that individual has sworn physically upon the Holy Gospels of God, having touched the book, that he was unable to—

Once the tax is paid, the consuls shall cause the defendant to be summoned by the guild messenger, so that within three days he may reach an agreement with the plaintiff, *or appear before them to perform and receive the fullness of justice.* If, however, within the said time or afterward the defendant denies the claim, the plaintiff shall pay to the guild chamberlain twelve denarii in small Florentine coins <note>original: "f. p." for "fiorini parvi"</note> for every pound, including the four denarii first paid by him. And thereafter, let such a lawsuit and dispute proceed by its own momentum <note>original: "suo marte"; literally "by its own Mars/war"</note>. Once the proofs have been made according to the usage of trade, the consuls shall decide the dispute without delay of time, condemning the loser to pay the winner all expenses incurred by him in the said dispute. Which decision and sentence the said consuls and their successors shall be bound to carry out and commit to execution, at the request of the creditor, or any of his partners, or heirs, or anyone holding a legal interest from him, with every objection set aside, by fining and seizing the property of those so condemned, according to what seems best to them; and by causing the debtors to be seized and imprisoned under such sentences, fines, and commands; and also by having them plundered and their goods distrained, and adjudging the plunder and seizures as settlement and payment to their creditors. And they shall be bound to do the aforementioned at all times, notwithstanding any holidays currently in effect.

f. ### XII. That all and singular persons practicing or exercising the said craft shall swear an oath and be subject to the Consuls of the said Guild.

*a. **c.** Regarding a simple summons issued by the said Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> for anyone to appear before them: if that person does not appear at the appointed time, they shall be fined five shillings in small Florentine pennies <note>original: "soldis quinque f. p." The simple report of the messenger *or the aforementioned assistant* shall be believed against those who do not permit themselves to be distrained.

**e.** Anyone whose goods have been distrained is bound to *redeem* <note>original: "luere"</note> their seized property or pledge within ten days from the day of the seizure. If they fail to do so, the Chamberlain of the said guild can, must, and is obliged to sell, pledge, dispose of, or alienate that property, recording the price in his ledger and applying it to the account and debt of the person distrained. If there is a surplus, he must return the remainder to the owner. The said Chamberlain may not hold any seized property for longer than ten days.

**f.** However, so that no doubt may arise concerning who are physicians, apothecaries, or mercers, we declare that all individuals practicing medicine or surgery, those who set bones, and those who treat the mouth <note>Early dentists</note> in the city or territory of Florence—however they may practice, whether with written prescriptions or without—shall be understood as doctors and be held and regarded as doctors. They shall be compelled to swear the oath and be subject to the aforementioned guild and its Consuls.

**g.** The Apothecaries <note>term: Spetiarii (Apothecaries/Pharmacists) - In medieval Florence, this guild also included merchants of spices, dyes, and luxury goods.</note> who must swear the oath and be subject as stated above are these: namely, all individuals selling or causing to be sold, at wholesale or retail, in the city or territory of Florence: pepper, saffron, honey, wax, sugar, powdered sugar, ginger, cinnamon, rock alum or Castile alum, candles, torches, treacle <note>A medicinal compound used as an antidote</note>, *trefola*, indigo, brazilwood, brazilwood shavings, raisins, kermes dye <note>original: "granam"</note>, sumac, madder, dwarf elder, mustard, vetch, *marine pitch*, tin, lead (worked or unworked), buckram, or any of the aforementioned things and all other things belonging or pertaining to the apothecary shop, or the art of the apothecaries, or any of these items.

## 14. Concerning the scales, balances, and other weights to be maintained.

*a.* The consuls <note>The elected leaders or magistrates of the guild</note> of this craft are bound to ensure and procure that one pair of large scales <note>original: "cazzarum"; these were heavy-duty scales used for bulk goods</note> be kept and maintained within the said craft for weighing up to the quantity of five hundred pounds. With these, all goods and merchandise sold within this craft shall be weighed for anyone wishing to have them weighed, so that every error arising from diverse steelyards and balances may be eliminated. The chamberlain <note>The guild's treasurer or financial officer</note> of this craft is bound to have and keep these large scales.

*b.* And the consuls are bound by their own oath to have one pair of large scales made in the month of January, along with iron weights. All men of this craft shall be bound to weigh with these when buying and selling from fifty pounds upward—and below that amount if the buyer so desires—and to keep these scales in a communal place for weighing.

*c.* The consuls and the chamberlain shall also ensure, under penalty of their salary, that one pair of fine scales be kept in the said craft for weighing cloves, mace, cubebs <note>A type of pepper used in medicine and cooking</note>, and all other fine goods. For these, a fee shall be paid to the chamberlain for the benefit of the craft by anyone who sells and has goods weighed with them, in this manner: for every ten units of fine goods, one penny; and for every hundredweight of goods worth 40 pounds in small Florentine pennies <note>original: "f. p." or "florenorum parvorum"</note> that is weighed with the large scales, three small Florentine pennies; and for all other merchandise where the hundredweight is worth 40 pounds or less, two pennies for every hundredweight. These pennies shall be paid only by the seller.

*d.* The buyer is bound and obligated to send such merchandise at his own expense to the place where the said scales are kept for the craft, and from that place to send it to the buyer's shop; and with the said scales, he is bound to weigh all merchandise at the buyer's request.

*e.* The consuls shall also take care in the month of January to have one double-standard of a straight dozen <note>original: "dodicine"; likely referring to a set of twelve standard weights</note> adjusted to the weight of the Commune of Florence, along with one pair of balances belonging to the university <note>The "universitas" or corporate body of the guild</note> of this craft. To this dozen and these balances, all weights and measures of the said craft shall be calibrated, both for the dozen and for the mark <note>A unit of weight for precious metals</note>. They shall have one chest in which all the weights of the said craft are to be stored and preserved by whomever the consuls see fit to appoint, and they shall be handed over to the new consuls and chamberlain at the start of their term.

*f.* And the consuls are bound every three months of their term to go or send representatives through all the shops and warehouses <note>original: "fundacos"; a term derived from Arabic for a combined warehouse and inn for merchants</note> of this craft, and cause them to be weighed...

# STATUTE OF 1314 II, XIV

...marks, doubles, and dozens; and if they find anyone not possessing equal and correct weights and measures, according to what is contained in the chapter of this constitution, they shall be required to take from him a penalty of five shillings in Florentine small pence <note>original: "soldos quinque f. p." - fiorini piccioli, the local silver currency</note> for each offense. **g.** Likewise, the Consuls <note>the elected leaders of the guild</note> of this Guild shall be required at the beginning of their term of office to have for the said Guild two pairs of scales for weighing saffron <note>original: "crocum sive zafferanum"</note>, one pair of which they shall deposit with some good and sufficient apothecary <term>spetiarium: a spice-seller or pharmacist</term> at the Gate of Saint Mary, and the other in the Old Market. With these scales, all and singular men of this Guild buying and selling saffron shall be required to weigh it, whenever the saffron bought or sold is ten pounds or more, under penalty of ten pounds in Florentine small pence, to be taken from every seller and buyer.

**h.** And the seller shall be required to give, for every pound of saffron sold, one <term>medagla: a small coin, usually worth half a penny</term> in the name of a fee <note>original: "diritture"</note> to the said merchant holding the scales for the said Guild. These pence the merchant himself shall faithfully collect and present to the Chamberlain <note>the guild's treasurer</note> of the said Guild.

**i.** And no broker <term>sensalis: a middleman who negotiated trades</term> may make any deal for any quantity of saffron from ten pounds upward, unless it is weighed with the said scales, under penalty of ten pounds for every deal. And such a broker making a deal in violation of this shall be placed under a ban. And the aforesaid rules shall apply to any saffron, whether foreign or local.

**l.** And no one of this Guild may buy from any foreigner or man outside this Guild <insert>nor from a man within the Guild (1)</insert> <margin>Addition made by the arbiters (a)</margin> any quantity of saffron, unless it is weighed with the said scales of the Guild and paid for, as has been said, by the seller, if it is of the weight of ten pounds or more, under the said penalty.

**m.** Likewise, the said Consuls and Chamberlain shall be required to have for the said Guild two sieves <term>cherbella: specialized screens for sorting spices</term>, namely one for sifting pepper, ginger, and incense, and another for indigo <note>a valuable blue dye</note>. These sieves the Chamberlain shall be required to lend to all those requesting them for sifting the aforesaid items. And they cannot be released from this duty, nor can a deadline be given to them beyond the month of February, under penalty of their salary.

**n.** And let no one of the said Guild dare to keep the Guild's sieves or scales during the nighttime, under penalty of one hundred shillings in Florentine small pence.

# II, XV, XVI STATUTE OF 1314

## XV. That he who sells by weight shall pay the weighing fee.

*a. It is decreed and ordained that whoever sells any goods of this craft by weight is obliged and bound to pay the <term>weighing fee</term><note>original: "ponderaturam" - a tax or fee paid for the official weighing of goods</note>, if the weight is fifty pounds or more. And the buyer is obliged and bound to have the sold goods transported at his own expense. And every member of this craft who buys or sells any item or merchandise is obliged and bound to have the weight of the sold merchandise and the price of said merchandise recorded by the official weigher of the Commune of Florence. And if any <term>broker</term><note>original: "sensalis" - a middleman who negotiated sales and acted as a witness to the contract</note> is present, he is obliged and bound to record the weight and price of said merchandise and the deadline for payment, under penalty of 20 silver <term>soldi</term><note>original: "soldorum f. p." - Florentine small denari/shillings</note> for each occurrence.*

b. And if such a sale should be called into doubt, or if there is a dispute over the item, the price, the weight, or the payment deadline, the written records of the buyer and seller shall be relied upon, provided they wrote them down and their records agree. Otherwise, the record of the broker shall be relied upon and given credit.

## XVI. How the seller is bound to sift pepper and other items.

*a. If anyone of this craft buys pepper, ginger, or incense from any person of this craft, and finds dust within them or any of them through fraud, the seller is bound—if the buyer so desires—to sift the goods and provide them sifted, and to make up the original weight, provided it is 25 pounds or more <margin>a. This was corrected to: from six pounds and up</margin>. If he does not do this and it is reported to the <term>consuls</term><note>The elected leaders of the guild</note>, the said consuls are bound to fine him ten silver soldi for each occurrence.*

b. However, if the buyer has carried the purchased item to his own shop, the seller is not bound to sift it after that transport, unless the buyer requested the sifting during the same day he made the purchase and had it brought to his shop.

c. And that everyone who sells indigo, or incense, or gum arabic and mastic—whether he be a citizen or a foreigner—is bound to have it sifted, as well as any other merchandise that requires sifting, at the will of the buyer, using the sieves of the craft, under penalty of 40 soldi.

(a) Corrected to: from six pounds and up <note>This indicates a tightening of regulations, requiring sifting for much smaller quantities</note>.

## XVII. Regarding the acceptance of the sack as part of the merchandise, if a dispute arises between the buyer and the seller concerning the sack.

a. If anyone should buy any merchandise from the goods of this Guild, they shall be bound and obligated to accept the sack as part of the merchandise <note>This means the weight of the sack is included in the total weight of the goods sold.</note> if a dispute arises between the buyer and the seller regarding the sack; namely, for any merchandise where a hundredweight <note>original: ".c." or centinarium, approximately 100 pounds.</note> is valued at ten pounds <note>The "pound" (libra) here is a unit of currency, the Florentine lira.</note> or less. And in such merchandise shall be included alum <note>A mineral used as a mordant in dyeing cloth.</note>, madder <note>A root used to produce red dye.</note>, cumin, grapes, mustard, anise, fennel, hemp tow <note>The coarse, broken fibers of hemp.</note>, and any other merchandise whose hundredweight is valued at ten pounds or less. This shall be understood to apply to merchandise kept in sacks—specifically in a single sack—fastened with rope or esparto cord.

b. Regarding goods contained in barrels or vats, a tare <note>An allowance made for the weight of the packaging.</note> must be deducted for every barrel of honey at ten pounds per load <note>original: "salma," a traditional measure of volume or weight.</note>. And for honey kept in vats or half-barrels, a tare must also be deducted. For a barrel weighing 100 pounds, or up to 130 pounds or less, the tare shall be 20 pounds; for a barrel weighing from 130 pounds up to 200 pounds, the tare shall be 25 pounds. For a pouch of saffron weighing 25 pounds or more, the seller is bound and obligated to give the pouch to the buyer without any charge.

c. All other goods and merchandise not mentioned above shall remain under the provision and oversight of the Consuls of this Guild.

d. If, however, crocus or saffron is sold in quantities of ten pounds or more, the seller is bound to provide the sack, if it is in a sack, without any charge. And no one of this Guild shall dare to mix Catalan saffron with local or Marchigian saffron <note>Saffron from the Marche region of Italy.</note>; but they are bound to show and provide Catalan as Catalan, local as local, and Marchigian as Marchigian, under the penalty contained in the statute.

And to the end that the merchants of this guild may be able to carry out their trade more freely and provide for themselves in their profits, it is decreed and ordained that there shall not be, nor ought there to be, any prohibition in the city of Florence or its district concerning the undermentioned goods and merchandise, namely: pepper, ginger, cinnamon, indigo <note>a blue dye</note>, incense, brazilwood <note>original: "verzino"; a wood used to produce red dye</note>, sugar, powdered sugar, and all types of alum <note>a mineral salt used as a fixative in dyeing</note>, cloves, nutmeg, mace, galangal <note>a ginger-like spice</note>, silk, and every kind of spice, kermes <note>original: "grana"; a red dye derived from insects</note>, sumac <note>original: "scotano"; used in tanning and dyeing</note>, quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, almonds, rice, dates, cubebs <note>a type of pepper</note>, madder <note>a plant used for red dye</note>, and every other good and spice that comes from overseas. Indeed, all the aforesaid things, or the aforesaid goods and any one of them, may be brought back and carried to the city and district of Florence, and also exported freely and without penalty, at the pleasure and will of anyone wishing to export them, or have them carried, in whatever manner and however it shall seem fit to them; saving the statutes and reforms of the Commune of *Florence*.

->XIX. *Concerning the requirement to have two pairs of scales,*<-
->*which shall be kept in the castle of Poggio Bonizio and*<-
->*in the marketplace of Marcialla.*<-

a. *Since many men and persons direct their steps to the markets of Poggio Bonizio <note>modern Poggibonsi</note> and Marcialla to buy saffron, and they buy it with coarse and unsuitable scales, about which the consuls of this guild have hitherto received many complaints, it is ordained that the consuls and the chamberlain <note>the guild's financial officer</note> of this guild, whose term of office shall begin on the calends of January next coming <note>January 1st</note>, shall ensure and see to it that throughout the said month two pairs of scales for weighing saffron are made and obtained; one of which is to be deposited and must be deposited with the syndic <note>a local representative or official</note> to be elected for this guild in the castle of Poggio Bonizio, and the other in the market of Marcialla.*

b. *And that each of the said syndics must weigh in his place, castle, and village all the saffron that shall be sold and bought in the said markets or places, and receive for the said guild for every weight of a pound or less one denarius; and from that amount upwards, two denarii for every weight.*

c. *These syndics shall have for their salary a fourth part of the denarii which they receive from the saffron they weigh. They must and are required to record these denarii, and are required to render an account of them to the syndics and chamberlain of this guild who shall be in office at the time.*

d. *And that no one shall dare or presume to buy or sell saffron in the said markets or places, except with the said scales, under penalty of three pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." for parvorum; the local currency</note> for each of them and for every weighing.*

# STATUTE OF 1314 II, XVIII-XXII

*e. ## XX. That the present ordinances must be read before the guild (1).

In the month of January, or in the month in which this constitution shall have been corrected and approved, the consuls shall be bound to have it read before the assembled guild, wherever it seems best to them to do so; and they shall command those present, and even those absent, that they must effectively observe all the chapters contained in the same constitution, under the penalties and bans contained in the chapters of the said constitution.

## XXI. That the consuls be present at the auction of the property of one who dies or departs with another's money.

If anyone of this guild should pass away or die, and his heirs, or the guardians of those heirs, or their legal representatives <note>original: "mundualdi"; a Lombard legal term for a male protector or guardian of a person under legal disability</note>, or his creditors—if there be no one to pay them—should wish to have the property and goods of such a deceased person, or of one who has departed with another's money, which he may have in the city or in the shop <note>original: "apotheca"</note> or elsewhere; if it has been reported to them, the consuls shall be bound, by themselves or by others of the guild whom they choose, to be present at the auction <note>original: "incantationi"; literally a 'calling out' or public sale to the highest bidder</note> of the said goods. They shall not permit the partner of such a deceased person, or of the one who departed with another's money, to be present at the auction of the said goods without the permission of the said heirs, guardians, or creditors; and they shall cause notice to be given to all the shops of this guild, so that from every shop they may go to the said auction, and they must help them in the aforesaid matters, in good faith and without fraud.

## XXII. Concerning the non-election of anyone committing a falsehood.

Whoever of this guild shall be found in any falsehood <note>referring to forgery, fraud, or professional dishonesty</note> concerning any matter of this guild, he may not forever [hold] any office or bene—
