The consuls in office at the time shall be bound and obligated to provide to the consuls, counselors, and other officials of the said guild, and to any others who have been injured or harmed by reason of their said offices <insert>or for any other reason whatsoever</insert> <margin>Marginal note from 1315, written by the same hand that wrote the painters' statute.</margin>, one good and suitable advocate <note>a legal representative or lawyer</note>, who is a true Guelph <note>The Guelphs were a political faction supporting the Pope; this requirement ensured political loyalty to the current Florentine government</note>, at the expense of the said guild, who must assist him until the end of the case. ### XXIIII. *On the approval of written records, and the faith to be placed in them.*

Since human bodies fall ill from unforeseen accidents, and thus require medicines and necessary things to cure them—and just as these events happen suddenly, so too do they suddenly require doctors and medicines—and medicines are often sent suddenly via boys, male servants, and female servants to those in need without any formal ceremony; and *after their recovery or health* is restored, those who were sick may stubbornly refuse to pay those who trusted them for the items given to them, which is discordant and not in accordance with the law; and lest these stationers <note>term: "stazionerii"; sellers of books and parchment who often shared space with apothecaries</note>, mercers <note>term: "merciarii"; traders in fine fabrics and small wares</note>, and apothecaries <note>term: "spetiarii"; pharmacists and spice merchants</note> find themselves thus deceived after acting in good faith by giving credit, it is decreed and ordained that the writings in the books of the stationers, mercers, and apothecaries—who give or send medicines or other things pertaining to the art of apothecaries and mercers to the sick or to other men—shall be believed and upheld regarding the things thus sent or given, and regarding the quantity and...

# II, XXVI STATUTE OF 1314

### XXVI. *Concerning new craftsmen and the creation of the matriculation roll.* <note>The "matricula" was the official register or membership list of a guild.</note>

a. *Since that which consists of all its parts is approved as most perfect, for the purpose of completing and restoring the college of the said guild <note>The "artem" or "guild" refers here to the specific trade organization governed by these laws</note>, we decree by this law that the Lord Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note>, whose term of office shall begin on the Kalends of January <note>January 1st</note>, in the current years of our Lord one thousand three hundred and ten, ninth indiction, under the virtue of their sworn oath and under penalty of ten pounds of small florins; a penalty which the syndics <note>Officials who audited the conduct of the consuls</note>, who shall audit them, are bound and obligated to condemn them to immediately; [the Consuls] are bound and obligated at the beginning of their office to make each and every craftsman of the said guild from the city and territory of Florence, both old and new, take an oath, and to pay to the aforesaid guild for their entry fee as is declared below, and to cause to be made a book or matriculation roll of their names and surnames; at the beginning of which book shall be written each and every craftsman of the said guild who principally practice the said trade in the city, boroughs, or suburbs, next to whom shall be written each and every deli-owner <note>original: "pizzicaiuoli" - sellers of salted meats, cheeses, and various foodstuffs</note> and other minor persons <note>original: "debiles persone" - literally "weak persons," referring to those with lower economic status or smaller business volume</note> who are principally bound to another guild and principally practice another trade, but are or shall be bound to this guild because they practice or shall practice some small part or branch of this trade in the city, boroughs, or suburbs.*

b. *Those from the countryside <note>original: "comitatini"</note> shall indeed be enrolled in a similar manner in another section of the aforesaid book.*

c. *All those who have come or shall come to the aforesaid guild principally in the city of Florence, its boroughs, or suburbs, or to take the oath anew, and have not paid for their entry, each of them shall be bound and obligated to pay to the chamberlain <note>The treasurer or financial officer</note> of the said guild for the expenses of the officials—and the consuls are bound to make them pay—ten pounds of small florins. Except that, if the person whose payment is being discussed has served the aforesaid guild for six years, he shall pay only five pounds of small florins.*

d. *All deli-owners and other minor persons mentioned above, who have hitherto come to the said guild, and those who shall come anew, and each of them, to swear to the said guild or to practice the said trade, shall pay and be bound to pay for the said expenses, for each of them, forty shillings of small florins.*

e. *However, if such a deli-owner wishes to practice the said trade principally, he shall be placed among the citizens in the aforesaid book and shall pay ten pounds, including the forty shillings which he first paid.*

### XXVII. Concerning the oath and the providing of security by brokers.

a. In the month of January every year, the consuls of this guild are bound and must act and ensure, in such a way, that each and every broker <term>sensales: intermediaries who negotiated sales for a commission</term> and agent <note>original: "prosenete"</note> shall swear upon the Holy Gospels of God to practice their craft in good faith, without fraud; and that they give and provide suitable security <note>original: "fideiussione"</note> to the said consuls receiving it on behalf of the said guild, regarding the observance of all statutes and chapters of this guild, and especially the statutes concerning brokers. And if anyone refuses to swear and provide security, he shall be driven out from the brokerage <note>original: "sensaria"</note>, and it shall be commanded to all members of the said guild, under penalty of 40 shillings in small Florentine pennies for the offender, to be collected as often as it occurs, that they shall make no market deal with such a broker.

b. And no broker may perform any brokerage or market deal for any items whose price exceeds the sum of 25 pounds in small Florentine pennies, unless he first brings together the buyer and seller to negotiate and confirm the purchase and sale, or gives the penny which is commonly called "God’s penny" <term>danaio di Dio: a small earnest payment or symbolic coin given to seal a contract, often later given to charity</term>, under penalty of 40 shillings, as often as it occurs.

c. ### XXVIIII. Concerning the punishment of those who offer petitions for the office of the consulate.

It is statuted and ordained that the consuls of this craft are bound and obliged by the bond of their oath, and under penalty of their salary, to fine anyone of this craft one hundred soldi in small florins <note>original: "f. p." for floreni parvi</note> whom they find and know through two witnesses of public repute to have offered or made petitions <note>soliciting or lobbying for votes</note> for the office of the consulate, or for any other office of this craft; and the one making petitions shall be barred from any office of this craft for five years. And regarding the aforesaid, anyone may be an accuser and informer, and shall have half of the fine, and his identity shall be kept in confidence.

# III, xxx STATUTE OF 1314

### XXX. Concerning the prohibition of bringing falsified saffron into the city of Florence.

*a.* All and singular members of this guild <note>The Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries, which regulated spices and medicines</note>, both masters and apprentices, shall be bound not to buy or cause to be bought, in the city of Florence or elsewhere, nor to sell, nor to bring into the city itself or its district, falsified saffron <note>original: "crocum falsum"; saffron was frequently adulterated with safflower or minerals due to its high value</note>. The consuls <note>term: consuls (elected leaders of the guild)</note> of this guild shall be bound to fine anyone acting to the contrary or possessing said falsified saffron one hundred pounds in small florins; they must also seize the saffron and have it publicly burned in the New Market <note>original: "foro novo"; the Mercato Nuovo was the center of Florentine trade</note>. An exception is made if falsified saffron is found in a small quantity in the possession of any grocer <note>original: "piczicaiuolo"; a small-scale retailer of foodstuffs</note> or other person of modest means, and they provide proof that they bought it as such from another; in that case, the consuls shall be bound to fine them only forty shillings in small florins. The consuls are bound to issue this forty-shilling fine with the advice of the guild council.

*b.* And no one of this guild shall dare to keep for sale Catalan saffron mixed with our local saffron, under penalty of ten pounds in small florins. "Local saffron" shall be understood as that from the Marches and Tuscany. Furthermore, no one of this guild shall presume to keep in their shop <note>original: "apotheca"</note> in any way or for any reason any saffron powder made by force <note>original: "pulverem zafferani fattum per vim"; likely referring to mechanical grinding that hid impurities or the use of artificial pressure to bind adulterants</note>, under penalty of ten pounds in small florins for each instance. They shall cause such powder to be burned in the presence of the men of this guild. Anyone keeping said powder for sale shall be barred forever from being called to any office or benefit. Both foreigners and citizens shall be bound by the aforesaid rules. The consuls of this guild are bound to denounce anyone acting against the aforesaid to the Podestà <note>term: Podestà (the chief magistrate of the city)</note> of Florence, under penalty of ten pounds for each of them. The chamberlain <note>term: camerarius (the guild's financial officer)</note> of said guild is bound and must fine the consuls if they fail to denounce them as stated, under penalty of twenty-five pounds in small florins. If the chamberlain does not fine the consuls as stated, the syndics <note>term: sindici (officials who audited the guild's accounts and conduct)</note> of said guild then in office shall be bound and must fine the consuls and the chamberlain, and each of them, twenty-five pounds in small florins. This chapter shall be absolute, and in no way can it be diminished or changed. Anyone may be an accuser regarding the aforesaid matters and shall receive half of the fine.

*c.* This chapter shall also apply to *dialtea* <note>an ointment made from marshmallow root</note>, *populio* <note>poplar ointment</note>, *aurino* <note>a golden-colored ointment or pigment</note>, oils, *marziaton* <note>martiaton, a complex "soldier's ointment" for aches</note>, theriac <note>term: triaca (a famous universal panacea containing dozens of ingredients)</note>, and generally to any other falsified thing. Regarding any things whatsoever that are falsified in any way, the said consuls can, are bound to, and must take cognizance <note>investigate and judge</note> in whatever manner and way they wish, and they must punish and fine those found guilty, however they are discovered, with the penalty set above for powder made by force, under penalty of twenty-five pounds in small florins to be taken from the consuls by the syndics.

->XXXI. On punishing those who buy, sell, or work with false wax in any place.<-

*a. It is ordained that no one of this guild <term>Artis: The Guild of Oil-merchants and Provisioners (Pizzicagnoli)</term> shall dare or presume to buy, or cause to be bought, work, or cause to be worked, sell, or cause to be sold, keep, or cause to be kept in any place false wax. The consuls of this guild are bound to fine anyone acting to the contrary fifty pounds in small florins <note>original: "f. p." — parvorum florenorum</note>, and they must seize the wax itself and turn it green <note>likely a method of marking the wax as industrial or unfit for candles</note>, and sell it for the benefit of the guild, within twenty days from the day the wax was found or reported to them, under penalty of losing their salary. And if the consuls themselves do not do this, the chamberlain <note>the guild's financial officer</note> of this guild must and is bound to carry out the said fine, under penalty of twenty-five pounds in small florins. And if the consuls and the chamberlain do not carry out the said fine, the syndics <note>legal auditors</note> of the said guild who are in office at the time are bound to fine the consuls and chamberlain ten pounds in small florins each.*

*b. And no one of this guild who has bought, sold, worked, or caused to be worked false wax may ever be elected to any office of this guild. Regarding the aforementioned matters, anyone may be an accuser and shall receive half of the fine. Except that if false wax is found in torches, or large candles, or in any item belonging to any grocer <note>original: "piczicaiuolo"</note> or anyone of this guild, and he did not work the wax himself and proves from whom he bought said wax, the person with whom it was found shall be fined forty shillings in small florins by the consuls. Nevertheless, the seller shall be fined fifty pounds in small florins, as stated above.*

*c. And no one of this guild, or outside of this guild, shall dare or presume to bring or cause to be brought to the city of Florence, in a bale or bales, a load or loads, or in any other manner, false wax. And if anyone of this guild, or any other person, brings or causes to be brought from outside the city of Florence false wax, and it is found with them, or they sell it to any person, the consuls of this guild are bound to compel them to return and restore the price to the buyer, and to seize the wax and have it sold, and put the proceeds into the guild's accounts, as stated above.*

### XXXII. On punishing those who have not worked good, pure, and legal wax.

*a.* It is ordained that everyone of the said guild must work good, pure, bright, and legal wax, and in every piece of waxwork they must place a wick of good and bright new cotton <note>original: "banbagie"</note>, not scorched; which wick must be bound with linen thread <note>original: "accia"</note> *and not with twine* <margin>or with fine twine</margin>, well and legally, according to the provision of the Consuls, without any deceit, fraud, or malice. And one should and may put in every pound of wax two ounces of cotton, and no more, without any scorched material. And this is understood to apply to torches <note>large ceremonial candles</note> only. And whenever any torch is found made against the aforesaid form, or within any shop of this guild, that has a wick of linen thread, or of anything other than cotton, or that has a wick exceeding the aforesaid weight, or is bound with twine, they shall fine the person with whom it was found 40 silver shillings <note>original: "soldis .XL. f. p." referring to Florentine piccoli</note>, and the same amount for the one who ordered the said torch to be made, and *the one who made it, if he can be found*. And credit shall be given to the finders and inspectors, or the messenger of the guild, regarding the aforesaid discovery.

*b.* And that all and singular, making or possessing torches, are bound and must seal those torches with their own seal, and write on the shafts of the said torch their name and surname; and everyone is bound to give a copy of their seal to the notary of the guild upon a certain ledger, or a certain large parchment specially designated for this, next to which copy he shall write his name and surname. And no one shall dare or presume to keep in his shop, or elsewhere, or sell, or cause to be sold any torch, unless, as has been said, it is sealed and inscribed, under penalty of 20 silver shillings for every torch, and for every instance.

*c.* And that no one, who has recovered any torch of his own or another's from any church, or from elsewhere, shall dare or presume to destroy that torch, unless he has first shown it and them to the officials of the wax-makers <term>ceraiuolorum: the guild members specializing in wax</term>, under penalty of 20 silver shillings for every torch. Which officials are bound to solicitously seek out, find, and investigate if anyone has acted against the aforesaid or any of the aforesaid points, or if he has failed in anything, and if those torches and any other torches of the city of Florence are made according to the form of the guild statute. And immediately upon finding any torch made in any way against the form of the statutes, or any point, article, or member—

### XXXIII. Concerning the punishment of those who make "hollowed" or "flowered" candles.

a. All and singular members of this guild making, or causing to be made, large wax candles <note>original: "cereos"</note>, are bound to make them perforated <note>likely referring to a hollow center for the wick</note> and not "hollowed out" <note>original: "bucciatos" - likely a deceptive practice of thinning the wax shell</note>, and they may be perforated through a third of a cubit <note>term: "bracchium" - a Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches</note> and no further. And all must be of right and just weight, and they are bound to give and cause them to be given of just weight, namely: that of a pound for a pound, and that of a half-pound for a half-pound, and so for each individual weight. And in every candle they must place a new wick of cotton <note>original: "banbagia"</note>, which must be of the weight of one quarter-ounce, and they shall make all candles of good and legal wax of three, four, six, eight, ten, and twelve ounces, and from there upwards as many as they wish, under penalty of ten shillings of small florins for each candle.

b. And they shall not dare or presume to make or cause to be made any "flowered" candles <note>original: "fioritos" - highly decorated or painted candles</note>, unless they be the candles of the communes and parishes of the countryside of Florence <note>original: "Florentie"</note>, to be offered on the vigil of Blessed John the Baptist <note>The patron saint of Florence</note> in the month of June, under penalty of ten pounds of small florins for each candle.

c. And those making "flowered" candles shall not be able, for ten years next following, to hold any office or benefit in the aforementioned guild.

d. And two of the consuls and the chamberlain, together with the messenger of this guild, are bound and must investigate and go about investigating the said candles, and weigh all those they find, and record them in writing. Which parties the consuls are bound to condemn, under penalty of their own salary.

### XXXIIII. *Regarding the prohibition of making cast wax images in molds.*

a. We decree that no member of this guild shall dare or presume to make, or cause to be made, any cast <term>maina</term> <note>A "maina" refers to a wax votive offering, often shaped like a body part or a whole figure, left at a shrine in fulfillment of a vow.</note> in a mold, *nor in any other way using a spindle for candles*, but must only make them, or cause them to be made, by hand. This shall be understood to apply to the figures of men, women, oxen, horses, and any other beast, or any other thing for which men and persons make various and diverse vows, and they shall sell them at a fair price.

b. And everyone who sells, or wishes to sell, these wax images is bound to seal them with their own seal, and must provide a copy of that seal to the <term>chamberlain</term> <note>The "camerarius" was the guild's treasurer and administrative official.</note> of the said guild. The chamberlain is bound and obligated to have such an example or copy presented to him; except that if someone vows to place in any location a ship, or a galley, a house, a castle, or any other building which cannot be made without wood, the person who makes it, or is commissioned to make it, may place wood within it, having first obtained permission from the <term>consuls</term> <note>The "consules" were the elected leaders of the guild.</note> of the said guild *or one of them*. Once permission is obtained, he is bound to weigh the said structure in the presence of the guild's chamberlain. Both the chamberlain and the seller of the structure are bound and obligated to record the weight.

c. And if it should happen later that the said structure is found to be of greater weight than was recorded by the guild chamberlain, the consuls are bound to fine the violator ten pounds *in small florins* <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccoli," the local currency of Florence.</note> *for each occurrence, under penalty of their own salary and under the bond of their oath.* And they must and are bound to investigate the aforementioned matters twice every month. The guild chamberlain is bound and obligated to go *at the request of any guild member to inspect the wax image or images they wish to make, to weigh them or have them weighed, and to record the weight and the copy of the seal with which they were marked, under penalty of forty shillings in small florins.* He shall have and receive *for his salary, each time, four pence in small florins*, which shall belong to the said chamberlain by full right.

d. And if any member of this guild wishes to make any large structure, he may and is permitted to place upon it wax plates made on a board, or a head made in a mold, having first obtained permission from the guild consuls.

e. And the consuls themselves are bound to ensure that anyone wishing to sell wax images, candles, or other items of this guild *in the Garden of Saint Michael* <note>The "Orto San Michele" (Orsanmichele) in Florence, a major site for trade and religious devotion where guilds often displayed their wares.</note> provides a guarantee and security to this guild *of five pounds in small florins*. And no one of the said guild shall dare or presume to charge more than ten shillings *in small florins* per pound for a hand-made wax image, under penalty of one hundred shillings *in small florins*.

# STATUTE OF 1314 III, XXXIV-XXXVII

†. It has been added that for each chapter and article of this chapter that is not observed, there shall be a penalty of 100 Florentine small shillings <note>original: "soldorum .c. f. p." referring to the *soldi di fiorini piccoli*, the common silver currency of Florence</note>, except in the article regarding the weight of wood; if a load <note>original: "maina," likely referring to a specific bundle or quantity of wood</note> is found to be of greater weight than what is recorded, in which case the penalty shall be ten Florentine small pounds.

### XXXV. On not selling or keeping poison in the city.

No citizen or foreigner <note>original: "foretanus," referring to those living outside the city walls or non-citizens</note> shall be allowed, nor is it permitted to them, to keep, sell, carry, or display poison in any manner or for any reason within the city of Florence or its district. Anyone acting to the contrary shall be punished fifty Florentine small pounds, for each offense. And all members of this guild <term>Artis: The "Arte" or Guild, the professional corporation governing this trade</term> are bound to denounce those who violate this. The Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the Guild</note> are bound to condemn the violator to the aforesaid penalty, and also to denounce such a delinquent to the Lord Podestà <note>The chief magistrate of the city</note>, under penalty of one hundred Florentine small shillings for each of them.

### XXXVI. On punishing one who commits theft.

The Lord Consuls shall take from anyone stealing, or caught in the act of stealing the goods of their partners, or of their masters, or of any other person of the said guild—concerning items pertaining to the guild itself—a penalty of ten Florentine small pounds for each offense. And they shall denounce the thief to the Florentine rulers <note>The city government</note> to seek justice for the victim, and they shall expel him from the fellowship of the said guild. However, for those already punished by the Commune of Florence, no further penalty shall be imposed by the Consuls of the said guild.

### XXXVII. On punishing one who takes a shop away from another.

a. No member of this guild, by himself or through another, may take or lease any shop <term>Apothecam: A workshop, storefront, or place of business</term> already leased to another member of this guild, nor dwell in it within a period of five years from the day on which the previous tenant left it and moved out. And if anyone of the said guild acts to the contrary—unless by license and express consent granted to him by a public document from the said first tenant—he shall be compelled by the Consuls to vacate the said shop, and he shall be deprived of his guild membership; nevertheless, he shall be condemned by the guild and the Consuls of the said guild to fifty Florentine small pounds. Half of this fine shall go to the Commune of Florence, one quarter shall go to the Chamberlain <note>The treasurer</note> of the said guild, and the other quarter shall go to the person from whom the shop was taken.

# III, XXXVIII-XXXVIIII STATUTE OF 1314

*b. And from the day that said proof against such a person is made, no member of this Guild shall have any dealings with him, under penalty of 100 small Florentine shillings <note>original: "soldorum .c. f. p." — the 'f. p.' refers to 'fiorini piccioli', the common silver currency of Florence</note>. And the Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the Guild</note> shall be held to enforce the aforesaid, under penalty of one hundred shillings for each of them.*

*c. And no member of this Guild shall dare, by himself or through another, to take or lease any shop among those burned at the time the fire was set in the city of Florence <margin>or afterwards, burned or destroyed for any cause whatsoever</margin> <note>This refers to the disastrous fires of 1304 which destroyed much of the city center</note>, whether subsequently rebuilt or not rebuilt within the aforementioned term, to be calculated from the day of the rebuilding of said shop, unless they have the permission of the person who held that shop before the fire, under the penalty aforesaid.*

### XXXVIII. Regarding the punishment of those who act as a guarantor for any Magnate before the Commune of Florence.

No member of this Guild shall dare to act as a guarantor or provide a security bond <term>malleveriam: a formal legal guarantee or bail</term> for any Magnate <note>The 'Magnates' were the old noble families of Florence, often restricted by law from certain political activities to protect the merchant class</note> before the Commune of Florence for any reason, under penalty of two hundred Florentine pounds. *And this statute shall not extend beyond acting as a guarantor for Magnates, and for this reason, such a guarantor shall not be considered to have committed perjury.*

### XXXVIIII. Regarding the punishment of those who do not observe the festivals and holy days contained in this statute.

*a. The Consuls are required to have a proclamation made to all shops of said Guild, or within their shops, that they must observe the festivals as decreed below, namely: the days of Easter, the Nativity (Christmas), and the Resurrection of the Lord, Pentecost, All Saints, and the festivals of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Saint John the Baptist <note>The patron saint of Florence</note>, and the Evangelist, and the twelve Apostles, Saint Barnabas, the Epiphany of the Lord, the day of Saint Stephen, and the first of May, and Good Friday, as well as the Sundays of the entire year. On these days, no one of this Guild shall dare to keep his shop open, except for the small shutter <term>sportellum: a small opening in the shop door for emergency sales</term>. Against those who do otherwise, and for each instance, the Consuls shall fine them ten Florentine shillings.*

*b. And on the days of the Nativity, Resurrection, Good Friday, Pentecost, and All Saints, and on Sundays, no one shall dare to grind anything in his shop or allow anything to be ground <note>original: "pistare" — likely referring to the grinding of pigments or medicinal ingredients</note>, under penalty of ten Florentine shillings for each person and each instance. And on the day when any member of this Guild is buried, they shall not dare to place or display anything upon their windows, or poles, or outside the shop, under the said penalty.*

# STATUTE OF 1314 III, XXXIX-XLII
45

c. And that during the festivities and feast days of the Blessed Reparata, Saint Zenobius, Saint Augustine, Saint Francis, Saint Dominic, Saint Martin, and the Holy Cross (a), no one of this guild <note>The Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries</note> ought to keep their shop open, except for the small service window <note>original: "sportellum"; a small hatch in the door used for urgent sales on holidays</note>. And regarding the aforementioned, the consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> are bound to investigate, or have an investigation made, and to believe the simple word of the investigator or messenger.

->XL. *Concerning electuaries and syrups.*<-

All and singular members of this guild making or causing to be made barley-sugar <note>original: "pennidias"; a pulled sugar sweet used for coughs</note> are bound to make them using a strainer or a filtering cloth, in good faith and without fraud. Against any violator, the consuls are bound to take ten pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli"</note> as a penalty, for each occurrence. And they must cause electuaries <note>medicinal pastes mixed with honey or syrup</note> to be made—those which are listed in the pharmacopoeia <note>original: "antidotario"; a book of standardized medical recipes</note> as being made with syrups—*with syrups*, and those with honey—with honey, in good faith and without fraud, unless it be the will of the buyers. It is permitted, however, for anyone to make electuaries with sugar that are usually made with honey; but they must not sell a medicine made with honey as a medicine made with sugar.

->XLI. *Concerning the blacklisting of debtors.*<-

The consuls of this guild are bound, at the request of any creditor of this guild who shows that they are owed any quantity of money, to command everyone of this guild that they must not conduct any trade with their debtor (if he is also of this guild), unless they first reach an agreement with him. Anyone acting to the contrary shall be punished by the consuls in the amount of one hundred shillings of small florins.

->XLII. *Concerning the punishment of the chamberlain who has profited against the honor of the guild.*<-

It is ordained that the new consuls are bound and ought to secretly discover and investigate if the chamberlain <note>the guild's treasurer or administrator</note> of the said guild has profited in any way against the honor of the aforesaid guild from any person. And if they find him to have acted to the contrary, or to have defrauded in any way, they are bound to punish him in the amount of five shillings of small florins for every shilling defrauded, for each occurrence.

# III, 43-45 STATUTE OF 1314

### 43. Regarding the penalty for one who redeems the clothes of the dead from gravediggers.

No one of this guild <note>The Guild of Apothecaries and Physicians</note> can or should redeem <note>buy back or reclaim</note> the clothes of the dead from <term>becamortis</term> <note>gravediggers or corpse-bearers; from the Italian 'beccamorti'</note>, or from priests, or any other person. Anyone acting to the contrary shall be punished by the <term>consuls</term> <note>the elected leaders of the guild</note>, for each instance, in the amount of one hundred small Florentine <term>soldi</term> <note>a silver coin; 20 soldi made one lira</note>. And anyone may be an accuser in this matter, and shall have half of the fine, and his identity shall be kept in confidence.

### 44. That no stationer is allowed to give any laxative medicine to anyone on his own advice.

No <term>apothecary</term> <note>original: "spetiarius"</note> or <term>stationer</term> <note>original: "staczonerius"; a seller of prepared goods or books, often associated with the medical trade</note> should give any <term>laxative medicine</term> <note>original: "medicinam solutivam"</note> to anyone without the advice of a physician, nor provide medical treatment in any way or for any reason, under penalty of ten small Florentine pounds, as often as it occurs. And regarding the aforesaid, anyone may be an accuser, and shall have half of the fine, and his identity shall be kept in confidence.

### 45. Regarding syrups and other electuaries.

*a. All and singular apothecaries, both masters and apprentices, whether they have physicians in their workshop or not, are bound to make syrups and all <term>electuaries</term> <note>medicinal pastes made with honey or sugar</note> and medicinal items well and lawfully* <gloss>well and lawfully added between the lines by the first hand</gloss>, *especially those which are made with sugar, which must be made with good powder from Cyprus mixed with powder from Babylon, under penalty of two pounds, and all must be done with the knowledge of a physician.*

*b.* And that no apothecary who has a physician <note>referring to shops that employed a resident doctor</note> shall work red powder from Alexandria into any medicinal antidote, <insert>[under the said penalty]</insert> <note>original: "sub dicta pena"; restored from Codex B</note>, as often as it occurs. And they may work and use the said powder from Alexandria in <term>confections</term> <note>original: "confettis"; spiced sweets or sugar-coated nuts</note> pertaining to banquets, or those which are presented to any foreigner, provided that this powder is not used in any medicinal antidote without the knowledge of a physician, under the said penalty.

*c.* And that the consuls are bound to cause this to be commanded to all apothecaries, both masters and apprentices, and also to make all and singular masters who make medicinal things swear that they will make them well and lawfully, and according to what is contained in the said chapter, under penalty of 40 small Florentine soldi for each of the said consuls.

# STATUTE OF 1314 III, 46-49

### 46. *On punishing those who offer sieves and other items.*

*No one of this craft shall dare or presume to offer, or cause to be offered to any person, fine cloth <note>original: "stamignam," a lightweight wool or linen fabric used for sifting</note>, torches, sieves, quilts, or any other item belonging to this craft, under penalty of three pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or "florenorum parvorum"</note>. Regarding the aforementioned, anyone may act as an accuser and shall receive half of the fine, and their identity shall be kept in confidence; and the word and assertion of three witnesses speaking from public reputation shall be believed. However, if a doctor <note>likely a pharmacist or medical practitioner associated with the guild</note> acts against this, six pounds shall be taken from him as a penalty, for each occurrence.*

### 47. *That no one of this craft shall enter into partnership with anyone who has absconded with another's money.*

*No one of this craft shall dare or presume to associate themselves or enter into a partnership with any person who is insolvent or fleeing with the money or goods of others, under penalty of ten pounds of small florins. And such a person who has absconded may hold no office or benefit from this guild, and shall be banned forever and placed under interdiction.*

### 48. *On not luring away or corrupting another's apprentice.*

*If anyone shall lure away or corrupt an apprentice belonging to another member of this craft, who was staying with him during the time of his contract, he shall be punished by forty shillings of small florins <insert>he shall be punished by ten pounds</insert> <margin>Marginal addition from 1315, likely written by the same hand that wrote the painters' statute.</margin>. And no one shall dare or presume to receive, accept, or harbor any apprentice of any master of the said craft, unless he has first completed his term with the master with whom he was previously placed, under the said penalty and for each occurrence.*

### 49. *On not opening letters.*

*No one of this craft shall dare or presume to open in any way any letter sent to another member of the said craft, under penalty of twenty-five pounds of small florins for every letter, and for every time, to be taken from him by the consuls <note>the elected leaders of the guild</note>, for each occurrence.*

# III, L-LIII STATUTE OF 1314

->L. Regarding the penalty for giving a commission.<-

No one of this guild <note>Latin: "ars"; referring to the professional corporation or guild</note> may or shall give to any citizen or foreigner any commission <note>Latin: "dirictum"; a kickback or brokerage fee</note> regarding any goods sold by the men of this guild. The consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> are bound to take from anyone acting to the contrary, by way of a penalty, 40 silver shillings <note>Latin: "soldos .XL. f. p."; f.p. refers to 'florenorum parvorum' or small Florentine denari</note> for each occurrence.

->LI. Regarding the punishment of those who have renounced the guild.<-

The consuls of this guild are bound and obligated to find and investigate whether those who have previously renounced, or shall in the future renounce this guild, continue to practice the aforementioned craft in whole or in part after said renunciation; and they shall compel all and each of those practicing it to return and swear an oath to the guild anew, and to pay for their entry and as a new master <note>original: "novo magistro"</note> <note>The Latin text is noted as being written this way in the original manuscript.</note> the amount contained in the form of the statutes; and nonetheless, they shall fine each person for each of the aforementioned offenses 25 pounds <note>Latin: "libris .xxv. f. p."</note>. The consuls are bound to the aforementioned tasks under penalty of ten pounds each, and they must compel such condemned persons to pay to the guild all levies imposed upon them in the intervening time—namely, from the day of renunciation until the day of return—and all debts contracted by him or any of his partners up to the said day of renunciation.

->LII. Regarding the punishment of one who goes with someone making a collection.<-

*It is ordained that no one of this guild may or should go with anyone who makes any collection <note>Latin: "accattum"; likely referring to unauthorized fundraising or begging</note> without the permission of the consuls, under a penalty to be taken from him at the discretion of the consuls. And this chapter is not to be understood as applying to members of religious orders.*

->LIII. Regarding the punishment of one clearing the goods of a foreigner.<-

No one of the said guild shall clear or cause to be cleared any merchandise of any foreigner <note>Latin: "foretani"; someone from outside the city-state of Florence</note> at any toll-gate <note>Latin: "pedagio"</note> or customs office, through the Commune of Flo-

# STATUTE OF 1314 III, LIII-LV

Florence, or his officials by extortion. Against anyone doing so, the consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> shall be bound to take as a penalty ten pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or "florenorum parvorum"</note>, as often as it occurs.

### LIIII. On punishing those who speak rudely to the consuls, or among themselves in their presence.

No person shall dare, during a lawsuit or otherwise, to speak with rudeness <note>original: "rusticitatem," implying unrefined or insulting speech</note> or use injurious words toward the consuls by reason of any case or office of the consulate, nor speak any injurious words among themselves in the presence of the officials of the lords consuls. If anyone acts to the contrary, he shall be fined by the consuls up to the amount of one hundred shillings in small florins, taking into account the severity of the rudeness and the injurious words. And it shall be sufficient proof in the aforesaid matters if the said consuls, or the chamberlain, or any one of them heard the aforementioned things.

### LV. That no physician may practice the art of medicine unless he has been examined.

a. *No new physician, whether a doctor of physical medicine or a surgeon, from wherever he may be, may practice the art of medicine or surgery in the city of Florence if he is not degreed <note>original: "conventatus," meaning one who has formally received a university degree</note>, unless he has been examined by the consuls of this Guild along with two Friars Minor <note>Franciscans</note> and two Preachers <note>Dominicans</note>, to be provided by the priors or guardians of the said orders.*

b. *And that no new physician can or should treat patients in the city of Florence or its territory <note>original: "comitatu," the surrounding countryside</note> unless he were a degreed physician before the examination was made of him. And if any physician is found in the city or territory of Florence who is an idiot <note>original: "ideota," meaning uneducated or lacking professional training</note> or unskilled, whether woman or man, practicing against the law, they shall be expelled by the society of this Guild, so that they cannot practice medicine in the city or territory of Florence. And no apothecary <note>term: spetiarius - a pharmacist or spice merchant who also sold medicinal ingredients</note> shall dare to keep such a physician, woman or man, in his shop or elsewhere, nor conduct any business with them, nor offer them any aid or assistance.*

c. *From anyone acting to the contrary, the consuls shall take as a penalty one hundred shillings in small florins for each instance. And anyone may be an accuser regarding the aforesaid, and shall receive half of the fine. And the consuls of this Guild are bound to carry out all the aforesaid under penalty of ten pounds of small florins for each of them. And they cannot be released from these duties in any way. And they are bound to denounce such a physician, male or female, to the Podestà <note>The chief magistrate of Florence</note> of Florence as a falsifier of this art.*

# III, LVI-LVIII STATUTE OF 1314

## LVI. *That every physician is bound to advise a sick person, about whom he has doubt, to receive penance.*

Whosoever physician <note>original: "medicus fisicus," referring to a doctor of internal medicine</note> or surgeon shall be called to anyone suffering from a continuous fever, or another dangerous illness, or a wound, or a dangerous abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note>, he shall be bound and ought to say these words to the sick person or to those standing by: "I am bound by the name of my oath to warn and advise such a sick person to receive penance for sins committed," and otherwise not to treat him, under penalty of one hundred shillings <note>original: "soldorum"</note>. And if a surgeon shall be called to the care of a sick person, or one wounded, having any lesion of the skull, whether a fracture, or a splintering <note>original: "rutilam"</note>, or a depression, or any dangerous abscess, or an anthrax carbuncle <note>original: "carbunculum antranei"</note>, or a cancer, and things similar to these, they shall be bound and ought to seek a partner physician or surgeon, and otherwise not to treat him, under penalty of 40 shillings in small florins <note>original: "f. p." for parvorum florenorum</note>.

## LVII. *That no physician should dare to speak rudely of another physician.*

No physician shall dare or presume to speak of another physician, secretly or openly, with rudeness <note>original: "rusticitatem," implying unrefined or insulting speech</note> or injurious words. And from him who does the contrary, the consuls <note>the elected leaders of the Guild</note> are bound to take, in the name of a penalty and as a penalty, 40 shillings in small florins, as often as it occurs. And if an accuser or denouncer shall legitimately prove the case against such an accused person, he shall have half of the fine, and his identity shall be kept in confidence, saving the jurisdiction of the Commune of Florence.

## LVIII. *On punishing a physician judging any wound as enormous or not enormous, or anyone toward life or toward death, without a partner physician.*

*a. It is ordained that no surgeon, by the precept of the Podestà <note>the high magistrate of the city</note>, the Captain, and their households, can or ought to sentence any man toward life or toward death, or judge any wound as enormous or not enormous, without the presence, counsel, and judgment of a convened doctor of medicine <note>original: "medici phisici conventati"</note>. And always for the giving of this sentence, the surgeon shall require the physician, and the physician the surgeon, under penalty of fifty pounds in small florins, to be taken by the consuls from anyone deciding against the said form.*

*b. And that no physicians, however many there may be, can receive on the occasion of any sentence for the aforementioned reports more than two gold florins, under penalty of fifty pounds in small florins. Half of which penalty shall belong to the denouncer, and his identity shall be kept in confidence.*

### *LVIIII. On punishing a physician who keeps an apothecary in his shop who has not paid his dues or sworn the oath to the aforementioned guild.*

No physician shall dare or presume to keep any apothecary <note>Latin: *spetiarium*; a pharmacist or spice-merchant</note> in his shop <note>Latin: *apotheca*; the place of business where medicines were prepared and sold</note> who has not paid the assessments and duties of the guild, or who has not sworn the oath to the aforementioned guild. Likewise, no apothecary shall presume to keep in his shop any physician who has not sworn the oath to this guild, or who has not paid the duties and assessments imposed upon him.

### *LX. That no consuls may contract any debt without the permission of the council.*

We ordain that no consulate and no consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> of the said guild, during their term of office, shall dare to acquire any money by obligating the guild itself to repay it, or contract any debt on behalf of the said guild, without the permission of the council of the said guild, under penalty of double the amount of that debt. And if they have contracted any debt for the said guild with the consent or permission of the council, they are bound to repay it before the end of their term of office, under the aforementioned penalty.

### *LXI. That no gathering of apprentices may be held at night.*

Since many damages and expenses often befall the craftsmen of the said guild because of the gathering of apprentices <note>Latin: *discipulorum*; students or trainees learning the trade</note> which takes place in the shop at night, it is ordained that no gathering of apprentices or other persons shall be held, or be allowed to be held, in any shop of the said guild at night, under penalty of ten pounds of small florins <note>Latin: *f. p.* or *florenorum parvorum*</note> for each apprentice. And the master shall be compelled to pay the said fine on behalf of the apprentice.

### *LXII. On punishing one who keeps unbolted pepper and spices not made with pepper and saffron.*

*a.* No member of the said guild shall dare or presume to keep pepper in his shop unless it has been bolted <note>Latin: *cribellatum*; sifted or strained to remove impurities</note>, under penalty of ten pounds of small florins if the pepper weighs twenty-five pounds or more; and if it is less, a penalty of one hundred shillings of small florins.
*b.* Likewise, no apothecary or craftsman of the said guild shall dare to keep spices in his shop unless they are made of pepper and saffron, or substances...

# III, LXII, LXIII STATUTE OF 1314
Page 52

...of greater value, under penalty of 40 small Florentine shillings <note>original: "soldorum .XL. f. p." refers to the *soldi piccoli*, a common currency of the period</note>. c. And that no wholesale merchant, or any other person, shall keep in his shop nor sell or cause to be sold *ground pepper* <note>original: "piperem minutum"</note>, nor shall any of the aforesaid or anyone else keep in his shop *ginger* or *ground cinnamon*, unless it has been well-sifted and cleaned of dust and sand; and just as has been said regarding the aforesaid, this shall be understood to apply to *nutmeg, mace* <note>original: "folio," referring to the leaf-like covering of the nutmeg</note>, and all *spices*.

d. Likewise, that no one shall make or keep *mixed* spices <note>original: "fattas," likely referring to pre-blended spice mixes which were easier to adulterate</note>, except those made from genuine spices, namely: *pepper, ginger, cinnamon, cloves, galangal, mace, nutmeg, grains of paradise* <note>original: "meleghettis," a pungent spice from West Africa</note>, *cardamom, betel leaf, saffron, spikenard,* and *clove stems*. And all the aforesaid items must be well-cleaned of any dust and sand.

e. Likewise, that anyone who is asked for spices of pepper and saffron is bound and obliged to give spices of *black pepper, whole and sifted, and of saffron, and of no other kind*.

f. Likewise, that in the said spices, or any others which one might keep *mixed*, one may include *long pepper or ground pepper*.

g. Likewise, that all those who make or wish to make, or cause to be made, *yellow* spices <note>A common medieval spice blend used for coloring food</note>, are bound to *color them yellow* and cause them to be colored yellow only with *saffron*, and not with any other powder or other ingredient. Furthermore, from anyone acting against any of the aforesaid cases, the consuls shall take five pounds <note>original: "libras quinque"</note> for each offense; and from any *grocer* <note>term: <term>piczicaiuolo</term> (a retailer of foodstuffs and spices)</note> acting against any of the aforesaid cases, *40 small Florentine shillings for each offense*. And by the present ordinances, it is not intended, nor shall it be, that the statute of the said guild speaking of counterfeit items or falsifications be in any way diminished, but rather they shall remain in their full strength and firmness.

### LXIII. That any accuser shall have *half of the fine*.

If anyone accuses or denounces any person or persons of this guild for any falsification, and the consuls are certain of it, he shall receive from the chamberlain <note>The guild's treasurer</note> of the said guild *half of the fine* which is collected from the accused, according to the form of this constitution; and the identity of the accuser and denouncer shall always be kept secret, saving the chapter concerning counterfeit saffron, which is found above.

# STATUTE OF 1314 — III, 64, 65

### 64. *On the penalty to be imposed by the syndics.*

If the <term>syndics</term> <note>officials appointed to audit and oversee the conduct of others</note> of this guild find that any former official of the said guild has committed a transgression in any way during his term of office, they shall fine him according to the form of the statute, if the statute addresses the matter; and if the penalty has not been determined by the constitution, they shall fine the said transgressor according to the nature of the crime and the status of the person.

### 65. *On the general conclusion and observation of the aforesaid statutes.*

a. We decree that all the aforementioned chapters, ordinances, and statutes of the present constitution are, and are understood, held, and maintained to be the chapters, ordinances, and statutes of the aforesaid guild and <term>university</term> <note>original: "universitatis"; here meaning the entire corporate body or legal community of the guild</note>. And that these chapters, ordinances, and statutes—in every one of their chapters, articles, members, and points—shall be valid, binding, and obtain full and irrevocable firmness, solely and simply as they stand, from now until the next two years to come. And if anyone should be of such audacity as to dare to say, propose, or <term>harangue</term> <note>original: "arrengare"; to speak formally in a public assembly</note> against the correction, amendment, and compilation made regarding the said chapters, whether secretly or openly, or should say that the present constitution and the chapters contained within it do not have the force and power of legitimate and approved statutes of the aforesaid guild, he shall by that very statement be considered <term>infamous</term> <note>a legal status involving the loss of reputation and certain civil rights</note> and shall fall—and be understood to have fallen—perpetually from all honors, offices, and benefits of the said guild; and nevertheless, he shall be fined by the <term>consuls</term> <note>the highest-ranking leaders of the guild</note> ten pounds of small florins <note>original: "libris decem f. p." (florenorum parvorum)</note> for each instance, under a double penalty, to be collected from each of the said consuls by the syndics.

b. And that the lords consuls of the said guild are bound to impose all penalties contained in this statute and to punish all excesses, wrongdoings, and crimes as has been stated and declared through the said statutes. And if a chapter does not speak on a matter, they must and can punish all transgressors at their own discretion, having inspected the nature of the crime and the transgressor <gloss>Corrected by the original hand from "quantity"</gloss>. And this chapter shall be precise and definitive, and shall be understood as a special provision derogatory to all other chapters of the said guild in every one of its articles and points, so and in such a way that nothing can be proposed or argued against it.

c. It was added by the <term>arbiters</term> <note>officials chosen to settle disputes or refine laws</note> of the said guild: and that the ordinances issued regarding <term>credits</term> <note>original: "credentiis"; likely referring to financial trusts or debts</note> by the consuls of the said guild are <term>void</term> <note>original: "capsa"; literally "boxed" or set aside/cancelled</note>.

# STATUTES OF THE SADDLERS
-> 59 <-

*In the name of God, amen. These are certain provisions, decrees, ordinances, and statutes pertaining to the branch of those merchants who cover, furnish, or equip, make, work, buy, and sell saddles, and perform and practice other things <note>original: "faciunt et exercent" written over an erasure</note> belonging to the aforementioned branch.*

### I. <note>The title of this section is missing in the original manuscript.</note>

*a. We grant to the men of the said branch the right to take, elect, and keep one man from among themselves—certainly a good and capable man—as an official; and to release and remove that official, and to substitute another in succession, as is set forth below. First, indeed, in the present month of May, or thereafter whenever they wish, having called together the artisans of the said branch in the place they have chosen, they shall call by voice in the accustomed manner the aforesaid official, who shall remain in that office from now through the entire month of December next following, in the current years of our Lord one thousand three hundred and fourteen <note>1314 AD</note>, in the 13th indiction <note>A 15-year cycle used in medieval dating to verify documents</note>.*

*b. Which official shall promise, swear, and be bound throughout the said time to manage, help, lead, and defend the men and persons of the said branch, and to do all other things which shall pertain to his aforementioned office. This election must be renewed every year in the said month of December, in the manner, way, and time that shall seem fitting to the officials who are in place at that time <note>original: "qui pro tempore fuerint"</note>, according to the method and form ordained above. And the office of the aforesaid official elected from the present time forward, and of each of them, shall last for one year.*

*c. And the son, father, or brother of the said outgoing official may not be elected to the aforesaid position, nor even his partner in his workshop <term>apotheca: a medieval term for a shop, stall, or place of business</term>.*

# II, III STATUTES OF THE SADDLERS <note>original: "Sellai"</note>

## II. *That the said official is bound to make every member of the said branch take a physical oath (1).*

a. The aforementioned official is bound, within ten days from the day he has sworn into his own office, to make each and every man of this craft—namely the masters—swear to this statute. Those so swearing are bound to observe these oaths from that time until the next following Calends of January <note>The first day of the month; in this context, January 1st.</note>.

b. Likewise, the official himself is bound to make them swear; and they themselves are bound to swear and observe the oath in this form, namely:

> "I, being a member of this branch, swear upon the Holy Gospels of God to observe, fulfill, hear, attend to, and not cease through fraud, and to obey each and every command—of whatever quantity or quality, provided they are just and honorable—which the official for the time being, or the messenger of the said branch, shall give me or cause to be given to me by reason of his craft and office, according to the good and pure understanding of the one giving the commands; and to observe each and every thing contained in these present statutes that I ought to observe, in good faith and without fraud, provided they are not against the honor and constitution of the Commune of Florence. And I promise to give and pay to the official of the said branch, or to the chamberlain <note>term: "camerario" (the guild's treasurer or financial officer)</note> of this branch, all penalties legally owed for any chapters not kept, or commands contained herein, or for any other just cause."

And the official himself is bound to swear to exercise his office well and legally, and to treat the artisans as is contained above in the first chapter.

c. If anyone should speak insulting words to this official by reason of his office, in the place where justice is administered by him, the official himself shall fine him 40 silver shillings <note>original: "soldis .XL. f. p." (Soldi Piccoli of Florence)</note> for each occurrence; and if the insult or insulting words are spoken to the same official elsewhere, the official shall fine him 20 silver shillings. Regarding this, the oath of the said official shall be upheld. The official shall see that these fines are executed within ten days from the day of the condemnation.

## III. *Concerning the penalty for a summoned person not appearing.*

If anyone, having been summoned on behalf of the aforementioned official, does not come to the place determined in the summons, or does not remain in that place at the will of the official, he shall pay as a penalty two silver shillings for each instance. If, however, he arrives after the official has begun to speak, he shall pay one shilling, unless he can justly defend himself before the official.

# STATUTES OF THE SADDLEMAKERS IV-VIII

### IV. *That the men of the craft are bound to maintain good fellowship among themselves.*

The men of this craft <note>Latin: *artis*; referring to the professional guild</note> are bound to maintain good fellowship among themselves and shall not cause any injury, harassment, or grievance to one another regarding any apprentice, partner, or laborer. The aforementioned official shall fine anyone acting to the contrary twenty *soldi* in small Florentine pennies <note>original: "soldis .xx. f. p." (denariorum florenorum parvorum)</note> for each occurrence. He shall collect this fine within the next ten days.

### V. *Regarding not performing work that was begun by another.*

No member of this guild shall dare to perform any work that was started by another member of this craft without the permission <note>original: "parabula"</note> of the one who began the work. The aforementioned official shall fine anyone who acts to the contrary ten *libre* in small Florentine pennies for each occurrence; provided that the one who began the work is able and willing to complete what he ought to complete in full, by order of the said official, for a fair price. The official shall collect this fine within ten days.

### VI. *Regarding not painting a piece that has not been covered in leather.*

Every member of this craft is bound not to have any piece painted that has not first been covered in leather <note>original: "incoiatum"; from the Italian 'cuoio' for leather. This ensures the structural integrity of the saddlery before decoration.</note>. The official shall fine anyone acting to the contrary ten *soldi* in small Florentine pennies for each occurrence, to be collected within ten days.

### VII. *Regarding the administration of justice and the receiving of complaints.*

The aforementioned official has the power, obligation, and duty to render and facilitate justice among the men of this craft—specifically concerning the deeds and business of the said craft and any other matter—and to receive complaints and petitions. He shall command a defendant who confesses to pay the plaintiff what he admits he owes within the next ten days. If, however, the defendant denies the claim, the official has the power and obligation to decide the case as he sees fit within thirty days, collecting a court fee <note>original: "diritturam"</note> from the losing party of six *denarii* for every *libra* involved in the case. The official may also, if he pleases, seek legal counsel at the expense of the parties regarding the case or cases brought before him.

### VIII. *Regarding not taking away a workshop.*

Every member of this craft is bound not to make any solicitation, or cause damage or injury to any member of this guild, regarding any workshop <note>original: "apotheca"; a shop or place of business</note> in which

<meta>catchword: in which</meta>

# STATUTES OF THE SADDLERS

*...any of the masters should dwell there, and not to take it for rent in any way without the license and permission of him or those who first held it. And concerning such license and permission, a public legal document must appear, drawn up by the hand of the notary of this guild or another reputable notary. And also [it shall not be taken] without the license and permission of the aforementioned official, unless the previous tenant had first vacated it for six continuous months. The aforementioned official shall fine anyone acting to the contrary ten pounds in small Florentine pennies <note>original: "libris decem f. p." - fiorini piccoli, the local silver-based currency</note> for each occurrence; and thereafter ensure it is observed in this manner. He shall collect this fine within the next ten days from the day of the sentencing.*

### VIIII. Concerning the observance of feast days.

*All and every member of this branch are bound to celebrate three continuous days at the Christmas of our Lord Jesus Christ and at his Resurrection <note>Easter</note>, not counting the day of the feast itself; and the four feasts of the Virgin Mary, and the twelve Apostles, Saint Lucy, and Saint Savior, and other feasts which the same official might command to be observed. On these days, they shall not work nor cause work to be done, except only that one may stay at the workshop <term>apotheca: a combined shop and workshop space</term> without opening the windows, nor placing outside any items pertaining to the said craft, nor opening the larger doors; but they may open the smaller doors of the workshop. However, on the feast days of the Blessed Mary and the aforementioned Apostles, they cannot and must not stay at the workshop, except as on the day of Easter <gloss>Except also that the aforementioned official might give license for working in the workshop</gloss> <note>This interlinear gloss is a later addition from 1315</note>. The aforementioned official shall fine those acting to the contrary twenty shillings in small Florentine pennies for each and every occurrence. He shall collect this penalty within ten days from the day of the sentencing.* <insert>and nights</insert> <note>This addition was made on June 29, 1314, by the notary Pietro di Ricco Bacherelli</note>

### X. Concerning the non-retention of apprentices.

*No master of this craft or partner can or should keep the apprentice <term>discipulus: a trainee learning the trade under a master</term> of any other master, unless he has served for the determined time, or unless he is held with the license and permission of that master with whom he was first placed, under penalty of one hundred shillings in small Florentine pennies. The aforementioned official shall collect this penalty within ten days from the day the sentencing is made.*

# STATUTES OF THE SADDLERS XI-XV
63

### XI. *On the correction of the statutes.*

*The aforementioned official <note>likely the guild master or rector</note> shall be permitted, with the counsel of two men of this guild whom he shall choose, and in the presence of the men of said guild, to make and ordain new chapters for the said guild, for the honor and good standing of the same guild, and to diminish, add to, and correct the present chapters. And those things which they have ordained and made shall be valid and binding and must be inviolably observed by every individual of the said guild, provided that they have been approved, and they must be approved, by the aforementioned Lord Consuls <note>the higher civic authorities of the city</note>. Otherwise—that is, if they were not approved—they shall not be valid, nor should they be observed.*

### XII. *On not purchasing stolen goods.*

*No one of this guild may knowingly buy or cause to be bought a stolen item. Against anyone doing so, the official shall condemn them to a fine of 20 silver shillings <note>original: "soldis .xx. f. p." referring to Florentine small denari</note>, for each occurrence. And he shall be compelled to restore the purchased item to whomever it belonged. This fine must be collected within ten days from the day of the condemnation.*

### XIII. (1) <margin>The title of this section is missing.</margin>

*On any day when someone of this guild dies or when a funeral service <note>original: "misterium," referring here to the funeral rites or guild mystery plays associated with mourning</note> is held for them, no one of this guild shall dare to keep their shop open, nor place any work upon the window <note>the "fenestram" was the street-facing counter where goods were displayed</note>, under penalty of ten silver shillings. The said official shall impose and collect this fine within ten days. It shall be permitted, however, for anyone to keep a small shutter <note>term: "sportellum" - a small door or hatch allowing light or limited access without being fully open for business</note> open on the aforementioned days.*

### XIIII. (1) <margin>The title of this section is missing.</margin>

*The aforementioned official, with the majority of the master craftsmen of the said guild, shall be able to absolve the aforementioned official from his oath of office, as well as other officials, in whole or in part, whenever it appears to them that the said officials are bound to some inconvenience by the form of any statute.*

### XV. *On the salary of the official, the chamberlain, and the councilors.*

*In this guild there are and must be the under-written officials, namely: one official, one chamberlain <note>the treasurer or financial officer</note>, and two councilors. And they must have salaries in this manner, namely: the official, one pound of pepper and three ounces of saffron; the chamberlain, six ounces of pepper and two of saffron; and each of the councilors, four ounces of pepper and one of saffron.* <note>Spices like pepper and saffron were high-status luxury goods often used as a form of currency or prestigious payment in medieval Europe.</note>

# XVI-XX STATUTES OF THE SADDLERS <note>original: "Statuto dei Sellai"</note>

### XVI. *Regarding the hiring of apprentices.*

*No one may hire any apprentice except by a public legal document and with a suitable guarantor, and in the presence of the aforementioned official. If at the master's expense, the term shall be no less than six years; if at the apprentice's expense, the term shall be no less than three years. The official shall fine anyone acting to the contrary 40 silver shillings <note>original: "soldis .XL. f. p." referring to Florentine piccoli, the local currency</note> for each offense. This fine must be collected by the said official within ten days from the day of the judgment.*

### XVII. *Regarding making handiwork from good timber.*

*Every member of this guild is bound to make items pertaining to said craft well and lawfully, and to make all saddles from good timber—namely from beech, maple, hornbeam, walnut, or olive—and not from any other, nor from poplar or other poor, weak wood, unless it be a Hungarian-style saddle <note>original: "sella unganesca"</note>, which may be made of poplar. Against anyone doing otherwise, the official is bound to take 20 shillings as a penalty for each offense, and to collect it within ten days.*

### XVIII. *Regarding the prohibition of pack-saddle makers carrying insignia.*

*The aforementioned official is bound not to permit any pack-saddle maker <term>bastarius: a maker of "basti," the heavy frames used for beasts of burden rather than riding horses</term> or maker of donkey-saddles to carry or keep any insignia of the saddlers of this craft in the army or elsewhere, unless he has sworn an oath under the consuls of this craft and to this short-code <note>original: "breve," the foundational document of the guild</note>. Against anyone doing otherwise, the official shall take 20 shillings <insert>40</insert> <gloss>Interlinear correction perhaps from April 1, 1315</gloss> in the name of a penalty for each offense.*

### XVIIII. *Regarding the messenger of the craft.*

*The official is bound to have one apprentice or another person as a messenger, for making the aforementioned requisitions and other tasks that belong to the office of a messenger. To whom he is bound to give for his salary of one year 20 silver shillings from the money of the said craft.*

### XX. *Regarding not giving a commission.*

*No one of this craft shall dare to give a commission <term>dirittum: likely a kickback or "right" of payment to an intermediary to secure work</term> to any person, under penalty of 20 shillings for each offense. The official shall collect this fine within ten days from the day of the judgment.*

->STATUTES OF THE SADDLERS XXI-XXIII<-

# XXI. <note>The rubric title is missing in the original manuscript.</note>

*No one of this craft shall make saddles from goat skin and sheep skin mixed together, unless it be in a pack-saddle <term>bardella: a light, padded pack-saddle</term>, on the side, or underneath the cloth. If anyone acts to the contrary, he shall be fined 20 small Florentine shillings for each saddle. The official is bound to collect this fine within ten days from the day the penalty was issued.*

# XXII. <note>The rubric title is missing in the original manuscript.</note>

*If any master of this craft should repair saddles or perform any work for any person who owes money to another member of this craft <insert>once a formal order has been issued to him by the official</insert> <note>original: "facto eidem precepto per officialem"</note>, he shall be fined 20 shillings for each instance, and he shall be bound to satisfy the creditor. This fine must be collected within three days from the day of the penalty.*

# XXIII. Regarding the providing of a banquet.

*It is decreed that if any apprentice of <gloss>this</gloss> <note>original: "huius"</note> craft from the city of Florence or its district wishes to attain the rank of master of said craft and practice said craft, and has served for the time ordained by the statutes of the craft, he is bound to provide a good and suitable banquet <term>conmestionem: a formal celebratory meal provided by a new master to his peers</term> for all the masters of said craft, or pay to the chamberlain of the said branch, receiving it on behalf of that branch, twelve Florentine pounds <insert>to provide a banquet for the whole city, and the twelve pounds are reduced to ten</insert> <note>original: "civitati facere comestionem in totum et libre .XII. sunt reducte ad .X."</note>. If, however, the said apprentice is a foreigner <note>meaning someone from outside the Florentine territory</note>, and has served in the city of Florence or its district for the ordained time and wishes to join said craft, he shall pay <insert>twenty pounds</insert> <note>original: "libras .XX."</note>. Excepted from this are the sons or grandsons <insert>descended from a son</insert> of any master of said craft who are of the lineage or house of such a master, who shall not be bound to serve or to pay anything <insert>and any citizen or inhabitant of the Florentine countryside who has served the craft shall pay fifteen pounds</insert>.*

# XXIIII–XXVII STATUTES OF THE SADDLERS’ GUILD

### XXIIII. *That it is permitted for masters to give work to apprentices.*

*It shall be permitted for any master of this branch <note>original: "membri"; referring to the specific division of the guild</note> to give work pertaining to the labor of said craft to any Florentine worker or inhabitant of the surrounding countryside <note>original: "comitatino"</note> who knows how to sew, and to keep him in his workshop <note>original: "apotheca"</note> for one year and no longer, without the permission of the official of the said branch. And no master shall dare to teach such a worker to sew with a border-strip <note>original: "ad bandellam"</note>, or on a frame <note>original: "telarium"</note>, or with a flat stitch <note>original: "puntum planum"</note>. Against anyone doing otherwise, the aforesaid official shall condemn them to a fine of 40 small Florentine shillings <note>original: "soldis .XL. f. p."</note> for each offense. Which fine must be collected within ten days by the aforesaid official.*

### XXV. *That no one may work for anyone, or associate with anyone, who is not enrolled in the register of the said craft.*

*No master of this craft may, or shall be permitted to, perform this craft for any person, of whatever condition they may be, or associate themselves with anyone who is not a master of this craft and found to be enrolled in the register <note>original: "matricula"</note> of the said craft, under penalty of fifty small Florentine pounds for each offense. And the official is bound to collect this fine within ten days from the day of the sentencing.*

### XXVI. *That no master may give work to any foreigner.*

*We ordain that no master shall dare to give work to any foreigner <note>original: "forensi"; meaning anyone born outside the Florentine territory</note> not born in the city, countryside, or district of Florence, whether he be an apprentice or a worker, unless first that apprentice or worker has paid and given to the chamberlain of the said branch, receiving it on behalf of the said branch, three small Florentine pounds, under penalty of one hundred small Florentine shillings for each offense <insert>(a)</insert>. Which fine the said official is bound to collect within ten days.*

### XXVII. *Regarding the division of fines and other income.*

*Half of all and singular fines, fees <note>original: "diritturarum"</note>, legal disputes, payments from new masters, and any other income...*

### *XXVIII. Regarding the rubric on not leasing shops already leased by another craftsman.*

*a. Likewise, to remove all fraud and every act of force, and to restrain malice, it is statuted and ordained that no craftsman of this guild, or anyone bound to this guild in any way, shall dare or presume to lease or cause to be leased any warehouse <term>fundacum: a large commercial building or warehouse</term> or shop <term>apoteca: a retail shop or workshop</term>, however leased, by any other craftsman of this guild, or of any other guild whatsoever, without the will, license, and consent of him, or those, who reside in such shops or warehouses, and who had leased those shops and warehouses themselves. Concerning which license and consent, a public instrument <note>a formal legal document</note> must appear, drawn up by the notary of the guild and in the presence of the consenting consuls of that guild to which the person belongs who provides such license and consent, or who voluntarily renounces the shop and warehouse before the same consuls, as stated, by public instrument, under penalty of one hundred pounds of small florins. Half of this penalty shall be applied to the Commune of Florence, and the remaining half must go to that craftsman or those craftsmen who resided in those shops and warehouses, and against whose will and consent such shops and warehouses were leased.*
