->REFORM OF 1314<-
I
71

*In the name of God, amen. Below are written certain statutes, ordinances, and corrections of statutes, made, published, and compiled by the new arbitrators of the said guild <note>The "Artis" or Guild, likely referring to a specific merchant or craft guild in an Italian commune</note>, in the years of the Lord's incarnation one thousand three hundred and fourteen, in the thirteenth indiction.*

## I.

*a. First, to the statute placed under the rubric <note>A "rubric" is a titled section or chapter in a legal document, traditionally written in red ink</note> concerning the election of consuls, they added these words, namely: that the consuls of the said guild, both present and future, are bound and must be held by the bond of their oath to be present, remain, and come to administer justice every Friday and Tuesday, from the morning until the hour of terce <note>approximately 9:00 AM</note>, and from the hour of nones <note>approximately 3:00 PM</note> until the hour of vespers <note>sunset</note>. And that all things contained in the said chapter placed under the rubric concerning the election of the lords consuls shall be extended to the aforesaid matters, just as to those things contained in the said chapter (1).*

*b. And that future consuls shall have for the salary of their office, from the money of the said guild, four pounds of small pennies <note>original: "libras quattuor f. p." referring to Florentine or local small denari</note> for each of them, and two pounds of pepper, and three ounces of saffron flower, and six bowls, and three large, new trenchers <note>term: incisoria (large wooden or metal plates used for cutting meat)</note>, at the times contained in the said chapter. And they shall have, or be able to have, nothing else (2).*

*c. And that the present consuls have and must have from the chamberlain <note>the guild's treasurer</note> of the said guild, for the labor which they have sustained and will sustain in standing to administer justice two days a week and for the amendment of these statutes, for a certain communal meal, six pounds of small pennies (3).*

# II-IIII REFORM OF 1314
72

->II.<-

*a. Likewise, to the statute placed under the rubric <note>A "rubric" is a titled section or chapter in a legal manuscript, traditionally written in red ink.</note> concerning the election of the chamberlain <note>original: "camerarius"; the guild's treasurer or financial administrator</note>, they added that the chamberlain of the said guild is bound and must, on every Tuesday and Friday of his term of office, at the hours and times when the consuls of the said guild meet, keep one boy for the services of the said guild. This boy is bound and must be present and remain with the said consuls and do all and singular things which shall be imposed upon him by the consuls of the said guild. If the said chamberlain does not keep this boy, the said chamberlain must be punished immediately by the consuls of the said guild by the loss of his entire salary (1).*
*b. And that the said chamberlain shall have for the salary of the said boy, from the money of the said guild, forty soldi in small florins <note>original: "soldos quadraginta f. p." (fiorini piccoli)</note> (2).*
*c. And that the said chamberlain is bound to send to the notary of the said guild, on the feast of All Saints of each year, a gift <note>original: "ensenium"; a customary gift or tribute</note> just as he does for the consuls of the said guild (3).*

->III.<-

*Likewise, to the statute placed under the rubric concerning the election of the councilors, it was added that the old consuls of the said guild shall be councilors of the said guild for the coming six months. And that the consuls of the said guild shall elect only six other councilors of the said guild (4) <margin>Cancelled by the arbitrators (1).</margin> (a).*

->IIII.<-

*Likewise, to the statute placed under the rubric concerning the election of the messenger <note>original: "nuntius"</note>, they added these words, namely: that the messenger of the said guild is bound and must be present and remain every day continuously for the services of the said guild at the shop <note>original: "apotheca"; here referring to the guild's official place of business or headquarters</note> of the aforesaid guild, where the notary of the said guild resides. And that otherwise he would have nothing, nor can or should he have anything from the aforesaid guild, unless for each day the chamberlain of the said guild withholds from the same messenger, when he is not in the said court, five soldi in small florins. And that the notary of the said guild is bound and must, under penalty of one hundred soldi in small florins, denounce that messenger on any day on which he does not come to the shop which is held for the aforesaid guild (5).*

# STATUTES OF THE PAINTERS

*These are certain provisions, statutes, and ordinances made, published, and compiled by the consuls of the said guild, by the authority and power granted to them by the aforesaid guild, pertaining to the branch of those apothecaries <note>original: "spetiariorum"; painters were often grouped with apothecaries because both traded in pigments and chemical substances</note> who buy, sell, and work with gold, silver, and beaten tin, glue, white lead, azure, cinnabar, and other colors, and perform other tasks looking toward and pertaining to the branch named above.*

->I.<-

*a. We grant to the men of the said branch the right to take up, elect, and keep one man from among themselves—certainly a good and capable man—as an official, and to release and remove that official and substitute another as shall seem fitting to them. This official shall promise, swear, and be bound throughout the entire time of his office to manage, help, lead, and defend the men and persons of the said branch, and to do all and singular other things which shall pertain to his aforementioned office. And the term of the newly elected official shall last from now until the first of July <note>original: "kalendas iulii"</note> next present, and from the said first day for the six months then immediately following. However, for an official elected from this day forward, the term of office shall last for six months.*

*b. Furthermore, the said official shall be bound to examine and investigate the deeds of the men of the said branch; and he can and must—with the advice of two counselors of the said branch to be chosen by the said official—having seen the acts and deeds, ordain through any of the craftsmen of the said guild such condemnations <note>legal penalties or fines</note> as and how many he wishes to make and form, and consign them to the notary of the said guild. And these condemnations, thus written and made public in the presence and by the will of the consuls of the said guild, shall have full legal standing.*

*c. The aforesaid official may also make against the men of the said guild, or any one of them, such and as many condemnations as he wishes to make and as shall seem fitting to him, according to the form of the statutes written below. And if the statutes do not speak on a matter, he may make such and as many condemnations against any men and persons of the said guild up to the amount of ten shillings in Florentine small pence <note>original: "soldorum decem f. p." (denariorum parvorum)</note>, and he may and shall demand those same condemnations—*

-># I-III STATUTES OF THE PAINTERS<-

*...be held within ten days (a), from the day the said condemnation was made. And the said official must stand for audit <note>original: "sindicatum" - a formal review of an official's conduct and finances</note> at the end of his term of office, just like the other officials of the said guild.*

*d. And the aforesaid official shall have for his salary for his said office, from the pence and money of the men of the said branch, twenty shillings in small florins (b), and one pound of pepper, and two ounces of saffron flower, six bowls, and two new trenchers <note>wooden plates or carving boards</note>.*

## II.

*The said official shall be bound at the beginning of his term to choose, appoint, and name two men and persons from the said branch, one of whom shall be the counselor-chamberlain and scribe of the affairs of the said guild, and the other shall be a counselor of the aforesaid guild; who shall advise the said chamberlain on the affairs and business of the said branch. And their term shall last as long as the term of the aforesaid official. The other, however, who shall be only a counselor, shall have half a pound of pepper, one ounce of saffron flower, one trencher, and two new bowls (c).*

## III.

*To the honor, praise, and reverence of Almighty God, and of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin His mother, and of all the Saints of God, we ordain that no one of the said branch may, dare, or presume to work, or perform any labor of the things of this guild on the below-written celebrated and festive days, or any one of them: namely, on Sundays, or any feast day of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the day of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ with the three following days, the day of Pentecost, All Saints, the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, Saint Stephen, Saint John the Evangelist, and the Holy Innocents, the Ascension of the Lord, and the twelve Apostles, Saint John the Baptist, the Blessed Lawrence, Saint...*

# STATUTES OF THE PAINTERS III-V

*...of Saint Zenobius and the Blessed Reparata <note>Saint Zenobius and Saint Reparata are the patron saints of Florence; their feast days were major public holidays</note>. Excepting that the aforementioned official may, and it shall be permitted for him to, grant a license to work on the said days or either of them, whenever and on whichever days he wishes, and as it shall seem appropriate to him, to whomever he wishes for necessities when they arise. This is provided that such a person, to whom the license was granted, gives to the chamberlain of the said branch a fourth part of what he earned on such a day or days. And excepting that anyone of the said branch may gild and varnish their works on the said days. And that same fourth part ought to be spent for the love of God <note>original: "Dei amore"; this indicates the funds were designated for charitable works or the poor</note>. Anyone acting against the aforementioned rules or any part of them shall be fined by the said official ten shillings in small florins <note>original: "soldis decem f. p." or "florenorum parvorum"</note> (1) for each offense.*

### IIII.

*To this end, so that no material for scandal may be generated among the craftsmen of this branch, we ordain that no one of the said branch may, dare, or presume to take any workshop <note>original: "apothecam"; in this context, a retail shop or artist's studio</note> leased to another of the said branch, or to dwell in it, if the first tenant has stayed in it and wishes to stay, and has paid the rent to the owner of the workshop. If, however, such a first tenant has not paid the rent, and the owner complains of this before the Consuls of the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers <note>original: "artis medicorum, spetiariorum et merciariorum"; the painters were legally organized as a branch of this larger guild</note>, or before the official of the said branch, then the consuls or official—having seen and clearly recognized the aforementioned to be true—may license anyone who wishes to take such a workshop to take it; and after the license is given, either specifically or generally, anyone of the said branch may lease such a workshop at his will.*

### V.

*a. We ordain that everyone of the said craft is bound and ought to observe the statutes and ordinances of the said craft, and to observe the promises made or to be made by them or any of them, and especially to the persons placed under, and who shall place themselves under, the jurisdiction of the said consuls and guild or the said official, for the sake of the said craft.*

# V-VIII STATUTES OF THE PAINTERS
80

**V.** And if anyone from outside the guild wishes to request anything from one of our craftsmen, they must first obligate themselves to satisfy the person from whom they are making the request, as is reasonably required. They shall pay four denarii <term>f. p. (fiorini piccioli)</term> <note>The "fiorino picciolo" was the "little florin," a silver-based currency used for daily transactions, distinct from the famous gold florin.</note> for the fee of every pound of the quantity they have requested or wish to request. Otherwise, they shall not be heard in any matter, under a penalty of ten shillings <term>f. p.</term> for anyone acting to the contrary, to be collected as often as the offense occurs.

### VI.

We decree that no one from the said membership should dare or presume, by themselves or through another, to complete any work begun by another master against the will of the one who started such work, provided the original creator wishes to complete the work and fulfill what they promised. If, however, the one who began the work does not observe their promises and does not complete the work after being requested to do so, any member of the said guild may complete that labor. Anyone acting to the contrary shall be condemned by the aforementioned official to restore and pay for all damages arising from the situation. A member shall be understood to have "begun" a work when, at the request of the person commissioning the work, they have remained at the task—or caused someone else to remain—for one full day, either designing or executing the work. If, however, a member begins a work without the request of the owner, they shall not be considered the "beginner" of the work, nor shall the work be considered "begun." Anyone acting to the contrary shall be fined forty shillings <term>f. p.</term> by the official, as often as it occurs.

### VII.

Likewise, no one of the said membership may dare or presume to work in any place, or perform any labor, with any person or persons who are not subject to the jurisdiction of the Consuls of the said guild, under a penalty of five shillings <term>f. p.</term> for every day they have worked with them, as often as it occurs.

### VIII.

Since the aforementioned membership is burdened by many expenses due to the taxes <note>original: "gabellas"</note> imposed and assessed upon this guild by the Commune of Florence, we ordain that whoever of the said membership wishes to practice the aforementioned art in the city of Florence, and has not served the said guild as contained in the chapter *concerning apprentices*, shall pay to the chamberlain of the said membership in the city of Florence...

# STATUTES OF THE PAINTERS VIII, IX
Page 81

*...for the entry fee <note>original: "pro intratura"</note> (a) and for the salary of the official to be paid by a new master, and as an aid to the aforementioned tax <note>original: "gabelle"</note>, ten pounds of small florins. To make this payment, however, blood brothers (b) or sons of any master of the said craft shall not be held liable or compelled; rather, they may exercise the said craft freely. However, they may not—before they have practiced the aforementioned craft for three years or more—keep any apprentice of their own, if the father or brother already keeps or has an apprentice. Furthermore, whoever serves the said craft as an apprentice, as is contained in the chapter **concerning apprentices**, shall pay only forty shillings for his entry.*

### IX.

*a. It is ordained that no one of the said membership may, dare, or presume, from now until the next three years, to take more than one apprentice for each master of the said membership. And that any craftsman, when he has hired an apprentice, must hire him for a term of at least three years at the apprentice's expense, or for a term of at least six years at the master's expense.*

*b. And that any apprentice who has placed himself, or wishes to place himself, as an apprentice with any master of the said membership to practice the aforementioned craft, must place himself by a public legal document <note>original: "publicum instrumentum"</note>, to be drawn up by the hand of the notary of the said craft. And that no one ought to keep him otherwise, under penalty of twenty shillings of small florins for each offense, and twenty shillings for every month that he might dismiss him from the aforementioned place during the time of the three or six years; and such an apprentice is bound and obligated to pay to the chamberlain <term>Chamberlain: The treasurer or financial administrator of the guild</term> of the said membership twenty shillings. And if anyone of the said membership keeps more than one apprentice against the aforementioned form, he shall be fined by the official of the membership—if such an apprentice is sixteen years of age or younger—two shillings for every day he keeps him; and if he exceeds the age of sixteen years, the one keeping him shall be fined five shillings for every day he keeps him.*

*c. However, anyone of the said membership may keep an apprentice for fifteen days before the hiring is finalized by a public document, so that he may see and recognize if the apprentice has the mental capacity <note>original: "capax ingenii"</note> for learning the craft.*

# VIII-XIII STATUTES OF THE PAINTERS

<note>original: "predictam, et consulere..."</note> ...the aforementioned [art], and to evaluate whether the apprentice is naturally capable or not. Once the term of the contract is completed, the master must report that same apprentice to the notary of the said guild, so that he may begin to earn a living from the aforementioned art.

### X.

To this end, so that everyone may reasonably bear the burdens imposed upon them, we ordain that no member of the said guild shall support any rebel, condemned person, or defiant individual of the said guild, nor anyone who has not paid a tax, fine, or duty reasonably levied against him. Furthermore, no one shall support anyone who has not served the master with whom he was placed, nor give him work, nor acquire any labor from him, nor work with him, nor give, lend, or provide him with tools <term>masseritias: the specialized tools and equipment of the painter's workshop</term>, under penalty of five shillings in small florins <note>original: "soldorum quinque f. p." referring to the fiorini piccioli, the local silver-based currency of Florence</note> for each occurrence.

### XI.

Likewise, no one of the said guild may, dare, or presume to design or create—on a banner, shield, or elsewhere, by himself or through others—the insignia of any tyrant or public enemy, or of any rebel against the Commune and People of Florence and the Guelph party <note>The Guelphs were the political faction supporting the Pope, dominant in Florence at this time</note>. Nor shall anyone design or make any image or die for any coinage without the permission of the officials appointed for this purpose by the Commune of Florence, under penalty of ten pounds in small florins, or more or less at the discretion of the consuls or the aforementioned official, considering the severity of the offense committed. And regarding what is said above about permission, it is understood that with such permission they may design or make the image or die of any coinage.

### XII.

Likewise, no one of the said guild may, dare, or presume to commit any fraud in the aforementioned art, such as applying or placing silver in place of gold, "half-gold" <note>an alloy of gold and silver</note> in place of fine gold, or German blue <note>azurite</note> in place of ultramarine <note>the much more expensive pigment made from lapis lazuli</note>, or similar deceptions whereby a work might be diminished in value. This is under penalty of forty shillings in small florins for each occurrence, and the offender must restore any damages resulting from the aforementioned malice or following from it.

### XIII.

Likewise, no member of the said guild shall dare or presume in any way to speak insults to the consuls, the notary, or any other official of the said guild or art, nor to resist the seizure of goods by the guild's messenger, under penalty of forty shillings in small florins for each occurrence, or more or less at the discretion of the consuls or the aforementioned official.

->STATUTES OF THE PAINTERS XIV-XVI<-
83

### XIV.

Since almost all matters cannot be fully clarified at present, we ordain that it shall be possible and lawful for the community of the aforementioned branch <note>The "branch" refers to the painters' specific group within the larger guild structure</note> to elect four good and law-abiding men from said branch, who <insert>together with the official and the counselors</insert> <margin>Added by a hand from 1316</margin> may clarify doubts regarding said art whenever they arise, and make provisions regarding salaries and other matters which are necessary for the office mentioned above. And whatever is done by them shall be valid and binding, as if they were the statutes of the aforementioned art, provided that, if expenses are incurred, those expenses do not exceed the sum of five pounds of small florins.

### XV.

Likewise, that all fines and income of the said art shall belong for one half to the chamberlain <note>The treasurer or financial officer</note> of the College of the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Mercers, and for the other half to the chamberlain of the said branch, for the benefit of said branch. And both the consuls of the said art and the official of the said branch are bound to the aforementioned terms and to each of the things mentioned.

### XVI.

Likewise, that the official of the said branch is bound and obligated to collect, or cause to be collected, all fines which he has imposed within ten days <insert>within one month</insert> <margin>Correction from June 18, 1316</margin>, counting from the day the fine was issued.

In the name of our Lord God Jesus Christ, amen. In the year of His incarnation one thousand three hundred <note>original: "trecento"</note> and sixteen, in the 14th indiction <note>A 15-year cycle used for dating medieval documents</note>, on the 18th day of the month of June, in the time of the noble and powerful knight Lord Rolandino de Galiucziis of Bologna, the honorable Vicar of the city and district of Florence on behalf of the Royal Majesty of Jerusalem and Sicily, all the above-written statutes and ordinances were approved, along with their additions and corrections—

# STATUTES OF THE PAINTERS
84

...contained, written, and set down in this book and constitution by the provident, wise, and discreet men:

> Master John, a physician, son of the late Lapo, acting for himself and in the place and name of
> Guccio Tocti of Uzzano, who committed his turn and voice <note>original: "vicem et vocem"; meaning his proxy and voting power</note> to the same; and
> Mectus Beliotti, acting for himself and in the place and name of
> Lord Fazio of Signa, a judge, who committed his turn and voice to the same; and
> Cambino Rocchi, a skinner <note>term: pelliparium (a furrier or leather worker)</note>,
> Grifo Ranerii, and
> Arrigo Federighi

as approvers for the Commune of Florence, deputized to approve the statutes and ordinances of the guilds of the city of Florence. Always reserved—at the beginning, middle, and end of this present approval—are all and singular ordinances of justice of the Commune and People of Florence, and all and singular statutes, ordinances, and council reforms of the city and its commune, present and future. Also reserved are the honor and reverence of the Holy Roman Church, of the said Royal Majesty, and of the said Lord Vicar and his court and successors; of the Lords Priors and the Standard-bearer of Justice <note>term: vexilliferi iustitie (the Gonfaloniere, a high-ranking official in the Florentine Republic)</note>; of the Lord Barigello <note>term: barigelli (the captain of the guard or police chief)</note> and his court and office; and of all other officials of the city and its commune, present and future.

And it is reserved that if the aforesaid statutes and ordinances, or any of them contained, written, and set down in this book and constitution—or their additions and corrections—should in any way detract from, contradict, or obstruct the said honors, or the statutes and ordinances of justice, they shall not be understood to be, nor shall they be, approved, corrected, or confirmed. Rather, insofar as they might obstruct, contradict, or oppose the aforesaid, they shall be understood to be and are void, corrected, and removed; they shall be of no efficacy or value, as if they had never been written in this book and present constitution.

I, Bene, son of the late Bencivenni of Rufina, by Imperial authority an ordinary judge and public notary, now scribe for the Commune of Florence, together with the said approvers specially deputized by the Commune itself, have publicly written all and singular the aforesaid things by mandate of the same approvers, and therefore I have signed below.

### [Book I]

#### I. *Concerning the election of the Lord Consuls and their prohibition.*

**a.** [The procedure to be observed in the election of consuls].
Around the middle of the month of June and around the middle of the month of December of each year, the consuls of the said Guild <note>The "Arte dei Medici e Speziali," one of the seven major guilds of Florence</note> currently in office shall be required—so that at least within three days of the end of each of the said months—to have the following things done regarding the election (1) of the new consuls of the said Guild, in the manners written below, namely: that the said Lord Consuls are required to assemble their advisors and those of the said Guild, so that at least two-thirds of the consuls and two-thirds of the advisors of the said Guild are gathered together in the house <note>The guild hall or headquarters</note> of the said Guild. And once gathered, these consuls and advisors shall elect and nominate sixteen good and loyal men of the said Guild: specifically four doctors, six apothecaries, and six merchants <note>The "merciai" or mercers/grocers</note>, true Guelphs <note>The political faction supporting the Pope, a requirement for holding office in Florence</note>, and not foreigners. And let it be understood that the member-group of the merchants, regarding the aforementioned things and all others (a), includes all the sub-groups (b) which are customarily called and understood to be under that name; these men they are required to elect and nominate in agreement. And if in this election and nomination there should be any discord among the consuls and advisors, two-thirds of the said consuls and advisors are required to perform and carry out the election and nomination. And they may also perform all the things written below.

**b.** Excepting nonetheless that, while the provision of the Commune of Florence regarding the "bagging" <term>insacchatione: the process of placing names of eligible candidates into bags (borse) to be drawn by lot</term> of the consuls shall last, those who are drawn from the bags of the said "baggings" shall be and are understood to be the consuls of the said Guild, according to the form of the provision and ordinance of the Commune of Florence made regarding the aforesaid matters.

**c.** Which sixteen men of the said Guild—namely four doctors, six apothecaries, and six merchants—*thus elected and nominated, must place and put*

(1) *B election.*

d. And the consuls of the said guild are bound to make the councilors of the said guild and the sixteen adjuncts <note>original: "arroti"; additional members called to assist a committee</note> take an oath.

# STATUTE OF 1349 I, 1

### 7

g. [Penalty for those electing to office and penalty for those accepting office who have not paid their debt to the guild].
Furthermore, let it be that anyone who elects someone who has not entirely paid everything they owed to the aforementioned guild shall be fined by the consuls <note>The 'Consoli' were the highest-ranking executive officials of a medieval guild</note> currently in office the sum of forty soldi in *small florins* <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli," the silver-based currency used for daily transactions in Florence</note> to the aforementioned guild. And no one may accept any office of the said guild contrary to the said form, under penalty of one hundred soldi in *small florins*, for which they must be immediately fined by the said consuls and removed from the said office by the consuls and the chamberlain <note>term: "camarlingho" - the treasurer or financial administrator of the guild</note> of the said guild, under penalty of one hundred soldi in *small florins* for each consul or chamberlain, for every such instance. And all others may be elected to the said office, and they are bound and must accept and take the oath.

h. [Penalty imposed on those not accepting an office of the said guild].
And if anyone does not accept it <gloss>original Latin note: "acceptaverit"</gloss> and will not accept it, let them give to this guild 25 pounds of *small florins*, and let them be removed from the said office, and another be put in their place.

i. [One-year prohibition from the day of leaving office].
And let there be a prohibition <note>term: "divieto" - a mandatory waiting period to prevent the same families or individuals from monopolizing power</note> from the said office for one year from the day the office was laid down. And that these consuls may not hold any office from the said guild for one year from the day the office was laid down, from which or through which a salary or gift might follow or be ordained.

l. [Prohibition for the shop-assistant of any consul].
Furthermore, no shopkeeper <note>term: "bottegaio" - likely referring here to a business partner or senior employee associated with a consul's workshop</note> of any consul may hold the office of the consulate for one year from the day the consulate was laid down, nor hold any office of the said guild for six months from the day the consulate was laid down.

m. [Form of the election of consuls].
Furthermore, in the election of consuls and in all and every other business conducted in the aforementioned guild, at least two-thirds <gloss>original note: "three" (corrected to "two" in the reform of December 1356)</gloss> of the consuls of the said guild must be present and give consent; otherwise, what they do is not valid. And if anyone is requested to form the council for the said election and does not actually come, they shall be fined ten soldi in *small florins* by the chamberlain of the said guild for the benefit of the guild, and the consuls are bound to make them pay this for every such instance, under the said penalty for each of the said consuls. Which election and its form we command to be performed and observed at such time when the provisions made by the Commune of Florence regarding the creation of consuls have expired, are lacking, or are quashed. And while and until they remain firm, we ordain that...

# STATUTE OF 1349 I, I, II

*p.* [*That two-thirds of the consuls and councilors may do all things that the whole body can do*]. <note>original: "Quod due partes consulum et consiliariorum possit omnia facere, que possunt omnes ipsi"</note> They further ordain and establish that in every gathering, college, work, or business of the said guild, or among the councilors of the said guild, it shall be considered a sufficient number if two-thirds of the said consuls or councilors are present; and whatever can and must be done by the office of the consuls shall be valid and binding if it is performed by two-thirds of the said consuls and councilors (1).

## II. Regarding the election of the chamberlain, his office, and prohibitions.

*a.* At the beginning of the month of January of each year, while the provision of the Commune of Florence regarding the creation of consuls is observed, the consuls of this guild—or two-thirds of them—together with their councilors and those of the said guild—or two-thirds of them—and sixteen <term>adjuncts</term> <note>agiunti: additional members called in to assist or oversee specific administrative tasks</note> from the men of the said guild, namely (2) four doctors, six apothecaries, and six mercers, to be elected and nominated by the said consuls, are bound and required to elect and nominate nine (a) <term>good men</term> <note>buoni huomini: a formal status for reputable citizens eligible for office</note> of the said guild and the branch of the apothecaries, being themselves apothecaries, of at least twenty-five years of age. These nine (b) apothecaries thus nominated must be put to a secret <term>scrutiny</term> <note>scruptino: a formal vote or ballot to determine fitness for office</note> among the said consuls, councilors, and adjuncts, provided that at least two-thirds of the consuls, two-thirds of the councilors, and two-thirds of the adjuncts are present at the said scrutiny. And those three who *shall have the most votes* in the said scrutiny shall remain and be understood to be <term>chamberlains</term> <note>camarlinghi: the financial treasurers responsible for the guild's funds and accounts</note> of the said guild for one year, and for the term of one year. That is: one, whom the said consuls choose, shall be the chamberlain and held as chamberlain of the said guild for the months of January, February, March, and April; and the second, whom the said consuls choose, shall be the chamberlain of the said guild for the months of May, June, July, and August; and the third shall be the chamberlain of the said guild for the months of September, October, November, and December. ### III. *Concerning the election of the notary and his office.*

*a. In the month of January of each year, as soon as they are able (2), the consuls currently in office shall be bound and obligated—the consuls of the said guild or the majority of them—by the bond of their oath and under penalty of 10 pounds for each consul, to proceed to the election of the notary and scribe of the said guild. This shall be done together with the guild's councilors and twenty-four "additions" <note>term: arroti (additional citizens called in to supplement a council for specific votes)</note>, namely: six doctors, nine apothecaries, and nine grocers, to be chosen by the said consuls. Having gathered in the house of the said guild, they shall choose from the best men of the guild, and in the stead and name of the said guild, elect and appoint a good and capable notary, a Florentine citizen <note>original: "fiorentinum"</note>, and a true Guelph <note>note: The Guelphs were the political faction supporting the Pope; membership was often a requirement for holding office in Florence</note>, whom they desire as notary and scribe of the said guild for a term of one year, with the office, authority, salary, and gifts described below.*

*b.* And at the said election, there shall be present the said consuls or the majority of them, the aforementioned councilors or the majority of them, and the twenty-four additions. And the election of the said notary shall be obtained by the majority of those consuls, councilors, and additions present there, by a secret ballot <note>original: "secreto scruptineo"</note> to be held among the consuls, councilors, and additions together.

And also each and every person condemned and who shall be condemned by the consuls of this guild, and the amounts of each person condemned and who shall be condemned, and the payment made or that shall be made by such condemned persons.

If the syndics <term>sindichi: officials appointed to audit and investigate the conduct of other officers</term> of this guild shall find any former official of the said guild to have committed a misdeed in any way during his office, let them condemn him according to the form of the statute; and if the statute does not speak to it, and if the penalty was not determined by the constitutions, let them condemn said delinquent according to the crime, and the quality and status of the person.

c. *And they shall stay and reside, and must stay and reside, at the house of the said guild every day that the notary of the said guild is present there;* and whoever does not do these things shall not receive a salary from the aforesaid guild or from the chamberlain <note>original: "camarlingho"; the guild's treasurer or financial officer</note> of the said guild.

d. e. *And the chamberlain of the said guild is bound to withhold from the salary of these messengers, and each of them, for every day they do not remain at the said guild to exercise their office and write for the aforesaid guild* and their office, five shillings in small florins; this is under penalty of ten shillings to be taken from such chamberlain by the notary of the said guild for the benefit of the guild. *The said notary is bound, under the same penalty to be taken by the chamberlain, to denounce to the consuls or the chamberlain of the said guild any such delinquent messenger every day and time that he does not remain to exercise the said office of messenger, as stated above.*

f. *And the said messengers shall have for their salary for their office each month* up to the amount of ten pounds in small florins—each of them receiving that portion of the ten pounds which the consuls deem appropriate; and *for every new member <note>original: "novitio"</note> whom they or any one of them shall bring in, twelve pence in small florins for each and every pound of what such new member pays as an entry fee to the guild;* for every formal request, six pence; and for every command and seizure, if it is for three pounds or less, 12 pence; and if it is from three pounds up to 15 pounds, 18 pence; and if it is from 15 pounds upward, two shillings; from then on, whatever the amount may be, the messengers shall not have more than that paid to them.

### XI. Regarding the election and office of the searchers of the guild.

We ordain that the consuls <note>The "consoli" were the highest-ranking elected officials of a medieval guild</note> of the aforesaid guild, at the beginning of their term, are required to elect and nominate as many and whichever "searchers" <note>term: cercatori (inspectors or investigators responsible for policing guild regulations)</note> of the said guild as they wish; these searchers are required and must notify, denounce, and report to the consuls of the said guild currently in office all and each person acting against the form of the statutes of the said guild, and those not observing the orders of the said guild. Regarding the testimony of these searchers and each of them, they shall be believed upon their oath and given full credit, and their identity shall be kept secret. And the notary and the chamberlain <note>term: camarlingho (the treasurer or financial officer of the guild)</note> of the said guild are required to remind the consuls to perform the said election. And if the consuls do not perform the said election, the chamberlain of the said guild may not send any gift or payment to those consuls; and the said searchers shall have, and the chamberlain of the said guild must pay to them, the fourth part of the fine <note>original: "condempnagione"</note> which is levied by reason of such report, referral, denunciation, and notification—that is, to the one who made such report and denunciation.

### XII. That the accuser shall have a portion of the fine.

If anyone accuses or denounces any member or members of this guild for any falsehood, and the consuls are certain of it, he shall receive from the chamberlain of the said guild the fourth part of the fine which is collected from the accused, according to the form of the statutes of this guild; and the identity of the accuser shall always be kept secret, always excepting the statutes and chapters of this guild regarding false saffron <note>term: gruogo falso (saffron was a highly valuable commodity often subject to adulteration or fraud)</note> and the physician judging any person to be severely wounded <note>term: fedito enorme (a legal category for serious physical assault requiring specific reporting)</note>.

### XIV. Concerning the sufficient number for a gathering.

Since in all gatherings made by the guild and the men of said guild, disputes may arise regarding the number of men of said guild who must be present to be sufficient for the assemblies, we therefore establish and ordain by this perpetual law that in each and every gathering or gatherings which shall be held in the future in this guild, sixty men of said guild gathered together shall be understood and considered a perfect and sufficient number. And those sixty present, thus gathered together with the consuls of the said guild, or two-thirds of those in agreement, may—and it shall then be lawful to—ordain, establish, decree, and do everything they wish; and that which is done, established, reformed, or decreed by them or by two-thirds of those present shall be valid and hold as if it were done and ordained by the entire guild and the aforementioned university <note>original: "università," here meaning the legal corporation or collective body of the guild</note> (1).

# STATUTE OF 1349 II, XVII-XVIIII

### XVIII. Regarding the annual registration of partners.

So that no dispute may arise among the craftsmen and merchants of the said guild, we ordain that every year in the months of January (2) and February, the consuls <note>the elected heads of the guild</note> of the said guild currently in office shall be required to command, through the messengers of the said guild, all the shopkeepers of the said guild—that is, one of the masters of every warehouse or shop—to bring in writing to the notary of the said guild, throughout the said months of January and February, each and every master and his partners in his shop and party, in whatever manner they may be in his warehouse or shop, whether enrolled or not enrolled in the register <term>matricola: the official membership roll of a guild</term> of the said guild. And they are required to have the aforesaid registration made under solemn oath, upon penalty of 10 pounds in small florins <note>original: "lire .x. di f. p." referring to the 'fiorini piccioli', the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note> for every person who is not reported to the aforementioned notary within the said term. The said consuls are bound by their oath of office to condemn to this fine every master of any warehouse or shop of the said guild who does not perform the said registration; and they must collect or cause such fines to be collected within one month. And they shall seek the truth of the aforesaid matters and proceed both openly and secretly, as it shall seem fit to the said consuls. And the notary of the said guild shall be required to make a book every year and write those registered into such a book. And no one of the said guild who has not been registered may or should hold any office or benefit in the aforesaid guild for that entire year.

### XXI. *That no gathering of apprentices may be held at night.*

# XXII. Regarding the commission of theft of items belonging to the said guild.

*a.* No master, apprentice <note>original: "discepoli"</note>, or laborer of the said guilds or any one of them shall dare or presume to commit theft of the merchandise, items, and goods belonging to the said guilds or any one of them, or of any other goods or items.

### XXIII. *That each and every person practicing the said Guild shall swear an oath to the aforementioned Guild, and be subject to the Consuls of the said Guild.*

a. *[That those disobedient to the consuls shall be fined 40 soldi].* <note>Original Latin: Quod inobedientes consulibus condempnentur in soldis .XL.</note> Each and every doctor, both physicians <note>practitioners of internal medicine</note> and surgeons, and each and every apothecary and mercer <note>merchants of small goods and textiles</note> of the city and territory of Florence shall be bound and must swear an oath to the aforementioned Guild and be subject to the Consuls <note>elected leaders</note> of the said Guild, and obey all their commands and sentences. (fiorini piccioli)</term>: the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions, distinct from the gold florin</note>, by the Consuls of the said Guild, for each instance.

b. *[Consuls shall demand old fines].* <note>Original Latin: Consules exigant condempnationes veteres</note> And if the said Consuls do not issue the fine, the successors of those Consuls shall be bound to issue the fine to such a disobedient person; and nonetheless, they are bound to collect, and see to the collection of, old fines <margin>The Consuls are required to collect and ensure the collection of debts <note>original: exigere et exigi facere teneantur</note></margin>.

c. *[One summoned simply who does not appear shall be fined 5 soldi].* <note>Original Latin: Requisitus simpliciter et non comparens condempnetur in soldis .v.</note> And regarding a simple summons, which the said Consuls shall have made for someone to appear before them, if they do not appear within the required term, they shall be fined five soldi of small florins; under penalty of double the said amount, they shall be fined by each of the said Consuls. And the said penalty of five soldi is not intended for the Councilors of the said Guild, but against them the statute placed under the rubric of the election of councilors shall apply.

d. *[He who does not permit himself to be distrained shall be fined 40 soldi. Quod si consules non fecerint, condempnentur per sindicos in duplum</note> And whoever shall have such audacity <note>original: aldacia, a variant of audacia</note> that they do not allow themselves to be distrained <note><term>pignorare</term>: the legal seizure of goods to satisfy a debt or fine</note> for whatever reason they ought to have been distrained by the messengers of the Guilds, the Consuls <insert>or messengers</insert> of the said Guild shall fine them forty soldi of small florins. Which fine, if they do not issue it, the syndics <note>officials who audited the guild's accounts</note> or indeed the new Consuls are bound to fine them double those 40 soldi, and as many times as it occurs. And the simple report of the said messenger shall be believed against those who do not allow themselves to be distrained.

II, XXIII-XXV          STATUTE OF 1349

according to the form of the statutes and ordinances of the said <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" (Arte) refers to the professional Guild, likely the Physicians and Apothecaries given the spices mentioned later.</note>; and to collect and cause to be collected the fines from those who do not obey and do not swear [the oath] as has been said.

## XXIV. That everyone is required to send for the recording of what they have paid or are due to receive.

a. We ordain that whatever craftsman of the said Guild, whether from the city or from the <term>contado</term> <note>The rural territory surrounding the city</note> of Florence and its district, shall sell anything to anyone on <term>credit</term> <note>original: "credenza"</note>, he is required to send to have written in the book of debts that which he should receive or have for such merchandise. And likewise, every debtor who pays or sends to any creditor of his any quantity of money is required to send to see written in the book of debts the quantity paid, provided that the quantity which he pays or is due to receive exceeds the sum of ten <term>small florins</term> <note>original: "lire dieci di f. p." (fiorini piccioli), the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note>, or from there upwards. And to the aforesaid things, they and each of them are bound by their own oath.

b. Ordaining that the things contained in the present statute do not prejudice, nor can or should prejudice, the creditors or their credits, and do not prejudice nor can prejudice any person or persons who had paid what they ought to pay. And the messengers of the Guild shall announce the aforesaid things in the month of January to the craftsmen of the said Guild.

## XXV. Of the scales <margin>Codex B: *of cases and scales* etc.</margin> and other weights that must be kept.

a. The Consuls of the said Guild are required to act and ensure that in and for the said Guild there is kept one pair of <term>large scales</term> <note>original: "cazere" or "cazze," likely heavy-duty balances for bulk goods</note> for weighing up to fifty pounds, with which the things and merchandise of the said Guild may be weighed for anyone who wishes to have them weighed, so that every error from diverse steelyards and balances may be eliminated. Which <gloss>scales</gloss> <note>original: "zace," a scribal variant of "cazze"</note> the <term>Chamberlain</term> <note>The treasurer or financial officer of the Guild</note> of this Guild is required to have and keep. And that the Consuls are bound by their own oath to have made in the month of January a pair of large scales with iron weights, with which all men of this Guild are required to weigh when buying and selling from fifty pounds and downwards, if the buyer wishes; and to keep these scales in a common place for weighing.

b. The Consuls and the Chamberlain shall also ensure, under penalty of their salary, that the said Guild has one pair of fine scales for weighing cloves, mace, cubebs <note>A type of pepper used in medicine and cooking</note>, and all other fine things, for which one pays to the Chamber—

# STATUTE OF 1349 II, XXV

*...chamberlain of the said guild for the said guild, from everyone who shall sell and have weighed with them, in this manner, namely: (1) for every ten <note>original: "dicina"</note> of fine goods, one penny; and for every hundred of goods which are worth fifty pounds and are weighed with the large scales <note>original: "zace grosse"</note>, three pennies in small florins; and for every other merchandise, of which the hundred is worth from fifty pounds downwards, two pennies per hundred. And these pennies shall be paid only by the seller. Which merchandise the buyer, at his own expense, is required to send to the place where the said scales shall be kept by the said guild, and from that place send them to the shop of the buyer; and with the said scales, he is required at the request of the buyer to weigh all the merchandise.*

*c. Let the consuls also take care to have in the month of January a double set of twelve weights <note>original: "dodicina"</note> directly adjusted (a) to the weight of the commune of Florence with (b) a pair of scales, which shall belong to the community of the guild; to which twelve weights and scales all weights and equipment of the said guild shall be adjusted, both of the twelve and of the marks <note>original: "marci" - a unit of weight for precious metals</note>. And let them have a chest in which they put all the weights of the said guild, and let them be kept by the person whom the said consuls shall ordain, and let them be delivered to the new consuls and to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the financial officer or treasurer of the guild</term> at the beginning of their office.*

*d. Furthermore, the consuls of this guild are required at the beginning of their office to have for the said guild a pair of scales to weigh crocus or rather saffron (c), with which scales all and every man of this guild and every other person holding or selling saffron is required to weigh when the saffron bought or sold shall be from two pounds upwards to fifty pounds, under the penalty of ten pounds in small florins, to be taken from every seller and buyer.*

*e. And the sellers are required to give for every pound of saffron sold to the said merchant holding the scales for the said guild four pennies in small florins. Which pennies the said merchant shall faithfully collect and give to the chamberlain of the said guild.*

*f. And no broker <note>original: "sensale"</note> may, dare, or presume to make any trade of any quantity of saffron from two pounds upwards, if it is not weighed with the aforesaid scales, under the penalty of ten pounds in small florins for every trade. And such broker, making that trade, shall be punished by prohibition <note>original: "divieto" - a legal ban from practicing one's profession for a set period</note> (2). And the aforesaid things shall take place for all saffron, both foreign and local.*

## II, XXV, XXVI STATUTE OF 1349

g. *And no one of this guild may buy from any foreigner <note>original: "forestieri," meaning someone from outside the city-state of Florence</note>, or from a man outside of this guild, or from within this guild, any quantity of saffron, unless it is weighed with the said scales and the payment is made as previously stated; and the same applies to selling, under the said penalty.*

h. *Furthermore, the said consuls <note>the elected leaders of the guild</note> are required to have two sieves for the said guild: one for sifting pepper, ginger, and incense, and the other for indigo. The chamberlain <note>term: camarlìngho; the guild's financial officer or treasurer</note> is required to lend these sieves to anyone who asks for them to sift the aforementioned items. And they cannot be exempt from this duty, nor have a deadline beyond the month of February, under penalty of their salary. And let no one of the said guild dare to keep the guild's sieves or scales during the night, under penalty of one hundred soldi in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli</note>.*

i. *It is also declared that whoever wishes to have items weighed with the steelyard scales <note>term: stadera; a portable balance with unequal arms</note> of the Commune of Florence may do so, and it shall be lawful for him. And whoever does not weigh with the steelyard of the Commune of Florence is bound to the observance of all the aforementioned things and to the said penalty.*

l. *Declaring also and ordaining that the lord consuls of the said guild who are in office—once the present statutes are approved by the Commune of Florence—shall sell to the brokers <note>term: sensali; middle-men who facilitated trades</note> of the said guild and to other men wishing to buy, the revenue and proceeds from the guild's scales for such price or prices, and for such time and term, as shall seem fit and pleasing to them and the majority of them, though not for a time longer than one year. And they are required to do the aforementioned things under penalty of ten pounds in small florins for each consul.*

m. [<insert>Brokers must be compelled to buy the proceeds of the scales</insert> <note>original Latin: "Sensales debent cogi ad emendum proventus bilanciarum"</note>]. *And since it is said that because of the brokers of this guild, the said guild receives great damage regarding the payments for weighing which are and should be done with the said scales; to avoid all malice, the aforementioned consuls in office can, are required to, and must—under penalty of losing their gift <note>likely their official stipend or bonus</note>—compel the brokers of this guild, legally and personally and by every way and means that pleases them most, including by fine and deprivation of guild membership, to buy the revenue and proceeds of the said scales for such time, term, price, and rent as shall seem fit to them. Provided that no sale of the said revenues and proceeds of the scales can be made for a time and term longer than one year, as is said above.*

### XXVI. That whoever sells by weight must pay for the weighing.

a. *We ordain that whoever sells by weight any item of this guild is required to and must pay for the weighing, if it is of a weight of fifty pounds...*

# STATUTE OF 1349 II, XXVI, XXVII

or from that amount upwards, *the buyer must have the sold items carried at his own expense.*

b. *And everyone of this guild who buys or sells any item or merchandise shall be bound and must have the weight of the sold merchandise and the price of the merchandise written down by the weigher of the Commune of Florence.* <note>The 'Commune' refers to the city government of Florence; using an official weigher ensured tax compliance and prevented fraud.</note>

c. *And if any broker intervenes, such broker shall be bound to write in his book the weight, the price, and the payment deadline, under penalty of 20 silver shillings <note>original: "soldi .xx. di f. p." referring to Florentine piccoli, the local silver currency</note>, for each instance.*

d. *And if such a sale should be in doubt, and there is a dispute over the item, price, weight, or payment deadline, the records of the buyers and sellers shall be relied upon, if they have written it down and agree on such writing; otherwise, the records of the broker shall be relied upon and given faith* (1).

## XXVII. How the seller is bound to sieve the pepper.

a. *If anyone of this guild buys pepper, ginger, or incense, or any other items or merchandise belonging to the aforesaid guild, from any person of this guild or from outside the guild and not subject to the said guild, if the buyer so pleases—even if no prior agreement was made—the seller is bound to sieve and provide the sieve to the buyer; and to fulfill the first weight, if it is from six pounds upwards. And if he does not do so, and it is denounced to the consuls <note>The 'consuls' were the elected leaders of the guild who acted as judges in trade disputes</note>, these consuls shall be bound to take from that seller a penalty of ten silver shillings, for each instance; and nonetheless sieve such item or merchandise; and if the buyer has carried the purchased item to his shop, the seller after said transport shall not be bound to sieve, unless the buyer has requested that it be sieved within the same day that he bought it and had it carried to his shop.*

b. *And everyone who sells indigo <note>original: "indico"</note>, incense, gum arabic, or mastic, whether citizen or foreigner, shall be bound to have it sieved at the will of the buyer with the sieves of the guild, under penalty of forty silver shillings for every bag weighing two hundred pounds. And this statute shall apply against all sellers, both within the guild and outside the guild.*

c. *It is ordained that such dust or siftings, which are extracted from such merchandise, may not be sold, bought, or kept by anyone, nor may any broker make a trade of such dust or siftings, under penalty of one hundred silver shillings for anyone who keeps, buys, or sells it, and for the broker who makes the trade. But such dust and siftings must, within three days from the day of such sieving...*

II, XXVII-XXVIIII &emsp;&emsp;&emsp; STATUTE OF 1349

[The sellers and buyers] must come within that time and term to present and assign [the goods] to the consuls <note>The elected leaders of the Guild</note> of the said Guild. And the consuls in office at that time shall ensure that such dust or siftings <note>Waste material or low-quality residue from spices or chemicals</note> are sold outside the city, territory, and district of Florence. And no broker <term>sensale: a middleman who negotiated sales for a commission</term> shall dare or presume to make any trade of such dust or siftings, under penalty of 40 shillings in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli, the local silver-based currency</note>, to be taken from said broker as many times as the offense occurs.

### XXVIII. *Regarding the acceptance of the sack as merchandise, if there is a dispute over the sack.*

*a. If anyone buys any merchandise pertaining to the Guild, they shall be required to accept the sack as part of the merchandise <note>meaning the weight of the sack is included in the sale price rather than deducted</note>, if a dispute over the sack arises between the buyer and seller; that is, for every merchandise where a hundredweight <term>cantare: a unit of weight, roughly 100-150 lbs depending on the region</term> is worth 10 pounds in small florins or less.*

*b. And such merchandise is understood to be alum, madder <note>a red dye plant</note>, cumin, grapes, mustard, anise, fennel, broom, hemp, and any other merchandise where the hundredweight is worth from 10 pounds downwards. And "merchandise" shall be understood as those things in sacks—specifically, in a single sack bound with rope or grass-cord. And for items in barrels or jars, a tare <note>a deduction for the weight of the empty container</note> must be made: for every barrel of honey, 10 pounds per load; and for honey in jars and pitchers, for a pitcher or jar weighing 100 pounds or up to 130 pounds or less, a tare of 20 pounds; and for those weighing from 130 to 200 pounds, a tare of 25 pounds shall be made. For a bag of saffron weighing 25 pounds or more, the seller must give the bag to the buyer without any charge. All other merchandise not mentioned above shall remain at the discretion of the consuls of this Guild. But if crocus <note>original: "gruogo," another term for saffron</note> or saffron is sold in quantities of 10 pounds or more, the seller is required to give the sack, if it is in a sack, without any charge.*

*c. And no one of this Guild shall dare to mix Catalan saffron with local or Marcher <note>from the Marche region of Italy</note> saffron; but he is required to show and provide Catalan as Catalan, local as local, and Marcher as Marcher, under penalty of 20 shillings in small florins for every pound of mixed saffron, to be taken from every carrier, seller, or anyone found [with it], as many times as it is discovered.*

### XXVIIII. *That there is not, nor should there be, any prohibition in the city of Florence regarding the underwritten things.*

*a. To avoid all fraud and malice which is often committed by some, especially by the officials in charge of prohibitions for the Wool Guild <note>The powerful Arte della Lana</note>, so that the merchants of this Guild may more freely practice their trade and provide for their earnings, it is decreed and ordained that there shall not be...*

## XXXII. Regarding not electing anyone who commits falsehood.

a. Whoever of this craft shall be found or discovered in any falsehood regarding any matter of this craft, may not forever be called or elected to any office or benefit, namely as rector, chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the guild's financial officer or treasurer</term>, arbiter, or councilors. And whoever shall be condemned for falsehood, the falsehood, the condemnation, and his prohibition shall be recorded for memory. And if he should be elected, it shall not be valid; and being elected, he shall not dare to accept said office, under penalty of one hundred shillings <note>soldi</note> for each time, and deprivation of such office. And that the notary be required to read all those prohibited at the time of the election of the consuls <term>consoli: the highest-ranking elected leaders of the guild</term>.

## XXXIII. Regarding giving aid to the artisans of the said craft.

a. The consuls, who shall be in office for the time, are bound and must give to the consuls, councilors, and the other officials of the said craft, and to all others to whom injury was moved or done by reason of their office or for any other reason—whether they be an official of the said craft or not—the counsel of the adjuncts <note>additional advisors or assistants</note>, in the below-written manner, namely: that if against anyone <margin>B: to whom</margin> of the said craft any cause or question shall be moved, the consuls who shall be in office for the time shall have their councilors and those of the said craft investigate whether such artisan has been legally injured or not. And if he shall be injured illegally, then the said consuls and councilors shall elect one good, expert judge, an advocate of the College of Florence, and one good, expert procurator <note>a legal representative or agent</note>, a true Guelph <note>The Guelphs were a political faction supporting the Pope; this requirement ensures political loyalty to the Florentine establishment</note>, at the expense of the said craft, at the will of the consuls, councilors, and the majority of them. These men must help such artisan until the end of the case. All of which things the said consuls are bound to do, if they are requested, under penalty of 10 pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." for fiorini piccioli</note>.

## XXXIIII. How the gold florin must be counted in payments.

a. We ordain that no one of this craft may, dare, or presume to count in any payment made to him for any thing or things of this craft, the florin at more than four pence <note>denari</note> more than what the money-changer <note>cambiatore</note>, at the time such payment is made, would want for his gold florin.

### XXXVIII. That the rural residents be enrolled separately from the citizens.

It is decreed and ordained that the rural residents <note>original: "contadini"; those living in the countryside (contado) outside the city walls</note> who are enrolled or shall be enrolled must be placed and recorded in the book in which the citizens are placed, following the main matriculation book with the prologue; and that the notary of the said guild is held and required to describe and place them in the book and register of the said guild, as stated above.

### XXXX. Those who may join this guild through the benefit of the guild.

It is decreed and ordained that the father for the son, and the son for the father, may join this guild without paying anything to the aforesaid guild <note>This refers to the "benefit of the guild," a hereditary right allowing direct male descendants to join for free</note>. And the biological brothers of the father shall be held and required to pay half (1) of what would have been paid according to the form of this guild statute. The daughter of a guild member may also join this guild through the benefit of her father, likewise paying nothing to the aforesaid guild; however, this daughter shall not pass any benefit to her own sons, even though she has been enrolled in the register of the aforesaid guild.

# II, 41-43 STATUTE OF 1349

## 42. Regarding not calling anyone who is buying at any shop.

<margin>*</margin>No one of the said guild may, dare, or presume to call or have someone call anyone who is in the process of buying any merchandise or things at any shop, to come to his own shop or to leave that shop. Whoever acts against this shall be condemned by the consuls <term>consoli: the elected leaders of the guild</term> to a fine of 40 shillings in small florins <term>f. p. (fiorini piccioli): the silver-based currency used for daily transactions in Florence</term>, for each occurrence.

## 43. *Regarding the payments that must be made to brokers for brokerage of the below-written things.*

a. In the month of January of every year, the consuls of this guild, with their council and that of the said guild, are bound and must, by secret scrutiny <note>a secret ballot or vote</note>, approve those who are and ought to be brokers <term>sensali: licensed middlemen who facilitated trade</term> and intermediaries <note>original: "prosoneti" - from the Greek 'proxenetes'</note> of the said guild, or rather those who exercise the craft or office of brokerage for the aforesaid guild. And those who shall be approved in the aforesaid scrutiny by the said consuls and councilors of the said guild, or by the majority of them, are bound and must swear an oath every year in the said month of January <insert>1</insert>. And the said consuls are bound and must act and ensure that the brokers thus approved in the said month swear upon the Holy Gospels of God to perform their craft of brokerage in good faith and without fraud, and that they give and provide suitable guarantors <insert>2</insert> to the said consuls or to the notary of the said guild receiving on behalf of the said guild <insert>3</insert>, to observe all the statutes of the said guild and especially the statute of the brokers <insert>4</insert>. And if anyone shall swear but will not provide security, he shall be expelled from the brokerage <insert>5</insert>. And it is commanded to everyone of the said guild that they shall make no market or trade with the said broker who is unwilling to swear, under the penalty of 40 shillings in small florins, for each occurrence, to be taken from whoever acts against this <insert>6</insert>.

d. e. And let no broker make or dare to make any claim of any right in the trades he has conducted.

f. g. ### 45. Regarding the prohibition of bringing false saffron into the city of Florence.

*a. All and every member of this guild, both masters and apprentices, are bound not to buy or cause to be bought within or without the city of Florence or elsewhere, nor to sell, nor cause to be brought to said city or its district, false or counterfeit saffron <note>original: "gruogo," an archaic Tuscan term for saffron (crocus)</note> (1). The consuls of this guild are bound to fine the possessor of said false saffron one hundred pounds in small florins; and they must seize said saffron and have it publicly burned in the New Market <note>The Mercato Nuovo, the commercial hub of medieval Florence</note>. Except that if false saffron is found in a small quantity in the possession of any grocer <note>original: "pizichaiuolo"</note> or other person of small means, and they testify that they bought it as such from others, the consuls are bound to fine them forty shillings in small florins; which fine they are bound to issue with the counsel of this guild.*

*b. And let no one of this guild dare to keep Catalan saffron mixed with our local saffron, but each member of said guild is bound to tell the buyer—if the buyer asks about the saffron—which is Catalan saffron and which is local. And local saffron shall be understood as saffron from the Marches and Tuscany.*

*c. And let no one of this guild presume to keep in any way or for any reason in their shop any saffron powder made by force <note>likely referring to ground saffron adulterated or crushed to hide impurities</note>, under penalty of ten pounds in small florins, and as many times as it is found, they shall have the powder burned before the men of this guild. And the one holding the aforementioned powder for sale may never again be called to any office or benefit.*

*d. And let no citizen, peasant, or foreigner dare or presume within the city, countryside, or district of Florence, or even elsewhere, to bring, sell, trade, gather, have, or keep "femminelle" <note>the yellow floral parts or styles of the crocus which lack the flavor and color of the red stigmas; used as an adulterant</note> of saffron, under penalty of twenty-five pounds in small florins for every person who violates this, and for every time, or more or less as it shall seem fit to the consuls presiding over the guild at that time, having respect for the quantity of such "femminelle."*

And if these consuls do not do so, the chamberlain of the said guild may, is bound to, and must carry out the said condemnation, under the penalty of 25 pounds of small florins. ### 47. On punishing those who do not work good, pure, and loyal wax, and how torches and candles must be made.

## 48. That the consuls are bound to condemn anyone who commits falsehood.

It is decreed and ordained that whoever, whether subject or not subject to the said craft, shall commit any falsehood <note>original: "falsità"; likely referring to fraud, forgery, or adulteration of goods</note> within the aforementioned craft or concerning the matters of the said craft, the aforementioned consuls are bound and must have condemned or acquitted whoever committed such falsehood within the next month following the day of the notification or denunciation made to them, under penalty of 40 shillings in small florins <term>f. p.: "fiorini piccioli," the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</term> for each consul. And nonetheless, they remain bound to carry out such condemnation or acquittal. And whoever is condemned for any falsehood may not be elected to any office of the aforementioned craft.

## 49. *On punishing those who keep unsifted pepper and spices made against the form written below.*

*a. No one of this craft shall dare or presume to keep pepper in his shop if it has not been sifted <note>original: "crivellato"; passed through a sieve to remove impurities</note>, under penalty of 10 pounds in small florins if the pepper weighs 25 pounds or more; and if it is less, 100 shillings in small florins.*

*b. Furthermore, no craftsman of this craft shall dare or presume to keep in his shop or at home spices, unless they are made of pepper and saffron <note>original: "gruogo"; an archaic term for saffron</note> and of more valuable things, under penalty of 40 shillings. And the consuls of the said craft are bound to search for the aforementioned things once every month.*

*c. And that no wholesale merchant or any other person shall sell, or cause to be sold, ground pepper in his shop; nor shall any of the aforementioned or others keep ground ginger or cinnamon in his shop unless it is well sifted and clean of dust and sand. And as has been said of ginger, the same shall be understood for nutmeg, mace <note>original: "folio"; referring to the outer covering of the nutmeg seed</note>, and every kind of spice.*

# II, L, LI STATUTE OF 1349

## LI. On punishing those who make images cast in a mold.

*a. We command that no one of this guild shall dare or presume to make or have made any image cast in a mold, but must make them only with their own hands, without any casting in a mold. And this is understood to apply to figures of men or women, or of any animal or things, in which men and persons offer vows in diverse and various ways. And these are to be sold for a fair price.* <note>This regulation ensures the quality of "ex-voto" offerings—devotional objects left at shrines—by requiring they be handmade rather than mass-produced by molds.</note>

*b. And everyone selling or wishing to sell an image shall be required to seal it with his own seal <margin>(1) Thus in the text.</margin>, and give a copy of the seal to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the financial officer or treasurer of the guild</term> of the said guild. Which chamberlain is required and must see that such a copy of such a seal is given to him.*

*c. Except that whoever should make a vow <margin>(2) Corrected from "votasse".</margin> to place in any location any ship, galley, house, castle, or any building that could not be made without wood, that he who has made it or has had it made, may put wood into it, having first obtained permission from the consuls of this guild or from the majority of them. Once this permission is obtained, he is required to weigh said building in the presence of the chamberlain of this guild. Which chamberlain and seller of said building are required and must record the weight, so that it can always be found; so that, if it is necessary to find said weight, that is, the building of such in-*
<meta>Text continues elsewhere; catchword "in-"</meta>

---

<note>original: "ciis, rotellis, bracciaiuolis..."</note> ...shields, bucklers, arm-guards, or other armor pertaining to the said guilds, without the license of the said consuls, under penalty of ten pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." for fiorini piccioli</note>, for each person acting against this and for each instance.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*e.* And also that no craftsman of the aforesaid guild, nor anyone working in them or any apprentice, shall dare or presume to arm or reinforce any work belonging to the said guild of shield-makers <term>tabulacciorum: makers of large wooden shields called 'tavolacci'</term>, unless he himself has made or sold such a piece, or unless he has permission from the one who made the piece, under penalty of ten shillings of small florins, for each person acting against this,

### LIII. *On punishing whoever shall take any shop away from another.*

a. No one of this guild shall dare or presume *by himself or through others to take or lease any shop already rented to someone of this guild, or to stay in it within the period of five years from the day that the previous tenant left it and moved out.* <note>This was a "non-compete" style protection to prevent members from outbidding each other or stealing locations</note>

b. And if anyone of the said guild *acts to the contrary, unless license and consent were first given to him by the said first tenant through a public instrument written by the hand of a public notary, he shall be forced by the consuls to vacate such a shop.* And nonetheless, he shall be fined by the consuls of the said guild one hundred pounds in small florins. And if the consuls find that anyone has consented or given permission or renounced the shop through force or fear, notwithstanding such consent or renunciation, even if a public instrument was made thereof, they shall cause the shop to be restored to the first tenant, and nonetheless condemn whoever took such a shop to a fine of one hundred pounds in small florins.

c. And no one of the said guild *shall dare or presume by himself or through others to take or lease any shop that was burned during the time that fire was set in the city of Florence, or since, whenever and for whatever reason they were burned, destroyed, or ruined and then rebuilt or not yet rebuilt, within the time mentioned above, to be calculated from the day of the rebuilding of such a shop, unless it is with the permission of the person who held that shop before it was set on fire, destroyed, or ruined, or from his sons, given to him by public instrument as in the point above, under the said penalty.* <note>This refers to the civil unrest and fires in Florence during the mid-14th century; the law protected the rights of original shopkeepers even if their place of business had been physically destroyed</note> And if a dispute should arise regarding this section or point, the consuls in office at the time, or two-thirds of them, with their advisors, or two-thirds of said advisors, may hear, proceed, and terminate the aforementioned matters briefly, summarily, and according to equity, as shall seem appropriate to them, considering the nature of the facts.

d. And that no one of the said guild shall dare or presume to lease or cause to be leased any warehouse or shop, by whatever means leased,
