# STATUTE OF 1349 — II, LVI
179

### *LVI. Regarding electuaries and syrups.*

*a. All and every person of this guild making or causing to be made <term>penidie</term> <note>A type of pulled sugar stick used as a cough remedy</note> are bound to make them using a <term>stamigna</term> <note>A fine wool strainer or sieve</note> or cloth to strain them, in good faith and without fraud. Against whoever should violate this, the consuls are bound to take a fine in the amount of 10 pounds of small florins, for each occurrence. And they must cause to be made <term>electuaries</term> <note>Medicinal pastes made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> that are made according to the <term>antidotary</term> <note>A formal dispensatory or book of medicinal recipes</note> of syrups, and those of honey with honey, in good faith and without <note>original: "sensa"</note> fraud, unless it is the will of the buyer or the physician. Nevertheless, it shall be permitted for anyone to make electuaries, which are usually made with honey, using sugar instead; but one must not sell medicine made with honey as a medicament made with sugar.*

*b. And all apothecaries, both masters and apprentices, are bound to make syrups and all electuaries and medicines well, loyally, and uprightly, especially those made with sugar, which should be made with good powder of Cyprus or powder of Babylon <note>Refers to high-quality imported sugars or spices</note>, with the knowledge of the physician, under the penalty of 40 shillings of small florins.*

*c. And no shopkeeper having a physician shall work red powder of Alexandria into any antidotary recipe, under the said penalty for each occurrence. And they may work and use the said powder of Alexandria in confections belonging to banquets or those presented to any foreigners, provided that this powder is not used in any medicinal antidotary without the knowledge of the physician, under the said penalty.*

*d. And the consuls are bound to command all apothecaries, both masters and apprentices, and furthermore to make all and every master who makes medicinal things swear that they shall make them well and loyally, according to what is contained in the said chapter, under the penalty of 40 shillings of small florins for each of the said consuls.*

# II, 57-59 STATUTE OF 1349

### 57. *On punishing the chamberlain who has profited in any way against the honor of the guild.*

It is ordained that the consuls <note>the elected leaders of the guild</note> are bound to secretly investigate and discover if the <term>chamberlain</term> <note>the guild's treasurer or financial officer</note> of the guild has gained anything against the honor of the aforesaid guild from any person; and if they find him to have acted against this or to have committed any fraud, they shall condemn him to ten pence of <term>Florentine small currency</term> <note>original: f. p. or "fiorini piccioli," the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note> for every penny defrauded, for each instance.

### 58. *On punishing those who buy back the clothes of the dead and offer items for any dead body (1).*

*a.* No one of this guild shall dare or presume to offer, or cause to be offered to any person, <term>staminas</term> <note>a lightweight wool cloth often used for shrouds or sieves</note>, torches, benches, coverlets, or any other items belonging to this guild <note>referring to the rental of funeral equipment</note>. And no one shall dare or presume to buy back the clothes of the dead from <term>gravediggers</term> <note>original: becchamorti</note> or priests or from any other person. And those acting to the contrary shall be punished in the amount of five pounds of <term>Florentine small currency</term>, for each instance. And regarding the aforesaid matters, anyone may be an accuser, and shall receive half of the <term>fine</term> <note>original: bando</note>, and his identity shall be kept in confidence. And these rules are understood to apply also against those who might offer any items for weddings or banquets. And in the aforesaid matters and each of them, the testimony of two witnesses proving public reputation shall suffice. And in the aforesaid matters, the consuls may also proceed and condemn as they wish, with or without proof. The conscience of the consuls alone shall be held as full proof. And to better investigate the aforesaid matters, the consuls may appoint searchers as they see fit.

*b.* And no <term>apothecary</term> <note>original: spetiale; a pharmacist who also dealt in spices, pigments, and waxes</note> or his apprentice may, dare, or presume to dress any dead person or carry items for a dead body, under the said penalty, for each instance.

### 59. *On punishing the apothecaries who give any laxative medicine to anyone.*

No <term>apothecary</term> or <term>stationer</term> <note>original: stazzonieri; often a shopkeeper or a specific type of apothecary</note> must give to anyone any <term>laxative medicine</term> <note>original: medicina solutiva</note> without the advice of a doctor, or provide medical treatment in any way or for any reason, under the penalty of ten pounds of <term>Florentine small currency</term>, for each instance. And for each of the aforesaid matters, anyone may be an accuser, and shall receive half of the fine, and his identity shall be kept in confidence.

---

### LX. *On punishing those who corrupt another's apprentice.*

If anyone shall entice away or corrupt the apprentice <note>The term "discepolo" refers to a young trainee bound by contract to a master craftsman</note> of any member of this guild, who was staying with him during the time of his contract, let him be punished in the amount of 10 pounds of small florins <note>original: "lire .x. di f. p." – the *fiorino picciolo* was the silver-based currency used for daily transactions in Florence</note>. And no one of this guild shall dare or presume to receive, retain, or harbor any apprentice of any master of this guild, nor give or lend to such an apprentice anything to work on or for the purpose of working, or any earnings, if he has not first completed the term with his master with whom he was first placed; nor even for six months following that completion, without the license of such first master, and unless he has first paid to said first master whatever it appears that such apprentice owes or ought to give to his first master. And in every case, before he receives and keeps him, he must have and ought to have license from the first master to take and retain him, under the penalty of 50 pounds of small florins for each person, in every case and as many times as it occurs, or more or less, at the discretion of the Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> presiding at the time. And regarding the aforementioned matters, the simple oath of the master shall be believed and upheld. And the Consuls are bound to condemn such delinquent or violator within eight days after it shall come to their notice.

### LXI. *That no one dare to keep another's apprentice without license.*

No one of this guild may or should keep or hire anyone as an apprentice or factor <note>An agent or business manager</note> for the aforementioned craft, who has been with any craftsman of this guild, unless his first master has first been satisfied and compensated for the time that he was bound to stay with or pay the first master. The violator shall be condemned to 10 pounds as many times as it occurs.

### LXII. *On keeping and teaching apprentices.*

Every master of the aforementioned crafts and each of them may and shall be permitted to take and keep an apprentice or apprentices to learn <gloss>to prepare <note>original: "parare" – likely a scribal error for "imparare" (to learn)</note></gloss> his craft in such manner, agreements, and salary as shall seem fit to him and as shall be agreed with them; provided that said apprentice is not older than 25 years of age, and they do not take him for a time and term of less than three years, under the penalty of five pounds of small florins for every master who violates this, and nevertheless such apprentice shall be compelled by the Consuls to leave.

b. And that every apprentice, who shall place himself with any master of the said crafts or any one of them, or another on his behalf, shall promise and provide a guarantor for...

### *LXIII. On punishing those who open the letters of others.*

No one of this guild, of whatever condition they may be, shall dare or presume in any way to open any letter sent to another, or to hide any letter sent to another, whether it concerns the guild or not, ***under the penalty of fifty pounds in small florins.***

### LXIIII. On punishing those who give a commission.

No one of this guild <note>The term "arte" refers to the professional guild or corporation</note> may or shall give to any citizen or foreigner any commission <note>original: "diricto"; likely a kickback or illegal fee</note> on any items sold by the men of this guild, under the penalty of 40 shillings in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli," the silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note>, for each occurrence. And the aforementioned rules do not apply to brokers <note>original: "sensali"</note>, to whom brokerage fees may be paid according to the form of the statutes. And the consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> are bound to have the aforementioned things announced to the craftsmen of the said guild, under the penalty of 40 shillings in small florins for each consul.

### LXV. On punishing those who renounce the guild and then practice the craft.

*a. The consuls of this guild are bound and must find and investigate if those who in the past have renounced, or will renounce in the future, this guild, exercise the aforementioned craft in whole or in part after said renunciation. And they are bound to compel all and each of those practicing to swear anew to the aforementioned guild, and to join the said guild again and pay for the entry fee and new mastership <note>original: "magistero"</note> what the craftsmen are bound to pay who come to this guild for entry and new mastership as a master not having a benefit <note>A "benefit" usually refers to reduced fees for sons or brothers of existing members</note>; that is: 4 gold florins if he is a citizen, and if a foreigner 8 gold florins, and if a peasant 2 gold florins, notwithstanding that he might have had any benefit from his father or brother or any other benefit according to the form of the statutes of this guild. Which benefit shall in no way profit anyone renouncing the aforementioned guild, but he shall immediately lose said benefit once such renunciation is made. And nonetheless, they shall fine each person, for each of the aforementioned things, 25 pounds in small florins.*

*b. And the consuls are bound to the aforementioned things under the penalty of 10 pounds in small florins for each of them for every instance, and they must compel such condemned persons to pay to the aforementioned guild all the taxes levied on them in the intervening time—that is, from the day of renunciation to the day of return—and all debts contracted by him or any of his partners up until the said day of renunciation.*

### LXVI. On punishing those who go with anyone making a purchase.

*We ordain that no one of this guild can or should go with or accompany anyone, or be with anyone, who is making a purchase <note>original: "acapto"; likely referring to forestalling or interfering in a wholesale transaction to influence the price</note>, under the penalty of 10 pounds in small florins, to be collected by the consuls.*

### *LXVII. On punishing those who clear the goods of any foreigners.*

No member of this guild shall clear or cause to be cleared any merchandise belonging to any foreigner <note>original: "foretano"; referring to someone from outside the jurisdiction of Florence</note> at any toll or duty owed to the Commune of Florence or to any official of such merchandise. And whoever acts to the contrary, the consuls shall condemn them, by virtue of the oath taken, to ten pounds of small florins <note>original: "lire .x. di f. p."; the 'fiorino picciolo' was the silver-based currency used for daily transactions, distinct from the gold florin</note> for each instance.

### *LXVIII. On punishing those who speak rudely or use injurious words toward the consuls.*

No person shall dare or presume, whether in a legal dispute or outside of one, to speak with rusticity <note>original: "rustichezze"; implying coarse, unrefined, or disrespectful language</note> or use injurious words toward the consuls or the notary of the said guild during their term of office, or toward any one of them, by reason or cause of any case or duty of the consulate or notary office; nor shall they speak any injurious words among themselves in the presence of the consuls or the notary. Furthermore, this applies even after the term of office has ended, regarding matters or causes that proceeded from or depended upon the said office. The violator shall be fined by the consuls of the said guild up to the amount of one hundred shillings, considering the severity of the rudeness and the injurious words. It shall be sufficient evidence in the aforesaid matters if the consuls, chamberlain, or notary, or any one of them, heard the words or declares to have heard them.

### *LXVIIII. On punishing the physician judging any wound, whether enormous or not.*

a. And in giving such a sentence, the surgeon must always request the physician, and the physician the surgeon, under penalty of 50 pounds of small florins.

Except that, if the doctor is able <margin>The original Latin text in manuscript B had "poterit" (will be able); a 16th-century hand corrected it to "dicit" (says).</margin> by public instrument, to be made by a good and loyal notary, to have a fellow doctor according to the form of the aforesaid statutes from the Podestà, judge, or official who has employed or wishes to employ him for these matters, and such Podestà, judge, or official to him such...

### LXXII. That no doctor shall share profits with any apothecary, and vice versa.

*a.* It is decreed and ordained that no doctor, whether a physician <note>a doctor of internal medicine</note> or a surgeon <term>cerusico: a practitioner who performed manual operations and treated external wounds</term>, of whatever status they may be, whether residing at an apothecary's shop or not, shall dare or presume to make a pact with any apothecary regarding any medicines which they might cause such apothecary to sell, nor shall they receive any portion of the payment for such medicines which they caused to be sold.

*b.* And that no apothecary shall dare, publicly or secretly, to give any doctor any portion of the payment for medicines sold by them, which were sold because of said doctor, under penalty of twenty-five Florentine pounds <note>original: "lire .xxv. di f. p."</note> for each person who violates this and for each time; the Consuls in office at the time are bound to condemn the violators to pay this fine to the aforementioned Guild. If they do not issue this condemnation, the syndics <note>auditors</note> appointed by the Guild to audit the former officials are bound and required to fine the Consuls double the said twenty-five pounds. And the aforementioned rules shall be announced by the Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries at the beginning of every month of January, May, and September by the Guild's messengers. Anyone who violates this may be accused or denounced by anyone at all, and the accuser's word shall be held as credible, and they shall receive a fourth of the fine. The chamberlain <note>treasurer</note> of the said Guild is bound to pay that fourth part of the fine to such accuser without any prejudice to them.

### LXXIII. On punishing those who keep in their shops anything not subject to the said guild.

No one of this guild shall dare or presume to keep in his shop any physician, apothecary <note>original: "medico spetiale"</note>, or merchant who is not obedient to the guild and to the consuls <note>The elected leaders and judicial officers of a medieval guild</note> of the said guild, and who has not sworn an oath and enrolled <note>original: "matricolato"; to be entered into the official register or 'matricala'</note> in the aforementioned guild, under penalty of 10 pounds of small Florentine denari <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli"</note> for each person and for every occurrence.

### LXXIIII. That no one may associate with anyone disobedient to the guild.

We ordain that no one of the said guild may, nor shall it be permitted to him, nor shall he dare or presume to associate or trade, or involve himself or have anything to do in any way, for any reason or cause, regarding any merchandise or things, or in any act or business of anyone disobedient to the said guild, under the penalty of one hundred shillings of small Florentine denari, for as many times as it occurs. And regarding the aforementioned and each of the aforementioned things, full faith shall be given and remain upon the word of two witnesses proving public reputation <note>original: "publica fama"; a legal standard based on the general knowledge of the community</note>.

### LXXV. To what the pewterers are bound.

*a.* We ordain that all and each of the pewterers <note>original: "stagnatai"; craftsmen working with tin and lead to create pewter</note>, both masters and apprentices, are bound and must ensure every production of tinned flasks <note>original: "fiaschi stagnati"</note> which they shall cause to be made, be made in the manners written below, namely: that in every work of tin they may put and use half an ounce of lead and no more for every pound of tin. And every pewterer, both master and apprentice, is bound to seal such work with the mark that shall be given by the consuls of the said guild. And such work shall be understood and must be sold as "excellent work" (a), except that works made only of lead must not be sealed as anything other than "excellent."

*b.* And that everyone of the said guild is bound and must perform each of the said works in good faith and without fraud. And these things extend to old works as well as to old and new, both those already made and those that shall be made.

### LXXVIIII. To what the painters are bound.

*a.* Since men defend and entrust their persons and lives under horse armor made of leather or iron, and since weak, vile, and falsely made leather armor is brought and continues to be brought to the city of Florence from outside, under the trust of which men often lose their person and life: it is decreed and ordained that leather horse armor must be made of leather (a) from ox, cow, bull, or buffalo, as is the custom in the aforementioned city of Florence, and not of any other leather, or of other beasts, or of any other beast (b) (1).

*b.* And that no painter or any other person of the aforesaid guild, [or any other person] (2), may dare or presume to keep or have kept in their shops horse armor made contrary to the aforesaid form, within the city of Florence or outside the city of Florence; nor paint them or have them painted; nor repair or have repaired those made contrary to the aforesaid form, under the penalty of five pounds <note>original: "lire"</note> of small florins for every piece of armor and for every instance. And "armor" shall be understood as the headpiece <note>original: "testiera"</note> by itself, the flank-pieces <note>original: "fianchali"</note> by itself, and the breastplates <note>original: "pectorali"</note> by itself (3).

## LXXX. Regarding disputes arising from the painting work of painters.

It is decreed and ordained that if any painter shall paint any hall, chamber, ceiling, or jetty <note>an overhanging upper story of a building</note>, or wall, or any other place, and if there should be a dispute regarding the payment for said painting between the painter and the one who commissioned such work, the consuls <term>Consuls: the elected officials who governed the guild</term> of the said guild can, are bound to, and must elect one or more painters, whomever and as many as they wish; and these painters may decide and terminate such dispute by estimating and declaring what is appropriate for such a painter for such painting. And once their declaration is made, it must be observed and carried out by them. And the consuls or the notary of the said guild, before such a declaration is made by them, shall ensure that from the amount demanded for such painting, 9 denari for every lira <note>a tax of approximately 3.75%</note> be paid to the chamberlain <term>Camarlingho: the guild's treasurer</term> of the guild. And once the declaration is made by the elected painters, the chamberlain of the said guild shall record half of that fee as income for himself and the guild, and give the other half to the said elected painters. And whoever acts to the contrary shall be fined 5 lire in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli, the local silver-based currency</note> by the consuls of the said guild as many times as they offend.

## LXXXI. To what the saddlers are bound.

And nonetheless, such frames made against the aforementioned form, and saddles furnished upon such frames made against the said form, shall be burned.

b. And every saddler, furnishing or making saddles, is bound and must furnish and make such saddles with good workmanship, specifically in the padding, saddle-flaps, and girths. And no saddler shall mix sheepskin with buckskin or cowhide; except that they may mix...

**f.** And no saddler may, dare, or presume to place or have placed his own mark upon the scrap-work or saddle of another, under the penalty of 40 shillings in small florins.

**g.** And no one may, dare, or presume to work or have work done in his shop or elsewhere on any day commanded by the Church to be observed <note>Sundays and Holy Days</note>, without the license of the consuls or the notary of the said guild, under the penalty of 40 shillings in small florins.

## LXXXII. That he who has served as an arbitrator may pay a certain portion of the fine to which he is condemned.

**a.** We ordain that whoever of the said guild shall be nominated or elected—by the consuls, by the parties, or in any other way—as an arbiter or arbitrator in any dispute, and because he has not rendered a judgment <note>original: "lodato," referring to the 'lodo' or formal arbitral award</note> has been fined by the said guild in any amount of money, he may and shall be permitted to pay for this reason to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the guild's treasurer</term> of the said guild, as full payment of such fine, two shillings per pound <note>a 10% settlement of the total fine</note> within ten days from the day such fine was issued. And once these two shillings in small florins are paid, he shall be absolved of such fine and may be cancelled from the record, as if he had paid the fine in its entirety; and nevertheless, he shall be compelled to render judgment on the said dispute.

### LXXXIII. That every year there should be a large book for the acts of the Guild.

### 87. On punishing those who make a false oath.

If anyone before the consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> and their notary or other officials of the said arts—being questioned by them or any one of them in any cause or process which was or had been made before them or by them or any one of them, whether for himself, or against him or any other person whatsoever—shall offer or make a false and untrue oath, they shall be punished and condemned by the said consuls in the sum of 40 shillings in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli, the local silver-based currency</note> for each instance and as many times as it occurs; and nonetheless he shall be compelled to perform whatever true thing he ought to have done before the said oath was made. And regarding these matters, the consuls shall have full discretion to proceed and punish by every way and means that shall seem necessary to them.

### 88. Concerning the condemnations that shall be made and not absolved.

a. It is decreed and ordained that the consuls of this company, who shall be in office for the time, are bound and must punish and condemn all and each of the men and persons of the said arts and companies who shall be found to have acted or committed offenses against the statutes and ordinances of the said arts, and who by virtue of their office, according to the law and the aforementioned statutes and any one of them, ought to and can be condemned. And they shall have these condemnations and each of them written down by the notary of the said company and then in the presence of the counselors of the said arts...

---

(a) *B* <note>Manuscript B</note> adds: Likewise, that no one of the said society, by word or sign, shall call out or cause to be called, or permit anyone to call out to someone wishing to buy or sell merchandise or things pertaining to the said arts or any of them, unless such a person wishing to buy or sell is in front of the shop <note>original: "apoteca"</note> of the one calling or causing/permitting the call; namely, from the middle of the street or square inward toward his own shop. Furthermore, no one, by word

<column-break/>

or deed, shall do or cause to be done or permit any injury to be done to anyone of the said arts or any of them regarding merchandise, things, or labors pertaining to the aforesaid arts; nor shall he go to view any merchandise until another of the said art [already there] has finished viewing it, unless by chance he is called by that first buyer, under penalty of ten shillings to be taken from each offender by the aforementioned consuls as often as it happens (1).

(1) This passage was canceled in 1349 by writing the two syllables of the word *va.... cat* <note>Latin for "it is void," written across the text to nullify it</note> over it.

### LXXXVIIII. Concerning those who are permitted and those who are prohibited from working in the crafts of the said guilds.

a. To provide for the needs of the masters, the women, and the artisans—whosoever they may be—who have need to work for a price and wage in the service of the said guilds, it is decreed and ordained that all and each of the masters <note>original: "maestri"</note> <insert>and of the members of the shield-makers' and belt-makers' guilds and any of them (a)</insert> of the said guilds, who have been in the past and are or shall be masters of these guilds, and their wives, sons, daughters, and mothers—and the wives of such masters when they remain widows and stay with their children in the houses of their husbands—may and shall be permitted to work in the mastery of the said guilds in the city of Florence, its boroughs, and suburbs, without making any payment to the said guild or to any other person, notwithstanding that such a master is not found in the matriculation roll <note>The "matricola" was the official register of guild members; being off the roll usually meant one could not practice the trade.</note> of the said guilds or any of them; provided that they do not perform such work for sale <note>meaning they could work for others for a wage, but not run their own retail shop</note>, nor keep an apprentice, nor teach the said craft to others.

b. And that such masters and widows, as has been said, wishing to work, shall each year in the month of January (or whenever it shall please the Consuls) give a surety bond <note>a financial guarantee of good conduct</note> of one hundred soldi in small florins <note>term: "fiorini piccoli" - the silver-based currency used for daily wages and local trade, as opposed to the gold florin</note> for each of them to the Consuls of the said company, to be recorded by the notary of the said guilds, to work well and loyally, to act, save, and manage in good faith and without fraud, and to obey the commands of the aforesaid Consuls and to observe the feast days, according to the form of the statutes of the said guild. And in the said manner, all artisans and those working for a price and wage may and shall be permitted to work as said, provided they provide the aforesaid surety and pay to the chamberlain <note>term: "camarlingho" - the guild's financial treasurer</note> of the said guilds every year in the month of January two soldi in small florins for each of them; and they shall not perform work for sale, nor keep apprentices or teach the craft, as said, under penalty of 40 soldi for each person who works without having provided the said surety and paid the two soldi.

c. And no master of the said guild may give work to any of the aforesaid persons who will not serve the guild according to the form of the statutes,

### 81. On punishing those who keep poison in their shop.

No one of this guild, citizen or foreigner, may, dare, or presume to keep, sell, or carry or show in any way or for any reason poison in the city, countryside, or district of Florence. And whoever acts to the contrary shall be punished in the amount of *one hundred pounds of small florins* <note>original: "lire cento di f. p." — the 'fiorino picciolo' was the silver-based currency used for daily transactions, distinct from the gold florin</note>, and for as many times [as they offend]; and everyone of this guild is bound to denounce whoever acts to the contrary. And by the consuls <note>the elected leaders of the guild</note>, the delinquent must be denounced to the Lord Podestà <note>the high foreign magistrate of the city</note>, under the penalty of one hundred shillings of small florins for each of them.

---

In the name of God, amen. In the year of His salutary incarnation 1348, second indiction, on the tenth day of the month of September [etc.].
[Lord Donato de' Velluti, judge, on behalf of the Guild of Judges and Notaries] (1).

That whoever is drawn as a consul <note>Consuls were the high-ranking elected officials who governed the guild</note> and has not paid—either himself or his family—the forced loans <term>prestanze: compulsory loans levied by the Florentine state on its citizens</term> for 30 years, his ballot shall be torn up; and that the guild notary is required to keep a record in a book of who pays the loans and bring it to the Merchant Court <note>The Mercantia was the supreme judicial body for all commercial and guild matters in Florence</note> at the time of the drawing <term>tracta: the process of drawing names from a leather bag to select officials</term> . . . . . *Page* 402
II. And similarly shall be done for those drawn within the guild house for any guild office . . . . . . . . . 405
III. That in the guild scrutinies <term>squittini: the process of vetting and voting on candidates to determine their eligibility for office</term> no one may be included or put to a vote who—himself or his family—has not paid the loans for 30 years . . . . . . . . . . . . . 405
IIII. That no one of illegitimate birth may, for himself or through others, exercise any office in the house of said guild . . . . 406
V. That whoever does not observe the feast days shall pay 20 shillings; and that five apothecaries <term>spetiali: pharmacists or spice merchants, the core members of this guild</term> may not keep their shops open on a feast day. 407
VI. That every new consul shall pay two florins <note>The gold florin was the primary currency of Florence</note> to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the guild's financial treasurer</term>, of which the chamberlain shall record as entry 5 shillings for every Tuesday and Friday that the consul fails to come to the guild. 407
VII. That legal cases must be concluded within 40 days, under penalty of 40 shillings for every consul. . . . . . . . . . . . 408
VIII. That the successor shall draw the provost of the doctors eight days before the end of his term of office . . . . . . . 409
VIIII. No subordinate <note>A person subject to the guild's jurisdiction</note> may file a lawsuit in any other court . 410
X. That the apprenticeship of barbers must be recorded in the guild and they must pay 5 shillings to the oratory . . . . . . . . 410

### 1415

I. That whoever practices the craft shall be compelled to swear an oath to it. 412

### 1416

I. That those enrolled in the guild <term>matricolati: official members listed on the guild's register, or 'matricola'</term> may transport any merchandise to Pisa and Florence by paying the usual tax <term>gabella: an indirect tax or duty on goods</term>, and shall not be required to pay anything else. . . . . . . 413

### 1418

I. That barbers shall not work on feast days, under penalty of 5 pounds in small florins <note>original: "llire .v. f. p." referring to lire fiorini piccioli, the silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note>. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 414

# II-VI REFORM OF 1351
->230<-

II. *a.* To chapter 23, namely that all and each practitioner of the said guild shall swear etc., they deleted <note>original: "cassorono"; referring to the legal act of striking out or annulling text</note> on the third leaf of the said chapter, on the first side of the said leaf, in the twelfth line, these words, namely: "shall have worked, made" (1).
*b.* And also on the second side of the said leaf they deleted, in the third line, these words, namely: "shall have made and caused to be made" (1).
*c.* And on the said side of the said leaf in the 24th line, after that word "purses" and before that word "gloves" they added <note>original: "agiunsono"</note> this word, namely: "pouches" <term>scarselle: a type of large purse or wallet often worn hanging from a belt</term> (1).

III. To chapter 45 regarding not bringing false saffron <note>Saffron was a valuable dye and spice; "false saffron" refers to adulterated or counterfeit goods</note> to the city of Florence etc., on the second side of the second leaf of the said chapter, they deleted these words, namely: "and also in pavises, large shields, and round shields not covered with sufficient leather, or against the form of the chapters of the said guild made" (2). <note>Pavises (palvesi), tavolacci, and rotelle were different types of medieval shields made of wood and leather.</note>

IIII. *a.* To chapter 50 regarding exercising the said guilds well and loyally, they deleted near the beginning of the said chapter these words, namely: "and that no one must mix thread with silk in his belts" etc. until "as it shall appear there; and whoever acts to the contrary shall be punished as a forger" (3).
*b.* And on the penultimate side of the said chapter they deleted these words, namely: "saving and reserved that if anyone should receive, have, or hold any of the aforesaid prohibited weapons" etc., until the end of the said chapter (4).

V. To chapter 55 regarding punishing those who will not observe the feast days etc., they deleted, on the second side of the second leaf of the said chapter, those words, namely: "and it is decreed and ordained that all and each belt-makers, shield-makers, and workers" etc., until where it says "the feast days" etc. (5).

VI. To chapter 90 (6) <note>The editor notes this should be corrected to 89</note> regarding those to whom it is granted and those to whom it is forbidden to involve themselves in the guild etc., they deleted, around the beginning <note>original: "principium"</note> of the said chapter, these words, namely: "and of the members of the guild or rather the ministry of the shield-makers and belt-makers and of each of them" (7).

# REFORM OF 1351 VII-VIIII

### VII. Regarding chapter 91 (1) on not buying or keeping foreign works, they revoked the said chapter entirely (2).
<note>1. Corrected to Chapter 90. 2. Compare with the addition to rubric 90. This indicates a shift toward free trade, allowing the sale of goods produced outside Florence.</note>

### VIII. One may keep non-counterfeit foreign works in the shop.

Furthermore, they decreed, ordered, and established that anyone of the said Guild may, and it shall be lawful for him, to sell and keep for sale in his shops or elsewhere, in any place, any merchandise pertaining to the said Guild or to any member of the said Guild, notwithstanding that such merchandise, goods, or other things may have been made or worked in any city, land, or place outside of Florence and its district, provided that such merchandise and things are not false, falsified, or sophisticated <note>adulterated or of inferior quality</note>, or made against the form of the statutes of the said Guild.

### VIIII. Regarding the physicians who must be placed in the ballot-pouch for judgments on severe wounds.

*a.* Furthermore, since it often happens that in the courts of the Rectors <note>high-ranking judicial officials</note> of the city of Florence, there is a need for the counsel, judgment, and deliberation of physicians and experts in medicine by reason of the trials that are daily argued or conducted in the said courts against those who offend and wound with severe injuries, involving facial disfigurement, debilitation of limbs, and similar cases; and since, from the time of the Mortality <note>The Black Death of 1348</note> until now, there has been and still is today a great defect and small quantity of sufficient physicians in the city of Florence, especially surgeons; and often insufficient foreign physicians urgently solicit the said Rectors and officials to grant them the commission of such judgments, and through their inexperience, very evident and enormous errors and defects are often committed in their said judgments; and wishing, as much as possible for the common utility, to prevent the aforesaid things and provide an opportune remedy, it is provided, deliberated, and ordered that from the physicians, both physical <note>internal medicine</note> and surgical, of the city of Florence and its countryside and district, there shall be made—by the Consuls of the said Guild who shall be in office at the time, with their councils and with those assistants (a)—by black beans <note>a method of secret voting</note> and

the aforesaid consuls and councilors and assistants (1).

(1) The gap in Source C is due to the fact that the translator skipped an entire line of Source B.

# REFORM OF 1351
## Page 9 [232]

white <note>referring to white voting beans or tokens used in the ballot</note>, and that all those doctors, both physicians <term>physicians: university-trained doctors of internal medicine</term> and surgeons <term>surgeons: practitioners focused on manual operations and external wounds</term>, who obtain two-thirds of the votes from those present in the said council or scrutiny, their names shall be written on separate slips, placed in bags, and put into two purses: that is, the physicians by themselves in one purse, and the surgeons by themselves in the other.

*b.* And that whenever the governors of the city of Florence, or any of the parties litigating before said governors, should request a doctor to advise or judge upon any question of a severe wound, the debilitation of limbs, or similar cases, they must draw from the said purses the names of two or more doctors, according to how many are requested by the governors, officials, or the parties, in such a way that at every consultation to be given, at least one physician or more is present. And when the said purses are exhausted and empty, a similar imbagging and scrutiny <note>original: "squittino," a formal vote for office</note> must be performed in the same manner.

*c.* And that no doctor, whether physician or surgeon, shall dare or presume to indicate or declare any wound to be a severe scar—with or without facial disfigurement—or that any debilitation must remain in any limb or not, or to proffer or make similar judgments or declarations. Nor shall they render or make any judgment, counsel, or declaration, in writing or otherwise, to any judge or official in any of the courts of the city of Florence, except for those alone who were placed in the bags and finally drawn from said bags in the aforementioned manner. (These doctors must be drawn in the presence of one or two of the Consuls of the Guild <note>The Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries</note> serving at that time, by the notary of the said Guild serving at that time). This is under the penalty of one hundred pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli</note> for every doctor, physician or surgeon, who judges, declares, or acts against the prescribed form in the aforementioned matters (1).

*d.* Those doctors who are drawn as stated and who judge, advise, or declare according to the said form, may and shall be permitted to ask, demand, and receive for their salary, labor, and reward for said judgment or counsel up to the amount of two gold florins; and they shall be content with said salary, under the same penalty.

In the name of God, amen. In the year of our Lord 1351, in the 5th Indiction <note>a 15-year cycle used for dating medieval documents</note>, on the 7th day of the month of December.
Sir Nicholò di Lapo, judge, for the Guild of Judges and Notaries,
Andrea di Cappone de' Capponi, for the Guild of Money Changers,

### [1353]

1353, 7th indiction, on the third day of the month of December.
The following are corrections and additions made to the chapters and orders described in the volume of the statutes of the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Merchants <term>merciai: merchants dealing in various goods, often textiles or luxury items</term> of Porta Santa Maria of the city of Florence, by the consuls of the said Guild currently residing in office.

I. That no one may practice medicine, unless they have first
received a degree or been examined.

a. # REFORM OF 1353

...to treat patients and practice the art of medicine, who previously used to perform the craft of blacksmiths and other mechanical arts <note>The "mechanical arts" were manual trades, then considered inferior to the "liberal arts" like medicine.</note>; and those things, which they do not know at all, they strive to do, by which things it often happens that those who are treated by such presumptuous persons are rather harmed and damaged than healed or freed from illness; therefore, to remove such things, we ordain, and by this law we establish that no one, of whatever condition and status he may be, [may practice] even if he were enrolled and matriculated or examined and approved as sufficient by four doctors expert in the art of medicine, to be elected and deputed for this by the consuls <note>The *Consoli* were the presiding officers of the Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries.</note> of the said art who shall be in office at the time, and by those medical consuls who at that time shall reside in the office of the consulate, if any then reside in the office of the consulate, of which approval a public instrument <note>A formal legal document.</note> should appear by the hand of the notary of the said art, or in the books and acts of the said art by the notary of the same art, under the penalty of 25 pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or *fiorini piccioli*</note> or less, at the discretion of the consuls of the said art existing at the time, for each person acting to the contrary, whether citizen or foreigner, to be taken from him by the consuls of the said art every time, even in fact and without making any formal condemnation. 

And that the consuls of the said art, who shall be in office at the time, be bound and must investigate the aforementioned practitioners acting against the said form, and punish and condemn anyone who acts to the contrary summarily and in fact, even omitting every legal solemnity, and collect and cause to be collected the fine. And at the beginning of each term of the consulate, they shall appoint over the aforementioned matters searchers <note>original: "cerchatori" - officials tasked with finding illegal practitioners</note>, as many and whomever they wish, to whose reports full faith shall be given (1).

b. Furthermore, the said consuls shall be bound and must, at the beginning of their office, elect and depute four doctors expert in the art and science of medicine, whomever (2) they wish, among whom there shall be at least one or more surgeons <note>original: "cerusico" - at this time, surgery was often distinguished from the internal medicine practiced by physicians.</note>, for the examination and approval of such doctors who wish to practice the art of medicine in the said city, countryside, or district of Florence. And those who shall be approved as sufficient by such approvers and examiners shall be held as capable and sufficient to practice the art of medicine; and it shall be permitted and lawful for him to treat patients in every place in the city, countryside, and district of Florence, provided that he submits himself and takes an oath to the said art, and has himself written in the matriculation roll <note>The official membership list of the Guild.</note> of the said art. And such approvals are to be made and must be made by those four doctors, to be elected as said, together with the medical consuls of the said art, if any doctor should reside in the office of the consulate at that time, by secret ballot...

## II. That no one may sell penny candles.

*a. Furthermore, that no apothecary and no other person shall dare or presume to have sold, or keep for sale in the city, countryside, or district, wax candles sold by the penny <note>original: "derratale" - refers to small, cheap candles sold for a fixed price of one 'denaro' or penny</note>, the weight of which is more than twelve candles per ounce, under penalty of 40 shillings in small florins <note>original: "f. p." for fiorini piccioli</note> for every pound. And that the consuls of the said guild, who shall be in office at the time, may and shall be permitted every month of their term, if it seems fit to them, to provide and ordain of what number the pound of penny candles is made and ought to be made. And no one may make these penny candles larger or in greater number than what shall be declared by the consuls existing at the time, under penalty for each person and for each time. And that the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the treasurer or financial officer</term> of the said guild be required every month to search through the guild and report whoever might violate this, and his report shall be upheld.*

*b. Declaring further that in every part of the present statute, where mention is made of obtaining something by vote, or under similar words, it shall be understood as obtained if it was done by secret scrutiny with black and white beans; and if it were proposed or shall be otherwise, it shall not be, nor be understood as, obtained.*

For the consuls <note>The elected executive leaders of a guild</note> of the Guild of Physicians, Apothecaries, and Grocers <note>original: "medici, spetiali e merciai"</note> of the city of Florence, regarding the chapters contained in the volume of the statutes of said Guild, and written by me, Francesco di Ciolo <margin>B. Cioli</margin>, notary and scribe for the Commune of Florence for the under-written officials, and furthermore by those same under-written officials admitted, corrected, and deliberated, as is contained in order below, namely:

I. *a.* First, considering that it often happens that the consuls of the said Guild do not assemble to administer justice <note>original: "render ragione" - literally "to render reason," referring to the guild's judicial functions in trade disputes</note> and to perform the other duties pertaining and belonging to their office—not only failing to meet four times a week, as they are bound and required to do by the form of the Guild's chapters, but often not even once a month. This results in no small damage and shame to the said Guild and to those who intend and wish to litigate in the Guild's court. Wishing to prevent the negligence and defects of the consuls and other officials, they established and ordained that the consuls of the said Guild for the time being, and also the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the financial officer or treasurer</term>, the notary or scribe, and also the messengers of the said Guild for the time being, and each of them, shall be bound and required to stay, come, and assemble in the Guild House to administer justice and perform the other duties belonging to their office on the days and hours in which they must come, stay, and be in the Guild House... according to the form of the Guild statutes (1).

They shall audit <note>original: "sindicheranno" - to perform a formal review of accounts and conduct</note>, immediately on the next following day after the successor of such chamberlain <note>original: "camarlingho" - the financial officer or treasurer of the guild</note> shall be drawn or elected. ## II. And consuls and the other officials must be marked for absence.

*a.* And for every day that he has not come and stayed as is said, five shillings of small florins from their salary, and gifts at least up to that quantity which the gift due to such official by reason of his said office from the said guild amounts to, if he were to have a gift; otherwise from his salary, if he shall have a salary, unless such official, as is said, marked <note>original: "apuntato" - literally 'pointed' or 'noted down' for an absence</note> and reported, shall have a legitimate excuse.

*b.* And let it be understood as a legitimate excuse, and as a legitimate excuse let it be admitted, if such official at the time of his said marking was ill or absent from the city of Florence by five miles or more, or in the office of the Priorate or Gonfaloniers of Justice <note>The highest executive offices of the Florentine Republic</note> or in any other office of the said Commune, or in the office of the five counselors of the University of Merchants <note>original: "Mercantia" - the judicial body governing trade and merchant disputes in Florence</note>; and at the time of his marking, he is personally exercising that office of the Commune or counselor of the Merchants; or if he is hindered or occupied by any other legitimate cause, for which hindrance or occupation he shall have had permission from the consuls of the said guild, or from the majority of them. Of which permission there should appear a record by the hand of the notary and scribe of the said guild; of which permission the said notary is bound to provide proof to such auditors and chamberlain.

*c.* Provided that <note>original: "Dummodo" - Latin legal term</note> they do not take anything from any messenger of the said guild for any marking made of them or any of them on any day or hour of any week, except for the markings made of him or them on Tuesday and Friday of any week.

*b.* And furthermore, we ordain and establish that the chamberlain of the said guild, whose office shall begin in the month of May next following, and the other chamberlains of the said guild to be elected or drawn in the future, and also the chamberlains of the said guild who shall be elected in the future, may, and it shall be lawful for them, and they are bound, and must [audit] all and each of the officials of the said guild who shall be elected or drawn in the future, or whose office has not yet begun, to audit them and hold them to account <term>sindicato: a formal audit or review of an official's conduct and finances at the end of their term</term> regarding the aforementioned penalties <note>original: "apuntature," referring to fines for absences or failures in duty</note>, and to have condemned or acquitted them at least within 10 days from the day such officials leave office, in such a way that first they have the notary of the said guild read to them—and the notary is likewise bound to read—the present statute, chapter, and order, and all other statutes and orders they may wish.

*c.* And furthermore, the said chamberlain may, is bound, and must, immediately after he and the auditors of the said guild have audited and held to account such officials of the said guild and their predecessors, at least within 12 days from the day they leave office, give and send to each of those consuls, the notary, and to the chamberlain himself and to the other officials of the said guild, to whom the gift from the guild must be given according to the form of the chapters of the said guild, those gifts and salaries which they ought to have according to the form of the statutes and orders of the guild, provided that there is first withheld or satisfied by such officials the condemnation <note>The payment of fines</note> which they have incurred or shall incur by reason of such penalties recorded against him or them, under penalty of five pounds of small florins for each person and each time and in each of the aforesaid cases. And this chapter, as to the things contained in the present chapter, shall be precise and shall derogate <note>To take precedence over or repeal parts of previous laws</note> all other chapters described in the volume of the chapters of the said guild.

# REFORM OF 1360 IV, V

### IV. That Michele di Nardo shall be the Chamberlain of the Works of San Bernaba.

Furthermore, considering that the Commune of Florence built and established the church of the victorious apostle Saint Barnabas <note>San Bernaba; the church was built to commemorate the Battle of Campaldino, fought on St. Barnabas' Day, June 11, 1289</note>, which is a church recommended by the Commune of Florence to the said Guild <note>The Silk Merchants' Guild, or 'Arte di Por Santa Maria'</note> in times past; and desiring that—to the perpetual memory of the victory which the Commune of Florence received through divine aid on the day of such a great feast against the Aretine Ghibellines <note>The Ghibellines were the pro-Imperial political faction, defeated by the pro-Papal Guelphs of Florence</note> and the other rebels and enemies of the said Commune, and for the honor and joy of the said Commune and the aforementioned Guild, and for the praise, glory, and reverence of Almighty God and the said victorious blessed apostle, and for the salvation of the souls of those who died in the battle of the said victory to achieve such a great triumph—the said church be built and enlarged; it is provided and ordained that Michele di Nardo, mercer <note>A dealer in textiles and fine fabrics</note> and craftsman of the said Guild, who in days past was elected and deputed by the Consuls of the said Guild as Chamberlain <note><term>Camarlingho</term>: the financial administrator or treasurer</note> for the affairs of the said church of San Barnabas, for a time and term of one year next following, beginning on the day of his election—which was recorded by Ser Nello di Ghetto, notary and scribe of the said Guild, on the day [blank]—shall be and is able and obligated to be the Chamberlain of the said Guild over the affairs of the said church for the above-mentioned term of one year, beginning on the said day, with that power <note>original: "balia"</note>, office, and authority that was and is attributed to him, both in the instrument of his election and by the Commune of Florence through the reform or provision of the Councils of the People and Commune of Florence, made in the month of April last passed in favor and for the augmentation of the said church.

### V. That the Consuls may elect the Chamberlain and the Overseer.

And that for the future, the Consuls of the said Guild, both present and those who shall be in office over time, together with their councilors and those of the said Guild, and with those added members <note><term>arroti</term>: citizens called in to supplement a committee or council</note> and craftsmen of the said Guild whom they wish to have for this purpose or without them, may and shall be permitted—for the increase and convenience of the said church, and so that the said church may be built and enlarged—to elect and depute, and also if it then seems fit, to place in the bags or purses <note>A reference to the Florentine system of "imborsazione," where names of eligible candidates were placed in bags to be drawn by lot</note> those Chamberlains, Overseers <note><term>operai</term>: officials in charge of the physical construction and maintenance of a religious building</note>, and officials from among the craftsmen and men of the said Guild, whomever and however many they wish, and in such manner and form and for such time and term and with such authority, judgment, power, and potency as the said Consuls, councilors, and added members, or the majority of them, shall deliberate, provide, and ordain (1).

# REFORM OF 1362

->[1362]<-

This is a new chapter regarding the sifting of saffron <note>original: "gruogo," an archaic term for saffron</note> before it is weighed, if it is of a weight of ten pounds or more, established by the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Merchants of Porta Santa Maria of the city of Florence.

### I. That the saffron must be sifted.

**a.** If anyone of this guild shall buy or sell saffron <note>original: "gruogo o vero zafferano"</note> within the city of Florence from any person of this guild, or from outside the guild, or from one not subject to said guild, unless a specific agreement has been made otherwise, the seller is required—before he weighs it—to sift it, and to give it sifted to the buyer if it is of a weight of ten pounds or more, under penalty of one hundred shillings <note>original: "soldi"</note> for each person and for each instance; and more or less at the discretion of the Consuls <note>the elected leaders of the guild</note> of said guild, having respect to the quantity of the saffron sold and weighed without being sifted.

### II. The sieve shall stay with the Chamberlain.

And so that the aforementioned things can be done conveniently, the Consuls of this guild shall procure, and are bound and obliged to procure, that for and by the said guild there be kept a basket <note>original: "corbello," likely referring here to the sifting basket or sieve</note> (a), which basket the Chamberlain <note>the guild's financial officer</note> of this guild is bound to have and keep at his shop. With this sieve, all men buying and selling are bound and obliged to sift all the saffron they buy or sell that is of a weight of 10 pounds or more. For the use of this sieve, one penny <note>original: "denari"</note> shall be paid to the Chamberlain of the guild, receiving it on behalf of the guild, for every pound of saffron that is sifted; the seller paying half and the buyer paying the other half. The buyer is bound to send the saffron at his own expense to the place where the sieve is kept by the guild, and from that place send it to his own shop.

### III. Penalty of 100 pounds for whoever does not sift it.

And if anyone shall buy or sell saffron not sifted with the said sieve of the guild, of a weight of ten pounds or more, the Consuls may and must condemn such buyer and seller, and each of them, to one hundred shillings in Florentine small pence <note>original: "f p." for fiorini piccioli</note>, or a greater or lesser amount, having respect to the quantity of the saffron sold and weighed without being sifted. And anyone may be an accuser regarding the aforementioned things and shall be believed <note>their testimony accepted</note>, and he shall have the fourth part of the fine.

---

(a) <note>original: "B cribellum." Latin for "sieve."</note>

# REFORM OF 1363 VIII, VIIII

### VIII. That brokers shall keep secrets.

Furthermore, every <term>broker</term><note>original: "sensale"; a licensed middleman who negotiated trades between merchants</note> is bound and must exercise the art and ministry of brokerage well, loyally, and faithfully. They must not commit deceit or fraud in the aforementioned matters in any way, and must keep secret every <term>transaction</term><note>original: "merchato"; refers here to the specific deal or trade being negotiated</note> and whatever they are assigned to do or trade by any craftsman of said guild or outside of the guild. They shall not manifest or reveal this to anyone else in any way, by themselves or through others, directly or indirectly, tacitly or expressly, until such time as that transaction or task commanded of them is entirely finished and carried out—unless it is by the will and consent of the person who commanded the transaction or business, or by the will and consent of the <term>Consuls</term><note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> of said guild, under penalty of 25 <term>pounds of small florins</term><note>original: "lire di f. p." (fiorini piccioli); the local currency used for daily transactions</note> for each person and for each instance.

### VIIII. And the salaries of brokers limited under the below-written penalties.

*a.* Furthermore, every broker may and is permitted to take, receive, and have for brokerage of the things for which they negotiate a transaction—both from the merchant and craftsman of said guild as well as those from outside the guild—only the salary or price noted below. That is, for each and every thing, calculated at double everything that they were able to take and have according to the form of the said statute placed under the rubric of payments to be made to brokers for the brokerage of the below-written things, in such a way that everything they were able to take or have by virtue of said statute is included within said double amount <note>This refers to a doubling of previous legal rates established in earlier statutes</note> (1).

*b.* Save nonetheless and except for saffron; for which saffron they may receive and have for brokerage for each pound of saffron they trade: only six <term>denari</term><note>Pence or small coins</note> of small florins from the seller and three denari of small florins from the buyer, and no more. And no broker may, dare, or presume to take, pick up, receive, or have for themselves or for others, directly or indirectly, for salary, brokerage, or remuneration of any transaction or any things for which they made a trade, more or otherwise than what is contained above, nor any gift or present, under penalty of 10 pounds of small florins for each person and for each instance (1).

# REFORM OF 1363 XVI
269

### XVI. That no one shall bring "femminelle" of wild saffron into Florence.

*a.* Furthermore, considering that many people, and especially foreigners not subject to the aforementioned Guild <note>The "Arte dei Medici e Speziali" or Guild of Physicians and Apothecaries, which regulated spice merchants</note>, bring and sell, or cause to be brought and sold in the city and territory of Florence, the *femminelle* <note>original: "femminelle"; these were the yellow stamens or floral waste of the crocus, which lack the dye and flavor of the red stigmas</note> of wild saffron <note>original: "gruogo"; bastard saffron or safflower, often used as an adulterant</note>, which in truth possess no goodness, efficacy, or value; and it often happens that with these *femminelle*, which have the appearance and likeness of true saffron, the genuine saffron is falsified and sophisticated <note>adulterated</note>, a thing held in abomination by all merchants and especially by the craftsmen of said Guild; therefore, in addition to the other statutes and orders mentioned above, in whatever way they were made in the past, it is decreed and ordained by this law that no citizen, peasant, or inhabitant of the city, territory, or district of Florence, nor any foreigner—even if not subject to the aforesaid Guild, of whatever state or condition they may be—may, dare, or presume in the city, territory, or district of Florence or elsewhere to bring, sell, or cause to be brought or sold, trade, gather, have, or hold in any way for themselves or others, directly or indirectly, *femminelle* of wild saffron, under the penalty of one hundred pounds in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli</note>, for each person and for each instance, or more or less as shall seem fit to the Consuls <note>the elected leaders of the Guild</note> of said Guild, having respect and consideration for the quantity of such *femminelle*. Of which penalty, half shall go to the said Guild, and the other half shall be attached to the Commune of Florence.

*b.* And the Consuls of the said Guild may, and are furthermore bound and obliged, through the messenger or chamberlain or other official of the aforesaid Guild, or others whom they wish, as many times and when and where and how it shall seem fit to them, to search and cause to be searched for the aforesaid things and to take or cause to be taken the said *femminelle* from any person or persons, even those not subject to the aforesaid Guild, even without the license, commission, or decree of any judge or official, or even by deed and their own authority; and they may cause those *femminelle* to be publicly burned, freely, lawfully, and without penalty. And anyone may [report] concerning the aforesaid things, and each of them. And whoever acts against or offends against the aforesaid things, or any of them, may be accused, denounced, or notified before the Consuls of the said Guild, secretly or openly, with a name or without a name, and their identity shall be kept secret; and they shall have the third part of the condemnation <note>the fine collected</note>, and in that case the other two parts of the condemnation shall be applied both to the aforesaid Guild and to the Commune of Florence. And that the Consuls of the said Guild may, and it shall be lawful for them, by virtue of their rendered oath, and they are bound and obliged concerning all and each of the aforesaid things, whether by way of accusation, denunciation, or notification, or by their own office, against...

<summary>This decree prohibits the import and sale of "femminelle" (saffron adulterants) in Florence to protect the quality of genuine saffron. It grants the Guild Consuls broad powers to search, seize, and publicly burn fraudulent goods without a warrant.</summary>

### I. What the gold-leaf beaters must observe.

Desiring that good workmanship be practiced by the craftsmen subject to the said guild, and especially by the gold-leaf beaters <term>orpellai: craftsmen who produced "orpello" or imitation gold leaf, often used for decoration</term>, and also so that the legal drafts of deceased notaries written on parchment, and also ecclesiastical books ordained for divine honor and praise, may be preserved and guarded and not sold or destroyed, it is established and ordained with prudent deliberation that all and each gold-leaf beater and those who draw the gold leaf <note>original: "siricanti gli orpelli"</note> in the city, territory, and district of Florence are bound and must prepare the leather in which they make said gold leaf well and loyally, as was customary; nor may any of them, under any sought-after pretext, make or work said gold leaf, or have it worked or made, upon sheets of written or erased parchment <note>This regulation prevented the destruction of valuable legal and religious manuscripts to be used as "gold-beater's skin" or scrap material.</note>. And whoever acts against the aforesaid things shall be fined by the Consuls of the said guild ten shillings in small florins <note>original: "f. p." for fiorini piccioli</note> for every dozen, and for every instance, to be taken from him by the said Consuls. And let no one of the guild dare or presume to sell or keep in his shop the said gold leaf made against the aforesaid form, under the aforesaid penalty. And the said gold leaf made against the aforesaid form must be publicly burned by the said Consuls or by their mandate, so that in the future no one dares to make or sell any gold leaf on the aforesaid written or erased parchment. And the Consuls of the said guild, whose office shall begin in the month of January next to come, are bound and must publish and command all these things to the gold-leaf beaters and the craftsmen of gold leaf and the other craftsmen of the guild. And these Consuls and each of them successively are bound and must, by virtue of their sworn oath, search and cause to be searched if there are any who act against this. # REFORM OF 1373 I

In each consulate <note>The term of office for the Guild's leaders</note>, the consuls of the said Guild shall be bound, at the beginning of their term, to assemble and cause to be assembled before them in the Guild hall twelve men from among the best men of the Guild—true Guelphs <note>Members of the political faction supporting the Papacy, a requirement for holding office in Florence</note> and those who keep or cause to be kept a shop for the goods of this Guild—specifically four from each member branch <note>The Guild was divided into three branches: Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers/Merchants</note>. Once these twelve have been summoned and gathered, the consuls and the majority of the twelve, in agreement and of one mind, shall be bound and must elect and nominate twelve good and loyal men, true Guelphs and not foreigners. Once nominated, these twelve so named must be put to a secret scrutiny <note>A formal vote or "squittino"</note> among the consuls and the gathered twelve; and those six of the twelve who receive the most votes in the said scrutiny shall be councilors of the Guild for the duration of the term of the consulate of the aforementioned consuls: namely, two doctors, two apothecaries, and two merchants.

And considering that, due to the busy occupations of the Guild members, the said summoning and gathering of the twelve members, the scrutiny, and the election of the councilors often fails to occur—which results in damage and shame to the Guild—it is decreed and ordained that the consuls of the Guild and two-thirds of them (even if others are absent or not requested), together with the councilors of the Guild and the majority of them, and with those members of the Guild whom the consuls and two-thirds of them wish to have present for the aforementioned matters—provided that at least twenty-four members of the Guild are present—may, shall be bound, and must nominate those members eligible for the office of councilors of the Guild according to the form of the Guild statutes. Among themselves and the aforementioned additions <note>original: "aroti" - additional members called in to reach a quorum</note>, they shall hold a solemn and secret scrutiny. Those who obtain the majority of votes from the consuls and the additions present shall be placed in a bag <note>original: "inborsare" - the Florentine system of "imborsazione" where names were placed in bags for random drawing</note>: namely, doctors by themselves, apothecaries by themselves, and merchants by themselves.

Once so "enbagged," at the start of each consulate, six members shall be drawn from the said bag—two for each branch—who have no prohibition <note>Legal or political disqualifications</note> according to the form of the Guild statutes. These men shall be, and are understood to be, councilors of the Guild for the duration of the term of the consuls who are then sitting in office at the time of the drawing. And should anyone, for any reason, be missing from the office, another councilor from the same branch may and must be drawn to replace the vacancy for the remaining time. And so on successively, once the bag is empty and even before, whenever it seems fit to the consuls, the consuls and the additions shall perform the enbagging of the councilors in a similar manner. And let it be noted that the enbagging of the said councilors and the office of councilors began on the 7th day of April...

recently passed, and also the drawing of names performed from the bags in which the councilors of the said guild were placed; and the things done by them and their office shall be valid and hold in everything and for everything, as if it had been done legitimately and according to the form of the statutes and orders of the said guild <note>original: "statuti e ordini della dett’arte"</note> (1).

### II. Method of scrutiny and syndics, and that their office shall last one year.

Furthermore, in the aforesaid manner and form, they provided and ordained that the consuls <note>The highest-ranking officials of the guild</note> of the said guild and two-thirds of them—even if others are absent or unsummoned—together with their councilors and the majority of them, and with those craftsmen of the guild whom the consuls wish to have present (provided that at least twenty-four craftsmen of the guild are present), can, are bound to, and must nominate those craftsmen of the guild eligible for the office of the syndics <note>term: syndics (sindichi) - officials responsible for auditing accounts and ensuring legal compliance</note> of the said guild, according to the form of the guild statutes. And among them, the councilors, and the aforementioned adjuncts <note>term: arroti - additional members called in to supplement a committee</note>, they shall submit them to a solemn and secret scrutiny <note>term: scruptineo - a formal vote or ballot</note>. And those who in the said scrutiny obtain two-thirds of the votes of the consuls, councilors, and adjuncts present must be placed in a bag <note>term: inborsare - the practice of putting names on slips of paper into a leather bag for random drawing, a hallmark of Florentine democracy</note>: specifically, doctors by themselves, apothecaries by themselves, and grocers by themselves.

From those thus placed in the bags, at the beginning of the month of January each year, two craftsmen of the guild must be drawn from the said bags—one for each member category—who do not have a prohibition <note>A legal disqualification, often due to recently holding office or owing taxes</note> according to the form of the guild statutes. These men shall be and are understood to be the syndics of the guild for a term of one year, with the office, authority <note>term: balìa - delegated power or legal jurisdiction</note>, and salary or customary gift as contained in the guild statutes.

And whenever anyone for any reason should be missing from the aforesaid office of the syndicate, another in his place from that same member category can and must be drawn for the remaining time. The person thus elected shall have the same authority, salary, or gift which he would have had if he had been drawn for an entire year. And so successively when the said bag is emptied, and even before, whenever it seems fit to the consuls, the aforesaid bagging of the syndics shall be performed by the consuls, councilors, and adjuncts in a similar manner.

And the bagging performed for the said syndics and the office of the syndics on the 7th day of April recently passed, and also the drawing of names from the bags, and the things done by them, shall be valid and hold as if done legitimately and rightly according to the form of the guild statutes (1).

(1) Reformed December 26, 1404, rubric III.

# REFORMS OF 1373, 1374 III

### III. That the messengers shall have 2 gold florins for their clothing beyond the usual amount.

Furthermore, considering the high cost of cloth and the quantity of money <note>original: "pecunia"</note> which the messengers <term>messi: officials who carried communications and performed administrative tasks for the guild</term> of the said guild must receive for the aforementioned guild for their clothing according to the form of the statutes of the said guild—which is not sufficient for them to buy honorable clothing for the aforementioned guild—it is therefore provided and ordained that the messengers of the said guild shall have and must have, beyond the quantity of money due to them by the form and according to the form of the statutes of the said guild for their clothing each year, for the price of the said clothing between both of them, two gold florins <note>The gold florin was the international reserve currency of the Middle Ages, minted in Florence</note>; that is, to each of the said messengers, one gold florin from the money of the said guild. And that the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the treasurer or financial officer</term> of the said guild, who shall be in office at the time, can, is bound to, and must—from the money of the said guild, beyond the quantity due to these messengers according to the form of the statutes of the said guild—give and pay them every year two gold florins for their clothing, freely, lawfully, and without penalty.

The following are corrections or rather chapters of the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Haberdashers <term>merciai: merchants who sold a wide variety of small goods, from needles to jewelry</term> of the city of Florence, and of all the members and craftsmen of the aforesaid guild.

### I. That the undertakers be subject to the jurisdiction of the consuls.

Inasmuch as infinite complaints are very often presented before the consuls of the said guild because of the immoderate extortions continually practiced by the undertakers <term>becchamorti: literally "corpse-peckers," a term for those who handled the burial of the dead</term>, and those employed and working to bury the bodies of the deceased and their assistants; and inasmuch as the said consuls and their office cannot provide a remedy regarding these extortions, chiefly because many of them are not found registered or enrolled in the guild’s membership book <note>original: "matricola"</note>, and therefore are not subject to the guild’s authority; which situation results in no small damage and loss to all the citizens of the city of Florence and is a reproach and shame to the said guild and its consuls; and especially since it is believed that such undertakers should be subject to the Guild of Apothecaries because they are related to the aforesaid craft <note>The connection likely stems from the apothecaries' role in providing spices and waxes for funerals</note>; therefore, for the good and utility of the citizens of the aforesaid city and the honor of the entire guild, they provided, decreed, and ordained that all and each person who works in any way to bury the bodies of the dead, or to announce funerals, or to invite mourners—who in the common tongue are called *becchamorti*—shall be understood to be and are subject to the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Haberdashers of the city of Florence and to the jurisdiction, reprimand, office, and power of the consuls of the said guild, notwithstanding that they may not be enrolled or registered in the guild’s membership book. ### IV. That no one may buy notarial registers or merchants' letter books, nor legal instruments, nor erase them.
