Save and except that stationers and book-sellers may keep, buy, and sell them as they are accustomed to do, except for the notarial registers, under the penalty of one hundred pounds of small florins <note>original: *lire cento di f. p.* (fiorini piccioli)</note> for each of them who acts to the contrary, for as many times as it occurs. This fine is to be applied and paid, one half to the Chamberlain and the Chamber of the *Mercantia* <note>The Court of Merchants in Florence which oversaw commercial disputes</note> and the University of Merchants of the city of Florence, receiving it for the said University; and the other half to the aforesaid Guild or to the Chamberlain of the said Guild, receiving it for the said Guild, if and insofar as the condemnation was made by the Consuls <note>The highest elected officials of a Guild</note> of the said Guild. And if the condemnation was made by the officials of the said University of the aforesaid city, the entire quantity of the said condemnation shall be applied to the said University. And that every foreign official of the *Mercantia* can, is bound to, and must investigate and search for all and each of the aforesaid things, and having found the guilty parties, punish and condemn them according to the aforesaid penalties, even summarily, without any trial or the observation of any solemnity. And furthermore, the Consuls of the said Guild who shall be in office at the time are bound to search for the aforesaid things and, having found the guilty parties, punish and condemn them under the bond of their oath.

# I. Authority of the Provost of Doctors to fine doctors.

First, considering that the statute placed in the present volume, written by Ser Michele di Bandella, notary, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1372, 11th indiction <note>A 15-year cycle used in medieval dating</note>, on the 20th day of the month of December, in which or by which authority was given to the Provost of the Doctors regarding certain matters contained in said statute; and considering that because the said Provost does not have the authority to fine disobedient doctors, for which reason the said doctors refuse to obey the said Provost, and refuse to carry out the disputations <note>Formal academic debates required for medical practice</note> and other laudable acts contained in the said statute; it is therefore decreed and ordained that the Provost of the Doctors shall have the power, authority, and mandate to punish and fine those doctors who are disobedient to him, for each instance, in the amount of up to 20 soldi in small florins <note>term: f. p. (fiorini piccioli), the silver-based currency used for daily transactions in Florence</note>; which fine the Consuls of the said Guild, presiding at the time, are bound and required to have collected by the Chamberlain, and by the Chamberlain of the said Guild applied to the Guild’s funds (1).

# II. That the Provost of the Doctors must observe the matters contained above.

Furthermore, it is decreed, provided, and ordained that the Provost of the Doctors for the time being shall be bound and required to ensure that disputations and the other laudable acts contained in the said statute are performed at the times, terms, manner, and form as contained in the said statute. And if any of these Provosts shall refuse to do the aforementioned things, or refuse to see them observed, or contravene <margin>Latin: *cessaverit seu... contra venerit* (shall have ceased or... come against)</margin> them in any way, he shall be punished and must be punished by the Consuls of the said Guild for each instance in the amount of 20 soldi in small florins; this fine shall be taken from the Provost in fact and without following any formal ceremony, and applied to the said Guild (2).

### III REFORM OF 1376

To seal every tomb in which they bury the dead, twenty *piccoli* shillings <note>original: "soldi venti pic."; the 'piccolo' was a smaller denomination of the Florentine silver soldo</note>. (a) Except if the deceased is buried in a company tomb <note>a communal vault belonging to a confraternity or guild</note>, they may not take more than 10 *piccoli* shillings per person.

b. Except that these matters and wages are not understood to apply to ecclesiastical persons, nor to knights, nor to judges, nor to doctoral physicians; with these, they may agree [on a price] discreetly. Indeed, the gravediggers <term>becchamorti: literally "corpse-peckers," the guild-regulated laborers responsible for handling bodies and burials</term> are required to watch over, observe, and report each and every piece of household goods and items belonging to the deceased, to the apothecary, or to others. And that, notwithstanding that they may take and demand their wages up to the said amount as stated above, they are nevertheless bound and must exercise discretion regarding the burials of small boys and girls and of the poor; they should demand and take lower wages than stated above, because it would be impossible to calculate (b) every labor that the said gravediggers endure regarding the burials of every dead person. Considering especially the labor endured in the burials of famous men and those of great standing, and also of knights and doctors, and also to be able to discern and declare the discretion of said gravediggers regarding the wages they must take for the burials of boys, girls, and the poor, it is decreed and ordained that by the office of each consulate of the said Guild <note>The Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries, which oversaw gravediggers</note> at the start of their term, there must be elected and deputized eight craftsmen of the said Guild—that is, two for each quarter of the city of Florence—whose office shall last the entire duration of the said consulate that makes the elections. These two, each for his own quarter, shall have to deliberate, ordain, and limit—should a dispute arise—the wages due to the said gravediggers; and whatever is decided by them, the gravediggers may take and no more. Saving, nevertheless, the above-mentioned chapters, which may not be prejudiced in any (d) way.

c. And so that the citizens of Florence are not defrauded or deceived by the said gravediggers, it is decreed and ordained that each of the said gravediggers must have a copy of the above-mentioned ordinances written or signed by the hand of the notary of the said Guild. Each of them must present and show this copy to whichever person is deputized to handle the burial expenses of that particular deceased person. # THE REFORM OF 1377

The manner and form previously observed prior to the <term>bagging and imborsation</term><note>The process of placing names into leather bags (borse) to be drawn by lot for office.</note> of the consuls, through which many inconveniences have arisen in the past during the conduct of the said <term>scrutinies</term><note>isquictini: the vetting process or elections to determine eligibility for office.</note>; considering especially that many young and unknown craftsmen of the said guild were elected by the consuls of the said guild as <term>adjuncts</term><note>arroti: additional members called in to supplement a committee or council.</note> to perform the aforementioned scrutinies, who often gave their <term>black beans</term><note>fave nere: used for "yes" votes in the Florentine balloting system.</note> to those who did not deserve the office of the consulate, and deprived those who were worthy of the said office by means of their <term>white beans</term><note>fave bianche: used for "no" votes.</note>; and considering that discretion resides in the elders, and especially in the expert and practical men, and they better know—and ought to know—their fellow craftsmen and who is worthy and who is not worthy of the aforementioned office; and therefore, for the good, utility, and peaceful and tranquil state and honor of the aforesaid guild and its craftsmen, it is provided, decreed, and ordained that in each and every scrutiny performed in the guild hall for the office of the consulate, in addition to the number of consuls and councilors of the said guild, there shall and must be forty-eight <term>adjunct</term> craftsmen of the said guild, eligible for the office of the consulate according to the form of the statutes and orders of the Commune of Florence and of the said guild, to be elected by the office of the consuls of the said guild. Of which forty-eight adjuncts, at least thirty-two at the time of the said election must have been consuls of the said guild at least once. This is expressly declared: that from any single shop or warehouse of the said guild, no more than one person may be elected as an adjunct; and no partner of any councilor may be elected as an adjunct. Which forty-eight adjuncts must be elected by the consuls of the guild currently in office, or by two-thirds of them, through a solemn and secret scrutiny celebrated by them and among them, or to be celebrated by black and white beans, in such a way that all the aforementioned adjuncts up to the said number of 48—who shall obtain the vote by the consuls or among the consuls or two-thirds of them, of whom at least 32 have been consuls of the guild at least once—can and must be present at the aforementioned scrutiny and cast their beans in the said scrutiny; and it shall suffice if two-thirds of the consuls, councilors, and adjuncts are present at the aforementioned scrutiny.

# II, III REFORM OF 1377

The office of the Ten of Liberty <note>The "Dieci della Libertà" was a Florentine magistracy responsible for protecting the city's freedoms and overseeing certain administrative duties</note> of the commune of Florence, [considering that] for litigants appearing before them, much labor falls upon the consuls and the craftsmen <term>artefici: skilled members of a guild</term> of the said guild, without any benefit to the said guild or its craftsmen; rather, in seeking the truth of the facts in the cases questioned before them, it is very often necessary to spend the guild's own money, which results in loss and detriment to the said guild and the aforementioned craftsmen. Furthermore, because those who submit their disputes to the aforementioned consuls—as their chosen judges and arbitrators—often commit offenses within the guild house, both against the persons of the said consuls and against the honor of the consuls and craftsmen of the entire guild; and because these offenders are not [currently] subject to their jurisdiction, they leave unpunished for their crimes and thus boast of their sins.

Therefore, it is provided, decreed, and ordained that for each and every dispute brought before the said consuls, a fee shall and must be paid for the settlement by commission <term>commissaria compositione: a legal settlement reached through appointed arbitrators</term> to the said guild, or to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the guild's treasurer or financial officer</term> of the guild receiving it on their behalf. That is: for every pound <note>lira</note> of the amount awarded, or of the value of the thing regarding which the judgment is made, two pence <note>denari</note> shall be paid. It is expressly declared that this fee shall not exceed, nor can it exceed, the amount of 10 pounds in small florins <note>f. p. stands for "fiorini piccioli," the silver-based currency used for local transactions in Florence</note>.

And that each and every person litigating before the said consuls by settlement through arbitration, in whatever manner—both the plaintiff and the defendant—during the time or term of the arbitration agreement made by the parties before the consuls or the office of the consuls of the guild, shall be understood to be and shall be subject to the jurisdiction, office, and authority <term>balia: full administrative and judicial power</term> of the said consuls, in every way and in all respects, as if they were enrolled and registered in the membership roll <term>matricola: the official register of guild members</term> of the said guild. And the office of the consuls of the guild may proceed against them, or any one of them, both by law and by fact, during the term of the arbitration, just as they may proceed against those registered and enrolled in the membership roll of the guild.

# REFORM OF 1377 III, IIII

...of the guild, or indeed of any member or ministry of the said guild, practicing in any manner within the countryside <note>original: "contado," the rural territory surrounding Florence</note> of Florence, shall be bound and obligated to pay to the said guild—or to the chamberlain <note>term: "camarlingho" (treasurer or financial officer)</note> of the said guild receiving on its behalf—the sum of 10 silver soldi <note>original: "soldi .x. di f. p." referring to Florentine small denari</note> every year during the month of August. This is to assist with the expenses which are daily required for the aforementioned guild. To ensure this payment is made, they may and must be compelled by the consuls or the chamberlain of the guild in the manner and form deliberated by the office of the guild consuls, once or more, as many times as necessary.

### IIII. The procedure for conducting the scrutiny for the Six of the Mercanzia.

Furthermore, for the honor and standing of the said guild, and so that those who are worthy may enjoy the offices and honors <margin>honors</margin> of the said guild, it is provided and ordained that in each and every scrutiny <note>term: "squittino" (the process of determining eligibility for office by ballot)</note> held in the guild house regarding the craftsmen of the guild for the office of the Seven Councilors of the University of the Mercanzia <note>note: The Mercanzia was the supreme commercial court and governing body of the Florentine guilds</note> and merchants of the city of Florence, there must be present the consuls and councilors of the guild—or at least two-thirds of them—and twenty "arroti" <note>term: "arroti" (additional members or 'adjuncts' summoned to enlarge a committee for important decisions)</note> who are craftsmen of the guild. All twenty of these adjuncts must have served as consuls of the guild at least once. These adjuncts are to be elected by the office of the guild consuls through a secret scrutiny conducted by them using black and white beans <note>note: A traditional voting method where black beans signified "yes" and white "no"</note>.

And each and every craftsman of the guild who is approved in the said scrutiny by the consuls, councilors, and adjuncts—which shall take place in the guild house for the office of the seven councilors aforesaid—by two-thirds of the consuls, councilors, and adjuncts present (provided that at least two-thirds of the total number are in attendance), shall have their names, first names, or surnames recorded in writing or by public instrument. This document shall be sealed with the seal of the guild and prepared by the guild notary for the official or the office of the Seven Councilors of the University of the Mercanzia of the city of Florence. This scrutiny must be recorded or written by the guild notary and by two religious friars <note>note: Clergy were often used as neutral observers to ensure the integrity of communal elections</note> who shall be elected by the office of the consuls, and one or two of the consuls currently in office, as decided by the consular office. The aforementioned scrutiny cannot and must not be conducted in any other way; and if it were so conducted, it shall be void and have no legal standing.

# IIII, V REFORM OF 1378

...or rather bags <note>original: "borse"; these were leather pouches containing the names of eligible citizens used for lottery-based elections</note>, in which were and are placed the names of the craftsmen of the said guild who were approved for the office of the consulate, and who must serve as consuls of the said guild. Specifically: one bag in which are placed the doctors, painters, gold-beaters, tinsel-makers, and chest-makers; and another in which are placed the apothecaries <note>original: "spetiali"; these were pharmacists who also traded in spices and pigments</note> holding shops outside the Old Market; and yet another in which are placed the apothecaries holding shops in the Old Market and around said market, and the warehousemen <note>original: "fundachieri"; wholesale merchants or keepers of storage houses</note>, wherever they reside in the city of Florence; and the other in which were and are placed the mercers <note>original: "merciai"; dealers in small goods and textiles</note> and others of the branch of said mercers. They provided, deliberated, and ordained—for the good and peaceful state of the said guild, and so that the honors and gifts of the said guild may be distributed and equalized as best as possible according to the rank of the said craftsmen—that in the future there shall be only three bags.

And the said four bags shall be reduced to only three in this manner, namely: that the first two bags of the said four—that is, the bag in which are placed the doctors, painters, gold-beaters, tinsel-makers, and chest-makers, and the other bag in which are placed the apothecaries holding shops outside the Old Market—and all those placed in the aforementioned two bags shall be mixed together into a single bag. Thus, from the said first two bags, there shall be made only one bag, in which shall currently be placed together all the doctors, painters, gold-beaters, tinsel-makers, chest-makers, and apothecaries holding shops outside the Old Market who have been approved in the scrutiny <note>original: "squictino"; the process of vetting and voting on candidates for eligibility</note> for the office of the consulate of the said guild. And the other bag shall be and remain fixed for the apothecaries of the Old Market and the warehousemen mentioned above. And similarly, the third bag shall remain fixed for the mercers and others belonging to the said branch who have been approved as consuls of the said guild in the said scrutiny.

### V. That there shall be six consuls.

a. And considering that at present seven consuls must be drawn from the said bags according to the statutes and orders of the said guild, they provided that, once the aforementioned mixing is done and the two bags are combined and reduced to one, there shall be drawn by lot and fortune only six craftsmen as consuls of the said guild for a term of four months. Their office, lasting for four continuous months, will happily begin with God's help on the first of January <note>original: "kalen di gennaio"</note> next, in the form and manner written below, namely: from the first bag, in which the doctors, painters, gold-beaters, tinsel-makers, chest-makers, and apothecaries from outside the Old Market must now be placed together...

### VIIII. Concerning the scales.

**a.** Furthermore, that the weights, steelyards <note>statee: a type of balance scale using a counterweight on a lever</note>, and scales of the said guild shall remain and be, and must continually remain and be, in the Old Market <note>Mercato Vecchio: the historic commercial center of Florence, now the site of the Piazza della Repubblica</note> or indeed in the guild house.

**c.** Furthermore, that all the aforesaid things and each of them must be observed and confirmed by the craftsmen of the said guild.

# I, II REFORM OF 1379

The officials and approvers, by every legal path and in the manner, form, and cause by which they best could—and especially by the force of the authority, power, and mandate <note>original: "balie," referring to an emergency committee with full powers</note> granted to them in this regard by any statutes and ordinances of the said Commune of Florence—have quashed, annulled, and rejected every deliberation and every ordinance and statute contained in the said old and new statutes of the said guild (contained above in the present volume) which spoke or were arranged against Ser Bartholomeus, son of Ser Nelli Ghetti, notary of the said guild; specifically regarding the dismissal and removal of the said Ser Bartholomeus from the office of the notary of the said guild. And furthermore, they have approved and confirmed all and singular statutes, ordinances, and deliberations, both old and new, of the said guild that speak and provide in favor of the said Ser Bartholomeus, and for and concerning his election or confirmation as notary and scribe of the said guild, made and published, and all and singular things contained in them, and every election, nomination, and confirmation of the said Ser Bartholomeus as notary and scribe of the said guild, made by the aforesaid guild or the craftsmen of that guild, whenever and however they were performed.

## II. A penalty of one hundred shillings <note>original: "soldorum centum"</note> imposed on Consuls who do not assemble.

And they must stay and remain there to exercise their said office and to effectively carry out the business of the said guild and their office, with all malice and scheming removed, unless such days are holidays. This is under penalty of one hundred shillings in small Florentine pennies <note>original: "soldorum centum f. p." (florenorum parvorum)</note> for each of them and for each time they act against the aforesaid or fail to assemble. This fine is to be collected from them and from anyone so acting by the official of the University of the Merchant Court <note>original: "Mercantie," the Mercanzia, which oversaw all Florentine guilds</note> and of the merchants of the city of Florence existing at that time, and applied to the university...

# THE REFORM OF 1380
312

city of Florence, presented and approved by the undersigned approvers of the statutes of the guilds of the city of Florence.

### I. In favor of Ser Bartholommeo.

Firstly, whereas the vacancy of the office of the notary of the said guild—which ends, according to the custom observed in the past, every year on the first day of the month of January—brings very great harm to the aforementioned guild and to the litigants <note>original: "causanti," those with active legal cases</note> in the court of the said guild; and especially since it often happens that the election of the said notary is delayed, sometimes until the end of the said month of January; adding to the statute of the said guild, placed under the rubric of the election of the notary and his office and prohibition (1) due to the preoccupations of the consuls <note>The "Consoli" were the high-ranking elected officials who governed the guild</note> and other occurring matters; and until the new election is made, neither can the cases proceed, nor can the other affairs of the said guild be performed or exercised; wishing to provide healthfully for the indemnity of the said guild and of those who plead before the said consuls, it is provided, established, and ordained: that Ser Bartholommeo, son of Ser Nello Ghetti, who for many times past and at present is the notary and scribe of the said guild, may and shall have the power to perform and exercise all and each of the affairs and businesses of the said guild, and to cause to be written and recorded all and each of the cases, writings, and acts which might need to be written or recorded in the court of the consuls of the said guild, until such time as a new election of the notary of the said guild is made according to the form of the statutes of the said guild, and as if he were truly the notary and scribe of the said guild, and as if his election had not yet ended or expired. And that the same Ser Bartholommeo, until a new election is made by public instrument for the notary of the said guild according to the form of the statutes of the said guild speaking of the election of the notary, shall be bound and understood to be the notary, and held as the notary and scribe of the said guild, in everything and for everything and as to every matter, with the <term>customary</term> <note>original Latin: "consuetis"</note> authority and salary that are contained in the statutes and ordinances of the said guild, and as if the election and the term of the election made for him still endured. Notwithstanding in the aforesaid things or any of them any laws, statutes, provisions, and ordinances of the said guild, which by the aforesaid things, and regarding the aforesaid things only, are intended to be and are specially and generally repealed (2).

## II. That the plaintiff, having made a request, shall pay the fee; and the denying defendant, before being heard, shall pay.

Furthermore, they provided, deliberated, decreed, and ordained that in any dispute that shall be moved or aired in the future before the consuls of the said Guild <note>original: "dett'arte"; likely referring to one of the major Florentine trade guilds</note>, before any legal act proceeds—provided a formal request has been made—the plaintiff <term>actore: the party bringing the lawsuit</term> shall pay and be bound to pay to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the financial officer or treasurer</term> of the said Guild, receiving on behalf of the Guild, the customary fee which must be paid according to the form of the Guild statutes. And that the defendant <term>reo o vero convenuto: the party being sued</term>, appearing and denying the claim, before being heard in the matter, shall pay and be bound to pay to the chamberlain of the said Guild, receiving on behalf of the Guild, the fee of four denari for every lira of everything he denies or of its estimated value. In which fee and other expenses incurred in the dispute by the said defendant, the consuls shall be bound—under the bond and virtue of their sworn oath—to condemn the losing plaintiff to pay or restore to the said defendant who prevails in the case.

## III. Regarding the gift for the consuls.

Furthermore, they provided, decreed, and ordained that every consul of the said Guild should and must have for his gift <note>A "presente" was a customary allotment of goods given to officials upon taking office</note> 25 maple wood bowls and 25 beech wood bowls, four pounds of pepper, four ounces of saffron, four pounds of wax candles, and one basket <note>original: "zana"</note>, and no more or otherwise. And that the current chamberlain of the Guild, and whoever shall be in office at the time, shall be bound to buy the said things with the Guild's money, and may and must give or send them to each consul of the said Guild, both present and future, for his and their gift, freely and without penalty, without any further deliberation being required by the consuls or the council of the Guild.

### IIII-VI REFORM OF 1383

### IIII. Regarding the gift for the councilors.

Furthermore, they provided, decreed, and ordained that the councilors of the said guild <note>The Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries (Arte dei Medici e Speziali), one of the seven major guilds of Florence</note>, both present and future, shall and must have a gift from the funds of the said guild, namely the value of one gift given to one of the consuls. ### V. Regarding the penalty for those who do not come at the command of the consuls.

Furthermore, they provided, decreed, and ordained that all and each of the craftsmen of the said guild who shall be personally cited and requested on behalf of the consuls to come or assemble at the house or within the house of the said guild to treat and ordain the affairs of the said guild, or for any other reason, and shall disdain to come or appear or assemble, shall be understood to be and are *ipso facto* <note>By the very fact</note> condemned, and shall fall under a penalty of 10 soldi in small florins <note>original: "f. p." - fiorini piccioli, the silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note> for each of them not appearing or not coming, as is said, and for every instance. Which condemnation the consuls of the said guild are bound to collect or have collected within the eight days immediately following, under the penalty of perjury and by virtue and bond of their rendered oath. This is expressed and declared that, notwithstanding the aforesaid things or any of the aforesaid things, if it shall be deliberated or declared by the consuls or by two-thirds of them that such person or persons not appearing, as is said, have a legitimate excuse, they shall be understood to be and are *ipso facto* free and absolved from the said condemnation of 10 soldi.

# I, II REFORM OF 1385

necessity of the said guild <note>original: "arte" - referring to a professional guild or trade corporation</note>, it is decreed and ordained that in the house of the said guild there is and must be a large book, in which shall be written all the affairs of the said guild and all the debtors and creditors of the said guild, present and future, for giving and for receiving, each one individually under his own entry <margin>Version B: and by himself</margin> by name and surname <margin>Version B continues: as much the principal as the guarantor, and the amount they must give and receive</margin>, and the reasons for everything that shall be paid and received by these debtors and creditors, the time, the agreements, and the contracts that they might have <margin>Version B: will have</margin> with the said guild; and it shall be called the "Mirror of the Guild" <note>The "Specchio" was a common name for a primary ledger or public record book in medieval Italy</note>. And it must be written by the hand of the chamberlains <term>camarlinghi: financial administrators or treasurers</term> of the said guild who shall be in office at the time, or by their deputy, and in the vernacular <note>Italian rather than Latin</note>, so that everyone may be able to read and understand it (1).

## II. That the consuls and the chamberlain swear to collect [debts].

And that the consuls <term>consoli: the highest elected officials of the guild</term> who shall be in office at the time, and their chamberlains, are bound and must, at the beginning of their office—in addition to the other promises and oaths they are bound to make according to the form of the statutes of the said guild—promise and swear into the hands of the notary of the said guild to collect, according to their power, from the debtors who owe the guild any quantity of money or other thing for whatever reason written in the said book, everything that shall appear in the said book as owed by them or any of them; and this applies to the principals as well as the guarantors <term>mallevadori: individuals who provide a financial guarantee for another's debt</term> and from their heirs or from their assets; and also to collect and cause to be collected all the fines <note>original: "condempnagioni"</note> that they shall issue; and also from all the new members <note>original: "novitii"</note> who shall enter <margin>Version B: will enter</margin> the guild during their time, everything they ought to give by reason of the entry fee <note>original: "entratura"</note> to the guild, for which the term assigned to them for payment has passed; provided that from now on no <margin>Version B: not any</margin> new member is received or recorded in the guild who does not then pay his entry fee in full, or truly does not provide sufficient security through good guarantors, one or more, to pay by the deadline assigned to them by the consuls for payment; and also to collect and cause to be collected everything that through the said book appears that the guild ought to receive and have from any person for any reason.

### III. That no one, except for the chamberlain, shall receive the guild’s money; and how the guild’s money should be paid.

Likewise, that the money of the said guild must come into the hands of the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the chief financial officer or treasurer of the guild</term> of the said guild, and not to any other official of the same. This chamberlain, and no other official of the said guild, must and can receive the money of the said guild; and that which he receives he must record as income, and he cannot, nor should he, spend it, nor in any way record it as an expenditure, except for that which is deliberated by the consuls <term>consoli: the elected executive leaders of the guild</term> and councilors of the said guild and two members from each branch, whom the consuls shall elect, or two-thirds of them—excepting that which he is permitted to pay and spend according to the form of the statutes of the said guild or of the Merchant Court <term>Mercatantia: the Mercanzia, the overarching judicial body governing all Florentine guilds</term> or by the command of the seven officials of the Merchant Court. And regarding the guild's money that he receives in the absence of the guild’s notary, he is required to send the receipt to the notary so that he may record it as income in his book. This money, which the chamberlain shall receive for any reason, he is required and must record in the said ledger <term>speccio: a "mirror" or public ledger used to track debts and payments</term> under the account of the person who pays, and nonetheless record it as income in his own book of entries. Furthermore, the said chamberlain is required to write upon every petition for which a fee is paid the amount of the fee he receives, both from the petitioner and from the person being petitioned.

### IIII. That cases should not be examined in the audience chamber.

Likewise, that the consuls of the said guild, on the eight judicial days <note>original: "octo dì giuridichi"</note> in which, according to the form of the statutes of the said guild, they are required and must gather to render justice and to hear the disputes of the litigants before them, must not, nor can they, hear, understand, examine, decide, or terminate any dispute of the litigants before them, unless it is in the customary place and bench of the house of the said guild. And that in the audience chamber <term>audienzia: the formal hall for hearings</term> of the house of the said guild, they must not, nor can they, gather to hear, examine, or assist <margin>B: terminate</margin> in any dispute of any litigant before them, unless it is on an extraordinary day, or one on which they are not required to gather, or truly for questions or matters pertaining to the guild itself, under penalty for each consul who acts against this of five small lire <term>piccoli: "denari piccoli," the silver-based currency used for daily transactions in Florence</term>.

### I. That the office of the syndics shall last 4 months.

First, they provided, ordered, and established that the office of the <term>syndics</term> <note>officials responsible for auditing accounts and ensuring legal compliance</note> of the said Guild shall, in the future, last for four continuous months and no longer. And that the <term>consuls</term> <note>the highest-ranking leaders of the Guild</note> of the said Guild, at the beginning of each consulate's term, are bound and must draw from the bags—in which the names of the <term>artisans</term> <note>guild members</note> of said Guild are currently placed or will be placed in the future—three artisans for the office of the syndics. Specifically, one shall be drawn for each bag or each member of the three branches of the Guild, for a term of the four months immediately following. These men so drawn shall have the same and total <term>balìa</term> <note>extraordinary power or authority</note>, authority, and power which the syndics of the said Guild used to have when their office lasted for one year. And these syndics shall receive a gift from the aforesaid Guild, and the <term>chamberlain</term> <note>the financial treasurer</note> of said Guild shall be bound to give a gift to each of them, valued at two <term>lire</term> <note>the local currency</note> each and no more; this amount includes any gift or sum of money which, by any statute or ordinance of the Guild, the syndics were entitled to receive from the Guild (1).

### VI. Concerning the tinsmiths.

Furthermore, considering that the branch of the tinsmiths and flask-makers <note>original: "stagniai e fiaschai"</note>, in which there used to be a great number of craftsmen in the city of Florence, has greatly diminished due to the defect of the craftsmen of said branch and because of the poor workmanship in tin. For a long time now, they have practiced making said tin works by putting more lead into them than is appropriate, or otherwise using it incorrectly. Because of this, the merchants who used to come to Florence for said works no longer come, but instead provide for themselves in other foreign countries. This results in great loss for the craftsmen and in loss and shame for all the citizens of this city. Therefore, for the public utility, it is provided and ordained that no tinsmith or flask-maker, in any way subject to the said Guild, can or should put lead into any work of tin; and that whoever from this point forward shall work or make any work of tin, is bound and must work and make such work from good and pure tin. And in it, they cannot nor should they put or infuse lead in any way, under penalty of 10 silver soldi <note>The "soldo" was a silver coin; 20 soldi made one Lira.</note> for each of them and for each work. Excepted from this are inkwells, pipes <note>original: "condocti"</note>, bells, and tacks <note>original: "bullecte"</note>, in which excepted things the statute of the said Guild that speaks of this shall hold place. And in the said excepted things, it is not intended by this statute that it be provided otherwise. And that the Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the Guild.</note> of the said Guild are bound and must, under penalty of perjury and 5 Lire for each of them, at least once every month of their term of office, search and cause to be searched [the shops], and cause the said works made contrary to the said form to be destroyed, and condemn the guilty to the said penalties.

### VII. Note of what the Consuls must do when a question is before them regarding the raising of rents.

Furthermore, it is provided, established, and ordained that in any dispute that might be before the Consuls of the said Guild between the owner or owners or lords of the shops or warehouses <note>original: "fondachi" — large commercial buildings used for both storage and trade.</note> in which the said Guild or any branch of the said Guild is practiced, and the tenant or renter, by reason of an increase in the rent of such shop or warehouse; the Consuls of the said Guild, before whom the question is debated, shall summon at least six merchants and craftsmen from among the closest neighbors of such shop or warehouse, and seek from them under oath whether a higher or lower rent should be paid for it. Which inquiry having been made, the Consuls shall decide the question according to what shall seem to their conscience that

### V. That the notary of the guild may keep an assistant with him.

Furthermore, they provided and ordained that the notary and scribe of the said guild may have and keep with him a good, expert notary, a Florentine citizen, as his assistant <note>original: "coaiutore"</note>, which assistant may enact, write, do, and exercise everything that the said notary and scribe can do.

### VI. That no one can be a consul who holds any office of the commune.

Furthermore, they provided and deliberated that for the future, whoever of the said guild shall be drawn for the office of the guild consulate, who holds any office of the Commune of Florence, whether inside or outside, salaried or not—if he were drawn such that the office should begin on the day of the commencement of the office of the consulate or before, except for the Council of the People and of the Commune of Florence—he cannot be drawn or taken for that office of the consulate or accept it; but as one having a prohibition <note>term: divieto (a legal disqualification preventing someone from holding two offices simultaneously)</note>, he must be put back into the bag <note>The "bag" (borsa) held the names of eligible citizens for random drawing of offices.</note>, under the penalty of 25 pounds of small florins <note>original: "llire .xxv. di f. p." ->REFORM OF 1391 VI, VII<-

[The first half of the fine] shall go to the University of the <term>Mercantia</term> <note>The overarching guild organization or "Merchant's Court" in Florence</note>, and the other half to the <term>camarlingho</term> <note>The chamberlain or treasurer</note> of the said guild. And that the <term>consoli</term> <note>Consuls; the highest-ranking elected officials of the guild</note> currently in office must have the merchants and craftsmen of the said guild collect the money that is customarily paid for offerings before the feast of Saint Barnabas and of the Blessed Mary for several days, as they wish. And the merchants and craftsmen are required to pay as the consuls shall ordain, under penalty of one-fourth more (1).

### VII. That certain statutes and the scrutineers be read.

Furthermore, considering that many statutes are in force regarding the prohibitions and provisions of the offices of the said guild, which statutes are not observed due to disuse; and considering that it is good to resist [corruption] at the beginning and to provide at the beginning—that is, when the <term>squittini</term> <note>Scrutinies; the process of vetting and voting on candidates for office</note> and the <term>nborsationi</term> <note>Imborsations; the placing of eligible names into bags for random drawing</note> for the offices are performed—they therefore provided and ordained that in the future, whenever any scrutiny is held for any office of the said guild, the consuls of the guild then in office, having gathered those who are to cast their <term>fave</term> <note>Literally "beans," used as ballots in Florentine elections</note> in such a scrutiny, are bound and must—under penalty of one hundred <term>soldi</term> of <term>f. p.</term> <note>fiorini piccoli; "small florins" or silver-based currency used for local transactions</note> to each of them by the <term>sindichi</term> <note>Syndics; officials appointed to audit and judge the conduct of outgoing officers</note> who shall audit them, to be taken or deducted from their gift <note>The "presente" or customary payment/stipend given to officials</note>—cause to be read before such scrutineers all and each of the statutes and orders of the guild which in any way concern those who are prohibited or barred from the offices of the said guild. 

And having read them, they must swear, or give or have the oath given to the others in the hands of their notary, to cast their beans discreetly and for those whom they deem appropriate according to the form of the orders of the guild. The notary of the said guild must remind the said consuls of the aforementioned things, and make a public instrument <note>A formal legal document</note> of this reminder, so that they cannot claim ignorance of this. 

Deliberating nonetheless, that whoever in the future shall accept any office of the said guild against the prohibition of the statutes of the guild, no gift from the guild or from its chamberlain should be sent to him. Rather, the syndics of the guild, under penalty of perjury, shall deliberate and are bound to deliberate at the time of the audit that for such a person who accepts [office] against the aforesaid form, no gift shall be sent to him by the chamberlain of the guild; and if the chamberlain should send such a gift, he shall be condemned by the syndics who audit him to pay back the same amount plus ten pounds of small florins. The notary, under the bond of an oath, is bound to always read and notify such syndics [of these rules].

### VIII. Orders concerning the branch of the barbers.

Furthermore, considering that many scandals and many disputes arise every day within the branch of the barbers, and desiring to prevent such scandals and disputes, they provided that in the future no barber may or should form or contract any new partnership with any other barber, whether a master or a former apprentice; nor shall any partnership made or contracted between any barbers be valid, hold weight, or be observed, unless—before such partnership begins—a formal written agreement of consent between the parties is solemnly made in the records of the said Guild and by the hand of the notary of the said Guild or his assistant. Nevertheless, any barber who acts or contracts any partnership contrary to the aforesaid form, which is not recorded in the acts as stated, shall *ipso facto* <note>Latin: "by the very fact"</note> be understood to be and shall be fined 10 pounds in small florins <note>original: "llire .x. di f. p." referring to the 'lira di fiorini piccioli', the local currency of account in Florence</note> to be given and paid to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the financial officer or treasurer of the guild</term> of the said Guild as a penalty; to which payment he can and must be compelled by the messengers of the said Guild, without any other formal condemnation being made against him.

### VIIII. Ordinances concerning the apprentices of the barbers.

Furthermore, considering that frequently the apprentices of the barbers have turned against their masters by leaving them at their own pleasure, and also by opening a new shop near the shop of their master to the loss and prejudice of said master—from whom, by such proximity, they take away earnings and clientele <note>original: "aviamento", referring to the 'goodwill' or established customer base of a business</note>—and desiring to prevent such deceits, they deliberated that no apprentice of the said branch of barbers, or anyone who has been an apprentice with any barber, may, dare, or presume in the future—within the next three years from the day he leaves his master—to open or manage a shop for himself or join in partnership with any master barber within 40 cubits <term>braccia: a Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm; 40 braccia is approximately 23 meters</term> of the shop of his master, under penalty of 50 pounds in small florins, (1) of which half shall go to the chamberlain of the said Guild for the Guild's use, and the other half to the master with whom he had been; for which penalty he must be summarily condemned by the consuls <term>consoli: the elected leaders and judges of the guild</term> of the said Guild. Nor may such an apprentice, or any apprentice of barbers, be permitted to leave his master to go stay with anyone else to open a new shop or join in partnership with anyone, or any other...

## II. When the offerings ought to be collected.

Furthermore, considering that for the taxes of the said guild—which are made every year for the offerings given on the feast of Saint Mary in the month of August and on the feast of the Blessed Barnabas <note>St. Barnabas (June 11) was a significant feast day in Florence, marking the victory at the Battle of Campaldino</note> until now—the collection of the said taxes has proceeded in an ordinary manner (1), and since nothing is then collected or demanded from those not paying on those days in which the said offerings <term>oblationi: ritual offerings or mandatory contributions made on feast days</term> are made, to the prejudice of the said guild and to the burden of those who are paying and obedient, it is provided and ordained that a register be made in and for the said guild. In this register, all and each of those described and matriculated <term>matricola: the official membership roll of the guild</term>, as well as those who shall be described or matriculated in the roll of the said guild, shall be noted and written in alphabetical order with organized spaces, so that next to the name of each person, the payments of several years can be written. And whoever is described in the said register must and shall be required every year, throughout the month of May, to give and pay to the chamberlain of the said guild—receiving on behalf of the said guild for the burden the guild bears for the offerings—twelve pence in small florins <note>original: "soldi .XII. di f. p." (fiorini piccioli), the silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note>, under penalty of double the amount. And once the month of May has passed, the chamberlain is bound and must, under penalty of perjury, collect and cause to be collected from everyone who has not paid within the term, without any remission, the ordained tax with the penalty of the double ordained above. Anyone who is found not to have paid his taxes at the time he is drawn or appointed to any office of the said guild, cannot and must not accept or exercise that office in any way, unless first to the chamberlain...

### III. That gifts be sent to the officials of the guild, and money should not be given to them.

Furthermore, considering that, both for the honor of the guild that sends them and for the merchants and artisans who receive the gifts for their offices, it is ordained that items should be sent as gifts; yet it sometimes happens that some ask for and collect money from the chamberlain rather than the ordained items, which is not an honorable thing; it is provided and ordained that the chamberlain of the said guild may not send to any outgoing official of the said guild anything for the said gifts except the ordained items. And that the syndics, who shall be deputized to audit, are required and must, within ten days of the month, have acquitted or condemned the consuls, chamberlain, and the other officials of the said guild according to the orders of the said guild, under the penalty of 10 lire in small florins for each person.

[The council ordered that if a doctor] send a companion, whether a physician <note>original: "fisico," a doctor of internal medicine</note> or a surgeon <term>cerusico: a practitioner who performed manual operations, distinct from the university-educated physician</term>, otherwise they must not treat the patient, under penalty of 40 soldi in small florins (1). ### VIII. That a book be made, in which all those of the College of Physicians are recorded.

Furthermore, they deliberated and provided—so that it may be known and manifest who are (3) and are understood to be members of the College of Physicians of the city of Florence—that for the future there shall be ordered and made by the said College a book. This book shall and must remain with the Provost of the said College, or else with the notary and scribe of the Guild and College of Physicians, Apothecaries, and Mercers <term>spetiali e merciai: the powerful Florentine guild (Arte) that included doctors, pharmacists, and merchants of spices and textiles</term>. In this book, the said notary shall write and note each and every person who is or shall be in the aforementioned College in this manner:

First, the names of each and every physician and doctor currently in the said College shall be noted and written in the said book, as will appear therein. And each and every person shall be understood to be of the aforementioned College who is found written in the said book by the hand of the notary of the said Guild, and no one else, unless they have been approved, found [eligible], and have paid as is ordered below. 

That is, for each and every person for whom it is deliberated and the motion is passed by the aforementioned College—or by two-thirds of the said College, or at least by two-thirds of the members from the city of Florence—via a secret ballot <term>scruptineo: a vote using black and white beans to ensure anonymity</term> to be inscribed in the book and register <term>matricola: the official membership roll of a guild</term> of the College by the notary of the said Guild or his assistant, they must be written and noted in the said book and register following those mentioned before. 

This shall be done only after the person to be inscribed has first taken an oath in the hands of the said notary to obey the lawful and honest commands of the Provost of the said College, and to observe the statutes—both those already made and those to be made—and the laudable observances of the said College. And they must first pay, if they are a citizen or native of the city or territory of Florence, two gold florins for entry into the aforementioned College; and if they are a foreigner, four gold florins for the said entry. Half of this shall go to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the financial officer or treasurer</term> of the said Guild, receiving it for the Guild, and the other half to the Provost of the College, or the notary of the Guild, or the chamberlain of the said College who shall be appointed to receive it for the said College.

# VIIII. Those who may participate in the examination of a candidate, and how much they should receive from the examinee.

Furthermore, they provided, deliberated, and ordained that no member of the aforementioned college <note>The College of Doctors and Apothecaries</note> who does not reside familiarly and continuously within the city of Florence may be present at any examination conducted for someone wishing to receive a doctorate, nor enjoy any privilege of the said college while residing with their family outside the city of Florence, until after their return to reside in the city of Florence they have lived there with their family for at least two months. And likewise, whoever is accustomed to residing there but moves their residence and family from the said city to another place, for as long as they reside in that other place, unless they have first returned and resided, as stated, for at least two months, they shall be deprived of the present and future examinations and other emoluments <note>fees or profits</note> that should come to them from such. And so that between the said college and the doctors of the said college and the person to be examined no scandal may arise by reason of the report made to them regarding the examination to be held; and so that by reason of the impossibility of paying the salary <note>the examination fee</note> which must be paid to the said doctors for the said examination, the person to be examined does not remain unproven or unapproved while observing the customary order, it is ordained that no member of the said college of physicians may receive for his salary more than one gold florin <note>term: fiorino d'oro; the standard high-value currency of Florence</note> at most, nor can he be forced to receive less, unless it has been deliberated and obtained by black and white beans <note>a method of secret voting using colored beans to signify 'yes' or 'no'</note> by the provost and two-thirds of the physicians of the said college. The provost shall receive double, that is, two gold florins, and at the assembly <gloss>original: in conventu</gloss> the cap <note>the ceremonial doctoral biretta</note> as is customary. And that the provost of the said college of physicians can and is also bound and must punish and fine each of the said doctors who does not observe the aforesaid things, or acts or goes against them, in the amount of 10 pounds of small florins <note>term: lire di fiorini piccioli; a lesser currency used for local fines</note> for each person and for every instance.

## X. No one who lectures in the Studio of Florence can be the Provost of the Physicians.

Furthermore, they provided and ordained that in the future no one can be the provost of the said college of physicians who is lecturing or has been deputed to lecture in the Studio of Florence <note>The "Studio Fiorentino" was the university of Florence, founded in 1321</note>. And whoever should be drawn as provost of the said college at a time when he is lecturing, being under a prohibition, shall be passed over and his name replaced in the bag <note>referring to the leather bags (borse) used in the Florentine lottery system for selecting officials</note>.

### III. It has no standing if the refusal is made through fear or threats.

And that which is said above regarding the refusal <note>original: "rifiutagione"; here referring to the formal relinquishing of a lease or right of entry</note> shall hold true, provided that said refusal was not made out of fear of threats or intimidation; and especially not due to any pact, command, or agreement made by the landlord or landlords <note>original: "hoste o hosti"</note> through which the property was refused. And no refusal made by one or some of the aforementioned parties shall be valid where there are multiple partners, unless the refusal is made by the majority of the partners who held the lease <note>original: "condocto"</note>, or who had rights or interests in the location. Except that, prior to the refusal, a partner must first offer the property to their fellow partner—should they want it for themselves—at the same price that could be obtained from other persons. 

But if several brothers <note>original: "frategli"; often used to denote close business associates or literal family members in a firm</note> or indeed partners have together leased any shop <term>bottega: a workshop or retail space</term>, warehouse <term>fondaco: a combined storage facility and merchant office</term>, or land, or have been established therein and later wish to divide, and should they not be in agreement on the manner of dividing said shop, or if a dispute should arise between them for that reason, the Consuls <note>The elected leaders of the Guild</term> of the said Guild can and must—at the petition of said partners or brothers or any one of them—appraise or have appraised in money the value of the rights to such shop or warehouse. And let lots be drawn for them; and to whomsoever the lot falls, that right of entry <note>original: "intratura"; the legal right to occupy a commercial space</note> shall remain and be granted, with the obligation to compensate the brothers or partners according to the manner in which said lots were cast.

---

### IIII. The refusal is not valid unless approved by the consuls and advisors.

And no refusal made by the men of the said Guild regarding any of the aforementioned places or things shall be valid unless it is first approved by the Consuls and advisors of the said Guild, or by two-thirds of them, by secret ballot <note>original: "scruptineo"</note> with black and white beans <note>A traditional Florentine voting method: black for 'yes', white for 'no'</note>. This must be done under oath, administered to each of them by the notary of the Guild or his assistant, to judge uprightly and according to their pure conscience; otherwise, the refusal shall be regarded as made not spontaneously, but through fear, and shall be treated as if it never occurred.

# VIII-X REFORM OF 1393

...or if anyone shall purchase anew, or acquire by any title, reason, or method, any such shops, warehouses, or lands, whether in whole or in part; and if he wishes to use it, in whole or in part, for himself or for his own residence, or for his own labor, craft, or service to be performed or exercised therein, against the will of the person who is found to be staying, working, or having work done therein, or who holds it under lease; [he may only do so] immediately after such new purchaser or acquirer has possessed it for five years, and not before.

## VIIII. He who has purchased fictitiously cannot evict the tenant.

And if anyone makes a fictitious purchase, or by any other fictitious pretext or title acquires or claims to have acquired any such shops, warehouses, or lands, he shall not be able, nor ought he in any way, to evict the <term>lessee</term> <note>original: "conductore"; a person holding a formal lease</note> or <term>tenant</term> <note>original: "pigionale"; one who pays "pigione" or rent, often for shorter terms</note> of such shop, warehouse, land, or person staying or residing therein; nor shall he take it from them, nor raise or move any dispute or innovation against them, under penalty of one hundred gold florins. This fine is to be collected from him by the consuls of the said Guild, with one half applied to the said Guild and the other half to the lessee or tenant who was thus wronged. Nevertheless, he shall be bound and must allow—and may be compelled by the consuls of the said Guild to allow—the said lessee and tenant to stay and reside therein; the consuls shall condemn and fine him once or more, and bar him from the Guild, as shall seem appropriate to the consuls of the said Guild <note>Refers to Rubric LIII, g</note>.

## X. Every purchase is understood to be fictitious until it is approved as true by the consuls and advisors.

And every purchase and each acquisition made of any such shops, warehouses, or lands shall be understood to be fictitious and not true until such time as it is approved as true by the consuls and advisors of the said Guild, in the same manner as stated above regarding the right of refusal <note>Refers to Rubric LIII, g</note>.

# REFORM OF 1393 XI, XII

### XI. He who is evicted and does not appear within five years shall not be heard thereafter.

And if within the said period of the said five years, the person from whom any such shops, warehouses <note>original: "fondachi" - a merchant's combined warehouse and residence</note>, or lands were taken, does not bring a grievance or complaint before the said Consuls of the said Guild <note>The "Consuls" were the elected officials who governed the guild and acted as judges in trade disputes</note> in such a way that it appears in the acts of the court of the said Guild, from that time forward he shall not be heard, nor shall anyone acting for him or anyone claiming any right through him.

### XII. He who does not pay the rent shall be compelled to pay and to provide security for the future.

And if any member of this Guild does not pay the customary rent to the landlord or landlords at the due or customary term, the Consuls of the said Guild shall be bound, at the petition of any landlord, to compel and burden such non-payer, by every effective means, those unwilling to pay what they owe to their landlords; and furthermore, [the tenant must] give and provide sufficient guarantors <note>original: "mallevadori" - individuals who legally pledged to pay the debt if the tenant defaulted</note> to pay the rent that they must pay for the future time, if that person wishes to keep that warehouse, shop, land, or place. If he does not make this payment, it must be made at least within one month thereafter. And if these guarantors do not pay within the term assigned by the Consuls of the said Guild—which term cannot exceed two months from the day the petition or written complaint regarding the aforementioned matters was brought to the Consuls of the said Guild—the Consuls themselves are bound immediately, by virtue of their sworn oath, in each of these cases, to give and grant license to the other or others to whom the landlord wishes to lease or let, and for anyone to take or hold such shop, warehouse, and land. 

Provided that first, in each of the aforesaid cases, the new person or persons taking, leasing, or acquiring the property shall first pay to the tenant who was staying, or who was found staying or living in such shop, warehouse, or land, everything that is due to him as the price for the right of "entry," "stay," and "residence" <note>original: "entratura, stantia e residentia" - these terms refer to the "goodwill" or the value of the established business location that a tenant built up</note> of such shop, warehouse, or land taken; which the first tenant or resident in such warehouse, shop, or land had or which belonged to him by reason of or by virtue of entry and stay, as has been said. And if there should be a dispute regarding the price or the amount of the price for such rights, the amount of such price shall be determined by the declaration made by the Consuls and Councilors of the said Guild, or by two-thirds of them, or by those to whom the said parties shall entrust the matter. # XII-XIIII REFORM OF 1393
### 356

The aforementioned matters shall extend to things present, past, and future, and shall apply to shops, warehouses <note>original: "fondachi" - a combined warehouse, office, and residence for merchants</note>, and lands existing outside in the countryside <note>original: "contado" - the rural territory surrounding and governed by Florence</note> and district of Florence, as well as within the city itself.

<header>REFORM OF 1394</header>

# I. That the consuls shall cause usury to be restored by those under their jurisdiction.

*a.* First, noticing and considering that—according to what has reached the ears and notice of the said officials—it has been heard that many craftsmen of the said Guild <note>The Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers (Medici e Speziali)</note>, enrolled in the said Guild and subject to it, have lent and do lend their money at usury <note>Interest-bearing loans, which were religiously and legally condemned at the time</note>. This thing is against the divine commandments and results in danger to their souls and in shame to the aforesaid Guild and its craftsmen. Wishing for the good and peace of the aforesaid Guild and craftsmen, and so that the said craftsmen, members, and subjects of the said Guild may more extensively carry out their merchandise and trade belonging to the said Guild, and convert their money into the craft of the said Guild, they provided that all and each of the statutes of the City of Florence and of the aforesaid Guild which speak against whoever lends for profit or usury are hereby approved, ratified, and affirmed. They provided, ordained, and decreed that in the future no doctor, apothecary, grocer, or craftsman of the said Guild, or subject to said Guild, shall dare or presume to lend at usury—whether against a pledge <note>Collateral</note> or by public instruments <note>Notarized contracts</note> or in any other manner of usury, directly or indirectly—to any person or persons, commune or corporation, of whatever condition or status they may be.

*b.* And if any of the aforesaid should act to the contrary, anyone so borrowing, and their heirs and successors, may and shall be permitted, once or more, to present a petition and complaint before the Consuls <note>The elected leaders and judges of the Guild</note> of the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers existing at that time, and to demand from the said doctors, apothecaries, grocers, and subjects of the Guild so lending at usury, that quantity or those sums of money which they had given or paid as usury, or in the name or by reason of usury.

*c.* And that the Consuls of the said Guild then in office, assembled according to custom, having heard the process of the said petition and complaint presented by the said borrower, shall be bound and must give and proffer sentence in favor of such person or persons so demanding the usury, against the said doctor, apothecary, grocer, or subject of the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers who, as is said, shall have lent. This sentence shall be for that quantity of money which they shall see that the said doctor, apothecary, grocer, member, or subject truly ought to give back for the said usury, or that the borrower ought to receive for the said usury taken from him.

*d.* And that, once the said sentence has been handed down by the aforementioned consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> according to the form of the statutes of the said guild against the said doctor, apothecary, or grocer—whether matriculated <note>A formal member of the guild</note> or subject to the said guild of doctors, apothecaries, and grocers—concerning the requested quantity or quantities, such doctor, apothecary, grocer, or craftsman matriculated or described in the said guild shall be bound and must effectively pay, in the name of a penalty for the said loan or exchange made by him, to the receiving chamberlain <note>The guild's treasurer</note> of the said guild, within ten days from the date of the sentence, an amount equal to one-fourth of the total quantity of money and gold florins <note>The standard gold currency of Florence</note> contained in the sentence given against such doctor, apothecary, grocer, or craftsman.

*e.* And that the said consuls are bound and must—under penalty of 25 lire each, to be applied to the University of the Merchantry <note>The Mercanzia, the overarching commercial court in Florence</note> and the merchants of the city of Florence—collect or cause to be collected the said penalty or fourth part from the said doctors, apothecaries, and grocers, whether matriculated or subject to the guild. They shall compel them through personal capture and detention, using any rector, judge, or official of the city of Florence. And the consuls of the said guild currently in office, along with any number of the *aroti* <note>Additional advisors or adjuncts to the guild council</note> of the said guild, may not and must not in any way waive, remit, cancel, or annul the said penalty. And if they act to the contrary, such action shall not be valid or hold any legal weight and shall be considered null.

*f.* And that the present or future notary of the said guild may not, nor should he dare or presume—under penalty of 25 lire of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli, the silver-based currency used for smaller transactions</note> to be deducted from his salary and applied to the guild—to write any proposal or deliberation made or intended to be made against the contents of this chapter. All other statutes and corrections of statutes concerning doctors, apothecaries, grocers, and craftsmen of the said guild, or those subject to it, existing in the volume of the guild's statutes regarding those who lend at usury <note>The practice of charging excessive interest, often legally or religiously prohibited</note>, are understood to be confirmed and approved by this present chapter.

*g.* And that the consuls of the said guild currently in office are bound and must, every year in the month of January, notify and bring to the memory of all doctors, apothecaries, grocers, and craftsmen of the guild this present statute and all it contains, so that they cannot claim or allege any ignorance regarding the aforementioned matters.

### I. How much the chamberlain should receive as a fee from those in litigation.

Firstly, considering that by the form of the statutes of the said guild, each litigant in the court of the said guild is bound and must—both the plaintiff making the demand and the defendant denying it—pay as a fee <note>original: "diritto"; a legal filing fee or tax on the value of the lawsuit</note> based on the amount demanded and the amount denied or that might be denied, to the chamberlain <note>term: "camarlingho" — the financial officer or treasurer of the guild</note> of the said guild, up to any amount, four pence <note>original: "denari quattro"</note> for every pound <note>original: "lira"</note>; and this often results in a very great burden for those who wish to bring claims in the said court for large sums of money; and therefore, wishing to make such a statute more fair and to correct it following the example of other courts where such a fee is paid, they provided and deliberated that for the future everyone, both the claimant and the denier, is bound and must pay to the chamberlain of the guild, in the name of the fee for the amount demanded or its estimated value, four pence per pound, provided that for whatever quantity and sum might be demanded or denied, however large it may be, such claimant or denier shall not pay, nor be bound, nor owe more than the amount of 30 pounds in small florins <note>term: "f. p." (fiorini piccoli) — the silver-based currency used for local wages and fees, distinct from the gold florin</note>; so that the amount of 30 pounds in small florins, paid as a fee by both the claimant and the denier, shall be understood to be and is sufficient payment for any amount which might be demanded or denied, however large it may be, and that the said fee be paid

And furthermore, that every election and appointment, drawing <note>extractione: the process of drawing names from a bag or purse for office</note>, or confirmation made in any way in the past of any notary as a notary or indeed as a scribe, or of any office of the said Guild <note>dett’arte: referring here to the Guild of Judges and Notaries or the Merchant Court</note> or University <note>università: used here in the medieval sense of a corporate body or association</note>, shall be and is understood to be by this reason null, void, revoked, and invalid. It shall not be valid or hold for any reason or manner, except for one year, beginning from the day mentioned therein. And if multiple elections, drawings, confirmations, or appointments were made of one notary as a notary or scribe or other official of the said Guild, these shall also be null and shall not be valid in any way, except for one year in total for all such elections, confirmations, or appointments. Nevertheless, the current year shall continue so that the present year may be completed according to the election, confirmation, drawing, or appointment already made. And from this moment forward, the aforementioned officials and statute-makers quashed, annulled, and revoked each and every election, appointment, drawing, and confirmation already made, and those yet to be made by anyone or in any manner, unless they are made for one year and in the manner and form aforesaid; provided that the election, confirmation, drawing, or appointment already made may complete the office of one year currently in progress, as stated.

c. And that no notary may further accept, take, perform, or exercise any office in any way, directly or indirectly, in or for the said Guild or University—whether by himself or through his coadjutor <note>assistant</note> or substitute or otherwise, or by himself or through others—nor go to or remain in that office, nor perform or cause to be performed anything pertaining to that office or dependent upon it. Furthermore, they may not request <note>rogare: the formal legal act of a notary witnessing and drafting a document</note> or write sentences of the Consuls or other acts of any such office, nor do any other thing, except for the instruments and writings of such elections, drawings, confirmations, or appointments that might be made, unless he has been elected, drawn, confirmed, or appointed as stated above, and in the manner and form aforesaid. And his confirmation, election, or drawing must appear by public writing <note>a formal notarized document</note>. And whoever acts or attempts to act against the aforesaid things contained in the present statute, addition, or order, or any part of them, by that very deed <note>original: "esso facto"; note (a) clarifies this as the Latin "ipso facto"</note> shall incur and be understood to have incurred the penalty of one hundred gold florins <note>fiorini d'oro: the high-value gold currency of Florence</note> for each person and for each instance. Half of this shall be paid and applied to the Chamberlain <note>camarlingho: the financial treasurer</note> of the Chamber of the Commune of Florence, receiving it for the Commune of Florence, and the other half to the Chamberlain or guardians of the University of Merchants and of the Merchant Court <note>Mercatantia: the powerful judicial body governing Florentine trade</note> of the city of Florence, receiving it for the said University; for which penalties they may indeed be condemned by the very deed.

# THE REFORMS OF 1401

# I. Those who may exercise the office for the chamberlain of the guild.

First, correcting the statute placed under the heading of the election of the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the chief financial officer or treasurer of a guild or municipality</term> and of his office and prohibition (1) on page VII, they provided, ordered, and deliberated that the chamberlain of the said Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers <note>original: "medici spetiali e merciai"</note>, who for the time shall be elected, drawn by lot, or deputed as chamberlain for the said guild and university, must and shall be bound to exercise his said office personally, by himself or by a son, a grandson of a son or of a brother born of the same father, or by his business partner, and not by others or in any other manner, under the penalty of 25 lire to be paid by anyone who acts to the contrary and for every such instance. And that no one else, of whatever condition they may be, shall dare or presume to perform or exercise the office of the said guild for any chamberlain, unless as a son, grandson, or partner of such a chamberlain who has been so drawn, elected, or assumed as chamberlain of the said guild, under the said penalty of 25 lire to be paid to the aforementioned guild. And if it should be done otherwise, or if any syndic <term>sindico: an official appointed to audit or review the accounts and conduct of outgoing officers</term>—who shall be appointed for the time to audit such a chamberlain—should act against the aforesaid rules, the expenses incurred by the said chamberlain who acted against the aforesaid rules in any way may not be admitted to his account or as an expenditure, under the said penalty of 25 small Florentine lire <note>original: "llire .xxv. f. p." referring to 'fiorini piccoli' or small silver-based currency</note> for every syndic, to be paid by them in fact to the chamberlain of the said guild (2).

In the name of God, amen. In the year of the Lord 1401, 10th indiction, on the 21st day of the month of December.
Sir Locto di Vanni Castellani,
Sir Bartholommeo di Tommaso Popoleschi,
Piero di Iacopo Baroncelli,
Alberto di Zanobi Alberti,
Chimento di Stefano,
Barduccio Octavanti,
Scolaio di Lapo Ciacchi, and
Lorenzo di Giovanni di Lorenzo, Florentine citizens, deputies [etc.], gathered in Florence in the house of the Guild of Master Woodworkers <note>original: "legnaiuoli grossi"</note> of the city of Florence [etc.], the aforementioned Sir Locto and Piero being absent [etc.], approved [etc.], of which approval it appears in the register of the said statutes by the hand of Ser Zanobi di Dato (a) from Gangalandi, Florentine notary [etc.].
