# II, III REFORM OF 1403

### II. That the overseers of Saint Barnabas must hold the feast of Saint Barnabas and what they may spend, namely 50 pounds.

Furthermore, considering that the amount of 35 pounds in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli," the local currency used for daily transactions in Florence</note>, which was provided and ordained in the past to be spent by the chamberlain <note>term: "camarlingho" (treasurer or financial administrator of the guild)</note> of the Works of Saint Barnabas <note>note: The "Opera di San Bernaba" was a religious and charitable committee within the guild responsible for the church or chapel dedicated to the saint</note> each year during and around the feast of Saint Barnabas, has not been sufficient due to rising costs, nor will it be sufficient in the future; and also wishing to prevent superfluous expenses from being incurred in the times to come during said feast, they provided, ordained, and deliberated that the overseers <note>term: "operai" (lay administrators responsible for the maintenance and activities of a religious building)</note> of said Works existing at any given time shall be bound and must provide for the aforementioned feast each year. They must organize it themselves or through those they appoint, and for said feast and matters connected to and depending on it, they may in no way spend whatever and however much seems fit to their discretion, provided that they cannot exceed the amount of 50 pounds in small florins. And the chamberlain of said Works is bound to pay and spend up to said amount of 50 pounds for and around said feast, as shall be deliberated by the said overseers. And whatever might be spent by the said chamberlain beyond or otherwise than what is ordained above, it shall be understood that the said chamberlain has spent it from his own personal funds, and it must not be credited to his accounts by the auditors <note>term: "sindichi" (officials appointed to review and verify the financial accounts of guild officers)</note> who shall audit him. And the said overseers, within eight days following the day the said feast is held, are bound and must show the account and reckoning of the expenses they have made regarding the said feast to the consuls <note>term: "consoli" (the highest-ranking elected leaders of the guild)</note> of said guild, so that such demonstration appears in and through the acts of said guild, under penalty of 10 pounds in small florins for each of them.

### III. That the chamberlain may not spend anything without the appropriation of the consuls.

Furthermore, considering that through various statutes of the said guild, the chamberlain is permitted in many cases to pay and spend the money of the said guild without an appropriation <note>term: "stanziamento" (a formal authorization or allocation of funds by a governing body)</note> from the consuls of the said guild—a thing which does not bring honor to the office of the said consuls—they provided, ordained, and deliberated that the chamberlain of the said guild for the time being may not give, pay, spend, or record as an expenditure any salaries, gifts, or any other thing, unless preceded by the appropriation of the consuls of the said guild; of which appropriation he is bound to provide proof to the auditors who shall audit him. Otherwise, it shall be understood that he has spent from his own pocket whatever—

# REFORM OF 1403 III, IV

...that he is found to have spent for the <term>syndics</term><note>officials appointed to audit accounts or represent the guild's interests</note>, for which he cannot show that an appropriation was made by the aforementioned <term>consuls</term><note>the highest elected leaders of the guild</note>. And that this <term>chamberlain</term><note>the treasurer or financial officer, known as the 'camarlingho'</note>, and also the chamberlain of the Works of Saint Barnabas, within eight days from the day their accounts are audited, shall be bound and must hand over and pay every amount of money from their office remaining with them to their successor, under penalty of an additional quarter of the sum and under penalty of losing the <insert>salary</insert> gift they were to receive for the exercise of such office. If the chamberlain of said guild should send this gift to one who has not observed the aforesaid rules, he shall be bound to return it to the said guild without fail.

### IV. Measure of beaten gold and silver.

Furthermore, considering that the craftsmen called <term>gold-beaters</term><note>artisans who hammer gold into extremely thin sheets or foil</note> are members of the said guild, and that for the prices of the beaten gold and silver they sell, no rule of weight or measure has been given, as is commonly given to all other merchandise; therefore, they provided etc. that these gold-beaters in the future may not, nor should they dare or presume to sell to any citizen or foreigner beaten gold or silver, the piece of which is smaller than the forms written below; that is, that every piece of pure gold or fine gold must and shall be of the size and according to the measure ordained by the consuls of the said guild. Which measure is more than a ninth part and less than an eighth part of a <term>braccio</term><note>a 'cubit' or 'arm's length,' a standard Florentine unit of measurement roughly equal to 58 centimeters</note> according to the Florentine measure; and every piece of <term>half-gold</term><note>gold leaf alloyed with silver or another metal</note> and of silver must and shall be of the size and according to the other larger measure ordained by the said consuls—namely, larger than an eighth part and smaller <margin>(1)</margin> than a seventh part of the aforementioned *braccio*, under the penalty of 12 <term>small florins</term><note>denari di fiorini piccoli, the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note> for every piece found to be smaller than the aforesaid measures or any one of them. And that the consuls must continually keep the said measures ordained by them in their possession or with the notary of the said guild, marked with their <term>stamp</term><note>an official seal or brand to guarantee authenticity</note>, and give the said measures so marked to the <term>searchers</term><note>inspectors appointed to uncover guild violations</note> who must search for prohibited things among the craftsmen of the said guild; and by these searchers, have them search with the said measure and investigate whether the aforesaid things are observed; and those found guilty, they shall punish and condemn according to the form of the present ordinance <margin>(2)</margin>.

# V. That no one may practice the craft unless they are first enrolled in the register.

Furthermore, considering that many have become accustomed to opening shops and practicing the craft of doctors, apothecaries, and grocers <note>The "Merciai" or grocers/merchants dealt in a wide variety of goods including spices, pigments, and textiles.</note>, or any branch of the said crafts, before they are enrolled in the register <term>matricola: the official membership roll of a guild</term> of the said craft; and wishing to prevent such presumption, they have provided etc. that in the future no one, of whatever state or condition they may be, may, dare, or presume to set up a shop or warehouse <term>fondaco: a combined warehouse and place of business</term>, or indeed perform any activity belonging to the said craft, or open a shop or work in one, or perform or cause to be performed any work, nor enroll themselves in partnership with anyone <margin>B: or associate with any enrolled member.</margin> in the said craft to practice any branch of the said craft, unless they first swear an oath or submit themselves to the aforementioned guild and have themselves recorded in the register of the said craft, and have paid in full to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the guild's treasurer</term> of the said craft, receiving on behalf of the craft, whatever is owed in the name of registration and entry fees according to the orders of the said craft. 

And whoever has already opened a shop or entered into a partnership or begun to practice any branch of the said craft without having first done what is stated above, must, within the coming month of January, be bound and required to have done the same as ordained above, or close the already opened shop and abstain entirely from the practice of the craft, under the penalty that <margin>B: to anyone.</margin> acts against the present ordinance as shall seem fitting to the consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild.</note> of the said craft existing at the time; which penalty shall not be greater than 15 pounds of small florins <note>original: "llire .xv. di f. p." (fiorini piccioli), the local currency used for smaller transactions.</note>, nor less than 10 pounds of small florins. Within which penalty the aforementioned consuls must condemn anyone who acts against this within eight days from the day it comes to their notice, under penalty of losing their present <note>A "present" or "presente" refers to the salary or stipend paid to the consuls for their service.</note>. Which present the chamberlain, whose responsibility it is, may not send to such consuls who have been negligent in the aforementioned matters; and if he should send it, it shall be understood that he has sent and paid it from his own funds. And these matters may be investigated at any time and by any office of syndication or consulate of the said craft, and such chamberlain may be compelled to restore to the guild from his own property as much as he sent against the form of the present ordinance.

## VI. That the barber shall not be heard unless he has first paid the fee.

Furthermore, they deliberated and provided that no barber, who might bring a verbal complaint <note>Barbers were often affiliated with the medical guilds as they performed minor surgeries and bloodletting.</note>, as they are accustomed to do, against a student of—

# REFORM OF 1403 VI-VIII

any matter that does not involve a specific determined amount, shall be heard, unless he first pays to the chamberlain <note>original: "camerlingho"; the guild's financial treasurer</note> of the said guild 10 soldi in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli," the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note>. And conversely, no apprentice of the barbers shall be heard in the said case against his master, unless he first pays five soldi in small florins in the name of the law.

### VII. What the messengers must receive from the chamberlain every year in the month of January.

Furthermore, considering the labors that fall upon the messengers <note>original: "messi"; officials responsible for delivering summons and notices</note> of the said guild, they provided that every year in the month of January, the chamberlain of the said guild is bound and must give to each of the messengers of the said guild half a pound of pepper, half an ounce of saffron, and two bowls.

### VIII. Concerning the observance of feast days.

<margin>(1) Rubric LV.</margin>
Furthermore, considering the statute which arranges for the punishment of those who do not observe the feast days and which days must be observed (1), and adding to, renewing, and correcting that statute, so that the craftsmen of the said guild—who through lack of habit do not know how to bring themselves to observe them—may be more strictly bound through fear of the penalty, they provided, ordered, and deliberated that the days of Easter and Sundays and the other days which are commanded by the Church to be observed, and also the feast of Saint Barnabas <note>June 11th; a significant Florentine holiday commemorating the Battle of Campaldino</note> which occurs in the month of June, must in the future be observed and celebrated by all craftsmen of the said guild. And on such days, no one shall dare or presume to keep a shop open, to sell, buy, or trade, unless they were things necessary for the bodies of the dead, or medicines, or other things necessary for the sick, or for some other necessity such that, if they did not sell, some scandal would likely arise, under the penalty of 20 soldi in small florins for each person and for each time. And that the notary and chamberlain of the said guild, and each of them, are bound and must urge the messengers to search and investigate whoever might attempt the contrary. And all and each of those, or any one of them, who shall be reported to have done the contrary, the notary of the said guild—under the penalty of five pounds in small florins—must note and record, and within the next two days following the date of such report, cause a distraint <note>original: "pegniorare"; the legal seizure of property to settle a debt or fine</note> to be made for the said penalty of 20 soldi in small florins. Once the pledge is taken, after eight days have passed from the day of the seizure, if that person whose property was seized has not paid or has not been declared by the consuls <note>the highest elected officials of the guild</note> as not owing—

### VIIII. That the apprentices of barbers cannot place themselves as apprentices near the shop of their first master.

Furthermore, having regard to the statute and order made in 1391 in which it is provided that no apprentice, who stays or had stayed as an apprentice with any barber, may—within three years from the day he leaves his master—set up or manage a shop for himself, nor join with any master barber near the shop of his said master within 40 *braccia* <note>A *braccio* (plural *braccia*) was a Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters. 40 braccia is approximately 23 meters.</note>, under the penalty contained in the said statute (2); and considering that no apprentice <margin>B: many apprentices</margin>, after the said ordinance was made, has left his master and—contrary to the form of the said statute and in fraud of the said statute—pretended to place themselves as apprentices with those who never were, nor are fit to be barbers, making legal instruments and writings of such apprenticeship so that he might well simulate and color his deception, to the damage of the masters from whom they departed and against the intent of the said statute; and wishing to prevent such deceptions, so that apprentices leaving in such a manner do not take away <margin>B: lest they snatch away</margin> the earnings from their masters, they provided etc. that for the future no apprentice of the said branch of barbers may, dare, or presume within the next three years from the day he leaves his master to set up or manage a shop for himself, nor join with any master to practice the said art, nor place himself with anyone as an apprentice, agent, or partner, or under any other titled name with any barber, nor in any way practice the art or trade of barbers by himself or through others with others near the shop of his said former master within 400 (3) *braccia* <note>The distance was significantly increased from 40 to 400 braccia (approx. 230 meters) to prevent competition.</note>, under penalty of 25 pounds in small florins, of which half shall go to the chamberlain of the said art receiving it for the said art, and the other half to the master from whom he had departed; in which 25 pounds in small florins the consuls <note>The *consoli* were the elected leaders of the guild who held judicial power over its members.</note> of the said art [shall fine] the one so acting by the fact itself <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>...

# REFORM OF 1404 IIII, V

## IIII. That the notary of the said guild shall administer the oath to the consuls.

Furthermore, they decreed, ordained, and provided that for the future, the current notary of the said guild <note>The notary was a key official responsible for legal documentation and ensuring procedures followed statutory law.</note> and whoever shall hold that office in time to come, on the first day that the consuls of the said guild gather in the guild house to exercise their office, shall be bound and required to administer the oath within said guild house. He must ensure they swear upon the Holy Gospels of God, physically touching the scriptures, to observe the statutes and orders of the said guild. Specifically, they must swear to uphold the statutes regarding those who are to be enrolled <term>matriculated; the process of becoming a formal member of a guild</term> in the said guild, and the manner to be observed in the <term>scrutinies; the process of vetting and electing candidates for office by secret ballot</term> which shall be held for the office of the consulate, as was recently decreed and ordained today above. This is under penalty of five pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli, the local currency used for daily transactions</note> for every time he omits the aforesaid duties, to be taken from him and applied to the guild, withheld from his salary. And if any of the aforesaid consuls is not present the first time the consuls gather in the guild house, he shall be bound and required to take the said oath in the manner and form aforesaid on the first day he is present with his other colleagues to exercise their office. And the said notary is bound to administer the oath to him in the manner and form aforesaid, under the penalty mentioned above. Adding further that, if the said oath is not sworn by the consuls or any one of them in the manner and form aforesaid, whatever is done by them or by such an individual who has not given the oath shall not be valid or hold weight, and shall be of no value or firmness.

## V. That the consuls and the sixty additions can do nothing unless half of the sixty have previously been consuls.

Furthermore, taking heed of a statute of the said guild <margin>Reform of December 29, 1391, rubric I</margin>, by which it is disposed and ordained that the consuls and councilors of the said guild, or two-thirds of them, together with sixty guild members added <term>arroti; additional citizens called to supplement a council for specific deliberations</term> to the said guild or more, may grant dispensations against any statute or ordinance of the said guild, and make new orders in said guild as it seems best and pleases them, and that they have that <term>balìa; extraordinary power or authority granted to a committee for a limited time</term> and authority which the entire guild possesses, as <margin>The words "as it seems best... which the entire guild possesses, as" are repeated in codex C.</margin> these and other things are more broadly contained in the said statute, they decreed—

# V, VI REFORM OF 1404

They decreed and ordained that the said consuls, councilors, and <term>arroti</term> <note>Additional members summoned to provide expert advice or to reach a quorum</note> aforementioned cannot do, dispense, settle, or ordain anything, nor perform any action, unless at least half of the said <term>arroti</term> have served as consuls of the said guild in the past, and not otherwise or in any other manner. And if anything should be done by them, if half of them have not been consuls as stated, it shall not be valid or binding and shall be void, null, and of no value, and must not be carried out. Furthermore, each of the said consuls, councilors, and <term>arroti</term> who has acted without observing the aforementioned rules shall fall under a penalty of 50 pounds in <term>small florins</term> <note>original: "llire .L. di f. p." (lire di fiorini piccoli), the standard local currency of account in Florence</note>. In which penalty they and each of them, for the present as for the future, were condemned; and they willed that they and each of them be considered condemned, the fine to be taken and seized as follows: one third to the Chamber of the Commune of Florence, one third to the <term>Mercatantia</term> <note>The Court of the Merchants, which oversaw all Florentine guilds</note> and the office of the <term>Mercatantia</term> of the city of Florence, and the remaining third to the said guild. Of this total penalty, a fourth part shall and must be given to the informer of the aforementioned matters, whether publicly or secretly, as it shall seem best and pleasing to the said informer. Canceling, voiding, and annulling any and all statutes and orders of the said guild that in any way, in whole or in part, might provide to the contrary.

### VI. That the officials of the guild may not receive money in place of their gifts.

Furthermore, so that the honors and preeminences granted by the said guild to the consuls, councilors, and <term>chamberlain</term> <note>The treasurer or financial administrator of the guild</note> of said guild—namely in the form of gifts or the presents which are sent by the said guild to honor them—may be preserved and maintained, they provided, legislated, and ordained that no consul, councilor, or chamberlain of the said guild, nor any one of them, may receive or have from the said guild by reason of his said office of the consulate, councilorship, or <term>chamberlainship</term> <note>original: "camarlingatico"</note>, anything except the gift customary and used by the said guild for the consuls, councilors, and chamberlain, if the guild is accustomed to give and send a gift to them or any of them. And if the chamberlain of the said guild, or his vice-chamberlain or purveyor, or any other person whatsoever for the said guild, should give or send to any consul, councilor, or chamberlain of the aforementioned guild (or to one who had previously held such office) money or any other thing outside of the aforementioned gift, by reason of his said office of the consulate, councilorship, or chamberlainship, he shall *ipso facto* <note>by the fact itself</note> incur and be understood to have incurred a penalty of 50 pounds in small florins for each—

# REFORM OF 1405

It is provided and ordained that the consuls <note>The elected heads of the guild</note> of the said guild, whose term of office begins in the month of January, together with the councilors of the said guild, shall be required every year to elect and nominate three good and loyal apothecaries <note>original: "spetiali" — members of the Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries who dealt in spices, medicines, and pigments</note> residing at a shop or warehouse, who must decide, terminate, and declare all and each [dispute] which may arise among the men of the said guild by reason of tare <note>original: "tara" — an allowance for the weight of packaging or impurities in bulk goods</note>, which might be requested regarding any allowance for saffron flowers <note>original: "fiori di gruogo"</note>, wax, naval pitch, ginger, cinnamon, and any other things; and whatever shall be determined by them shall be valid and hold and must be observed. And considering that their office should last for one year next following, and noting that the said office of tares in the said guild had not been ordained or used by the consuls existing at the time, and holding for certain that the said office is useful for removing the disputes which arise every day, correcting the said statute and adding to that statute, they provided, ordained, and deliberated:

### I. How the weighers are elected and their authority.

*a.* First, that the present consuls and those who shall be for the time, together with the councilors of the said guild and those adjunct members <note>original: "arroti" — additional citizens called to assist the guild councils</note> of the craftsmen of the said guild whom the said consuls wish, may and must perform a scrutiny <note>original: "scruptinare" — a secret ballot or vetting process</note> of the apothecaries of the said guild residing at a warehouse or shop of the said guild; and those who obtain the vote by two-thirds of those present shall be placed in a bag to be prepared for this purpose. And from the said bag, at the beginning of the term of each consulate, two of the said names in the bag must be drawn, whose office shall last for the entire duration of the consulate's term. To the office of these officials it shall belong and pertain to view, correct, weigh <note>original: "tarare"</note>, and set a price for the merchandise and things of the said guild sold and given at retail, for which a market price has not been expressly made; and to correct and amend the records of such things sold, over which a difference arises between the seller or buyer, and to set them at their price, as shall seem fit to their discretion.

*b.* Furthermore, they shall be held and must discreetly measure and cause to be measured all and each and any stammel <note>original: "stamignia" — a type of fine wool cloth or sieve-cloth</note> which shall be sold by the craftsmen of the said guild or bought by the craftsmen of the said guild. And that no one subject to the said guild may have [cloth] measured by anyone other than the aforesaid weighers <note>original: "taratori"</note>, under the penalty of five pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." — fiorini piccioli</note> for every piece of stammel, for which the consuls of the said guild existing at the time must condemn [the offender] on each occasion. # REFORM OF 1405 I

[The] inspectors <note>original: "taratori" - officials appointed to weigh, measure, or assess the quality and tare weight of goods</note> of any merchandise and records of merchandise, sold without an express market price, are required to have each party <note>the buyer and the seller</note> pay two denari per lira of the [total sum] (1) that the said merchandise or the records of said merchandise produced to them should fetch.

c. And for every piece of stamin <note>original: "stamignia" - a coarse woolen cloth or linsey-woolsey</note> that is measured, each party—the buyer and the seller—must give the said inspectors 18 denari per side.

d. And for every bale that must be inspected using a sieve <note>original: "crivello" - used to separate impurities from bulk goods</note>, each party shall pay two soldi in small florins <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli" - the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note> to the said inspectors, except for almonds, rice, cumin, and other merchandise of similar or lesser price, for which each party must pay one soldo per bale.

e. And for every package—that is, bale, bundle, barrel, jar, or other binding of merchandise and things—which is inspected without a sieve, each party shall pay the said inspectors one soldo in small florins, except for things and merchandise valued at four florins per hundredweight or less, for which each party must pay six denari in small florins.

f. And for fine merchandise and items which must be examined and inspected by them—namely saffron, cloves, scraps <note>original: "frusti" - likely small pieces of precious cloth or materials</note>, nutmeg, aloe, mastic, spikenard, azure <note>lapis lazuli or blue pigment</note>, gold, silver, beaten tin, confections, and similar things—each party must pay the said inspectors one denaro per lira.

g. Furthermore, the said inspectors must keep with them a book, to be purchased by the chamberlain <note>original: "camarlingho" - the treasurer or financial officer</note> of the said Guild, in which they shall write or cause to be written as expenses every quantity of money received by them during their term of office by reason of the aforesaid things or any of them. And at the end of their term, they are required to assign and give to the chamberlain of the said Guild the sum of all the money received by them by reason of their office. The chamberlain is required and must record this money as entry <note>income</note>. And the auditors <note>original: "sindichi" - officials responsible for reviewing accounts</note> of the said Guild are required to review the accounts of the entries and exits <note>credits and debits</note> of the said inspectors. And once the aforesaid account has been seen by the auditors, the chamberlain of the said Guild is required and must give to the said inspectors, as their gift or rather salary, half of all the money received by them, to be shared between the two of them. This is added and expressed: that the consuls <note>the highest-ranking leaders of the Guild</note> currently in office, after the next coming year has passed, may at any time reduce the said gift of the inspectors to a fixed amount, as shall seem fit to their discretion, having taken into consideration the profit <note>original: "fructo"</note> that the Guild receives from the office of the said inspectors.

### II. No one may measure except for the official measurers.

Furthermore, no person subject to the said Guild may, shall dare, or presume to have any fine wool cloths <note>original: "stamigne," a lightweight woolen fabric</note> which they might buy or sell, measured by anyone other than the aforementioned official measurers <note>original: "taratori," officials responsible for verifying weights and measures</note>. And no apothecary <term>spetiale: a member of the guild who dealt in medicines, spices, and often pigments or wax</term> or other person subject to the said Guild shall dare or be able to calculate the value of any written account of goods sold, even if requested by the parties involved; instead, they must send it to the aforementioned measurers to be appraised by them in the manner and form described above. This is under penalty for anyone who acts to the contrary of five pounds of small florins <note>original: "lire cinque di f. p." (fiorini piccioli)</note> for each time they have something measured or appraised against the aforementioned form, to be collected by the Consuls <term>consoli: the elected leaders of the Guild</term> of the said Guild.

### III. That a standard rod and sieves remain in the Guild hall.

Furthermore, the above-mentioned Consuls are bound and required, for the observation and convenience of the aforementioned matters, to have a marked measuring rod <note>original: "canna," a linear measure roughly equal to 2 meters</note> made for measuring, as well as those sieves <note>original: "crivelli"</note> that shall seem appropriate to them. These must remain in the Guild house or elsewhere, as shall be ordained by the Consuls.

### IIII. How the wax candles of the parishes, peoples, and communes are to be made.

Furthermore, wishing to provide regulations regarding the wax candles of the parishes <note>original: "pivieri," rural districts centered around a baptismal church</note>, peoples, and communes, which are made by the apothecaries and offered on the [feast day] of Saint John the Baptist, so that the Works <note>The "Opera," the board of works responsible for the maintenance of the Baptistery</note> of the aforementioned Saint John may receive what is due from the said peoples, parishes, and communes; and so that the apothecaries are given cause to work the said candles well and loyally, attending to a statute of the Guild written above under the rubric of punishing those who do not work good, pure, and loyal wax and how torches and candles ought to be made (1), correcting the said statute and adding to the said statute, they provided, ordained, and deliberated that:

Whosoever of the said Guild in the future shall work, or cause to be worked, or sell any of the said candles that is not entirely of new wax and of a single type of wax, or in which there is more than half an ounce of wick for every pound, or which does not have the entire wick made of new cotton and new thread <note>original: "accia," linen or hemp thread</note>, shall fall under a penalty of 25 pounds of small florins for every candle and for every time anyone acts to the contrary. Half of this amount shall go to the Chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the financial officer</term> of the Chamber of the Commune of Florence for the said Commune.

# REFORM OF 1405, 1406 IV

...the receiver, and the other half to the chamberlain <note>camarlingho: the financial officer or treasurer</note> of the said guild for the benefit of the receiving guild. And if such a candle were declared to be good and worked according to the prescribed form [without the name being covered], the said declaration shall not hold and cannot or should not be written or noted by the notary of the said guild, but treated as if it had never been made.

In honor of God and of Saint Luke <note>The patron saint of painters</note> and of all the celestial court, and for the salvation of the souls of the men and persons of the said company who have died, and of the persons flowing into the said hospital and those who in the past have died and been buried therein; and whereas always in the past, for a long time until now, it was the custom for the men and persons of the said company to come there on the appointed day and, with reverence and as a religious observance, to be present and remain there, and to obey the captains of the said company and remain subject and obedient to their commands and admonitions, and to pay willingly and sincerely that which was ordained by them or by their constitutions; [all this] in honor of God and of the said blessed Saint Luke and for the growth of this company.

And that the notary of each of the said guilds is bound to notify their consuls the first time the said consuls gather, under penalty of five pounds to the said notary of the said guild.

# I, II REFORM OF 1413

## I. That in order to hold the office of the consulate, two-thirds of the members must have previously served as consuls; and the same applies to the office of the Six of the Merchant Court.

a. First, regarding the great importance of conducting the <term>scrutiny</term> <note>original: "squittino"; a process of vetting and voting on candidates for office to ensure they were eligible and loyal</note> and everything that follows from it and proceeds daily: whenever a scrutiny is held within the Guild for the office of the consulate of the said Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers, the following method must be observed in the election of the <term>additional electors</term> <note>original: "arroti"; citizens co-opted or added to a committee to broaden representation or expertise during the scrutiny process</note> who perform such a scrutiny. That is: the additional electors, who shall be chosen according to the orders of the said Guild, must have been consuls of the said Guild at some time in the past—at least two-thirds of all such electors. And if the said scrutiny, or anything depending on it, should be conducted otherwise or in any other manner, it shall not be valid or binding and shall have no efficacy or value, as if it had never been done. And if anything is done to the contrary of what is stated above, the consuls of the said Guild shall incur a fine of fifty pounds in <term>small florins</term> <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli"; the silver-based currency used for daily transactions in Florence</note> each; one half to be applied to the University of the Merchant Court, and the other half to the aforesaid Guild.

b. Similarly, the same procedure shall be followed and must be done in the future within the Guild for the scrutiny of the office of the Six Councilors of the University of the Merchant Court <note>The "Mercantia" or Merchant Court was the supreme commercial tribunal in Florence, overseeing all the guilds</note>. That is, the additional electors chosen by the consuls of the said Guild to perform the said scrutiny must have been consuls of the said Guild at least once in the past, to the extent of two-thirds of their number. Otherwise, the said scrutiny shall not be valid or binding, and shall be of no efficacy or moment. And if it is done to the contrary, the consuls of the said Guild then in office shall incur—and from this moment are understood to have incurred—a fine of 50 pounds in small florins each, for every instance; half to be applied to the aforesaid University of the Merchant Court, and the other half to the aforesaid Guild.

# VI, VII REFORM OF 1414

the consulate, they are bound and must deposit with the <term>chamberlain</term><note>camarlingho: the financial officer or treasurer of the guild</note> of the said guild, for each of them, two gold florins. And these funds thus recorded as income by the chamberlain may in no way be returned or restored by the said chamberlain or his successor to the Consul from whose money they came, unless the Consuls, councilors, and <term>syndics</term><note>sindichi: officials appointed to audit or oversee the conduct of guild officers</note> of the guild, or two-thirds of them, declare that the said Consul had a legitimate excuse for the days he did not go to the guild. ### VII. That cases must be terminated within 40 days, penalty
->40 soldi for each consul.<-

# REFORMS OF 1415, 1416

### I. That anyone who practices the craft be compelled to swear to it.

First, they provided, decreed, and ordered that all and each person performing any branch of the said craft, and who practice the said craft—or in the future shall practice or perform it—in the city of Pisa or in the suburb of San Marco of the said city, is and shall be understood to be subject to the said craft. They may be compelled by any rector or official, at the petition of the consuls of the aforesaid craft, to swear to the said craft <note>This refers to a formal oath of obedience to the guild's statutes and authorities</note> and to do everything that the other craftsmen of the said craft must do or are doing; provided that they cannot be compelled to pay for the matriculation <term>matricola: the official register of guild members and the fee paid to be entered into it</term> more or otherwise than such craftsmen were accustomed to pay before the city of Pisa was under the Commune of Florence. This is nonetheless added: that no one who was registered in the matriculation of the craftsmen of the said city of Pisa before that city came under the Commune of Florence can in any way be compelled or burdened to pay for the said matriculation; and furthermore, that all and each of the other craftsmen of the said craft, performing and practicing the aforesaid craft in the countryside or district of Pisa, are and shall be understood to be subject to the said craft, except that they cannot be compelled to pay anything to the aforesaid craft for their matriculation or by reason of their registration. I, Marchionne, the above-written notary, have signed.

# REFORMS OF 1421, 1422

Francesco d'Antonio Palmieri, representing the Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries <note>original: "medici e spetiali"</note>, Francesco di Christofano, furrier, representing the Guild of Furriers and Skinners <note>original: "vaiai e pillicciai"</note>, Cambio di Piero, locksmith, representing the Guild of Locksmiths <note>original: "chiavaiuoli"</note>, Florentine citizens, deputies [etc.], having seen the chapter written below presented to them on behalf of the Captains of the Guelph Party <note>The Guelph Party was a powerful political faction in Florence that supported the Papacy and held significant influence over city governance.</note>, the tenor of which is this:

### I. That the feast of Saint Denis be observed by the craftsmen.

Firstly, considering the victory and the triumph given from heaven to the city of Florence over the city of Pisa on the day of the most glorious Saint Denis the Areopagite <note>Florence conquered Pisa in 1406; this decree formalizes the religious commemoration of that military victory.</note>, and therefore, for the exaltation of the community of Guelphs of the city of Florence, they provided, ordained, and deliberated that every year, in perpetuity, on the ninth day of the month of October, on which day is the feast of the said Saint Denis, no one of the said guild or those subject to the said Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries, shall dare or presume to keep a shop open on the said day; but they are bound and must observe the said feast of Saint Denis every year, just as the other feasts in the city of Florence are observed, and it shall be counted among the said feasts by the craftsmen of the said guild, under the penalty, for each one who acts to the contrary, of fifty pounds of small florins <note>original: "lire cinquanta di f. p." (fiorini piccioli)</note>, to be applied one half to the Commune of Florence, and the other half to the said guild.

Having seen and considered all and each of the statutes, chapters, and orders of the said Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries, which are contained in the present volume of statutes previously approved [etc.], they approved [etc.], of which approval [etc.] appears in the record of the said statutes by the hand of Ser Bartolommeo di Giovanni Dini from Laterino, a Florentine notary.

## II, III REFORM OF 1422

As has been stated, [the official] is bound and required, before the commencement of his said office of the consulate, to pay to the aforementioned oratory <note>A small chapel or house of prayer belonging to the guild</note>—or to a person lawfully receiving on behalf of said oratory—that which he is required to pay according to the form of the statutes and orders of the said guild, namely 6 gold florins. And if he does not pay before the beginning of his said office, he may not gather with his other companions and colleagues, nor exercise his aforementioned office, until he has paid the said 6 gold florins, under the penalty of 50 pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or "fiorini piccioli," the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note> to be taken from each violator and applied to the said guild. 

And the said person, who has not first paid as stated, cannot cast any <term>fava</term> <note>literally "bean"; these were used as secret ballots for voting in communal and guild councils</note> in his said office. Neither the notary of the guild, nor his assistant, nor anyone else may receive any ballot from such a person who has not paid first, under the said penalty. 

And if it should happen that anyone has not paid within the time established and ordered above, he may not have or receive any gift, nor anything in place of a gift, by reason of his office; nor may any be sent to him, under the penalty of 25 pounds of small florins for the one who receives it, and for each consul of the guild who deliberates to the contrary, and for the <term>camarlingho</term> <note>the guild's chamberlain or treasurer</note> of the guild who sends or causes such a gift to be sent or permitted. The same penalty applies to the notary or the <term>proveditore</term> <note>the purveyor or administrative manager</note> of the guild if they consent to the aforementioned things, or if any of them consents in any way. 

Regarding the aforementioned matters, the officials shall be subject to <term>sindicato</term> <note>a formal audit or review of an official's conduct at the end of their term</note>, and every office of the guild's syndics <note>officials appointed to investigate and punish misconduct</note> may take notice of these matters; and having found the guilty parties, they may punish and condemn them as disposed above and at any time. Nevertheless, that consul who has not paid before the time of the commencement of the said consulate, or during the time of the said office, remains a debtor to the said oratory for the quantity of 6 gold florins, and shall be compelled to pay in full. By reason of the loss of the said gift, nothing shall or can be diminished from the said sum of 6 gold florins for which he remains a debtor in the manner aforesaid.

# REFORM OF 1422 III

...any money or any other thing in place of such presents and gifts owed to him, more or otherwise than is disposed by the statutes and orders of the said Guild <note>The "Arte" refers to one of the powerful professional corporations or guilds that governed Florentine economic and political life</note>, which results in the shame of the said Guild. Wishing to provide for and ensure that in times to come such an impropriety does not occur, having conducted and obtained a scrutiny <note>A formal vote or ballot</note> as described above, they provided, ordered, and deliberated that:

No one who in the future shall be a consul, counselor, syndic, or chamberlain <term>Camarlingho: the treasurer or financial administrator of the guild</term> of the said Guild, or who has held any office of the said Guild by reason or respect of which he ought to have received or had from the said Guild any present or gift, shall dare or presume to take, receive, or retain for the said such present or gift—or indeed in place of such present or gift—money or anything else, more than is permitted by the statutes and orders of the aforesaid Guild, under the penalty of 25 pounds of small florins <note>original: "llire .xxv. di f. p." referring to *lire di fiorini piccoli*, the local currency used for daily transactions</note> for each person acting to the contrary, or if he should otherwise take, receive, or retain such a present; and for every such instance, the fine is to be taken from him and applied to the said Guild.

And if it should happen that any of the said officials of the said Guild should otherwise take, receive, or retain such a present or gift, the chamberlain of the said Guild—who sent or caused such a present to be sent, or indeed gave or caused it to be given or permitted it in any other way than is disposed above—shall be understood to be and is condemned to 25 pounds <margin>Corrected from *libre* (pounds)</margin> of small florins, to be taken from him and applied to the said Guild. 

And furthermore the notary, the provider of the said Guild, and each of them individually shall be understood to be and are condemned in the same amount, that is, 25 pounds of small florins to be taken from them and applied to the said Guild, if they permit the said presents or gifts or any of them to be sent or given to any of the said officials otherwise or in any other manner than is said above, for each of them and for every instance. 

And the syndics <term>Sindichi: officials charged with auditing and legal oversight</term> of the said Guild, who shall be in office at the time, must investigate those acting against the aforesaid things, and having found them guilty, declare and condemn them to give to the said Guild as is said above, under the penalty of 25 pounds of small florins for each of the said syndics who do not condemn the said delinquents in the aforesaid matters and for each person acting to the contrary. And that the said presents or any of them cannot be given or sent by the said Guild to any of the said officials, unless <margin>Latin: *nisi* (unless)</margin> before such giving it appears in the acts of the said Guild by the hand of the notary of the said Guild or his assistant.

### IIII. That there shall be no more than 3 messengers in the house of the said Guild.

Furthermore, considering that for several years now the said Guild and University <note>The term "University" here refers to the legal corporate body of the guild members, not an educational institution.</note> has kept four continuous messengers for the services of the said Guild, and that in times past there used to be only two, at which time there were no fewer occupations in the Guild than there are at present, but rather more; and recognizing that the Guild can and should be well served and satisfied by three messengers, and that the said Guild and University pays and supports its ordinary expenses with difficulty—to which diligent attention must be paid so that the said University can maintain itself in its current good state without [excessive] costs to the merchants and craftsmen of the said Guild—in every way etc. they provided and ordained that for the future, the said Guild and University, or rather the Consuls <note>The elected heads of the guild.</note> and any officials of the said Guild existing at the time, cannot and must not take, elect, or depute to serve the said Guild more than the number of three messengers at one time, but only three and up to the number of three and no more, notwithstanding any statutes or ordinances of the said Guild or of the Municipality of Florence <note>original: "comune di Firenze"</note> disposing to the contrary in any way, or any other custom used to the contrary. And which three messengers must receive for their salary and clothing—that is, each of them individually—that which is disposed by the orders of the said Guild to be paid to each messenger of the said Guild and no more.

### V. That before anyone (a) is received into the membership roll, it must be deliberated by the Consuls.

Furthermore, considering that, according to the statutes and orders of the said Guild, everyone who wishes to come before the magistracy of the said Guild and be placed and described in the membership roll <term>matricola: the official register or matriculation book of guild members</term> of the said Guild among the other members, is received into the roll of said Guild by the notary of the Guild receiving on behalf of the Consuls of the Guild, and thus it was always observed; and that no one in the past was ever refused, but everyone was always received and accepted; and that it has already happened, and in the future could happen, that someone was received into the roll by whose person this Guild was not honored and could be dishonored; wishing to provide for such inconveniences and to give cause to everyone who wishes to be received into the roll of the said Guild to conduct themselves well, in every way etc. they provided, ordained, and deliberated as above that in the future no one can be received or admitted to the roll or described in the roll of the said Guild by the

# REFORM OF 1425
I

### I. That no one may bring a complaint in any court against anyone whom the consuls appear to claim jurisdiction over, under penalty of 50 lire.

**a.** The said statute-makers, considering that the community of the aforementioned city is preserved and increased through the preservation and growth of the <term>guilds</term> <note>Italian: *arti*. These were powerful professional corporations that governed Florentine economy and politics.</note> of the city of Florence; and that by reason of certain customs contrary to the duty of honesty and good morals, and against the statutes and ordinances of the guilds—which have been practiced by many for a short time now <insert>is</insert> <note>original: "est"</note> to the damage and shame of the said guild and against its ordinances as stated above—the aforementioned guilds, and especially the **Guild of Apothecaries and Mercers** <note>Italian: *arte degli spetiali e merciai*. This guild included pharmacists, doctors, and merchants of fine goods like spices and silks.</note>, would fall into ruin; so that, if timely remedies were not provided, the said guilds would become nullities, and especially the said guild [of Apothecaries], and for this reason the said guilds of the aforementioned city would receive the greatest injury; [therefore] for the preservation of the said guilds and the said community, so that the aforementioned custom may be entirely removed, they provided, ordained, and deliberated that in the future no one, of whatever quality, subjected to the said guild in any way, may or should go in any way to any other court of the city or <term>territory</term> <note>Italian: *contado*. The rural area surrounding Florence under its jurisdiction.</note> of Florence against any person, nor bring any complaint or submit any petition or in any way demand any quantity of money or other things which he should or pretends to have, receive, or hold for any reason or cause from or against any person, of whatever state and condition they may be, subjected to the said guild in any way, unless it is in the court of the said guild before the office of the **Consuls** <note>The elected leaders and judges of the guild.</note> of the said guild, under the penalty of 50 <term>small florin lire</term> <note>Italian: *llire .L. di f. p.* (lire di fiorini piccioli). The standard silver-based currency for local transactions.</note> for each person and for each time they act to the contrary. In which penalty each violator is understood to be and is incurred and condemned *ipso facto* <note>Latin: "by the fact itself," meaning the penalty is automatic.</note>, even without any other declaration or act.

**b.** This is nonetheless saved, excepted, and reserved: namely, that if license were granted by the Consuls of the said guild—having first obtained a vote by the said Consuls by **black and white beans** <note>The traditional Florentine method of secret balloting: usually black for "yes" and white for "no."</note>—to go to another court; or if the Consuls of the said guild should not dispatch any case moved or that might be moved in the said court of the guild within the time contained in the statutes and orders of the said guild; then in the said cases, and each or any of them, it shall be lawful for such a plaintiff to go to another court of the city or territory of Florence, and to lawfully transfer that case and any other case without penalty, and not by any other way or other manner, directly or indirectly.

***

<margin>(a) B adds *is*.</margin>

<summary>This document establishes the legal monopoly of the Guild of Apothecaries and Mercers over disputes involving its members, forbidding them from seeking justice in outside Florentine courts without explicit permission from the Guild Consuls.</summary>

# REFORMS OF 1425, 1426

*c.* And the aforementioned things shall not be understood to apply, nor shall they take place, against those who have an execution <note>A legal seizure of property or person to satisfy a debt</note> ready and in effect against their debtors; in which case it shall be permitted to anyone—when by right and according to the statutes and orders of the Commune of Florence and the University of Merchants <note>original: "università di Mercantia," the overarching commercial court in Florence</note> it is permitted for someone to be able to have their debtor seized in fact—to have him seized in fact, and not otherwise, nor by asking or pleading through any other way, under the said penalty.

*d.* And furthermore, the aforementioned things shall not be understood to apply to those prohibitions or contracts and matters for which a public guaranteed instrument <note>A notarized document with a "guarantigia" clause allowing for immediate execution without a full trial</note> appears, over which, according to the orders of the aforementioned Guild and the Consuls of said Guild, they do not have jurisdiction; unless they are instruments for the leasing of warehouses or shops of the said Guild, over which, according to the orders of the said Guild, they would have jurisdiction. And that everyone can and shall be permitted, openly or secretly, to notify and denounce <note>original: "tamburare," referring to the practice of placing anonymous accusations in a "tamburo" or slotted box</note> anyone acting to the contrary, and they shall have and be given the fourth part of 50 Pounds of small florins <note>original: "f. p." or fiorini piccioli</note> freely, without any remission. And that the Consuls of the said Guild, who shall be in office for the time being, are bound and must dispatch and terminate the disputes moved and which shall be moved before them and within the Guild, within the time and term and by that mode and form as is disposed by the orders of the said Guild, under the penalties and to the penalties contained in the statutes and orders of the said Guild.

The present chapter and all other statutes, chapters, and ordinances contained in the present volume of this book of the Guild of the Apothecaries <note>original: "arte degli spetiali," the guild including pharmacists, doctors, and spice merchants</note> having been seen and considered, by virtue of their office [etc.], they approved, ratified, and confirmed [etc.], of which approval it appears in the master copy of the said statutes [etc.] by the hand of Ser Iacopo di Fei di Ser Scolaio de’ Ridolfi, Florentine citizen and notary.

# REFORM OF 1432 I, II

### I. [That a "Book of the Mirror" be made in the house of the said guild] <note>original: "Quod fiat liber speculi in domo dicte artis". The "Mirror" (Specchio) was a common name for a ledger used to track tax or fee defaulters.</note> (1).

First, that there be ordered and made within the said guild <term>arte: a professional guild or corporation</term> a book named the "Book of the Mirror." In this book shall be recorded and placed all and each of those enrolled in the said guild and those subject to it who are in the city of Florence, or who are citizens indebted to the said guild for any reason, at the discretion of the <term>consoli: the Consuls, the highest-ranking elected officials of the guild</term> presiding at the time. Those who are described <margin>B: so described</margin> in the said book as debtors of the guild must be struck off and removed from <margin>B adds: and from</margin> any office to which <margin>B adds: it happens</margin> they or any of them might be drawn <note>The "drawing" refers to the extraction of names from a leather bag (borse) to select officials by lot.</note> in the house of the said guild or for the guild's offices in the future, until they have paid and have been canceled from the said Book of the Mirror. And let it be understood that the same shall be observed regarding the sons—provided they are under the <term>podestà: legal authority or power</term> of the father—and the heirs of any such debtors so described in the said book. This is added nonetheless: that before such debtors of the guild are placed in the aforementioned Mirror, they must be notified personally by one of the guild's messengers, once or twice at their home, on different <margin>B adds: days</margin>, informing them that they have been placed and described as debtors of the aforesaid guild in and upon the said Book of the Mirror (2).

### II. [That no one placed in the Book of the Mirror can be put to a vote for any guild office] <note>original: "Quod nullus positus ad librum speculi possit micti ad partitum ad aliquod officium artis".</note>.

And that none of such debtors, so described and placed in the said Book of the Mirror, can or should be put to a vote <note>original: "mandare... a partito"</note> for any office, or to perform any office in the house of the said guild, during the time they are a debtor of the guild and so described in the said Book of the Mirror. This is under penalty of 50 pounds of small florins <note>original: "llire .L. di f. p." (lire di fiorini piccioli)</note> to be paid by the notary of the said guild who permits the opposite to be done; this fine is to be taken from him for each person and each instance and applied to the guild's funds. This applies to everyone drawn for any office in the guild house who is at that time described in the Book of the Mirror as a debtor and is not struck from such office. And no drawing <note>the selection of names</note> and no <term>squittino: the scrutiny or secret ballot process for electing officials</term> can be held in the guild house unless the aforementioned Book of the Mirror is present and open in such a way that it may be seen by everyone, under penalty of 50 pounds.

### III. [*That no consul of the said guild appearing in the "Mirror" at the time of his drawing may receive a gift*]. <note>original Latin: "Quod nullus consul dicte artis existens ad speculum tempore sue extractionis possit habere ensenium"</note>

That anyone who in the future is drawn as a consul of the said guild and is, at the time of his drawing, in any way a debtor to the said guild—and is placed and described in and upon the Book of the Mirror <note>The "Specchio" or Mirror was a public record of citizens who were in arrears on their taxes or guild dues, effectively "reflecting" their status and barring them from office</note> by reason of his matriculation <term>matricola: the official register of guild members</term> or his entry fee, or because he is a debtor to Saint Mary of the Trumpet <note>original: "sancta Maria della Tromba," a church in Florence associated with guild charities and administrative fees</note> by reason of being newly appointed or due to be appointed to the office of the consulate of the said guild, or for any other debt for which he is found or described in and upon the said Book of the Mirror as stated—cannot receive, nor have sent to him, the customary gift that would be owed to him for his said office of the consulate to which he was drawn. This is under penalty of 10 pounds of small florins for each of the syndics <term>sindichi: officials responsible for auditing and legal oversight</term> of the said guild who deliberate that such a gift should be sent, and 10 pounds of small florins for the notary who records the deliberation made by the said syndics to send him such a gift; these fines are to be taken from them and applied to the said guild for each and every instance. 

With this addition and modification, however: that any of the said consuls of the said guild who are so drawn and remain, if they have paid the debt they owe to the said guild (for which they were described in the guild book in the said Book of the Mirror) on the first day of entering their office or before, and are cancelled from the said Book of the Mirror for the said debt, they may and should have and receive the aforementioned gift freely and without penalty. In such a case, the aforementioned syndics may deliberate that the said gift be sent to him, and the notary of the said guild may record the said deliberation without any prohibition, notwithstanding the aforementioned things. (2)

### IV. [That the messengers of the guild shall receive nothing from the fees paid by members for their matriculation].

Furthermore, no payment shall be made, nor can be made, by the chamberlain <note>The *camarlingho* was the financial officer or treasurer of the guild</note> of the said guild for the time being, to the messengers or servants of the said guild as their right or fee, by reason of monies that are to be paid for matriculation <note>The formal process of registering as a member of a guild</note> or by those who shall matriculate in the said guild for their registration and entry; except for those monies which are paid to the guild by those already matriculated or who shall matriculate in the said guild, after they have been recorded in the book and upon the "Book of the Mirror" <note>The *Specchio* (Mirror) was a tax record or ledger used to track debtors and those ineligible for office due to unpaid dues</note> of the said guild, by reason of a distraint <note>The seizure of property to compel payment of a debt</note> or burden that was placed upon such debtors recorded in the said Book of the Mirror by the said messengers or servants or any one of them. For which burdens, after the said burdened parties have paid the guild, it is understood and permitted that the messengers may take and receive from those so burdened one shilling per pound of the said debt for which they were burdened, solely from the money of the said burdened parties <note>Correction in the original hand from "burdens"</note> and not from the guild, notwithstanding any statutes or ordinances of the said Commune to the contrary. They may nonetheless, and it shall be lawful for them to receive from whoever shall matriculate in the said guild five shillings in small florins <note>original: *f. p.* or *fiorini piccioli*, the local silver-based currency used for daily transactions</note> for each of them, according to the established custom.

### V. [That the auditors of the guild are bound to reconcile the notary's book and file with the chamberlain's income].

Furthermore, the auditors <note>The *sindici* were officials appointed to review and "audit" the conduct and accounts of outgoing officers</note> of the said guild, who for the time being shall audit the consuls <note>The highest-ranking elected leaders of the guild</note> and the other outgoing officials of the said guild, when they review the accounts of the guild existing at that time, are bound and must reconcile all the files of petitions with the book of the notary of the said guild and with the income of the chamberlain of the said guild; so that if less was paid than should have been for any petitions, requests, or business of the guild, they shall rectify it. They are bound and must, within one month from the day of entering their office, have audited such consuls, officials, and chamberlains, according to what is laid down by the ordinances of the guild. Which, if they have not done within the said time, the gift due to them from the guild for the said [service] cannot and must not be sent to them.

their office of the <term>syndicate</term><note>The committee responsible for auditing and legal oversight</note>, under the penalty of 10 pounds of small florins <note>original: "llire .x. di f. p." referring to the *fiorino picciolo*</note> to the <term>chamberlain</term><note>The guild's treasurer</note> and to the <term>provost</term> of the said guild to be taken from them, if they send the aforementioned [document] and applied to the said guild.

VI. **[That messengers must remit money they have collected within three days]** <note>original Latin: "Quod numptii mictant denarios quos exegerint ad introitum infra tres dies"</note>.

Furthermore, that whichever of the messengers or servants of the said guild should in the future take from anyone, or on behalf of any debtor of the said guild, any quantity of money in the city of Florence, he is bound and must have that money recorded by the chamberlain of the said guild as income within the next three days from the day he received it; and if he receives it from anyone or on behalf of any debtor of the said guild outside the city of Florence, he is bound and must have that money recorded by the chamberlain of the said guild as income within three days from the day that said messenger has returned to the city of Florence. If this is not done, it is understood that such messenger or servant of the said guild shall be, and is, removed from his said office of messenger or servant without any further deliberation being made.

VII. **[That whoever has been drawn for any office of the guild and has previously exercised the office of the consulate or another office of another guild, shall be struck out as ineligible]** <note>original Latin: "Quod quicumque fuerit extractus ad aliquod officium artis et primo exercuerit officium consulatus vel aliud officium alterius artis, straculetur tamquam inhabilis"</note>.

Furthermore, that whichever of the men and persons of the said guild shall be drawn <note>original: "tracto", referring to the practice of drawing names from a leather bag or "borse" for office</note> and appointed in the house of the said guild to any office of the said guild, and in the past has exercised any office—namely the office of the <term>consulate</term>, councilors, syndicate, or chamberlainship—of any [other] guild, he must be struck out as ineligible by the notary of the said guild from such office and removed from said office. And none of the aforesaid, who had exercised any of the aforesaid offices of any other guild, can be removed or put to a vote <margin>(a)</margin> to exercise any office of the said guild in the future in the house of the said guild, under penalty of 25 pounds of small florins to the provost of the consuls of the said guild and to the notary of the said guild, who should permit the contrary to be done, to be taken from them and applied to the said guild. This is nonetheless excepted, saved, reserved, and modified: namely, if any of those aforementioned of the said guild, who will have exercised any of the aforesaid offices in the house of the [other] guild <margin>(b)</margin>, shall renounce all and each of the offices to which he might happen in the future to be drawn or elected...

# I, II REFORM OF 1434

From the month of January <note>original: "gennaio"</note> (1) just passed until now, those [ordinances] which were then approved and confirmed by the statutory officials of the commune, their immediate predecessors in office, containing and providing for the conducting or not conducting of any <term>scrutiny</term> <note>original: "squittino"; a secret ballot process used in Florence to determine eligibility for office</note>, or concerning the mode or form that must be maintained regarding the scrutinies, or concerning any office of the Guild or of the <term>purses</term> <note>original: "borse"; leather bags containing the names of eligible candidates for office</note> regarding any benefit or favor for those who had been or were in the offices of the Six Councilors of the <term>Mercantia</term> <note>The Merchant Court of Florence, which oversaw commercial disputes and guild regulations</note> or of the Consuls of their Guild, whether by election or by drawing lots <note>original: "extractione"</note>, or granting or inducing any prohibition or veto or anything dependent or connected thereto, even under whatever general or special words they might contain or comprise (2), are understood to be, and are, by way of annulment and correction, entirely annulled, revoked, disapproved, and quashed. And from this moment forward, in said modes and forms and others by which they best could, by virtue of any of their authority, power, and <term>balìa</term> <note>An emergency committee or the extraordinary power granted to such a body</note>, they annulled, quashed, and revoked them, and willed that they be observed by no one, under penalty of one thousand lire for whoever acts against this or observes them, for each instance to be taken from them, with one half applied to the Commune of Florence and the other to the aforementioned University of the Mercantia.

### II. [Revocation of certain ordinances].

Furthermore, having seen and understood an ordinance made and formed by the statutory officials of the commune in the year 1429 and in the month of November of said year, providing that, when the scrutinies of the Consuls for the fifteen Minor Guilds are held together with one another, whoever has obtained the vote in said Guild through the Guild notaries must be reduced and referred—together with the others who have obtained [the vote] at the Mercantia—all the <term>artisans</term> <note>original: "artefici"; members of the professional guilds</note> of said Guild who in times past had been in the offices of the Lords Priors and the <term>Gonfaloniers</term> <note>Standard-bearers of Justice, the highest office in the Florentine government</note> of the Company of the People, the Twelve Good Men, the Captains of the Guelph Party, the Priors, Colleges, and Secretaries of said Party, and the Six Councilors of the Mercantia, who at that time shall be twenty-five years of age, even if they had not obtained the vote in the Guild; and the said statutory officials, knowing it to be dishonest that, against the will of the artisans of the aforementioned Guilds, someone who does not obtain the vote in the Guild should be referred to the Mercantia, and especially because the artisans know each other better and have full knowledge of their qualities and conditions, for the aforementioned reasons and others, they quashed and revoked the said statute in the manners and cases above, and all other statutes and orders that might regard or provide for the aforementioned things.

# VIIII-X REFORM OF 1434

...to bring to the Merchant’s Court <note>original: "Mercantia"; the central judicial and regulatory body for Florentine guilds</note> any person or persons, even if they have obtained the vote within their guild, who are not of the ages listed below for the following offices: namely, for the office of the **six counselors of the Merchant’s Court**, the age of 16 years or older; for **consul of a guild**, the age of 10 years <note>This surprisingly low age likely refers to ceremonial roles or specific legal standing for minors in family businesses, or perhaps a transcription error in the original manuscript for 20 (XX) or 30 (XXX)</note>; for **chamberlain of the University of Merchants**, 25 years; for **electors of foreign officials** and **statutory officials of the commune** in charge of approving or rejecting the statutes of the Merchant’s Court and other guilds, 30 years. And let it be understood that a year once started is considered completed. Nevertheless, the privileges of the office of the consulate of the **Wool Guild** <note>The "Arte della Lana," one of the wealthiest and most powerful guilds in Florence</note> are reserved. This is under penalty of 50 lire to be paid to the said University by any notary who acts against the aforesaid rules or records names as above; furthermore, those who are reported in such a way shall have their names torn up and cannot be put to a vote in the Merchant’s Court.

### X. [That the six of the Merchant’s Court and the guild consuls, who were elected in the year 1433, shall have no benefit by virtue of said offices, just as if they had not been elected].

This applies specifically and only to those who were elected in the year **1433** or from then until now inclusively for any of the offices mentioned above; from now on, it shall be as if they had never held said offices, nor been drawn or elected to them.

Furthermore, the aforesaid statutory officials, having observed the ordinances [etc.], approved, ratified, and confirmed all the statutes and ordinances contained and written in the present volume; and they annulled and quashed any others not written in this volume, if any existed. XI. **[No partnership of barbers shall be valid unless a record of it is made in the acts of the said guild]** <note>original Latin: "Nulla societas barbitonsorum valeat, nisi de ea fiat scriptura in actis dicte artis"</note>.

Considering that questions and disputes often arise between barber partners and between barber masters and disciples, because their dealings are not noted and described in and upon their books—since they are not fit to keep books and accounts like the other merchants of the said guild—and wishing to provide for their peace, and so that they do not litigate as often happens, they provided, ordered, and deliberated that for the future no partnership of any barbers shall hold or be valid or be put into effect by those barbers (or as many as wish to join) by virtue of any agreement made together or that they shall make, unless express mention of such partnership and their pacts is made in the acts and books of the acts of the said guild; and in the event that mention of the aforesaid things is made in the said books, such partnership shall be valid and hold and must be put into execution for those partners, and not otherwise or in any other way.

XII. **[No one shall be understood to be a disciple of any barber unless such discipleship appears in the acts of the said guild]** <note>original Latin: "Nullus intelligatur esse discipulus barbitonsoris alicuius, nisi de tali discipulatu appareat in actis dicte artis"</note>.

And that no one shall be understood to be a disciple of any barber, if such discipleship does not appear in the acts of the said guild; but anyone who in the future stays as a disciple with any barber may go away and depart from his said master and practice that craft wherever he wishes, if a record of such discipleship does not appear in the acts of the said guild, as has been said. And that no disciple of a barber may set himself up as a disciple or as a master near the shop of his master from whom he departed, within <term>forty braccia</term> <note>A "braccio" (plural braccia) was a Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters. Forty braccia is approximately 23 meters.</note>, for three years from the day of his departure, according to the form of the statutes of the said guild, notwithstanding any license given to the said...

## I. *That a "Book of the Mirror" be made in the house of said guild.*

First, wishing to intend and intending toward the honor, state, and growth <note>Latin: *augumentationem*</note> of the aforesaid guild, and to give cause to anyone subject to or enrolled <note>Latin: *matriculato*</note> in said guild for acting well and pursuing better ends, and also to make them diligent and prompt in paying said guild and in doing more quickly for said guild that which ought to be paid and done by those enrolled and subject to said guild [etc.], they have provided, ordained, deliberated, and established in this manner, namely: that there be ordered and made in said guild a certain book named ***the book of the mirror*** <note>Italian: *il libro dello specchio*; a "Specchio" (Mirror) was a common Florentine administrative ledger used to track tax debtors and disqualify them from office</note>, in which book all and singular persons enrolled in said guild and subject to said guild who reside in the city of Florence, or who are citizen debtors of said guild for any reason within the time and term written below—namely, through the whole of the present month of April—must be described and placed. Those thus described in said book as debtors of said guild must be excluded <note>Latin: *extraculari*; specifically referring to being kept out of the "eyes" or holes of the voting bags</note> and disqualified <note>Latin: *haboleri*</note> from any offices to which it may happen in the future that they or any of them are drawn in the house of said guild, and from the offices of said guild, until they have paid and been canceled from said book of the mirror. And let that same rule be understood regarding sons remaining under the power of a father, as well as the heirs of any such debtors so described in said book. This is added, however: that first, and before such debtors of said guild are placed in the aforesaid mirror, it must be notified to them personally by one of the messengers of said guild once, or at their house twice on different days, how they are placed and described in said book of the mirror as debtors of the aforesaid guild (1).
