# II, III REFORM OF 1436

## II. No one placed in the "Mirror" book may be put to a vote for any office of the guild.

And that no such debtors, thus recorded and placed in the said "Mirror" book <note>The *Speculum* or "Mirror" was a ledger used in Renaissance Florence to list citizens or guild members in arrears on their taxes or dues, effectively "reflecting" their legal standing.</note>, can or should be put to a vote for any office, or for the holding of any office in the said guild, during the time in which they are a debtor to the said guild and recorded in the said "Mirror" book. This is under penalty of fifty pounds to be taken from the notary of the said guild for each and every time he allows the opposite to happen, with the fine applied to the guild's funds. This applies to anyone drawn for any office in the house of the said guild who is recorded at that time in the said "Mirror" book as a debtor of the guild, and such a person shall not be cleared <note>original: *stracularetur*; referring to the process of being cleared or "scratched off" from the list of ineligible debtors</note> for said office. 

And that no drawing <note>original: *extractio*; the process of pulling names from a leather bag (*borse*) to select officials by lot</note> and no scrutiny <note>original: *scruptineum*; a vote or examination of candidates</note> can be performed or held in the house of the said guild regarding men and persons if the aforementioned "Mirror" book is not present and open, so that it may be seen by everyone. This is under penalty of fifty pounds in small florins <note>original: *f. p.* or *fiorini piccoli*, the silver-based currency used for daily transactions as opposed to the gold florin</note> for any consul of the said guild who is present to perform or permit the opposite to happen, for each occurrence, and the loss of the honorary gift <note>original: *ensenii*; a traditional payment or gift given to officials for their service</note> owed to him for the office of the consulate, according to the form of the statutes and ordinances of the said guild. 

However, the notary of the said guild must notify and tell the same consuls what is contained in the present chapter, so that the said consuls are informed of the aforesaid matters and may better remember them. And if any of the said debtors is put to a vote and should win, he shall not be "pursed" <note>original: *imbursetur*; the act of placing a name into the bags for future office selection</note> for said office. <insert>(1)</insert> <margin>(1) Compare with the reform of December 26, 1432, rubric II.</margin>

## III. That no consul of the said guild who is in the "Mirror" at the time of his drawing may receive an honorary gift.

That whoever hereafter is drawn as a consul of the said guild and is, at the time of his drawing, in any way a debtor to the said guild—being placed and recorded in and upon the said "Mirror" book by reason of his matriculation <note>The fee for joining the guild register</note> or his entry fee, or because he is a debtor to Saint Mary of the Trumpet <note>original: *sancte Marie della Tronba*; a church in Florence closely associated with the guilds</note> by reason of his assumption of the office of the consulate of the said guild (whether recently done or to be done), or for any other debt for which he is found and recorded in and upon the said "Mirror" book as stated—he cannot receive, nor can there be sent to him, the honorary gift <note>original: *emsenium*</note> owed to him for his said office of the consulate to which he was drawn. 

This is under penalty of ten pounds in small florins for each of the syndics <note>original: *sindicis*; officials responsible for auditing and legal oversight</note> of the said guild who shall have deliberated that the said gift ought to be sent to him, and ten pounds in small florins for the notary of the said guild.

<summary>These guild statutes from 1436 prohibit members with outstanding debts (listed in the "Mirror" book) from holding office or receiving honorary payments. They mandate that the debt ledger be physically present and open during all elections to ensure transparency and accountability among the consuls and notaries.</summary>

V, VI REFORM OF 1436
448

any of them through a public instrument to be drawn up by the hand of a public notary, so that it may be legally valid and stand, provided that for the person who has made such a renunciation, the provisions stated in the present chapter shall no longer apply <note>original: "non habeant ea que in presenti capitulo dicta sunt"</note> (1).

# VI. Regarding the creation of the purse of the conservators and their prohibition from office.

*a.* Likewise, they have provided, ordained, and deliberated that the consuls <note>The highest-ranking officials of the guild</note> and councilors of the said guild <note>original: "artis" - referring to a professional guild or trade association</note>, or two-thirds of them, together with the body of the said guild according to the form of the statute and ordinance of the said guild, in the present month of April, shall hold and must hold in the house of the said guild a scrutiny <note>term: "scruptineum" - a formal vote or vetting process to determine eligibility for office</note> of the merchants and craftsmen of the said guild. In this scrutiny, all men of the said guild shall be put to the vote who formerly were or are consuls of the said guild, and who have been seen to be in the pouches <note>term: "marsupiis" - leather bags used to hold the names of eligible candidates for random drawing</note> of the said guild for the office of consuls, who are thirty years of age or older. Additionally, seventy other men, whether merchants or craftsmen of the said guild who have not been consuls nor seen in the pouches for consuls, as shall seem fit to the consuls of the said guild, who are also thirty years of age or older, shall be included. 

And those who, when put to the vote, shall obtain two-thirds of the black beans <note>Black beans were used to signify a "yes" vote in the balloting process</note> or more, shall be "enpursed" <note>placed into the eligibility bag</note> and kept in a certain purse in the house of the said guild and in the chest of offices of the said guild. This purse shall be named the **purse of the conservators of the ordinances** of the said guild. In the month of May, by the consuls of the said guild, at the time when other officials of the said guild are drawn, four men and persons shall be drawn in the house of the said guild, who shall be named the **conservators of the statutes and ordinances** of the said guild. 

However, it is provided that two members of the same family or kinship group <note>original: "consorterie"</note>, nor two business partners, may hold said office at the same time. Anyone drawn for such an office shall be understood to have a prohibition <note>term: "devetum" - a mandatory waiting period during which a person cannot hold the same or another office to prevent the concentration of power</note> for three future years from the day the office is laid down from accepting or exercising the same office. His kinsman and partner shall be understood to have a prohibition for one year from the day the office is laid down. Furthermore, no one may hold said office who holds or exercises any other office of the said guild. Anyone in said office shall be understood to have a prohibition against any other office to which he might happen to be drawn or appointed while serving in the aforementioned office, except for the office of the consulate of the said guild, which he may obtain, take, and accept. However, if any of the aforementioned conservators is drawn as a consul of the said guild, he shall by that very fact lose and forfeit <unclear>his position as conservator</unclear>.

# VIII. The Gift for the Conservators.

The said Conservators can, are bound to, and must gather in the Guild Hall every Monday and every Thursday, barring any just impediment, and on any other day as necessary. If any condemnation is issued against the men and persons of the said Guild regarding the aforementioned matters by the Consuls and Conservators, the said Conservators ought to receive and have from the Guild, at the end of their term of office, a gift <note>original: "ensenium"; a customary honorarium or token of appreciation</note> for each of them. This gift shall be of the same value and made of the same materials as the gift given to the Chamberlain <note>original: "camerario"; the guild's treasurer</note> of the said Guild, according to the guild's ordinances. This applies only if, during their term of office, enough condemnations were made and enough money was collected by the Guild from them to cover the cost of such gifts, and not otherwise. However, if a smaller amount of money was collected, the value of their gift must be reduced accordingly, so that the Guild does not and cannot pay anything from its own funds beyond the money actually collected from these fines.

# VIIII. What the Conservators are required to do.

Likewise, they have provided, ordained, and deliberated that the said Conservators can, are bound to, and must enforce the collection of debts from any debtor of the said Guild, however they may be obligated and for whatever reason. This applies to those enrolled in the register and those subject to the Guild as well as those who are not; to private persons as well as others; and to the Commune of Florence <note>original: "communi Florentie"</note> as well as any other person, place, college, or corporation. However, no money from any condemnation or any money to be collected should come into their own hands; rather, all sums of money from the aforesaid must be paid to the Chamberlain of the said Guild. If any of the said Conservators should take or receive any amount of the Guild's money from the aforesaid, he shall be understood to be—and shall be—incurring [the penalty]...

### X. What brokers should receive for their brokerage fees.

Likewise, considering the few affairs that the brokers <term>sensali: middle-men or agents who negotiated sales between merchants</term> of the said guild have, and considering the small prices they can take for brokerage of the merchandise of the Apothecaries' branch <note>original: "menbro degli spetiali"</note>, according to an order and statute of said guild made in December 1363 (1), which statute has not been observed for a long time now and is not observed; and that often from foreigners and even from men and persons of the said guild, greedy prices for brokerage of merchandise have been taken by brokers, whether they buy or sell; wishing to apply an opportune remedy to this, we ordain and provide first that every broker of our guild may and shall be permitted to take and have for brokerage of the things and merchandise of the Apothecaries' branch—of which they might make a trade—from the merchant or craftsman of said guild as well as from those outside the guild, only the salary and price noted below, specifically: from each seller the price written below in its entirety, and half of the price written below from the buyer. And that no one may take as salary for brokerage or as remuneration for any trade or for any things of which he made a trade, more or otherwise than is contained below, neither as a gift nor as a present, under penalty of ten pounds of small lire <note>original: "lire dieci pic."</note> for each time. And anyone may be an accuser of this. And those such brokers shall be corrected and punished as is contained in the statute of the said guild made in 1363 under the rubric or order that begins "Also that every broker..."

### XI. That brokers should be paid for any merchandise sold in bulk, even if no broker is present at the market.
<note>original Latin title: "Quod sensalibus solvatur de qualibet mercantia vendenda in grossum quamquam non intersit mercato aliquis ut sensalis."</note>

Likewise, to provide for the brokers <term>sensali: official middlemen who facilitated trades and ensured they were legal</term> of the said Guild, so that they can and are bound and obliged to perform their brokerage duties more faithfully, with more care, and uprightly: we deliberate, ordain, and provide that every person subject to the said Guild who should buy any merchandise belonging to the member-group of the apothecaries <term>spetiali: pharmacists/apothecaries who also dealt in spices, dyes, and chemicals</term> in bulk—that is, one bale or more, or one barrel or more—for which purchase no specific broker of the said Guild was named by either the seller or the buyer; then and in that case, it is understood that all the brokers of the said Guild, approved by the Consuls and Councilors of the said Guild as required by the orders of said Guild, must be paid the brokerage fee <note>original: "senseria"</note> for such merchandise.

## XII. No broker may facilitate the sale of merchandise from those not subject to said Guild, except in bulk.

September of each year (1), that such approvals or elections of the said **brokers** <note>original: "sensali" — intermediaries who facilitated trade deals for a commission</note> of the said **guild** <note>original: "arte" — the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers</note> must be performed once every year by the **consuls** <note>the highest elected officials of the guild</note> and councilors of the said guild and no more, in the manner and form as disposed by the aforementioned orders of the said guild, namely by the consuls who begin their office in the month of January. b. And the **notary** of the said guild is bound and must send out a proclamation through the guild, by which it is notified by one of the messengers of the said guild among the merchants and craftsmen of the said guild that no one should dare or presume to buy or sell—through the hands of those brokers who were not approved within the three times as said above—any **merchandise** <note>original: "mercatantia"</note> belonging to the branch of the apothecaries, under penalty of two *lire picciole* <note>small silver/copper coins of Florence</note> for each trade made through their hands or any one of them. Which proclamation the said notary must have made on behalf of the consuls of the said guild. ### XV. No "weigher" may delegate his office to another, except by prior deliberation of the consuls and councilors.

Likewise, since it is ordained by the regulations of the said guild that every four months two "weighers" <term>taratori: officials responsible for checking weights and calculating "tare" or deductions for packaging</term> of the said guild are to be drawn, with the authority and power mentioned in the regulations of the said guild (1), and since it has been customary that such weighers sometimes delegate their office to others, who sometimes do not exercise such office with the discretion and caution that is proper, they have provided, deliberated, and ordained that none of these weighers may, nor shall it be lawful for them to, appoint another in their place, except by prior deliberation of the consuls and councilors of the said guild.

### to any barber, unless such apprenticeship 
### appears in the records of the said craft.

Likewise, in order to clarify who may be called an apprentice, they have deliberated that no one shall be understood to be the apprentice of any barber <note>original: "barbitonsoris"</note> unless such apprenticeship appears in the records of the said craft. Furthermore, anyone who stands hereafter as an apprentice with any barber may depart and withdraw from his said master and practice the craft itself wherever he wishes, unless a written record of his said apprenticeship appears in the acts of the said craft, as has been stated.

### XX. An apprentice departing from his master 
### barber may not practice the craft within 
### 400 cubits of that shop for three years.

Likewise, no barber's apprentice may establish himself as an apprentice or as a master near the shop <note>original: "apotecam"</note> of his master from whom he departed, within a distance of four hundred cubits <term>bracchia: a Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters</term>, for three years from the day of his departure according to the form of the statute of the said craft. This applies notwithstanding any license granted or to be granted to the said apprentice by his said master, unless and insofar as the said license appears in the records of the said craft, and not otherwise or in any other manner.

### XXI. That for merchandise purchased, the fee 
### shall be paid to the brokers, namely half by 
### the seller and half by the buyer.

Likewise, wishing to act for the honor, growth, and benefit of the said craft and of everyone subject to the said craft, they deliberated, provided, and ordained that for all the prices of each piece of merchandise that was ordained by the said craft in 1429 (1), and approved by the present makers of the statutes regarding the orders of the brokers <note>original: "sensali"</note>, the seller must pay those prices and amounts, and the buyer must pay half of the amount written for each item.

---

(1) The brokerage fees <note>original: "senserie"</note> were established by the statute-makers not in 1429, but in 1436. Compare the reform of December 28, 1436, rubric X.

# XXII REFORM OF 1436

### XXII. That brokers must bring in writing every week to the house of the said guild the trades made by them in that week.

Likewise, to remove every scandal that could arise or depend on any trade made by any <term>broker</term><note>original: "sensale"; an intermediary who negotiated sales between merchants for a commission</note>, as many scandals often arise through the negligence of not writing them down, they therefore deliberated and ordained that every broker, approved by and subject to the said <term>guild</term><note>original: "arte"; the professional corporation governing a specific trade</note>, must bring or cause to be brought in writing all the trades he has made in the past seven days—that is, from one Monday until the following Monday—making a note of the day the trade was made, what the <term>merchandise</term><note>original: "mercatantia"</note> was, the price, the terms, the quantity, and the exact weight, and the names of the buyer and the seller on a double sheet of paper (or more if they do not fit). And he must present this sheet by the end of the following Monday after the trades were made, either giving it or causing it to be given into the hands of the <term>provost</term><note>original: "proveditore"; the official responsible for the guild's daily administration and oversight</note> who is currently in office or shall be in the future.

And if that Monday should be a commanded feast day, he must bring it on the first following day that is not a feast day, and he must have it placed on a <term>file-string</term><note>original: "filza"; a traditional method of archiving documents by threading them onto a cord or wire</note> which stays with the provost of the said guild. And whichever broker does not bring or cause to be brought the said written trades on the aforementioned appointed day, then and in that case the said broker shall be understood to have fallen into a penalty of twenty <term>soldi piccioli</term><note>original: "soldi picc."; small denomination currency used in Florence</note>, of which the <term>notary</term><note>original: "notaio"</note> of the said guild must have eight soldi, the provost eight soldi, and among all the <term>servants</term><note>original: "famigli"; guild attendants or messengers</note> four soldi.

And this penalty shall be understood to have the same effect as the condemnations made by the office of the Consuls, and they cannot be removed except by the body of the guild. And the notary and the provost can and must record as a debtor any such broker who has fallen into the said penalty; and if that broker does not pay the aforementioned penalty within ten days from the day he fell into it, then from ten days onward he must pay a quarter more, and from twenty days onward he shall pay double. This surplus of a quarter and the additional amount must be paid and recorded as income by the <term>general chamberlain</term><note>original: "camarlimgho"; the chief financial officer or treasurer</note> of the said guild.

And for such a penalty or surplus, they may be seized in property and in person; and let this penalty be understood for every time he acts against this—that is, for every Monday and every ordained day that he fails to bring the trades made. And this penalty of twenty soldi for each time must be paid into the hands of the provost of the said guild, which money the provost must keep account of or record as income in a book called the "Book of the Orders of the Brokers"; and every month he can and must pay from these collected <term>fines</term><note>original: "condampnagioni"</note> eight soldi per pound to the notary, and...

# REFORM OF 1436 — SECTIONS XXII, XXIII

...to himself eight *soldi* <note>A silver coin; 20 soldi made one lira</note> per *lira*, and among all the servants four *soldi* per *lira*. And in the said book must be written all the regulations for the brokers <term>sensali: middle-men or brokers who facilitated trade between merchants</term> established in 1429 (1) and approved by the aforementioned approvers. Also this chapter [must be included]; and if any broker or other subordinate wishes to see or read it, or wishes to see the recorded trades which must be written in the file, the said provider <term>proveditore: a guild official responsible for administration and oversight</term> must show it to any subordinate who wishes to see it. The provider must also record in the said book from which broker he received his writing, and the day he brought or sent it. And if any broker acts against the regulations for brokers, for each instance he shall be understood to have fallen under the penalties set out in those regulations; and the notary and the provider must record such a condemnation and list him as a debtor, just as is done with those condemned by the consuls <note>The highest elected officials of the guild</note> of said guild. Then the provider can and must collect such fines and seize their property or person.

### XXIII. Every broker must have the statutes of the guild read to him during every consulate.
<note>original Latin: "Quilibet sensalis sibi legi faciat quolibet consulatu statuta artis"</note>

Likewise, every broker approved as stated above must, three times every year—that is, at every term of the consular office—within fifteen days of the first month of the entry of each new consulate, come to the said guild and have the aforementioned regulations read to him. Then, in the hands of the notary, he must swear—touching the letters [of the Gospels] with his hands—to observe everything written in the aforesaid regulations, and further promise to conduct their brokerage well and discreetly, without any fraud or barratry <note>barattaria: deceptive practices or illegal exchanges</note>. 

The notary and provider must record their oath, and the aforementioned brokers must also give the notary of the said guild five *soldi piccioli* <note>small deniers/pennies</note> each before they make the aforementioned oath. And if within the said time any of the aforementioned brokers does not come to make the oath and payment, then and in that case, once the time has passed, the said broker shall be understood to have incurred a penalty of five *lire picciole*. This penalty shall be understood to have the same effect as the condemnations made by the consuls. Thus they can and must be collected as stated above, and this penalty must be paid to the general chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the treasurer or financial officer</term> of the guild. Furthermore, if any broker or subordinate of this guild has in times past violated the above regulations, every [past] penalty is understood to be annulled, but these regulations must henceforth be perfectly observed.

### XXIIII. Any broker making a sale of which he has not made a written record shall incur a penalty.
<note>original Latin: "Sensalis aliquis faciens aliquod mercatum, de quo non fecerit scripturam, incidat in penam."</note>

Likewise, if any broker <term>sensale; a licensed middleman who negotiated trades</term>, whether approved or not approved, should make any trade of any merchandise belonging to the branch of the apothecaries <term>spetiali; pharmacists and dealers in spices, dyes, and medicines</term>, of which trade there does not appear a precise written record in the book of said broker, and also on the said sheet that they must bring to the Guild; and if they receive any payment for said trade from either the seller or the buyer, then and in that case this trade shall be understood to have been done deceitfully and with the intent to violate the orders of the brokers mentioned above. And for every trade made in such a manner, the said broker shall be understood to have fallen under a penalty of ten pounds in small florins <note>lire picc.; "piccole" or small currency used for daily transactions</note>. Which penalty shall be understood to have the same effect and value as the condemnations issued by the Consuls; and thus they must be recorded as debtors just as if they had violated any other part of the said orders. And this condemnation must be collected in the same way as the fine for failing to bring the sheet of trades; and anyone may be an accuser in this matter. Such condemnation must be paid and distributed in this manner, namely: one third to the General Chamberlain <term>camarlimgho; the guild's chief financial officer</term> of the Guild, and one third the Provider <term>proveditore; an administrative official</term> of the Guild must enter into the accounts and keep record of, and then distribute those funds in this manner, namely: eight shillings per pound to the Notary, and eight shillings per pound to the Provider, and four shillings per pound to all the servants <term>famigli; lower-level guild employees or messengers</term> of the Guild. And the other third part shall belong to the informer; and if the said informer does not want it, it must be paid to the General Chamberlain of the Guild.

### XXV. What the Consuls are permitted to spend and allocate.
<note>original Latin: "Quid consules possint spendere et stantiare."</note>

Likewise, they have provided, deliberated, and ordained that the Chamberlain <term>camerarius; Latin form of camarlimgho</term> of the said Guild, both present and future, can and shall be permitted to pay—by virtue of the allocations to be made by the Consuls of the said Guild—only and exclusively the ordinary expenses of the said Guild, namely: gifts <term>ensenia; formal gifts or honors</term> and for the giving and sending of gifts to the Consuls and other officials of the said Guild; the salaries owed to any ministers of the said Guild according to the form of the statutes and ordinances of the aforesaid Guild; the special and general offerings to be made by the Consuls of the said Guild, both in conjunction with the Office of the Six of the Merchant Court <term>Mercantie; the Mercanzia, the high court for all guilds in Florence</term> and with the whole body of the aforesaid Guild; bequests for pious causes or otherwise made by the said Guild, whether for girls of marriageable age <note>dowries for poor women</note> or for the poor, or in any other way whatsoever; and for refreshments <note>collationibus; light meals or gatherings</note> held by the Consuls of the said Guild up to the amount of twelve pounds in small florins for each Consul—

of the city of Florence, and as it shall be disposed, ordained, and provided for by the guild itself—following a diligent and secret scrutiny <note>original: "scruptineo"; a formal vote or vetting process for candidates</note> [etc.] solemnly celebrated among them—they have provided, ordained, and deliberated in this manner and form, namely:

### I. That fourteen members of the Balia shall be elected.

First, that the said present Consuls <note>The highest-ranking officials of the guild</note>, or two-thirds of them acting in agreement, can, must, and are bound—between now and the end of the month of December next—to elect and appoint fourteen (and up to fourteen) upright and discreet merchants and craftsmen of the said guild in the city of Florence. These Consuls and the said fourteen so elected shall be called "those of the *Balia* <note>term: Balia; a committee granted extraordinary powers for a specific task or duration</note> of the Guild of Doctors, Apothecaries, and Grocers."

# REFORM OF 1439 III, IV

<note>original: "namenta"</note> regulations of the said guild, once or several times and as it shall seem fit to them or to two-thirds of them, provided that in such elections to be made or in the <term>scrutinies</term> <note>A "scrutiny" was a formal process of vetting candidates to ensure they were eligible and politically acceptable for office</note> to be held, there shall not intervene among those to be elected—whether by the aforesaid consuls or by those of the <term>Balia</term> <note>The Balia was a powerful emergency committee or board with temporary dictatorial powers to enact reforms</note>—more than one person per family and one per any single business partnership. ### IV. Those of the Balia may create regulations.

Likewise, the aforesaid members of the Balia may and shall be permitted to make, within and for the said guild, regarding the aforementioned matters, and to ordain and deliberate on provisions, regulations, deliberations, and any statutes whatsoever, and to revoke them and provide and deliberate anew, as it shall seem fit and pleasing to them. And whatever shall be done, ordained, deliberated, and provided by them shall be valid and binding, and can and must be observed and carried into execution, just as if it had been done, provided, and ordained by the said guild and university <note>In this context, "universitas" refers to the entire corporate body or legal community of the guild</note> and by the body of the said guild, and as if they had been approved by the statutory officials of the guilds of the city and territory of Florence, any exception of law or fact being rejected, notwithstanding any obstacle or any statute or law disposing to the contrary.

# REFORMS OF 1454 I, II

## I. Concerning the Scrutinies. <note>original: "De scruptineis." A scrutiny was a formal process of voting by ballot to determine eligibility for office.</note> (1) <margin>The titles of sections I, II, III, VI, VIII, IX and following were added by a hand from the second half of the 16th century.</margin>

First, the aforementioned <term>statutarii</term> <note>officials appointed to revise or draft the guild statutes</note>, intending and wishing to attend to the honor, state, and growth of the aforesaid Guild, provided [etc.] in this manner, namely: And first, by quashing, revoking, and annulling every and any statute and order of said Guild that spoke of or in any way disposed of the <term>arroti</term> <note>additional members or "adjuncts" called in to assist in a vote or election</note> and their conditions, which were to be made or indeed elected or deputed by the Consuls of said Guild in any <term>squittini</term> <note>scrutinies/elections</note> that were to be held or will be held in the house of said Guild for the office of the Six Councilors of the <term>Merchatantia</term> <note>The Mercanzia, the overarching judicial body governing the Florentine guilds</note> or of the Consulate of said Guild, which were to be brought to the Mercanzia; that the Consuls of said Guild cannot, nor must they in any way conduct said scrutinies or any of them, or elect said adjuncts for said scrutinies, except in the manner and form and how and how many as will be stated below, and under the penalty written hereafter, namely: (2) <margin>Three and a half blank lines follow in the original manuscript.</margin>

## II. Concerning the scrutiny of the Six of the Court of the Mercanzia. <note>original: "De scruptineo sex curiae Mercantiae."</note>

*a.* That for the scrutiny of the Six of the Mercanzia, which is held in the house of said Guild, thirty adjuncts can and must be elected, and no more nor less, all being <term>matricolati</term> <note>formally enrolled members of the guild</note> in the said Guild. Nor can more than one of said adjuncts be elected per <term>consorteria</term> <note>a family association or clan</note>, house, family, or company, or shop. And that all and each of said adjuncts must be thirty years of age, and furthermore that all and each of said adjuncts must have these qualities in their own persons, namely: that each of them has held and exercised the office of the Six of the Mercanzia for said Guild, or indeed the Consulate of said Guild from any scrutiny celebrated from the year 1434 until now or in the future. Which adjuncts, who shall be so elected and of said qualities, and two-thirds of them being present together with the Consuls of said Guild, may and shall be permitted to scrutinize and conduct said scrutinies for the office of the Six of the Mercanzia; provided truly that the election of said adjuncts cannot nor must be done more than once for the same scrutiny. And if by chance it should happen that one had to re-scrutinize or indeed add to or correct the scrutiny made because of some flaw said to be in it or for any other reason, one cannot take other adjuncts or exchange any of them or make any other new election than of those same ones first elected and deputed, and not otherwise nor in any other way may any of said scrutinies be conducted.

## II. REFORM OF 1454

*b.* And in submitting names for the vote and in conducting the said <term>scrutinies</term> <note>original: "squittini"; these were the processes of vetting and electing candidates for public or guild office</note>, and each of them, this method and form described below shall be observed, namely: first, the names shall be drawn from the <term>pouch</term> <note>original: "borsa"; leather bags containing the names of eligible citizens used in Florence's lottery-based electoral system</note> in this specific order: first the Lords <note>The Signoria, the highest executive body</note>, then the Consuls of the said Guild, then the Knights, then the Doctors, then the Colleges of the Palace, then the Captains of the Guelph Party, then the Ten of War <note>original: "dieci di balia"</note>, then the Eight of the Guard, and then the Six of the Merchant Court <note>original: "sei della Merchatantia"</note>. Then, and after these, three pouches shall be made. In the first pouch shall be placed all the <term>additions</term> <note>original: "arroti"; extra members added to a committee</note> of such scrutiny and all the merchants of said guild who have been or were seen <note>nominated or eligible</note> at any time for the Six of the Merchant Court for said guild, or as Consuls of said guild in any scrutiny celebrated from the year 1434 until now; all the aforementioned shall be together and drawn by lot and fortune. In the second pouch shall be placed all those who have the "benefit" <note>eligibility passed through family lineage</note> of a father, paternal grandfather, paternal uncle, or paternal brother or son, who had been or were seen for the office of the Six of the Merchant Court for said guild or as Consul of said guild, from any scrutiny made from the said year 1434 until now or in the future. In the third pouch shall be placed all the other merchants of said guild who have gone or wish to go to the vote as it shall seem fit to the Consuls who are present at the celebration of such scrutiny, and in such number as shall seem fit and pleasing to the said Consuls, always remaining firm in not submitting to the vote those who, according to the order written below, cannot go. And regarding age, let it be observed as they were commanded by the Six of the Merchant Court.

*c.* And that otherwise, nor in any other way, can or should the said scrutinies or any of them be performed, under the penalty of one hundred gold florins <note>A very substantial fine, as the gold florin was the dominant currency of international trade</note> for each of the Consuls of said guild who acts or deliberates against the aforesaid things, or does not observe all the aforesaid things as said above and as will be said below; and similarly for the Notary of said guild and his <term>coadjutor</term> <note>original: "chuitatore"; an assistant or deputy</note> who receives any vote or conducts a scrutiny against the form of the present statute. And let it be understood that the said Notary shall be removed from his said office and cannot be elected to it within the five years immediately following. And nonetheless, whatever is done to the contrary shall not be valid, nor hold, nor can such a scrutiny made against the said form—or where the above things are not fully observed—be sent to the Merchant Court in any way, under the aforesaid penalty. And so that those who must go by lot are submitted to the vote by lot and fortune as said above, first and before the said scrutiny begins, an oath shall be administered to the Notary of said guild and his coadjutor, or whoever else submits the names to the vote, to submit them by lot and fortune, and without any advantage of one over the other.

# REFORM OF 1454 III-V

### III. Concerning the scrutiny for the consulate.

Also, in the scrutiny <note>Italian: *squittino*; the process of vetting and voting on candidates by secret ballot</note> for the office of the consulate of the said guild, thirty-six adjuncts <note>Italian: *arroti*; additional citizens called to assist in the electoral process</note> can and must be elected, and no more nor less, who are matriculated <note>officially enrolled members</note> of the said guild; nor can more than one be elected per family group <note>Italian: *consorteria*</note>, house, company, or shop. And all and each of the said adjuncts must be thirty years of age, and each of them must have been either "seen" <note>Italian: *veduto*; meaning their name was previously drawn from the ballot purse even if they did not serve</note> for the Six of the Mercatantia <note>The Merchant Court of Florence</note> for the said guild, or have been a consul and exercised the office of the consulate of said guild, in any scrutiny celebrated from the year 1434 or in the future; except that six within the said number, and no more, may be those who have not been "seen" or served as consuls or as the Six of the Mercatantia, provided they are not less than the aforementioned age of thirty years. These adjuncts, who shall be so elected and two-thirds of them being present, together with the consuls of the said guild, may and shall be permitted, when it occurs, to scrutinize and conduct the said scrutinies for the office of the consulate of the said guild. And it cannot or should not be done otherwise or in any other way, under the penalties written below.

### IV.

Also, in the casting of votes <note>Italian: *mandare a partito*</note>, the form, order, and method given above in the order for the scrutiny of the Six of the Mercatantia must be observed in this scrutiny in every respect, exactly as is contained and written therein. And thus, in this scrutiny of the consulate, it must be observed, under the penalties for any of the consuls and the notary of the said guild or his coadjutor <note>Italian: *chuitatore*; an assistant or deputy official</note> who does not observe the aforesaid things, as is narrated and written therein. And whatever is done or deliberated to the contrary shall not be valid, nor hold, nor can or should it be observed, nor sent to the Mercatantia. And the same oath shall be given and administered to the notary or his coadjutor or whoever else casts the votes, as is disposed in the scrutiny for the office of the Six. And the election of the said adjuncts cannot be made more than once for the same scrutiny; nor can any be exchanged if it should happen that a re-scrutiny is required, or if one had to add to the scrutiny already made or make any correction, or by any other way or means, no other adjuncts may be taken than those first elected and deputed. And if it is done otherwise, it shall not be valid nor hold, under the penalties aforesaid.

## VI. Those who cannot be put to a vote.
<note>original Latin heading: "Qui non possunt mitti ad partitum"</note>

Likewise, that no one who shall newly come and be received into the matriculation <note>term: matriculation (matricola); the official register of guild members</note> of said Guild may be put to a vote for any office or in any scrutiny that shall be made in the house of said Guild for the office of the Six of the Merchant Court or for the Consulate of said Guild, unless five full years have passed from the day he was received and matriculated in said Guild. With this exception and limitation, namely: that whoever shall come and be received into the matriculation by the benefit of his father or paternal grandfather, blood brother of his father, or blood uncle of his father—who had previously been matriculated for five full years or more—may be put to a vote in any of said scrutinies as if his own person had been matriculated for five full years. And the aforesaid things are not understood to apply to anyone who had been enrolled and matriculated prior to the day of the approval of this statute.

# REFORM OF 1454 VII

...the first four must be at least twenty-five years of age. And these thirty men, of the aforementioned quality and drawn <note>The "tratta" was the process of drawing names from a leather bag (borsa) to select officials.</note> as described above and below, shall be understood to be and shall constitute the Council of the said Guild. And the Consuls <note>The highest-ranking officials of the guild.</note> of the said Guild who shall be in office at the time, or two-thirds of them, together with the said thirty members of the Council, or two-thirds of them—provided the motion is passed by two-thirds of the total number of Consuls and the thirty Council members—shall have the power and authority to deliberate, order, decree, and provide everything and anything in whatever manner they see fit and pleasing. And the said Consuls, together with the Council members or two-thirds of them as stated, shall be understood to have all that authority, power, and <term>balìa</term> <note>A term for extraordinary judicial or legislative power granted for a specific period.</note> that the full body of the said Guild usually possesses. Their term of office shall last for one year, beginning each year on the first day of May. No more than one person from any single kinship group, house, family, company, or workshop may serve on the said Council. Anyone who is currently a Consul of the said Guild or one of our Magnificent Lords <note>The "Signori," the highest executive body of the Florentine Republic.</note> shall be prohibited from serving on the Council. 

If anyone is absent at the time the names are drawn, or if it is understood that such a person would have to serve in absentia for any part of the term, or if anyone is in office outside the city of Florence, or any other person is absent outside the city, territory, or district of Florence, and such a person is drawn for the Council and is otherwise eligible, his name-slip <note>original: "cedola"</note> shall be placed into another bag for those already drawn. When the first bag is empty, all those who were set aside from that first bag shall be put back in, along with all others who have newly become eligible up to that day. 

And whenever the Council needs to assemble, if any member is summoned either in person or by other means and does not arrive at the appointed day and hour due to some impediment or absence—according to the declaration of the Consuls and a vote held among them according to the regulations—then, and in that case, a substitute or substitutes may be drawn to replace the person or persons who are missing. The person originally drawn shall lose all his stipend <note>original: "presente"</note> for the said office, and it shall be given to his substitute or successor. Furthermore, if anyone on the Council is later drawn as a Consul, or is absent serving in another office outside the city of Florence, or is one of the Lords, or is missing for any other reason when the Council meets, a substitute may be drawn once the absence is declared. As stated, the first person drawn loses his stipend, which is given to his successor. 

And if anyone is drawn for the Council and, at the time of the drawing, is "at the mirror" <note>original: "allo spechio." This refers to the *Specchio*, a register of citizens who were ineligible for office because they were in arrears on their taxes.</note>, his name-slip shall be placed in the bag of those drawn and shall not be torn up. And each member of the said Council shall receive as his stipend for the said office <term>two small lire in pepper and saffron</term> <note>It was common in medieval guilds for officials to be paid in valuable spices rather than just coin.</note>.

# VIII, VIIII           REFORM OF 1454

### VIII. Regarding litigation over entry fees and other matters.

Likewise, they provided, deliberated, decreed, and ordained—and by so providing, decreeing, and ordaining—they abolished and annulled the office of the **councilors** <note>Italian: *consiglieri*; these were standing advisors to the guild leaders</note> of the said guild. And [they decreed] that in the said guild there shall no longer be councilors, nor shall any further drawing of names <note>Italian: *tratta*; the process of pulling names from a bag to select officials</note> be conducted for the said office of councilors. And because, according to the regulations of said guild, provisions are made regarding certain legal cases—such as those concerning the rents and **entry fees** <note>Italian: *entrature*; fees paid by a new tenant to take over a shop lease</note> of the shops of the craftsmen of said guild—certain deliberations or sentences must be made by the **consuls** <note>Italian: *consoli*; the highest-ranking elected officials of the guild</note> together with the said office of councilors, and similarly for other things arranged by the regulations; therefore, whenever such a case or cases should occur, the consuls of said guild are bound and required to place into a bag the names of all thirty members of the Council currently in office, and draw six of them by lot and fortune. And the said six drawn shall be, and are understood to be, the councilors of said guild specifically for that case, litigation, and question, or for whatever other such case might arise, for as long as the said case or incident lasts, provided it does not exceed their term of office. When such a case occurs, none of the said six councilors may be a consul, or a kinsman <note>Italian: *consorto*</note> or business partner of a consul, nor may there be more than one per household, company, or shop, nor anyone under the age of thirty completed years, nor anyone absent, according to the rules regarding absentees of the Council set forth in the regulation above.

### VIIII. Method of proposing provisions.

Likewise, they deliberated, provided, decreed, and ordained that in the said Council, no proposal may or should be made by the office or the **proponent** <note>Italian: *proposto*; the presiding officer for the day</note> of the consuls of said guild, nor any **vote** <note>Italian: *partito*; a formal motion or ballot</note> be put forward, unless the provision has first been obtained and won among the consuls themselves by two-thirds or more of them in agreement. And that no provision, order, reform, or other matter may be proposed more than one day in any single month; and on that day, no more than six proposals may be made, neither by way of "will" <note>Italian: *volontà*; likely referring to an informal or discretionary motion</note> nor by any other way or means. And when any proposal is made in the said Council, the **beans** <note>Italian: *fave*; used as secret ballots, typically black for "no" and white for "yes"</note> shall be cast covered and in secret, and the vote shall be collected by the servants of said guild in the **ballot boxes** <note>Italian: *bossoli*</note> ordained for this purpose according to the usual use and custom. And all the said ballot boxes shall then be recorded by the **notary** of said guild into a single other large box; then that box, where all the beans of such a vote placed in said Council are held, shall be emptied into the basin; then the beans shall be counted by the notary of said guild or his **assistant** <note>Italian: *chuitatore*; likely a clerk or coadjutor</note>. And in no other way, nor by any other form or path shall [the vote be valid]

# REFORMS OF 1454, 1455
## VIII

...no proposal may be brought forward that is not secret and conducted in the aforementioned manner. And if it should be done otherwise or in any other form, it shall not be valid, nor hold weight, nor can or should it be observed; nor shall any written record of it be made by the notary of the said Guild or his coadjutor <note>original: "chuitatore," an assistant or deputy to the notary</note>. And likewise, this shall be observed in whatever vote is held among the scrutinizers <note>original: "squittinanti," those responsible for the 'squittinio' or secret ballot process</note> of any election of the said Guild, whether for the office of the Six, or the Consulate, or indeed any other election of the said Guild. And nevertheless, whichever of the Consuls of the said Guild, or the notary or his assistant, who acts to the contrary shall incur a penalty of five hundred small lire; and the said notary and his assistant, in addition to this, shall be removed from their said office and cannot be reinstated or restored to it for the five years immediately following.

# I–III REFORM OF 1461

488

...no imposition of offerings or taxes may be made in any way upon any craftsmen, subjects, or registered members of the said guild <note>The Guild of Physicians and Apothecaries</note>, unless it has first been deliberated and approved by the consuls and council of the said guild, according to the form and manner of the statute and authority granted to that council. And if it should be done otherwise, it shall not be valid, nor hold weight, nor can or should it be observed or put into execution in any way.

## II. Concerning white wax: it must be the same underneath as on top.
<note>original Latin heading: "Pro cera alba sit de supter ut est supra"</note>

Furthermore, they provided, deliberated, decreed, and ordained that from this day forward, no apothecary <term>spetiale; a member of the guild who dealt in medicines, spices, and wax</term>, craftsman, or subject of said guild, nor any other person, may—nor shall it be lawful for them to—work white wax into wax tapers <note>original: "cerotti"</note>, torches <note>original: "falchole"</note>, candles, or in any other work or manner, which is not white underneath as it is on top and made of that same wax, quality, and color; rather, it must be pure, good, clean, and white, both underneath and on top. And whoever should act to the contrary must be punished and condemned in this manner, namely: that whoever works or indeed has or keeps in any way white worked wax contrary to said form and manner—that is, if it is not the same underneath as on top and of the same quality and color as the outside—shall lose all that wax worked contrary to said form and manner, and it shall belong to the aforementioned guild. Furthermore, they shall be understood to have incurred and be condemned to a penalty of ten *soldi di piccioli* <note>small Florentine silver/copper coins</note> for every pound of the weight of said tapers or wax worked in any way against this rule. Thus, the worker shall pay the condemnation based on the weight, and this may and must be put into execution *ipso facto* <note>Latin: "by the fact itself"; meaning automatically without a trial</note>, without any other declaration or sentence, by the masters of said guild, without any exception.

## III. That throughout the entire month of June the books of the craftsmen shall be brought to the guild.
<note>original Latin heading: "Quod per totum mensem iunii reducentur libri artificum in arte"</note>

Furthermore, they provided, deliberated, decreed, and ordained that every year throughout the entire month of June, any craftsman or subject of said guild who keeps a shop for himself or for others for any of the branches of said guild, shall be required within said time and term to produce to the said guild his principal account book of such shop and show it to the notary of said guild. The notary must record the title of the book, and the craftsman must provide and take an oath to state and reveal who were or are his partners <note>original: "compagni"</note>. The notary must make a note of these partners at the foot of said title, so that it may always be clearly seen who owns the shops and who belongs to any shop by way of partnership, under penalty of twenty-five lire.

<summary>This page outlines guild regulations from 1461 regarding internal taxation, quality control for white wax products to prevent fraud, and the mandatory annual registration of business account books and partnerships.</summary>

...small <note>The text likely refers to a fine or penalty in "piccoli," a smaller denomination of Florentine currency.</note> to anyone who does not produce or show said book every year within the stated time, to be taken from him and applied to the said guild.

### IIII. That scrutinies shall be held only and for one member.
<note>original Latin heading: "Quod fient scruptinia solum et pro uno membro"</note>

Furthermore, considering that only the ballot bag <term>borsa; the leather bag containing the name-slips (polize) of eligible candidates used in Florence's lottery-based election system</term> of the syndics <term>sindachi; officials responsible for auditing accounts and ensuring legal compliance</term> of said guild remains to be drawn by separate membership groups, and every other bag is unified for all members together, in order to reduce every bag to a union of all members, they provided, deliberated, decreed, and ordained that the three bags of the syndics be reduced to a single one, and all the name-slips <note>original: "polize"</note> be reduced and put into a single bag. And thus for every scrutiny <term>squittino; the process of vetting and voting on the eligibility of candidates</term> to be held for the said syndics in the future, each person shall be voted upon as a single member; and those who pass shall all be put together into one bag only and no more.

### V. No one can exercise the office of chamberlain who has previously exercised it, unless four months have elapsed.
<note>original Latin heading: "Non potest exercere offitium camerarii qui alias exercuerit, nisi elaxis .IIII. mensibus"</note>

Furthermore, that anyone who in the future exercises or has already exercised, for himself or for others, the office of chamberlain <term>camerlingo; the guild's treasurer</term> of said guild or weigher <term>taratore; an official responsible for checking the weight and quality of goods</term>, may not exercise any of said offices for others within four months. And likewise, he shall have a prohibition against exercising such office for another four months then next following; and it is understood that none of his sons, brothers, fathers, uncles, or paternal grandfathers, nor any of his apprentices or partners, may exercise any of said offices for others within four months from the day that any of his aforementioned relatives, as stated above, had exercised it. This is not to be understood to mean that if someone has exercised it for others, and then is drawn for himself, he cannot then exercise it for himself; rather, he may freely exercise it for himself. But afterwards, he may not succeed for others in the manner stated above, under penalty of one hundred gold florins <note>The gold florin was the prestigious international currency of Florence</note> to anyone acting to the contrary, to be taken from him and applied to the said guild.

### VI. The manner of leasing the guild’s property.
<note>original Latin heading: "Modus locandi bona artis"</note>

Furthermore, they provided, deliberated, decreed, and ordained that, when it should happen that any leasing <note>original: "alloghagione"</note> of real estate, houses, or shops of said guild—or those belonging to said guild in any way—must be made, or indeed if they must be re-leased to whoever was already inside or who had leased those goods before or at another time, the said leasings must be done by the consuls <term>consoli; the chief magistrates or presiding officers of the guild</term> of said guild or two-thirds of them, and six others drawn, and that...

...they must be drawn, every time such a case occurs, from the bag <term>borsa; the leather bag containing the name-slips of eligible candidates</term> of the thirty members of the council present at that time in the said guild. That is, the thirty men who are serving on the council of the guild at that time shall be placed in a bag, and six shall be drawn from that number by lot and luck. These six drawn in this way, together with the said consuls <term>consoli; the highest-ranking executive officers of the guild</term> and two-thirds of their number, may make any lease, but for no longer than five years. Nor after that period can any other lease or extension of said property be made, except in the final year before the rent expires. And anything and everything done to the contrary shall not be valid, nor hold, nor can or should it be observed in any way.

### VII. Councilors shall not have a prohibition.
<note>original Latin: "Non habeant devetum consiliarii"</note>

Likewise, from now on, anyone who is a member of the council of the guild shall not be understood, during their time on the council, to have any prohibition <term>divieto; a legal "ban" or waiting period that prevented an official from holding the same or another office immediately after a term to prevent corruption</term> against the drawing for the office of chamberlain <term>camarlingho; the treasurer or financial officer</term>, syndics <term>sindachi; officials who audited accounts and ensured legal compliance</term>, or assessors <term>taratori; officials responsible for checking weights, measures, or tax assessments</term>, or any other office of the said guild. Instead, they may freely serve on the council and simultaneously hold any other of these guild offices for which they are drawn or for which they qualify at the same time.

### VIII. The drawing shall be done at the discretion of the consuls.
<note>original Latin: "Fiat extractio de coscientia consulum"</note>

Likewise, since according to the regulations of the said guild, when the drawing <term>tratta; the process of pulling name-slips from the election bags</term> for offices within the guild is held, it is required to do so in the presence of twelve witnesses, and most of the time these are apprentices and workers <term>discepoli et fattori; lower-level shop assistants and laborers</term> from the workshops of the guild—a practice which does not bring honor to the guild—they have therefore provided, deliberated, decreed, and ordained that, notwithstanding any other statute, the said drawing may and must be done either with the said witnesses or without them, as it seems best and pleases the consuls who happen to be conducting the drawing of the said offices at that time.

### VIIII. A councilor shall not be replaced except by the consuls' decision.
<note>original Latin: "Non extrahatur loco consulum qui fuit consiliarius"</note>

Likewise, if anyone on the guild council is subsequently drawn for our Magnificent Lords <note>The Signoria, the supreme governing body of the Republic of Florence.</note>, or as a consul of the guild, or for any office outside of Florence, a substitute <term>scambio; a replacement official drawn to fill a sudden vacancy</term> cannot and must not be drawn unless the council is to be assembled and it has first been deliberated by the consuls of the guild that a drawing for such a replacement should proceed.

It also grants consuls more discretion over election procedures to maintain the guild's prestige by moving away from using apprentices as witnesses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the specific legislative adjustments of the 1461 reform for the Guild of Physicians and Apothecaries. REFORM OF 1461 X, XI

### X. The Overseer has no prohibition.
<note>original Latin: "Provisor non habet devetum"</note>

Likewise, considering that the current Overseer <term>provveditore; a permanent official who managed the guild's administrative and legal affairs</term> of the said guild is currently prohibited from exercising the office of the consulate <term>consolato; the board of Consuls who served as the guild's highest executive and judicial leaders</term> of said guild; and considering that this prohibition <term>divieto; a mandatory waiting period between terms of office designed to prevent the concentration of power</term> was always removed for his predecessor, who thus exercised the office of the consulate several times while being Overseer; therefore, they provided, deliberated, established, and ordained that the said current Overseer shall not be understood, by reason of being Overseer, to have any prohibition against exercising the office of the consulate of the said guild.

### XI. Concerning the order to be made to a debtor at the request of a creditor based on the debtor’s account book.
<note>original Latin: "De precepto libri fiendo debitori ad petitionem creditoris super libro debitoris"</note>

Likewise, noting that according to the ordinances of the said guild, any plaintiff <note>original: "actor"</note> seeking a debt of a certain quantity of money or other things from a debtor is bound and required to have that debtor cited for a first, second, and third citation on different days and times, after first paying the required fee <term>dirittura; the legal fee for filing a claim</term>, as these and other related matters are more fully established in the volume of the statutes of the said guild; 

and considering that according to the ordinances of the Merchant Court <term>Mercantia; the supreme commercial tribunal in Florence that acted as an oversight body for all the guilds</term> of the city of Florence, anyone who is a creditor in or upon the account books of his debtor is not required, once the fee is paid, to seek or obtain any other sentence, but once eight days have elapsed from the day the citation was made to such a debtor, such an order, notification, or citation has the same quality, force, and authority as if it were a sentence legally delivered in the said court; 

wherefore anyone, whether from this guild or even from outside this guild, who is in such a way a creditor of a subject of this guild, or against whom the said consuls have jurisdiction, tends to bring his complaint to the said Merchant Court rather than to the court of this guild; 

and wishing to provide for the utility and honor of the said guild, they have deliberated, established, and ordained that henceforth, whoever is a creditor upon the account book or in the books of any of his debtors, and wishes to give or present a petition against him or them in the court of this guild—alleging in his petition the book and papers <note>original: "librum et cartas"</note> as evidence of such debt, where he is the creditor and the time in which the debtor held that book—a single citation made against such a defendant shall suffice. Therefore, it shall be held and be as if he had been cited according to the form of the statutes and ordinances of the said guild and the Commune of Florence; and thus it may and shall be possible for the consuls of the said guild to pass a sentence against him or them, which is and shall be understood to be valid and legally delivered according to the form of the statutes of the said guild, notwithstanding anything else to the contrary.

<summary>This page records two administrative changes: it allows the guild's Overseer to serve as a Consul and streamlines the guild's debt-collection process by reducing the required number of court citations to one, matching the efficiency of the Florentine Merchant Court.</summary>

# XII REFORMS OF 1461, 1462

### XII. That the consuls shall have authority over those not registered in the present guild.
<note>original Latin: "Quod consules habeant auctoritatem contra non matriculatos in presenti arte"</note>

Likewise, the consuls of the said guild shall have, and be understood to have, full jurisdiction, authority, and power over all and singular men and persons not registered <term>matriculati; individuals officially enrolled in the guild's "matricola" or membership register</term> in this present guild and university for any debts or obligations, business, and matters, or any other acts they have performed or are required to perform with another subject of the said guild. The said consuls, both present and future, or two-thirds of them, shall have the power and validity to hear, proceed, pronounce, define, and declare sentences and condemnations against them and any one of them, just as if they were described and registered in the membership book of the said guild.

And having also seen all and singular other statutes and ordinances of the said Guild of Apothecaries <term>spetiarii; the guild members who handled drugs, spices, and often pigments</term> and their corrections [etc.], they approved and confirmed them [etc.].

Giovanni di Francesco di Neri Cechi, ordinary judge and public notary [etc.].

### III. That whoever is a debtor of 20 soldi or more may not hold any guild office. <note>original Latin: "Qui esset debitor in soldis .xx. et ultra non possit exercere aliquod offitium artis."</note>

# REFORM OF 1468 IV-VI

...as if he were to be enrolled <note>original: "matricolare"; to be officially entered into the guild's register, known as the Matricola.</note>. And if the notary or the provider <term>provveditore; a high-ranking administrative official responsible for the guild's finances and records</term> should record such a person to be enrolled without first observing each and every one of the above-written rules, each of them shall incur a fine of one hundred lire <term>lira; a unit of currency; 100 lire was a substantial fine, often exceeding an official's annual salary</term> for each and every instance. And the aforementioned rules shall not be understood to apply to any foreigner, nor to anyone who does not possess or bear the weight of taxes in the city or territory of Florence. Likewise, whoever possesses at least one hundred lire of capital as stated, the consuls of the said guild may settle with him for payment in whatever way and form seems best to them.

## V. 

Likewise, they provided that the number of members of the Council of the said guild—where it is currently thirty—shall be, and is intended to be from this time forward, twenty-four. Their term shall last four months, beginning on the first day of next May, and each member shall have, at the end of his term of office, two wooden bowls containing one pound of pepper <note>Spices like pepper were valuable commodities often used by guilds as a form of payment or ritual gift for officials.</note>. Likewise, from this time forward, candidates shall be vetted <note>original: "squittinino"; referring to the "scrutinio," a process of voting by ballot to determine if a candidate was "fit" for office</note> in the same manner as the office of the consuls and every other office of the guild.

->VI. That brokers may not be more than six.<- 
<note>original Latin: "Quod sensales non possint esse amplius quam sex."</note>

Considering that the aforementioned guild is not properly governed regarding the matter of brokers <term>sensali; middlemen who facilitated trades between merchants and were regulated by the guild</term>, and wishing to provide for this in a way that meets the needs of the said guild and the honor and utility of its craftsmen, the consuls provided and ordained in this way and form: first, that the number of brokers of the said guild shall be, and is intended to be, six brokers and no more, in any way or form. Of these, two shall be for the branch of the mercers <term>merciai; traders in cloth, jewelry, and small luxury goods</term> and the remainder for the branch of the apothecaries <term>spetiali; dealers in spices and medicines</term>; nonetheless, each broker may act as a mediator for either branch. Their office shall last until the end of the month of next January, the election of whom is to be carried out by the consuls of the said guild during this present month of August. And thereafter, each year in the month of January, the confirmation <note>original: "rafferma"; a vote to re-elect or confirm an official for another term</note> of the said brokers must be proposed by the consuls of the said guild together with a sufficient number of the Council of the said guild, each broker individually. And if such a confirmation is obtained, he is understood to be confirmed for one year, starting on the first day of January of that year. They may not be proposed for a vote more than three times per day, nor for more than three days. # VI-X REFORM OF 1468

...he must be removed from his said office and cannot be re-elected to such office within one year. And in place of those or that person who was not confirmed by the consuls and the council of the said guild, a replacement must be elected.

### VII. That the consuls are required to assemble the council every year in the month of January for the confirmation of brokers.
<note>original: "Quod consules quotanno de mense ianuarii teneantur cohadunari consilium pro confirmatione sensalium."</note>

Likewise, that the consuls <term>consoli; the chief magistrates of the guild responsible for its administration and judicial matters</term> who shall enter office each year in the month of January, are bound to assemble the council of the said guild during the said month of January at least once and make a proposal for such re-confirmation, under penalty of ten lire for each of the said consuls, which must be withheld from their payment at the end of their term of office.

### VIII. That the brokers should exercise their craft lawfully.
<note>original: "Quod sensales legaliter eorum artem exerceant."</note>

Likewise, that the said brokers <term>sensali; official middlemen who facilitated trade between merchants and were strictly regulated to prevent market manipulation</term> and each of them are bound and must exercise their said craft of brokerage <term>senseria; the business or office of a broker</term> well and loyally, and must not commit deceit or fraud in any way. They must keep secret all the deals that were entrusted to them or any one of them, and not reveal them to others in any way without the will of the person who entrusted them and of the consuls of the said guild, and they must keep diligent records.

### VIIII. That the brokers cannot enter into any partnership within the said guild, nor perform any work for themselves in the said trade.
<note>original: "Quod sensales non possint aliquam contrahere societatem in aliqua dicta arte, nec aliquid pro se in dicta arte exercere."</note>

Likewise, that none of the said brokers may or shall presume to contract or have any company, alliance, or agreement with any craftsman of the said guild, of whatever sort it may be, nor work for themselves or have any work or trade of the said guild performed for them, under penalty of fifty lire for each person and for each instance. <note>This regulation was intended to prevent "sensali" from having a personal financial interest in the goods they were brokering, ensuring they remained neutral intermediaries.</note>

### X. How a broker may be elected in place of a vacancy.
<note>original: "Quomodo eligere possit sensalem loco vacantis."</note>

Likewise, if it should happen that within the year before the month of January of each year, any of the said brokers' positions should become vacant...

REFORM OF 1468 X-XIII
<page-num>501</page-num>

...exercise or by death or by being dismissed or by refusing or for any other reason, the consuls who shall be in office at the time, after the consulate that was current when the case occurred, and two-thirds of them, may elect a replacement in the event of such a case, death, or any vacancy.

### XI. That brokers are bound on the first of every month to report to the provisor all trades they have made in the past month.
<note>original: "Quod sensales in kalendis cuiuslibet mensis tenentur referre provisori omnes mercatos quos fecerint in mensé preteriti."</note>

Likewise, considering that it was provided by those who had authority over the said guild, that the rates of the brokerage fees <term>senseria; the commission paid to a broker for facilitating a deal</term> that the brokers were to take were revised so that they were all increased by five soldi per lira, and on the other hand it was provided that the brokers should pay five soldi per lira of their earnings; and therefore it is provided that from now on the brokers of the said guild and any one of them are bound and must, under penalty of one hundred small lire, have reported to the provisor <term>providitore; an official responsible for the guild’s financial oversight and auditing</term> of said guild in writing by the first day of every month all the trades that such broker had made in the previous month, in the same manner as they currently do. And that the provisor of the said guild, within the eight days immediately following, must have calculated the account of what and how much they have earned from such brokerage for that month, so that he may provide notice and a cross-reference for the weigher <term>pesatore; the official in charge of the public scales who verified the quantity of goods</term> who is to be appointed by the said guild.

### XII. That no one shall dare to perform any brokerage of things belonging to the said guild.
<note>original: "Quod nullus audeat aliquam senseriam facere rerum ad dictam artem spectantium."</note>

Likewise, that no person, of whatever state or condition they may be, shall dare or presume to perform any brokerage of things or merchandise belonging to the said guild or subject to the said guild, under penalty of twenty-five small lire for each and every time. And whoever reports such a violation shall have a quarter of that fine.

### XIII. That nothing belonging to the said guild can be weighed except with the scales and balances of the guild.
<note>original: "Quod non possit ponderari aliquid spectans ad dictam artem, nisi cum bilancis et statera artis."</note>

So that the merchandise belonging to the said guild may be handled in the same manner as those of the other guilds, such as those of the Guild of Porta Santa Maria <note>The Guild of Porta Santa Maria was the common name for the Silk Guild (Seta), one of the most powerful trade organizations in Florence.</note>, so that whoever buys or sells them must have them measured...

# XIII-XIIII REFORM OF 1468

...measure and weigh at the Guild of Porta Santa Maria <note>The Silk Guild of Florence, also known as the *Arte di Por Santa Maria*, which oversaw the trade of silk and various luxury goods.</note> with the measure and weight ordained by them for that purpose. And since provisions have already been made for the said guild regarding saffron, stamine <term>stamignie; a lightweight wool or cotton fabric, often used for sieves or clothing</term>, and likewise for other merchandise such as manna, rhubarb, and the like; and the said consuls, desiring that the aforementioned guild follow the practices of other guilds in matters that are honorable for the guild; therefore, they provided that from this time forward, no one subject to the said guild may buy or sell any merchandise in bulk belonging to the said guild that is not weighed with the scales of the said guild, or specifically with the steelyard <term>stadera; a portable balance scale using a hook and a sliding weight</term> that must be commissioned for the said guild by its consuls. For this reason, anyone who has to weigh saffron and rhubarb, manna, scammony <term>schamonea; a plant resin used as a strong purgative</term>, turpeth <term>turbitti; a medicinal root from the morning glory family used in medieval physics</term>, and similar fine items, shall pay that amount which is presently ordained. And likewise for measuring stamine or other goods, they shall pay that amount which is ordained by the regulations of the said guild. And everything else that must be weighed of any other merchandise belonging to the said guild shall pay for such weighing to the said guild that amount which shall be provided and ordained by the consuls of the said guild and two-thirds of them, once or more throughout this present month of August. And such merchants who have such merchandise weighed must pay five soldi per lira of the total amount that the broker <term>sensale; a middleman who facilitated trades</term> who acted as the mediator <note>original: "mizano"</note> in such sale and purchase would have received; and they shall withhold that amount from the said brokers' brokerage fee <term>senseria</term> if a broker was involved. And the buyer or seller who is not subject to the guild shall pay; those who are subject to the guild shall pay for those who are not, up to the amount the broker would have to give, up to five soldi per lira.

### XIIII. Likewise, so that whoever has to weigh such merchandise shall not suffer any trouble or inconvenience, and also so that the weight may be just and true, and everyone—both the seller and the buyer—may have their due; 

they provided that the consuls of the said guild and two-thirds of them must have one or more steelyards made, as shall seem necessary to them and to two-thirds of them. Which steelyard must be in the form that seems best to them; and it, or they, must remain in the said guild’s office, so that whoever wishes to weigh may and must do so at their convenience. And should it be necessary to send it outside of the said guild office, the said consuls may send it. And the said consuls and two-thirds of them are bound to ensure that the said merchandise is justly weighed, and for this purpose they shall appoint one of the guild’s servants <term>famigli; staff members who performed administrative or manual tasks for the guild</term>, specifically the one whom the said consuls deem most fit and suitable for the said exercise.
