# REFORMS OF 1468, 1469 XV

### XV. Penalty for those holding, selling, and acting against the above-written rules.

Item, so that the aforementioned things are observed, from this time forward, any merchant or any person whatsoever subject in any way to the aforementioned guild, who against the said procedure should buy or sell any merchandise that has not been weighed or measured as stated above, by the very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> is understood to have incurred a penalty of five *lire piccioli* <note>The *lira picciola* was a standard unit of Florentine "small" currency used in daily transactions.</note> for each and every time, and for every bale, barrel, or bundle that they actually sold or bought. The guild and its provider <note>A *proveditore* was a guild official responsible for administrative oversight and enforcement.</note> may demand this fine and record them as a debtor, even without any other formal declaration or legal act. And the aforementioned things shall begin and be understood to take effect on the first day of the coming month of September.

And having seen all other statutes and ordinances of the said guild of apothecaries <note>original: "spetiariorum"</note> and their corrections, etc., they approved and confirmed all and singular the said statutes, chapters, and ordinances, both those newly presented before them and all others contained in the present volume of statutes, etc.

->Piero di Carlo Vive, ordinary judge and public notary, etc.<-

->REFORM OF 1483 I<-

# I. On the manner of appointing the official of the said guild. <note>original: "De modo creandi provisorem dicte artis"; the Latin title specifies the legal procedure for electing the guild's administrator.</note>

As the office of the provider <term>proveditore; the chief administrative and financial officer of the guild, responsible for its daily management</term> of the said guild is of great importance, it is therefore necessary for the said office to be held by men who are experienced, capable, and fit for its governance. Considering that within the regulations of this guild there is currently no statute providing a rule, form, or method for how the said provider should carry out his duties, nor how long his term of office should last, nor anything regarding what he must do or observe by virtue of his office—from which follows great inconvenience, to the harm and shame of the said guild—the said reformers and statute-makers of this guild, wishing to provide a beneficial remedy for such inconveniences, have provided, legislated, deliberated, and ordained in this manner and form, namely:

That the office of the current consuls <term>consoli; the elected heads of a Florentine guild</term> must, together with those advisors <note>original: "arroti"; additional citizens called in to assist the guild leaders in special deliberations or elections</note> who shall be mentioned below, conduct and celebrate a scrutiny <term>squittino; a formal process of vetting and voting on candidates for office</term> for the office of the provider of the said guild. This must be done under penalty of 25 large florins <note>original: "fiorini larghi"; the standard high-value gold currency of Florence</note> to be paid by each of the said consuls and applied to the guild's funds, if they have not performed it during their term of office in the customary manner of other scrutinies, using secret ballots and registers.

And whoever in the said scrutiny shall win the vote by two-thirds of the black beans <note>original: "fave nere"; in Florentine elections, a black bean represented a "yes" vote and a white bean represented a "no" vote</note>, may and must have his name placed on two slips in a bag designated for this purpose. From this bag, every year in the month of January, one person eligible for the said office must be drawn. This is under penalty of 25 large florins for any of the consuls of the said guild who do not have the said drawing performed at the appointed time, which penalty shall be applied to the said guild.

And whoever is thus drawn and found eligible shall be understood to be, and shall be, the provider of the said guild for a term of one year, beginning on the 25th day of the month of March <note>The 25th of March, the Feast of the Annunciation, was the official start of the New Year in the Florentine calendar</note>. And within eight days from the day of his drawing, he shall be bound, in the presence of the consuls of the said guild, to swear upon God’s Holy Gospels, touching the scriptures with his hands, to observe everything contained within the present regulations concerning the said provider, as well as any other regulations that speak or might speak of the said provider, provided they do not contradict these present orders.

Furthermore, he shall be bound to provide four suitable and sufficient guarantors <term>mallevadori; individuals who legally pledged their own wealth to guarantee the official's financial honesty</term> from among the men of the said guild. These guarantors must be approved by a vote of the consuls of the said guild, with each one obligating himself for the sum of one hundred large florins. All those who have been seen <note>meaning those who have previously been officially nominated or held office</note> in the office of the consuls of the said guild and are at least twenty-four years of age shall be put to the vote in the said scrutiny. The same prohibitions <term>divieto; rules preventing members of the same family or those with unpaid taxes from holding office simultaneously</term> that are applied by the Mercatanzia <note>original: "Merchatantia"; the overarching commercial court that governed all Florentine guilds</note> to the drawing of the consuls of the said guild shall also apply to the drawing of this provider. The said provider shall have as a salary...

...four sealed florins <term>fiorini di sugello; a standard currency used in Florence for official accounting</term> per month, which cannot be paid to the said provider without the appropriation and deliberation of the consuls of the said guild currently in office. Furthermore, he shall have all those emoluments as the provider of the said guild has been accustomed to having in times past, as established by the regulations.

## II. The provider of the said guild is required to exercise his office in person. However, he may appoint a substitute. <note>original: "Teneatur provisor dicte artis personaliter exercere eius officium. Possit tamen substituere."</note>

The said provider shall be required to exercise his office in person; he may nonetheless substitute a son, brother, or the son of a biological brother, provided they are thirty years of age or older and are first approved by the consuls and the council of the said guild. Anyone who is drawn as provider and wishes to refuse the office may do so within six days, provided they pay twenty soldi to the chamberlain <term>camarlingho; the treasurer or financial officer responsible for the guild's funds</term> of the said guild. In the same manner, syndics <note>legal representatives of the guild</note> and notaries may also refuse.

## III. The said provider is required to keep detailed accounts of rental money, and not to grant any lease to debtors of the said guild for a certain amount. <note>original: "Teneatur dictus provisor retinere computa particularia de pecunia affiti, et non facere aliquam locationem debitoribus dicte artis de certa summa."</note>

The said provider shall be held and obligated, with all due care and diligence, to keep an account in a large ledger and to reconcile the income and expenses of the chamberlain of the said guild. He must keep particular records and accounts of the rents and leases of the said guild, the form of the contracts <term>alloghagioni; the legal act of leasing out guild-owned properties or assets</term>, the alms, and every other matter, separately and distinctly from one another, and in a clear and open manner. 

He shall not grant any lease to anyone who owes a debt greater than half of one year’s rent, nor without a guarantor <term>mallevadore; a person who legally pledges to pay if the primary debtor defaults</term> approved by the consuls of the said guild currently in office. Anything done otherwise shall be void, and he is required to collect and ensure the collection of all ordinary and extraordinary income and revenues from all debtors of the said guild, and to keep a diligent account of everything in agreement with each debtor. He cannot and must not take money or anything else without making a receipt <note>original: "poliza"; a written record or voucher of the transaction</note> in his own hand for the person paying on the day he receives such money or items; and should he or others on his behalf receive such money or items in Florence, or within four miles of it, [he must record it] within two days—from beyond four miles, within eight days thereafter—

...following, he must have them entered as income by the chamberlain <term>camarlingo; the treasurer or financial officer responsible for the guild's funds</term> of the said guild. Nor may he retain anything as his own property without a proper appropriation. And whenever he fails to observe or lacks in any of the aforementioned matters, it shall be understood that he is deprived of office and subject to a double penalty, which shall be applied to the said guild; anyone may act as an informant and shall earn a fourth of the fine that is entered as income. And for all the aforementioned things, the said provider and each of his four guarantors <term>mallevadori; individuals who legally pledged to cover the provider's financial liabilities</term> shall be understood to be obligated, not exceeding the sum of one hundred large florins <term>fiorini larghi; high-quality gold coins used in Florence for significant transactions</term> for each of his said guarantors. And at the end of his said office, each year on the 15th day of March, two syndics <term>sindaci; officials appointed to audit accounts or represent the guild's legal interests</term> must be drawn from the same purse <note>the leather bag containing the names of eligible guild members for election</note> from which the said provider is drawn, being at least thirty years of age.

### IIII. Every year, on the 15th day of March, syndics shall be drawn to review the provider's accounts. Prohibition of syndics. <note>original: "Quolibet anno, die 15 martii extrahantur sindici ad revidendum rationes provisori. Deveta sindicorum."</note>

All relatives and business associates of the said provider shall be prohibited from holding the said office of syndics, and the name-slips of said drawn syndics must be returned to the purse. Which syndics, once drawn, must have settled all the books and writings of the said provider within one month from the day of their drawing, as well as everything that the said provider had administered during his term of office, in whatever manner and for whatever reason. And for everything they find the said provider has failed to do as contained above, they must list him as a debtor; and of that which he was made a debtor by virtue of their report and was put toward the drawing, they shall have a fourth part. Furthermore, they shall receive for their labor from the said guild one large florin each, after the report of the said settlement has been made by them and approved by the consuls <term>consoli; the governing board of the guild</term> of the said guild. And regarding what is contained in the said report, it is understood that the said primary provider remains obligated for the whole, along with the four guarantors, each for the aforementioned amounts of one hundred large florins per person.

### V. Every year at the appropriate times, the drawing of the provider and syndics shall be held. <note>original: "Quolibet anno debitis temporibus fiat tratta provisoris et sindicorum."</note>

The consuls of the said guild shall be held responsible (under penalty of 50 large florins for each, applied to the said guild as above, and from which they cannot be released except by a vote of the consuls and coun-

# V-VIII REFORM OF 1483
<page-num>514</page-num>

...council of the said guild, having obtained the vote by three-quarters of the black beans <note>original: "fave nere"; black beans were used as "yes" votes in Florentine ballots, while white beans signified "no"</note>, and it being impossible to propose more than three days, nor more than three times per day to make a proposal), to perform at the proper times each year the drawing <term>tratta; the process of drawing names from a leather bag (purse) to select officials</term> of the said provider and the said syndics <term>sindachi; officials appointed to audit accounts and ensure legal compliance</term>. The said provider shall have a prohibition <term>divieto; a legal restriction preventing an official or their family from holding other specific offices to prevent a monopoly on power</term> from the office of the consulate of the said guild and from every other office of the said guild, including himself and his sons. No provider may remain in office more than one year, and he shall have a prohibition for one year from the day he leaves office. And a similar prohibition shall apply to the syndics of the said guild.

### VI. Every year the notary of the said guild shall be bound to read the present ordinances to the new provider of the said guild. <note>original: "Quolibet anno notarius dicte artis teneatur legere presentia ordinamenta novo provisori dicte artis."</note>

The notary of the said guild shall be bound, under penalty of fifteen large florins each year, at the drawing of the said provider and in the presence of the consuls of the said guild, to read the present ordinance to the said provider, so that everything he must do and observe may be known to him.

### VII. Election of the provider for three years. <note>original: "Electio provisoris pro tribus annis."</note>

And because the scrutiny <term>squittino; the formal process of vetting and voting on the eligibility of guild members for office</term> of the said provider has not yet been completed, and the guild finds itself in need of governance and of being restored and settled regarding its records—and needing to be corrected <note>original: "amata"; likely a scribal error or archaic usage for "ammendata" (amended), referring to fixing the "disorders" mentioned next</note> concerning its other disorders—and since delaying would multiply these into greater disorders and inconveniences; for these reasons, they have elected and deputized as provider of the said guild—with the obligations, conditions, salaries, office, duties, and qualities stated above, for a term of the next three future years, beginning on the 25th day of the present month of March 1483 and ending as follows, and in no way for longer—the prudent man Marco di Benintendi d'Antonio Pucci.

->The 20th day of the month of April, 1483.<-

### VIII. Election of the notary for three years. <note>original: "Electio notarii pro tribus annis."</note>

Likewise, the above-mentioned statutaries <term>statutarii; committee members appointed to draft or revise the guild's statutes</term> elected and reconfirmed as notary of the said guild Ser Lotto, son of Ser Francesco, son of Ser Tommaso de' Masi, for a term of three years beginning on the 20th day of the month of March just past, with the salary and other usual benefits.

# REFORM OF 1483 IX-XI
<page-num>515</page-num>
<header>REFORM OF 1483 IX-XI</header>

->On the 24th day of the month of April, 1483.<-

### IX. Each year in the month of January, officials shall be drawn for Saint Barnabas and for the monastery of the converts.

The aforementioned statute-makers and reformers, having observed the necessary formalities <note>original: "servatis servandis etc."; a standard legal phrase indicating all procedural requirements were met</note>, etc., and in every way, etc., have deliberated that one purse <term>marsupium; a leather pouch or bag used to hold the names of eligible candidates for office</term> be prepared for the officials of Saint Barnabas and the monastery (1) of the converts <note>original: "monasterium convertitarum"; the Monastero delle Convertite was a Florentine institution for "reformed" prostitutes</note>. In this purse shall be placed the names of all those who obtained the aforementioned vote through two slips <term>apodissas; ballots or certificates of eligibility</term>. From this, each year in the month of January, three officials shall be drawn for the Works of Saint Barnabas <note>referring to the church or charitable works associated with St. Barnabas</note> and three for the monastery of the converts. These men must be at least forty-four years of age complete, and they shall be drawn according to the form of the statutes of the said guild.

### X. The bagging and drawing of the chamberlain.

Likewise, that in a certain newly made purse shall be placed the names of all those who have until now been seen to serve as consuls <term>consules; the highest-ranking executive officials of the guild</term> and for the office of the consulate of the said guild for one slip. From this, at the beginning of each consulate, one person shall be drawn as chamberlain <term>camerarius; the treasurer or financial administrator</term> of the said guild. He shall serve for a term of four months, beginning on the day that such consulate commences. This shall be observed from time to time, and the statutes of the said guild shall be followed regarding the term of the said chamberlain, as well as his age and other requirements contained in the statutes.

### XI. Regarding the inspectors of the said guild.

Likewise, the said statute-makers and reformers, noticing how in the drawing of the inspectors <term>taratoribus; officials responsible for checking "tare" weights and the purity of spices and medicines</term> of the said guild, which occurs at each consulate, those drawn often appoint an apothecary <term>aromatarium; a specialist in spices, herbs, and drugs</term> in their place to perform the inspection because they themselves lack the expertise. Since someone is sometimes appointed who is not as knowledgeable as is fitting, they have therefore deliberated that the said inspectors thus drawn cannot and must not in any way appoint anyone in their place, unless that person is approved by the consuls of the said guild and by two-thirds of their number. Anything done to the contrary shall be void.

->On the said day<-

# XII REFORM OF 1483
<page-num>516</page-num>
<header>XII REFORM OF 1483</header>

### XII. How the chamberlain shall pay the money of the said guild. <note>original Latin: "Quomodo camerarius solvat pecuniam dicte artis"</note>

a. That the chamberlain <term>camarlingho; the treasurer responsible for the guild's finances</term>, who will be in office from the next Calends of May <note>the 1st of May, 1483</note> onward for the said guild, may and is permitted to pay—by appropriation <term>stantiamento; an official authorization or budget allocation</term> made by the consuls <term>consoli; the chief magistrates and leaders of the guild</term> of the said guild in office—the ordinary expenses of the said guild. These include gifts <note>original: "presenti"; formal gifts or tributes often sent to high-ranking city officials or other guilds</note> to be given and sent to the consuls and other offices of the said guild, and the salaries of any servant of the said guild according to the form of the guild's statutes. This also includes general, particular, and special offerings to be made by the consuls of the guild, whether in cooperation with the Office of the Six of the Merchant Court <term>Merchatantia; the Mercanzia, Florence's high court for commercial and guild disputes</term> or with the community of the said guild. It further includes bequests made for pious causes or elsewhere for girls who are to be married <note>referring to the *Monte delle doti*, where the guild might provide dowries for the daughters of impoverished members</note>, as well as any other bequests, provided he does not pay more than is disposed by the wills or bequests. Payments should follow the orders where such orders exist, such as for the collections to be made by the consuls of the guild up to the sum of twelve *lire piccoli* <term>the "small" silver-based pound used for local transactions in Florence</term> and no more for any consulate. According to the orders, this includes salaries for the priests who serve or will serve the oratory of the Old Market <note>original: "Merchato vechio"; the Mercato Vecchio was the site of the guild's religious center</note>, not exceeding the sum of four *lire piccoli* <note>original: "lire quattro fiorini piccoli"; likely a clerical error for "lire di piccioli"</note> per month. This also covers what is spent for wax, paper, books, ink, and wood for the said guild; for the wax used at the oratory of the Old Market; for the wax used before the consuls of the guild; for the wax for our Lady in the guild <note>likely an image or altar of the Virgin Mary within the guild hall</note>; and for oil for the guild's lamp and for the oratory of the Old Market, not exceeding the sum of eighty *lire piccoli* in the whole year. In this, the consciences of the consuls or whoever makes the appropriation are charged <note>a solemn reminder that they are morally and spiritually responsible to God for the honest use of these funds</note>, and they must first give an oath to the provider <term>proveditore; the administrative overseer</term> that they will swear to this.

b. And beyond the aforementioned things, any other money to be paid for useful, necessary, or honorable expenses of the aforementioned guild may be paid and recorded as an outflow by the said chamberlain. This is allowed when it has been appropriated and deliberated by the consuls of the guild, obtaining a favorable vote <term>partito</term> among the said consuls and the Great Council of the said guild. The vote must be obtained by three-quarters of the black beans <note>Florentines voted by placing beans in a bag: black for "yes," white for "no"</note>, charging the consciences of the said consuls, who must swear that they believe these expenses to be useful, necessary, and honorable for the said guild. And whatever is done to the contrary shall be of no value. Should the chamberlain pay otherwise, let it be understood that he pays out of his own pocket, and he shall incur a penalty of twelve *lire piccoli* for each entry that he pays or records as an outflow against the said form. And the syndics <term>sindachi; officials appointed to audit and review the accounts of guild officers</term> who shall be drawn or deputed to audit such chamberlains must audit according to the said or[der]—

### XIII. Regarding the tenants and leaseholders of the said guild. <note>original Latin: "Pro pensionariis et fittaiuolis dicte artis"</note>

Item, considering that the said guild owns several shops <term>botteghe</term> and properties and holds them for rent or lease, and because it is necessary to repair them where and when needed to maintain them, and desiring that they be repaired both effectively and only when necessary and not otherwise, they [the reformers] deliberated: that when any tenant <term>pigionale</term> or leaseholder <term>fittaiuolo</term> of such properties or shops wishes to incur any expenses for the said reasons, they may not do so, nor have them done, without the license of the consuls of the said guild. However, with the license of the said consuls, they may do so, provided the amount does not exceed four small lire. And such expenses so incurred must be recorded in the account of such tenants or leaseholders as income and expenditure, and by the appropriation of the consuls and council of the said guild.

And if it is necessary to spend more, up to ten small lire per year, this may be done and recorded in the account of the said tenants and leaseholders as income and expenditure, and by the appropriation of the consuls and council of the said guild. And they may not be repaired otherwise. And if a larger sum needs to be spent, it cannot be done without the deliberation and appropriation of the consuls and council, which shall be ordained as described below. And the said chamberlain, regarding the said sums and as stated above, may record them as expenditure by virtue of the deliberation and appropriation as stated above, and not otherwise. And should he act to the contrary, the said chamberlain shall fall under a penalty of ten small lire for each entry, applied to the said guild, and furthermore, the payment shall be void.

<header>XIV-XVII REFORMS OF 1483</header>

### XIV. No change may be made to any statute, except in a certain manner.
<note>original Latin: "Non possit fieri aliqua innovatio alicuius statuti, nisi certo modo"</note>

And furthermore, considering that the said <term>statutarii; the officials responsible for drafting and revising the guild’s statutes</term> believe that changing statutes and orders frequently results in shame for the said guild, and likewise, when they are well-examined, it results in honor for the said guild; therefore, they deliberated and decreed that from this day forward, no statute may be changed <note>original: "innovare"</note>, except by the deliberation of the <term>consoli; the chief executives or "consuls" of the guild</term> together with the <term>consiglio maggiore; the Grand Council, the guild's primary legislative body</term>, which must be organized as described below.

### XV. No disposal of the assets of the said guild may be made, except in a certain manner.
<note>original Latin: "Non possit fieri aliqua alienatio de bonis dicte artis, nisi certo modo"</note>

And that the said consuls or other offices or officials of the said guild may not sell or transfer <note>original: "alienare"</note> any immovable property <note>real estate like houses or shops</note> of the said guild, or property pledged to the guild in any way, nor may they barter them, nor may they even purchase any assets. But should it be necessary to do any of these things, they may be done by the consuls and the aforementioned Grand Council.

### XVI. No scrutiny for any office may be held, except in a certain manner.
<note>original Latin: "Non possit fieri scruptineus alicuius offitii, nisi certo modo"</note>

And that the said consuls may not conduct any <term>squittino; the "scrutiny," a process of balloting and vetting to determine who was eligible for office</term> for any office of the said guild, unless the vote <note>original: "partito"</note> is first obtained by the said consuls together with the Grand Council of the said guild. The aforementioned rules shall not apply when it is commanded by the <term>Sei della Merchatantia; the "Six of the Mercanzia," the magistrates of Florence's commercial court who oversaw all guilds</term> that a scrutiny should be held for the Six of the Mercanzia or for the consulate according to the orders, or if it were deliberated or decreed by the statute-makers of the Commune <note>the city government of Florence</note>. In such cases, the scrutiny for the Six of the Mercanzia and the consulate shall be conducted in that manner and form, and with those <term>arroti; "additions," extra members or electors added to a committee for a specific task</term> as shall be declared by the said consuls.

### XVII. How the leasing of the assets of the said guild should be done.
<note>original Latin: "Quomodo fiant locationes de bonis dicte artis"</note>

No <term>alloghagione; the formal act of leasing or renting out property</term> of any assets of the said guild may be made, except according to the form of the statutes of the said guild. And no shop or house of the said guild may be leased unless the consuls of the aforementioned guild first, at least one month in advance, cause a notice <note>original: "scritta"</note> to be posted <note>original: "apichare"</note> on the said shop or house, by which they notify that the said consuls intend to rent out <term>apig[i]onare; to lease or put up for rent</term> the said house or shop on a certain day.

### XVIII. Method of forming the Grand Council of the said guild.
<note>original Latin: "Modus faciendi consilium maius dicte artis"</note>

And the said <term>statutarii; officials in charge of revising the guild's laws</term> and reformers, desiring that the said guild be reformed so that the provisions and deliberations on important matters are well and healthily decided and decreed, in the best way they could, deliberated, ordered, and decreed that in the said guild a <term>purse; a 'borsa' or bag used for drawing names for office</term> be made, into which shall be placed the names of all those who, up until today, have been "seen" <note>This refers to candidates whose names were drawn and who passed the eligibility check, even if they didn't end up serving at that specific time.</note> or actually drawn at any time for the office of the six counselors of the <term>Mercatantia; the commercial court or 'Merchant Tribunal' of Florence</term>. And no one can be part of this new council who is not at least forty-four years of age. And when the drawing for this council is made, the tickets <note>original: "polize"</note> of those who are drawn and are eligible should be put into another purse, until there are no more left in the first purse. And then that second purse shall be emptied back into the first, and so it shall continue from time to time. This council, together with the consuls of the said guild, shall have and are understood to have the same authority over the affairs of the said guild and each of its members—that authority, power, and <term>balia; full executive and legislative power</term>—which the entire body of the guild has or can have, provided the vote is carried among them by at least three-quarters of the <term>black beans; 'fave nere', used as secret ballots where black beans represented 'yes' votes</term> of the said council. And the said council of six shall last for one year, beginning every year—

### XVIIII. For the servants and attendants of the said guild.
<note>original Latin: "Pro famulis et domicellis dicte artis"</note>

The said officials, considering those things that bring honor and utility to the said guild, and considering that the income of the said guild has decreased due to **bad times** <note>original: "chattivo temporale," likely referring to poor economic conditions, perhaps due to bad harvests or plague, affecting the guild's revenue</note> while the guild's expenses have not decreased in any part, and wishing to provide in a way that is most useful and ensures the said guild is served as required, therefore ordained in this manner and form, namely:

a. That every year in the month of April, the consuls currently in office are bound and required, under penalty of 25 <term>large florins</term> for each person who acts to the contrary (to be paid to the said guild), to put to a vote or <term>scrutinize; 'squittinare,' the process of balloting or vetting candidates</term> among the said consuls and the ordinary council of twelve all the <term>servants; 'famigli'</term> or <term>attendants; 'donzegli'</term> of the said guild. And those who obtain two-thirds of the votes of the said consuls and council shall be understood as elected servants and assistant servants of the said guild, with the salary and emoluments established by the statutes. In such a vote, no servant can be proposed more than nine times in three days, nor more than three times per day. And those, or the one, who is not approved within the said time shall be considered dismissed and removed from such <term>service; 'exercitio'</term>, nor can they, directly or indirectly, perform the work in any way, under penalty of fifty large florins for them and for whoever employs them in the said service.

I. The Lord Consuls have considered how great an importance lies in passing sentences and auditing accounts for sums of 100 lire and upward. Furthermore, having been reminded by some of the leading and loyal members of the honor and reputation of this Guild that they ought to provide for such matters and establish some order and method therein, it is therefore provided, decreed, and ordained: that the present consuls, together with twenty <term>adjuncts; extra members called in to assist in decision-making</term>—specifically those who have sat or been <term>nominated; original: "veduti" (seen), referring to those whose names were drawn for office but who were disqualified for minor reasons, though still considered eligible for high councils</term> as the six members of the <term>Mercatantia; the high court of the merchant guilds in Florence</term>, provided they are available to be chosen. # REFORMS OF 1491 I
### 525

...to be, and shall be, two-thirds or more of the said nominees, who must be summoned by the said <term>consuls; the chief magistrates and administrators of the guild</term> currently in office, and also by those who will be in office in the future, whenever it is necessary to conduct such <term>scrutinies; the formal process of voting by ballot to select eligible officials</term>.

*b.* And all those who obtain such a vote by two-thirds of those voting in the scrutiny must be, and shall be, entered on an individual slip by the said consuls, together with the notary, into a bag which must be newly made for said <term>guild; the professional association of physicians and apothecaries</term>. This bag shall be placed in the guild’s chest where the other bags are kept. This bag shall be called the "Recourse Bag for Delivering Sentences of One Hundred <term>Lire; a silver-based currency used for smaller transactions</term> and upward." Regarding this bag: whenever the current consuls of the guild wish to pronounce any sentences exceeding the sum of one hundred lire—whether to condemn or to acquit—they are required, at the request of either party, to draw six names from those entered into said bag. And those drawn, together with the future consuls, are required and obligated to deliver a sentence on the case brought before them within ten days of their drawing. In the event that any of those drawn cannot be found for such a judgment, due to a physical impediment or other <term>legitimate cause; a legally recognized excuse such as illness or being out of the city</term>, in this case, upon the declaration of the said consuls and once it is clarified that the person is unable to serve due to some defect of person or other legitimate cause, they are required and obligated to substitute another from said bag in his place and return the first name to the bag. Furthermore, all those who in the future shall exercise the office of the consulate—that is, those who up to the present day have not yet sat as consuls—must be put to a vote every year in the month of December before the <note>original: "squittinanti"</note> voters appointed by the consuls serving in that month. The consuls may not elect them in any other way or form than what is stated above. And those who are put to a vote and approved by two-thirds of the voters, the said consuls together with the notary are required and obligated to enter those who have succeeded into the said Recourse Bag, under penalty of 100 <term>large florins; the high-value gold currency of Florence</term> for each of the consuls, and also for the notary, should they fail to observe what is stated above.

*c.* Furthermore, the litigating parties, when such a recourse drawing is to be held, may each name up to six <note>original: "sospecti" In this legal context, these are people the litigants 'suspect' of bias and wish to recuse from the panel.</note> challenged persons, and no more. And such sentences, pronounced and given in the manner and form aforesaid and handled according to the present order, whether they be acquittals or condemnations, shall be valid and binding and must be carried out. They shall enjoy all the privileges and favors that were ever granted and attributed by the ordinances of this guild at any time.

I, II REFORMS OF 1491

d. And because every labor deserves a reward, it is therefore provided and ordained that such litigants, when they must initiate such a <term>recourse; a formal appeal or review of a case by additional judges</term>, are required and must have deposited ten lire into the hands of the <term>chamberlain; the guild's treasurer and financial officer</term>. Once the names for the recourse have been drawn and a sentence is delivered (or even if it is not), these funds are to be spent as the <term>consuls; the chief magistrates of the guild</term> see fit and pleasing, and those expenses shall be sent to each of the said consuls and to each of those drawn, divided equally among them. And these ten lire shall be returned or not, according to what shall be declared by the sentence of the said consuls and <term>arroti; additional members drawn from the bag to assist the consuls</term>, or by two-thirds of them. And these matters shall be observed in their entirety, as stated above, notwithstanding any other law or statute.

## II. Penalties for consuls who do not expedite cases.

And it is further provided, in order to circumvent a statute made a long time ago in this guild, which states that for any case brought before the consuls, if they have not resolved it within 45 days, the person who brought the case may, without any prohibition once that time has passed, go to the <term>Mercantia; the high court of the Merchant Guild which oversaw all Florentine trade disputes</term>. In order that such inconveniences do not arise in the future, and also for the honor of the guild, it is disposed by this present statute that the consuls who serve in the future are required and must, within the said 45 days after the due requests have been made, have such a case resolved and a sentence given, provided the sum is from 100 <term>lire; the standard silver-based currency</term> upward. 

And if the said consuls do not resolve it within that term, they shall be understood to have fallen under a penalty of 50 lire each. And if such a case is for 100 lire or more, they are required and must within those 45 days, at the request of either party, draw the men for the recourse within that term, in the manner and form described elsewhere, under the penalty of fifty lire each. And if it is not requested by the party, in this case the said consuls, by not drawing the said recourse, shall not be considered to have fallen under the said penalty; nor, by this present statute, may the litigants seek any other judgment than that of their superiors, under the penalty of <term>one hundred large florins; the prestigious gold coin of Florence, a very high fine</term> for whoever acts against this; but the penalty shall only be understood to fall upon the aforementioned consuls when it has been requested by either party and they did not comply, together with the notary, who is required to give notice to the said consuls within that term of those sentences that are pending, in the manner and form stated above. 

And for whoever is found in any way to have fallen under the aforementioned penalties, it is provided that the consuls who succeed them after their term of office are required and must collect the aforementioned penalties; and once collected, in whole or in part, they must have them entered into the accounts by their <term>chamberlain</term>.

# REFORMS OF 1491 II-IIII

And if it should happen that those so convicted, for whatever reason it may be, do not pay, it is provided by this present statute that each of them may not enjoy any benefit of the said guild until they have paid in full.

## III. On the Expedition of Cases and the Notary's Diligence.

And it is further provided that if a case is brought before a <term>consulate; the term of office for the guild's presiding magistrates</term> of said guild, which is only permitted to last 44 days and no more without resolving such a case, and if it should pass to their successors, in this instance it is understood that the said case shall be resumed so that those who succeed them may examine it well and give a just judgment. And it shall not be understood that because the said case was lost for 45 days and under two consulates, any of the said <term>consuls; the chief magistrates of the guild</term> have fallen into any prejudice; rather, the penalty mentioned above shall only apply to those consuls under whom the case was pending during the 45-day term. 

And because the aforementioned cases first come to the notice of the <term>notary; the official responsible for the guild’s legal records and administration</term>, and he makes a record of them according to the order of the case, it could happen that through the negligence of the notary in bringing it to the attention of the said consuls, they might fall into the said penalty. To avoid such an error, it is provided, and so that such notaries are diligent, that by this statute and order they are required and must, within the said 45 days, notify the said consuls (gathered in sufficient number) three times and on different days, beginning within ten days of the case being filed, and following then every ten days for each time. And if such a notary does not observe such diligence, and the said consuls fall into a penalty through the failure of the said notary, it is understood that the entire penalty the consuls would have paid shall fall upon the said notary. And the said consuls may recoup that amount from the said notary in whatever way and form seems best and pleases them; it being understood nonetheless that any such notary who acts contrary to what is said above shall be dismissed, and never at any time shall he hold any office or benefit in the said guild.

## IIII. On the Bags of the Ministers and the Scrutiny.

And it was also provided that regarding any disorder found in the <term>bags; the leather pouches ("borse") containing the names of citizens eligible for office, drawn at random</term> of the ministers of the house—such as the <term>chamberlain; the guild's treasurer</term>, <term>overseers; officials in charge of guild property or works</term>, <term>assessors; officials who adjusted fees or weights</term>, <term>syndics; auditors of guild accounts</term>, and the council—it is provided by this present statute that the current consuls have the power to correct them in whatever way and form seems best and pleases them. 

Nonetheless, they may not place into the bags anyone other than those who, through the last <term>scrutiny; the "squittino," a formal process of vetting and voting on eligible candidates</term> performed, have been approved by a single <term>ballot; "poliza," the slip of paper indicating a favorable vote</term> and no more, under penalty of one hundred <term>large florins; the high-value gold currency of Florence</term> for whoever acts to the contrary, to be paid in the manner and form stated above; and they shall exercise their office in the customary manner and form, according to what is disposed by the orders.

->V-VII REFORMS OF 1491<-

### V. For those who collect for the guild.

Furthermore, it is provided that, in order to eliminate the frauds that could be committed and so that the said <term>guild; the "Arte" or professional association</term> may receive its due, it is ordained by this present statute that any official of the house—whether he be the <term>purveyor; an administrative official (provveditore)</term>, the notary, the <term>beadle; a guild servant or messenger (famiglio)</term>, or any other official—who collects any revenue for the said guild, is required and must have that sum recorded as income by the <term>chamberlain; the treasurer or financial officer (camarlingo)</term> of the said guild within two days from the day he collected it from those who have paid. This is under penalty of 25 <term>large florins; high-value gold coins used in Florence</term>, to be paid as stated above, and with the additional penalty that whoever violates this statute shall be unable to enjoy any benefit from the said guild.

### VI. Regarding deposits.

And it is further provided that, if in the future it should happen that any deposits are made into the said guild, as often occurs, they must be placed into the hands of the chamberlain and no one else. And whoever should receive such a deposit because the chamberlain was not at his office, that person is required to pay and give it to the said chamberlain within the time frame mentioned above. The chamberlain must keep these in a "book of deposits," under the aforementioned penalty. Such deposits are not to be returned without a <term>vote; a formal resolution (partito)</term> of the consuls. And if any of the said chamberlains, upon leaving office, still holds such funds, he is required within fifteen days of his departure to have transferred them to his successor, under penalty of double the amount, as stated above. And the present chapter is understood to be, and shall be, an addition to any other statute that speaks of such matters.

### VII. Concerning monies ordained for pious causes. <note>original Latin: "De pecuniis ordinatis ad pias causas"</note>

And it is further provided by this present statute that whatever money shall come into the hands of the chamberlain of the said guild for the time being—whether for a <term>pittance; a charitable distribution of food or alms (piatanza)</term>, for providing dowries to marry off young girls, or other alms—those specific funds may not be spent on anything other than that for which they were designated by the <term>bequest; a gift left in a will (lascio)</term>. And if anyone should put such money to another use, the said <term>consuls; the guild's presiding magistrates</term> and the chamberlain who paid it shall be required to ensure out of their own pockets that the legacies made for God are carried out according to the will of the deceased. It is understood that any <term>taxes; or financial burdens (graveza)</term> or other expenses that have been incurred, or may be incurred in the future, against those bequeathed assets shall be deducted first.

<summary>This page outlines strict financial protocols for guild officials, mandating that all collected funds and deposits be handled exclusively by the chamberlain within tight deadlines. It also establishes personal liability for officials to ensure charitable bequests, such as dowries and alms, are used strictly according to the donor's wishes.</summary>

# REFORM OF 1517

Giovanni di Piero Acciaiuoli, for the Merchant Guild <note>original Latin: "pro arte merchatorum"</note> (1),
Luca di Luigi Guicciardini, for the Money Changers' Guild <note>original Latin: "pro arte cambii"</note> (1),
Gianfrancesco di Antonio de’ Nobili, for the Wool Guild <note>original Latin: "pro arte lane"</note> (1),
Carlo di Leonardo del Benino, for the Guild of Porta Santa Maria <note>The Silk Guild; original Latin: "pro arte porte sancte Marie"</note> (1),
Agostino di Francesco Dini, for the Apothecaries’ Guild <note>original Latin: "pro arte aromathariorum"</note>,
Lorenzo di Niccolò Benintendi, for the minor guilds <note>original Latin: "pro artibus minoribus"</note> (1);
Florentine citizens, officials, and statute-makers, legitimately drawn [by lot, etc.], having reviewed the statutes and ordinances of this very Guild of Physicians and Apothecaries of the city of Florence previously written above in this book, and having reviewed the ordinances written below presented before them on behalf of the said guild and university <note>In this context, "university" refers to a corporate legal body or association, not an educational institution</note> of physicians and apothecaries, the tenor of which is as follows, namely:

### I. Concerning the barbers.

The honorable lords consuls of the present guild and university of physicians and apothecaries of the city of Florence, together with the council or rather the councilors of the said guild and university, gathered in sufficient number in the house of the said guild to exercise their office as is the custom, have considered how many controversies have occurred in times past between the company and men of Saint Catherine of the Barbers <note>The religious and professional confraternity that governed the social life of barbers</note> and some of its barbers, and how some barbers have denied the jurisdiction of these consuls. They have alleged that in many matters—and especially concerning the said company—the consuls have no jurisdiction over these barbers, which has resulted in dishonor and disobedience toward the aforementioned guild and university. It is especially considered a grievance that the most lowly members subject to the present guild and university, such as the barbers, have the audacity to refuse to submit to the declarations and decisions made by the presiding consuls of the guild. Therefore, so that in the future such barbers have no cause to boast against the aforementioned guild, nor to disobey the decisions or commands of the consuls in any matter, it is hereby provided, established, and ordained that the presiding consuls of the aforementioned guild and university (and two-thirds of them) have, and are understood to have, full and most ample power and authority over all barbers and the body and university of barbers. This includes masters as well as laborers, disciples, and apprentices of whatever state, quality, or condition they may be, and over any one of them, to be able to sentence, declare, define, and terminate—

<insert>(1) *Merchant, money-changing, wool, Porta Santa Maria, minor* [guilds] were added later, in the hand of the notary Luca di Ruggiero de’ Caccucci.</insert>

# REFORMS OF 1517, 1518

...to settle any and every dispute, of whatever nature they may be, whether among private individuals or between them and the said Company of Saint Catherine <note>The religious and social fraternity associated specifically with the barbers</note>; and to have the power, between the said company and the aforementioned barbers, to negotiate and to reorganize, amend, correct, revoke, cancel, confirm, and approve their chapters <note>The individual articles of their governing statutes</note>, adding or removing anything in its entirety as it shall seem fit and pleasing to the consuls who shall be in office for the time being in the said guild, or to two-thirds of them. And everything that shall be declared, negotiated, added, or removed in the future by the current consuls of the said guild, or in any way enacted, declared, or sentenced as stated above regarding the said barbers and regarding the said company and the aforementioned barbers, must be inviolably observed in the future by every barber—both masters and apprentices or workers—who are in any way subject to the said guild. Any of the aforementioned who fail to observe or act against these rules shall be understood to have immediately incurred a fine of ten small lire <note>original: "lire dieci picc."</note>, or more or less, at the discretion of the said lords consuls.

Declaring nonetheless that whatever shall be declared, enacted, sentenced, or ordered in the future by the consuls of the said guild currently in office, cannot be altered or annulled, nor removed in any part, except by a vote of the consuls together with the council and councilors of the aforementioned guild and university <note>In this context, "university" refers to the corporate legal body of the guild</note>, and by a two-thirds majority of them.

And concerning all and singular the matters mentioned above, after a discussion was held among them [etc.], and the necessary formalities observed [etc.], they approved and confirmed the statute mentioned just above and all and singular the statutes and ordinances of the said guild and university [etc.] with all black beans <note>In Florentine guild voting, black beans represented a "yes" vote and white beans a "no" vote. A unanimous vote is indicated here.</note>.

I, Luca Roggeri of Caccucce <note>original Latin: "Lucas Roggerii de Cacuccis"</note>, ordinary judge and public notary and Florentine citizen [etc.], was present at all the matters written below, and having been requested to record them, I have written and summarized them; being occupied with other matters, I have commissioned Antonio, son of Ser Giovanni Battista [etc.], to publish them.

I, Giovanni Battista, son of the late Antonio Gaspero, apothecary of Terranuova, notary, ordinary judge, and Florentine public notary, by the commission given to me by the aforementioned notary Ser Luca, have faithfully taken these records from the acts and notarizations of the same Ser Luca and have reduced them into this public form [etc.].

<meta>This page continues the administrative reforms of the Florentine guilds from 1525 into 1526. It specifically addresses a conflict of interest regarding members who are also enrolled in the Notaries' Guild, aiming to keep professional legal recorders separate from the guild's leadership roles.</meta>

# REFORMS OF 1525, 1526 . . . . . I
35

I. He who practices the profession of a notary—namely, he who is enrolled in the register of the Notaries' Guild—cannot hold any office within this guild. <note>original: "Qui exercet artem notarii, videlicet quod sit inscriptus in matriculam in arte notariorum non possit exercere officium aliquod in arte."</note>

The respectable lords consuls <note>The elected leaders of the guild</note> of the present guild and university, together with the council and advisors of the said guild, have observed that during the scrutinies <term>squictini; the process of vetting and electing candidates by drawing names from bags</term> for the consulships held in the present guild, certain sons of citizens of said guild have been balloted and won. These individuals later became and enrolled as notaries; <margin>and since they have been notaries <note>original: "et da poi che si sono stati notai"; added in the margin by the notary Bartolomeo de Meis in 1525.</note></margin> they have been drawn as consuls of the aforementioned guild. This is inappropriate and a cause of confusion: that those who have chosen to be, are, and wish to act as notaries should compete for or participate in the offices of the citizens. This is especially true considering that in times past, it was never the custom for any notary to hold a position in said guild, neither as consul nor in any other office. To avoid every inconvenience and disorder that could arise in the future for such a reason, it is hereby provided, established, and ordained:

In the future, anyone who is a notary and enrolled in the register <note>original: "matricola"</note> of the Guild of Notaries of the city of Florence cannot, must not, and shall not be considered a man of the present guild. Instead, he must be entirely struck from all offices for which he might be drawn in the future in this guild or the consulship. The chancellor of this guild for the time being shall be bound and obligated, under penalty of fifty *lire picciole* <note>The local "small" currency of Florence</note> for each time he acts to the contrary, to tear up the ballot <note>original: "poliza"</note> of any such person drawn as consul or for another office who is a notary at the time of the drawing. He shall remove him from the office and draw a replacement in his stead. However, it is not intended that this present provision includes doctors <note>Referring to "Doctors of Law," high-ranking legal scholars who were often members of the Guild of Judges and Notaries but held higher social status than simple notaries</note> who might be enrolled in the said Guild of Notaries.

Having seen the said provision, the aforementioned statutory lords, gathered as above—though Ser Antonio de’ Vespucci, their colleague, was absent [etc.]—approved the above-written provision and everything contained within it [etc.].

The same Bartolomeo di Antonio de’ Meis, notary [etc.].

->[1526]<-

In the name of God, amen. In the year of our Lord since his health-giving incarnation one thousand five hundred and twenty-six, fourteenth indiction <note>A 15-year cycle used for dating legal documents in Europe</note>,

### REFORMS OF 1526-1529

# REFORM OF 1556

and observed and done as was duly sought and required, not only for the universal good and convenience, but for the honor of the said craft and university <term>università; in this context, the guild as a corporate body</term>, to the effect especially that, according to the commission from His Illustrious Excellency <note>Duke Cosimo I de' Medici, who tightened control over the guilds during his reign</note>, all that which is required should be clarified and determined in the best and most honorable way and form possible; and being optimally informed of what has been used and observed from 1547 backward by virtue of the old statutes (1) and thereafter from ’47 (2) to the present by vigor of the new ones, regarding the making of said works well, and conversely, poorly; desiring and intending that everything conforms well, and as much as possible to remove every malice and license from those who have no fear, nor take account of committing and using fraud, deception, and falsity; having seen and considered all things to be seen and considered, and observed those to be observed, by virtue of the said rescript <note>a formal written decree</note> and of whatever authority, power, and office <term>balia; a committee granted temporary emergency powers</term> given and granted to them, in every best way, having passed the vote, they have provided, statuted, ordered, and deliberated as follows on this paper. And first:

### I. Regarding wind-torches.

That the torches, which are called "wind-torches," and in the old statute [called] "load-torches" <term>da soma; large torches often carried in processions</term> and for providing light to the body of our Lord Jesus Christ <note>The Feast of Corpus Christi, when the Eucharist was carried through the streets</note> and those specific to funerals, offerings, magistrates, and masquerades—given that it is the same body and workmanship—must always be made and composed of good, clean, merchantable wax and not mixed in any way. They must be of similar wax and not of different types, and the inside must be the same as the outside, without any deceit, fraud, or malice. For the base to be placed upon, they may put and work wicks <term>lucignoli</term> of said similar wax, even if it is used and pressed, provided that it is always entirely clean, pure, merchantable, and not mixed in any way; and they must tie them with linen yarn or thin twine well and legally. For every pound of wax, they may put no more than three and a half ounces of said wicks, thus composed and tied, for each torch. And the cover of each torch must always be well and conveniently made of plenty of new, good, clean, and merchantable wax, not used nor mixed in any way. Each torch can be at most three and a half to four cubits <term>braccia; a Florentine unit of length, approximately 58 centimeters</term> in length, and from ten to fifteen pounds <term>libre</term> in weight. And all the aforementioned things and every part of them must be entirely clean of any deceit, fraud, and malice. And thus they shall be worked and made in each and every part.

REFORM OF 1556 II-IIII

## II. Concerning torches, otherwise known as square torches.

Likewise, for the torches which are called square torches <term>quadroni; large torches with a square cross-section, often used in formal processions</term>, one must first make and compose the wicks of new cotton <term>banbagia; raw cotton used for wicks</term> that is pure, merchant-grade, and not used, nor mixed in any way; they may be tied with flaxen thread <term>accia; coarse, raw flax or hemp fiber</term> and thin twine securely, as was stated above regarding the other torches. The wax must be new, clean, good, and merchant-grade on both the top and the bottom, and of the same kind—not diverse nor recycled in any way. For the core <term>imposto; the internal "filling" or structural layer of a large torch</term>, the same wax must be used as is required and appropriate in every respect. For every pound <note>The Florentine pound (libbra) was approximately 339 grams</note> of wax, one must use and work into each said torch one and a half ounces <note>An ounce (oncia) was 1/12 of a pound, roughly 28 grams</note> of the said new cotton for the wicks. These are to be made to a weight of six to seven pounds and a length of two and a half to three cubits <term>braccia; the Florentine cubit was approximately 58 centimeters</term> each, and may be either twisted or straight as is desired by the one who commissions them.

## III. Concerning tapers, small torches, candles, taper-sticks, and other similar items.

Likewise, baptismal tapers <note>original: "ceri da figlocci," literally "tapers for godchildren," used during the sacrament of baptism</note>, or rather small torches, candles, taper-sticks, and other similar works may be crafted, kept, and sold at any weight and length that is most convenient and pleasing to the maker or the client. They must be made of new, clean, good, and merchant-grade wax and cotton, not mixed in any way, and entirely consistent throughout. For every one of these items weighing ten pounds or less, the makers are bound and required to use entirely new wax and new cotton; for every pound of wax, they must use one ounce of the said cotton, and no more, nor in any other manner.

## IIII. Concerning tapers for parishes, congregations, communities, and others.

Likewise, for tapers used by rural parishes <term>pievieri; referring to the "pieve," a central baptismal church in the countryside</term>, urban congregations <term>populi</term>, communities, and in any other manner or form—not including those that are pierced or embossed <note>original: "traforati nè i bucciati," referring to decorative wax with cut-out or textured "bark-like" patterns</note>—weighing ten pounds and up, it shall be permitted, as is appropriate, to use good, clean, merchant-grade recycled wax only for the core. However, the exterior must always be made and composed of entirely new, clean, good, and merchant-grade wax. The wicks of any of these tapers must always be made of new, good cotton, not mixed in any way. The coating <note>original: "coperta," the outer visible layer of the candle</note> of each must be of a sufficient thickness of the said new wax, and the core should be no more than what the work requires. For every pound of wax in these wicks, they may use one and a half ounces of the said new cotton, neither mixed nor tied in any manner.

V-VIII REFORM OF 1556

### V. The candles of 4 denari each shall be 75 per pound.

Likewise, the candles that are called "one *quattrino* <note>A *quattrino* was a small copper coin worth four *denari*</note> each"—that is, small box candles <term>da chassetta; small, everyday candles often sold in boxes or cases for domestic use</term>—must be seventy-five in number per pound <note>The Florentine pound was roughly 339 grams</note> and no more. They must be worked and composed of new, pure, good, merchant-grade cotton <term>banbagia; raw cotton used for wicks</term> and wax of a similar high quality throughout, and not of different materials; and in each wick, three threads of the said cotton must be placed.

### VI. Funeral candles.

Likewise, funeral candles <note>original: "chandele da morti"</note> may be worked in whatever number and weight is convenient as pleases the person who buys them or has them made. They must always be made of entirely new, clean, good, and merchant-grade wax and cotton, and not mixed in any way. For those numbered forty or fewer <note>meaning larger candles where 40 or fewer make up a pound</note>, they are required to make each wick with six threads; and for those numbered from 40 upwards <note>smaller candles</note>, with four threads of the said cotton, without any deceit, fraud, or malice.

### VII. Pierced and textured tapers.

Likewise, pierced <term>traforati; decorative tapers with cut-out patterns</term> and textured tapers <term>bucciati; tapers with a rough or "barked" surface</term> must not and shall not be made; and in this regard, everything that is laid out in the old statute shall be observed in its entirety. <note>These decorative styles were often banned because the holes or rough textures could be used to hide low-quality wax or impurities inside the candle.</note>

### VIII. That everyone who keeps or works with said wax products is subject to these rules.

Likewise, every and any person—of whatever state, grade, or condition they may be, and even if not currently subject to the said Guild and University <term>arte et università; the professional corporation or guild</term>, and however exempt or privileged—who works, keeps, sells, or has sold, worked, or kept any of the said works or compositions in any way, whether in the city or throughout the entire dominion and State of His Illustrious Excellency <note>Referring to Cosimo I de' Medici, Duke of Florence</note> in any place or part, is required and must observe and do everything that is declared and ordained in the present document, loyally and faithfully and without any deceit, fraud, or malice in every respect and not otherwise. This is under penalty for whoever acts against or causes others to act against these rules in any part or chapter of the things ordained above and below; they shall be condemned, and are hereby condemned for every instance and for every piece of work, to the same penalties and prejudices ordained and declared in every respect by the Law of '47 <note>The previous major legislative reform of 1547</note>.

REFORM OF 1556 VIII-X
551

...reporting on all of this, everything as is due and appropriate in every best way for the effects and for the purposes mentioned above and written below, and each of them respectively.

## VIIII. Sealing works from 4 ounces upwards.

Item, that everyone who makes or has these works made is bound and must—in addition to the things mentioned above—seal or have sealed those items that weigh four ounces <note>A Florentine ounce was approximately 28 grams</note> and up with their own seal. This must be done in the way and form that was required in the past and is currently required by virtue of the said statutes and orders, under the penalties and legal consequences contained and set forth therein.

## X. Concerning wax works and wicks worked and made in the past.

Item, considering that, because of the regulations ordained and established in the present document, the aforementioned apothecaries <term>spetiali; members of the Guild of Doctors and Apothecaries who also held the monopoly on professional wax-working</term> or others might possess wax works and wicks that were not made according to the standards now declared and fixed—including those that would no longer be permitted to be kept or worked—and wishing to provide for this in the best possible way, they ordained and deliberated that all apothecaries and every other person mentioned above are bound and must provide a written list <note>original: "nota in scriptis"</note>. 

This is to be done so that it may clearly be documented in the Guild: specifically, those in Florence must deliver it into the hands of the Chancellor of the aforementioned Guild, and those outside—namely throughout the dominion—into the hands of whomever the Consuls <term>consoli; the elected leaders of the Guild</term> of the said Guild shall ordain and judge to be appropriate. This list must include all wicks of every sort that they have in any way made, bought, had made, or that belong to them in any other way, and likewise for all wax works and compositions of whatever sort. 

And the said Chancellor, and likewise the others respectively to be deputized and elected as noted above, are bound and must make a diligent note of them in a book prepared for such a purpose, which is sufficient and appropriate. And let it be understood that this applies only to those items made from the day the command was issued backwards, and not to those to be made thereafter. 

Furthermore, the said works and wicks that are found to be good, clean, and without any fraud, deceit, or malice—even if they are already sealed with the personal seal of the person who made them or had them made—must be sealed again with the seal of the Guild, by whomever and in whatever manner the Consuls of the said Guild shall see fit. Only once they are thus sealed may they be kept, sold, and bought, and not otherwise, nor in any other way. 

Declaring that those found to be bad, fraudulent, falsified, or sophisticated <note>meaning adulterated with cheaper materials like fats or tallows</note> cannot and must not be accepted or sealed in any way; rather, even if they are [already] sealed...

X-XII REFORM OF 1556

...must be entirely condemned and, having been so condemned, shall remain as forgeries in every respect, as provided for in the Law of 1447 regarding the said Guild. It is further enacted that if, after this decree has been issued, any of the said works made previously are found that were not sealed or declared as stated above, in such a case, anyone who has acted contrary to this for any of the said works and for every instance shall be and remain convicted of forgery, as ordained by the said Law of 1447. In such a case, they are hereby condemned—even if the work is actually of good quality—as a forgery as described above.

### XI. They may not keep unsealed works, nor buy them from persons who cannot sell them.

Item, that they may not, nor must they in any way keep, sell, or buy any work weighing four ounces or more that is not stamped with the proper seal of the person who made it. Nor should they have or buy any work or composition, whether sealed or not, of whatever sort, quality, or quantity it may be, except from persons whom they know can and must truly and legally sell or provide them in any lawful and appropriate manner. This is under penalty of losing the works and, furthermore, being condemned to other penalties and damages as shall freely seem fit and pleasing to the Consuls of the said Guild <note>The Consuls were the elected officials who governed the Guild's affairs and held judicial power over its members</note> and to two-thirds of their number <note>Refers to the required "two-thirds" majority for a legal ruling</note> in office at the time of the aforementioned case, having considered and respected the magnitude of the offense and the status of the offender.

### XII. The sums for which those who buy from others must be condemned.

Item, whereas it sometimes happens that apothecaries and craftsmen buy works and items belonging to the trade which, although they are sealed, are later found to be shoddy or counterfeit. Given this situation, it has come under consideration that a distinction must be made between those who buy them and are knowledgeable enough to recognize their shoddiness or falsity, and those who are not. For those in whose possession such items are found remain condemned for them, and then seek to be acquitted by virtue of the statute of the said Guild by claiming they did not make them or have them made, but bought them as such from others. Therefore, considering the words of the statute which says that if they were found with any small grocer <term>pizichagniolo; a seller of salted meats, cheeses, and basic household supplies who was permitted to sell some wax products</term> or other unskilled person who testifies to having bought them from others already in that false state, they shall be punished in shillings...

REFORM OF 1556 XII-XIII

...forty <term>piccoli</term> <note>The "piccolo" was a small Florentine copper coin of low value</note> and the seller shall incur the penalty mentioned above. Desiring to eliminate all malice, fraud, and deception that could be committed regarding these matters, and to provide the best possible remedy against those—especially those who cannot be excused by ignorance—who might buy such items under some pretext to the detriment of the public and solely for their own profit and benefit, they [the Guild leaders] ordained and deliberated that for those who, if they wish, have and can have knowledge of whether said works are good or not, no excuse or reason shall be accepted concerning their having bought such false items from others. Instead, they shall remain entirely liable and be condemned in every respect, just as if they had made the items themselves.

And that the <term>pizicagnoli</term> <note>Retailers or grocers who sold a variety of foodstuffs and household goods, including candles and wax items</note> or other similar persons, who by chance buy them to resell in their shops and thus keep them without having made them or had them made, if they show and prove from whom they bought them, shall be fined two <term>lire</term> <note>A unit of currency; at this time, one lira was worth 20 soldi</note> and the seller shall face the primary penalty established above for this offense. 

And thus, in any of the aforementioned cases, whether said persons had knowledge of the fraud or not, the decision shall rest entirely upon the declaration and vote of the Consuls of said Guild and two-thirds of their number, to be decided according to the guild's regulations. This shall be granted to whoever requests it, as it shall freely seem fit and pleasing to their Lordships, burdening their consciences in this matter, after first taking an oath in the hands of the Chancellor of said Guild that such an excuse is the truth and ought to be accepted, and all in the best possible manner. Declaring that in no way shall anyone who has made or sold them as stated be free from penalty, but shall remain condemned and be so sentenced in every respect, as is ordained and deliberated by the aforementioned statutes.

### XIII. That no prejudice is intended to the statute on false goods.

Item, they ordained and deliberated that, by virtue of the present provision, no prejudice <note>In a legal sense, "prejudice" means to harm, invalidate, or override an existing law</note> can or should be done, nor shall any be done in any way, to the statute of said Guild regarding "false things" (counterfeits), nor even to any other statute or order of the present Guild and corporation, except in those matters and parts where they are contrary to and provide against the things ordained, made, and declared in the present document. And that in every other part and matter, they shall remain and be in their full force, order, and manner in every respect as they were before the present provision was made. And thus they must be observed inviolably, under the penalties and damages contained and established in them respectively, in every best way possible.

# REFORMS OF 1556, 1558

### XIV. Apothecaries must have a copy of this provision and statute.

Also, to the end that the <term>apothecaries</term> <note>The *spetiali* (apothecaries) were not just pharmacists, but also sold pigments, spices, and wax, and were members of one of Florence’s most prestigious guilds.</note> and the others mentioned above, both in the city and in the territory and State of His Illustrious Excellency <note>This refers to Cosimo I de' Medici, the Duke of Florence.</note>, do not, nor can or should, plead any ignorance of the matters ordered and established above, they [the Guild leaders] deliberated that all apothecaries must have a copy of the present provision, word for word <note>original: "de verbo ad verbum"</note> as it is written and made by the hand of the chancellor of said guild or his assistant, or indeed printed as the <term>Consuls</term> <note>The *consoli* were the elected officials who governed the guild's affairs and enforced its rules.</note> shall judge most appropriate. They must always keep it in their shop, displayed and public, so that anyone can see, read, and understand it. For this, they shall pay whatever the aforementioned Consuls declare must be paid, to whom and how it seems best to them. Any of said apothecaries who does not have it, or does not keep it as stated, shall face a penalty of ten <term>lire</term> or more, at the discretion of said Consuls. As many times as he is found not to have it or keep it as ordered above, let it be understood that he has incurred said penalties, and he must always be fined until he has and keeps it as stated. Notifying everyone that a diligent account will be kept of all the aforementioned things, and searches will be conducted everywhere, as and when it pleases the Consuls, and no excuse shall be accepted.

And as they have ordered above, they decreed, deliberated, and commanded that these rules must be inviolably observed in the best possible way, in every respect, provided that it pleases His Illustrious Excellency from the day that the things ordered and made in said provision are accepted and confirmed by Him, and not before, nor otherwise (1).

->[1558]<-

In the name of God, amen. In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ from His saving incarnation, one thousand five hundred and fifty-eight, in the first indiction, on the 28th day of the month of March. Acted in Florence, in the ducal palace and in the audience of the magnificent <term>Council and Secret Practice</term> <note>The *Pratica Segreta* was a high-level advisory council to the Medici dukes, dealing with administrative and legislative matters.</note> of His Illustrious Excellency (2). <note>original Latin: "In Dei nomine, amen. Anno Domini nostri Iesu Christi ab eius salutifera incharnatione millesimo quingentesimo quinquagesimo octavo, indictione prima, die vero .XXVIII. mensis martii. Actum Florentiae, in palatio ducali et in audientia magnifici Consilii et Praticae secretae suae Excellentiae ill.mae"</note>
