# REFORM OF 1558

## I. Regulation and distribution of taxes among the brokers.

The Most Illustrious and Excellent Lord Duke of Florence [Cosimo I de' Medici], and on behalf of His Illustrious Excellency, his magnificent and excellent <term>Secret Practice</term> <note>The *Pratica Segreta* was a high-level advisory council that handled administrative and legal matters for the Medici dukes.</note>, appointed for the correction, approval, and rejection of the statutes and ordinances of the present <term>Guild and University</term> <note>The term *università* here refers to the corporate body or "university" of the guild members, not an educational institution.</note> (1) of the city of Florence, gathered and assembled together for the exercise of their office in sufficient number in their usual place of residence and hearing, as is the custom; having seen and considered the below-written statutes and ordinances on behalf of the <term>Guild and University of Apothecaries</term> <note>The *Arte dei Medici e Speziali*, which included doctors, apothecaries, and spice merchants.</note>, Mercers, and other members annexed to the same in the city of Florence and its domain, presented and submitted to their Lordships and most worthy office—by commission of his aforementioned Most Illustrious Excellency—by the below-written four reformers of the stated Guild and University, the tenor of which is as follows, namely:

->1557, on the fifth day of April.<-

**Niccolaio di Giovanni di Niccolaio Davanzati**,
**Mazingho di maestro Ugholino di messer Paradiso Mazzinghi**,
**Zanobi di Giovanni di Stagio Barducci** and
**Iacopo di maestro Giovanni di maestro Antonio Rosati**, honorable Florentine citizens, reformers and statute-makers of said Guild and University, elected, assumed, and appointed according to the orders and statutes thereof and thus confirmed and approved by His Illustrious Excellency, together collectively gathered in the place of the usual residence and hearing of said Guild and University, as is the custom; having seen and considered the statutes, both old and new, of the aforementioned Guild regarding the <term>brokers</term> <note>The *sensali* were licensed middlemen who facilitated trades between merchants and were strictly regulated by the guild.</note> ordered and made; and having seen that recently, under the date of February 12 last, 1556 <note>The Florentine calendar often began the year in March; 1556 here likely refers to 1557 in modern dating.</note>, it pleased His Illustrious Excellency to order his magnificent Secret Practice that the number of brokers should remain at eight, once the [current] number of eleven who are there today has decreased, as appears in the deliberation, the tenor of which is this, namely: 

"On the 16th day of January 1556 <note>original: "Die XVI ianuarii 1556"</note>. His Excellency is satisfied that the number of brokers be reduced to eight, who must be <term>voted upon</term> <note>The term *squittinare* refers to the process of 'scrutiny' or balloting used in Florentine elections.</note> by the aforementioned reformers; and those persons who are successful <note>original: "rimarranno vinte," literally "remain as winners" of the vote.</note> shall be sent sealed to the Secret Practice without publishing them otherwise, and the Practice must approve or reject them until eight remain. Copy. I, F. Vinta, wrote this"; [on the] 12th day.

(1) <gloss>of the present guild and university [written] over an erasure.</gloss>

# REFORM OF 1558

In February 1556, the magnificent <term>Secret Practice</term> <note>The *Pratica Segreta* was Duke Cosimo I’s primary advisory council for administrative and legislative matters.</note>, having received from the aforementioned reformers of the <term>Guild of Apothecaries</term> <note>The *Arte dei Medici e Speziali*, which governed doctors, pharmacists, and merchants of spices and dyes.</note> eight <term>brokers</term> <note>The *sensali* were official intermediaries who facilitated trades and guaranteed the quality of transactions within the guild.</note> of said guild approved by them, plus three additional brokers not yet approved, totaling eleven in a sealed document signed by their own hands; and furthermore, having received information that Bernardo di Rinieri di Gratia and Vincentio di Alexandro Galli are the two other brokers of said guild, bringing the total to fourteen; and having seen the said approval of the eight, and having again discussed and examined the matter, they reported to His Excellency, by way of opinion and judgment: that Bernardo di Rinieri di Gratia, who is currently in military service <note>original: "al soldo"</note>, and Vincentio di Alexandro Galli, who no longer wishes to practice the <term>brokerage</term> of said guild, should be cancelled and removed without further prejudice to them; and that the other eleven brokers who remain, among whom are the eight approved by the reformers, should all remain in their practice during their lifetime. And after the death of the first three, the remaining eight shall be understood to be the permanent number of brokers, which must be maintained by appointing new brokers to replace those who might be missing due to death or other legitimate impediment. His Excellency wrote back: "It is well. Copy. <note>original: "Sta bene. Copia."</note> I, Francesco Vinta, have written [this]." <note>Francesco Vinta (1507–1581) was a high-ranking secretary to the Medici dukes.</note>

And seeing as they are thus understood to be and are elected, under the obligations and other rules as ordained by the aforementioned statutes, and therefore needing first to come to the declaration of the <term>taxes</term> <note>The *taxa* was an annual assessment or licensing fee paid by the brokers to the guild or state.</note> usually placed upon them at the discretion of the magistrate, year after year successively; having seen and considered everything that was to be seen and considered, by virtue of any of their authority, in every best way, they provided and ordained that the said brokers, whose names are written below, be required for this year—which began on the first day of the month of last January 1556 and follows through to finish at the end of December 1557—to pay as their tax, to each of them respectively assigned as follows, namely:

# REFORM OF 1558 I, II

all of which taxes, as declared above, amount to the sum of 175 <term>small lire</term> <note>original: "lire picc." (lire picciole); the standard local currency of Florence used for daily transactions, distinct from the gold florin.</note>. And they must pay them beforehand to the <term>chamberlain</term> <note>The *camarlingo* was the guild’s chief financial officer or treasurer.</note> of said guild before the time of their <term>reappointments</term> <note>The *rafferme* were the annual reviews where the guild leaders officially renewed a broker's license to work.</note>, which usually take place every year in the month of December; and whatever additional amount seems appropriate to the <term>consuls</term> <note>The *consoli* were the elected officials who governed the guild's affairs.</note> currently in office at that time, and to two-thirds of them, to be paid for said account to be distributed among the said brokers and each of them respectively, as their lordships shall best judge; deliberating and declaring that at no time can or should the aforementioned sum of 175 small lire be decreased for the said guild, but rather, if it seems right to the said consuls, it may be increased, distributing it as stated among the brokers who will be there from time to time, even if the number of eight is not reached, should that number have decreased at that time for any reason whatsoever. And thus the brokers existing at that time, even if fewer in number, must and shall support and make such tax payments freely and without any exception, as stated, before they are reappointed.

### II. What the brokers must pay for every package.

Item, seeing also that by virtue of said statutes, the aforementioned brokers, besides the said taxes, are obligated to pay to the said guild for every <term>package</term> <note>original: "collo"; a general term for a bale, bundle, or unit of merchandise.</note> of the goods, things, and merchandise belonging to the said guild—whether weighed or not with the guild’s <term>steelyards</term> <note>A *stadera* is a type of balance scale using a sliding weight; the guild held the legal monopoly on official weighing instruments.</note>—that they might sell, cause to be sold, or intervene in in any way, that amount which has been ordained for them by the consuls to pay to said guild. Considering that regarding other ordained methods, they <note>The brokers.</note> were greatly deceiving the guild with their cunning and malice, and having received information about this, especially from the said brokers themselves, it was found in truth that the guild has not obtained nor is obtaining—nor, if things continued as in the past, would it obtain—that which is its due and proper; and having examined the method by which one must and should proceed so that the guild obtains and can obtain its due, and having seen and considered everything that was to be seen and considered, in every best way they provided, decreed, and ordained that for the future the aforementioned brokers are bound and must give and pay to the aforementioned guild into the hands of its chamberlain, as follows below, for every package of all goods and merchandise included both in the guild's statutes and in the <term>customs extracts</term> <note>The "stracto delle gabelle" refers to the official list of taxes and duties levied by the city of Florence on imported and exported goods.</note> of Florence, whether weighed or not with the steelyards or balances or other weights of said guild.

III. (1) *a*. Expressly declaring and decreeing that, where in the aforementioned and declared packages of said goods and merchandise it is specified by number or weight "not to exceed one hundred," and from one hundred upwards, the payment to said guild has not been provided for: the aforementioned <term>brokers</term> <note>original: "sensali"; licensed trade intermediaries</note> are required to pay "one hundred for one hundred" <note>meaning a proportional rate based on the base unit of 100</note> up to the sum of three hundred, as is respectively stated for each; and from 300 upwards in any amount, for whatever bale that exceeds 300, four small soldi <note>original: "soldi picc."; referring to the *piccolo*, the standard small-denomination currency of Florence</note>, meaning the first 300 amounts to 6 soldi; that from then on they shall pay ten small soldi for every bale and whatever more is appropriate for the bale as stated, referring one to the other and vice versa, that which and how much is owed according to the aforesaid rules. And thus and as much as above for all bales respectively, the said brokers are bound and must pay and observe in everything and for everything in the best possible manner.

->III-V REFORMS OF 1558<-

b. [Merchandise must be sold in the presence of the seller and buyer]. And that they may not, nor must they in any way act as <term>intermediaries</term> <note>original: "mezani"</note>, nor intervene to sell, cause to be sold, or buy, nor transfer to others in whole or in part such goods and <term>merchandise</term> <note>original: "mercantie"</note> that are not weighed while both the seller and the buyer—or others legally receiving for them—are present, using the <term>steelyards</term> <note>original: "stadere"; a scale with a weighted arm used for heavy goods</note> or balances or other weights of the said guild, as is appropriate by virtue of its orders. Except, nonetheless, when a case arises where they are weighed with other scales, which the <term>consuls</term> <note>original: "consoli"; the elected leaders of the guild</note> of said guild could not prohibit for such weighing at that time (the determination of whether this is the case or not must rest upon the declaration of the said consuls and two-thirds of them); in such a case, the <term>brokers</term> <note>original: "sensali"</note> shall have been permitted to do so.

c. [They must notify the guild's weigher when items are weighed with other scales]. And this being done, they declared and ordered that they are immediately bound to give a full and true notice of such weights and <term>packages</term> <note>original: "colli"</note> weighed with those other scales to the <term>weigher</term> <note>original: "pesatore"</note> of the said guild; and first, they must write them in the book that each of them is required to have and keep according to the statutes, in an orderly fashion and where the other packages and goods weighed with the scales of the said guild are required to be recorded.

### IIII. [The weigher must record them in the weighing book].

And that the aforementioned weigher must and shall be immediately obliged to write all the said packages and goods weighed on other scales, having received such notice, in the book of weighings, in order, day by day, together with the others; and of all these, he must give a true and full account in every respect to the <term>chamberlain</term> <note>original: "camarlingho"; the guild's treasurer or financial officer</note> of the said guild.

### V. [The brokers must record the weighings in their own book].

And that for each of the said packages, respectively weighed or not as mentioned, each of the aforementioned brokers must keep a true and diligent account and write them in order in his book of trades, as appears and is ordered in every respect by the <term>ancient statute</term> <note>original: "statuto antiquo"</note> written above in this [volume] on page 35 under rubric 43 (1), which governs the payments of brokers. This book must be organized, kept, and produced as [it is disposed] (2) in said statute.

...if he does <insert>not</insert> <note>The word "not" (non) was added between the lines by a 1558 hand</note> give and provide such a note as described above, [he shall be fined] seven <term>lire picciole</term> <note>The "small" lira was the standard silver-based accounting currency in Florence</note> for every debtor <term>broker</term> <note>original: "sensale"</note> not reported and for every instance, to be taken from him and applied as stated above.

### XII. The auditors must review the superintendent’s account to see if he has complied.

And that the <term>auditors</term> <note>original: "sindachi"; officials responsible for financial oversight</note> assigned to the said <term>unit-fees</term> <note>original: "colli"; taxes on packages or bales of goods</note>, as deputized above, who are in office during that time—and two of them acting in agreement—must fully review the records of the said <term>superintendent</term> <note>original: "provveditore"</note> to see if he has complied as stated above. Wherever they find he has failed, they are required to record him as a debtor in the said auditors' book and condemn him to pay such a penalty, declaring the total sum and the cause in every detail, as is required and appropriate. And as a reward for their labor, they shall have half of everything that is withheld from the said superintendent’s salary as stated above, or which he pays in cash to the <term>chamberlain’s</term> <note>original: "camarlingho"; the guild's treasurer</note> income. And if the aforementioned auditors do not collect this within fifteen days of their condemnation of the superintendent, they ordained that, once the said time has passed, they shall be made creditors [of the guild] without any further formal authorization, to be paid by him as stated above. And that the <term>consuls</term> <note>original: "consoli"; the high-ranking leaders of the guild</note>, at every request of the said auditors, are required and must compel him to pay and deduct the said penalty in full and without any exception.

### XIII. a. [Salary of 7 lire for each of the auditors].

Likewise, they declared that the said auditors, as soon as they have reviewed, balanced, and declared—and thus recorded—all the said accounts for the brokers as stated above, shall receive, in addition to the other emoluments which (as mentioned) should respectively be given to them as a reward and compensation for their labor, seven <term>lire picciole</term> each. Thus, among all three, they shall receive twenty-one <term>lire picciole</term>, without any further formal authorization for payment; in such a case, this amount shall be paid to them freely by the chamberlain of the said <term>guild</term> <note>original: "arte"</note> and recorded as an expenditure, just as if an authorization had been made according to the guild's regulations.

### b. [Prohibition of the auditors].

The said auditors shall be subject to the same <term>prohibition</term> <note>original: "divieto"; a mandatory waiting period that prevented officials from holding the same office or multiple offices consecutively to prevent the consolidation of power</note> that applies to every member of the council, according to the regulations of the said guild. And the <term>chancellor</term> <note>original: "cancelliere"; the guild's legal secretary</note>, once they are drawn <note>officials were typically chosen by drawing names from a leather bag (the "borse")</note>, must record them on the board where the consuls are listed.

<margin>Brokers may take 2 lire 10 soldi for every apprentice they arrange for, having to pay 10 soldi to the Guild</margin>. For every apprentice (<term>garzone</term>) that they arrange for or place with any master, whether an apothecary (<term>spetiale</term>) or a mercer (<term>merciaio</term>) at a shop, fifty *piccoli* soldi <note>the standard "small" currency of Florence</note> are to be paid by the apprentice; of this, the broker shall keep forty *piccoli* soldi for himself, and he receives ten soldi for the Guild and then pays them to the chamberlain (<term>camarlingho</term>) in the manner stated for the packages.

And the aforementioned brokers (<term>sensali</term>) may not, nor should they, receive or have more, nor otherwise, for their brokerage fees (<term>senserie</term>) than what is ordained and declared above, under penalty of fifty *piccoli* lire for anyone acting against this, for every instance and as many times as they shall do so, to be taken from them and applied to the Guild, and further at the discretion of the Consuls <note>the high-ranking officials who governed the Guild</note>; and a fourth of every fine shall go to the notifier. And in addition to the said penalties, the brokers must be immediately compelled and condemned to return and give back whatever excess they had taken from anyone who had given it for such cause or account. ->REFORM OF 1558 XVI–XVIIII<-

[and the consuls] must condemn anyone acting against these rules <note>original: "contra faciente"</note> to the said penalties (1) through every executive path and method, as it shall seem fit and freely please the consuls and two-thirds of them.

### XVII. [The manner of approving brokers].

Also, that all the said brokers <term>sensali: agents who brokered labor contracts and trade deals</term> are understood to be, and are, elected and deputed to the said Guild; and they were so elected and deputed both for the branch of the apothecaries <term>spetiali: pharmacists and spice merchants</term> and for that of the mercers <term>merciai: dealers in cloths and small wares</term>, and for any of them. And every year in the month of December (2), at the accustomed time and in the manner according to the orders of said Guild, they must undergo a ballot <term>partito: a formal vote or division used in Florentine governance</term> to be re-confirmed in their posts <note>original: "raffermi"</note> with the accustomed obligations and other matters between the consuls and councilors of said Guild and six apothecary merchants, elected by the consuls; the vote is to be won by a two-thirds majority (3). And if anyone should not succeed in the vote, they declared that such a vote must be approved by His Most Illustrious Excellency <note>This refers to Cosimo I de' Medici, Duke of Florence, whose oversight of the guilds was absolute</note>, and whatever is deliberated by him shall be observed regarding the said broker, and not otherwise, should the aforementioned case arise at any time.

### XVIII. [Brokers may not be re-confirmed, nor practice, if they have not paid].

Also, to the effect that the brokers do not take advantage of, nor hold in their hands—as has been found in the past with the majority of them—that which belongs to the Guild, they [the reformers] deliberated that every year, before they undergo their re-confirmations, they must have fully paid the chamberlain <term>camarlingho: the guild’s chief financial officer or treasurer</term> of said Guild the taxes imposed on each of them by the consuls during that time, as stated above. Furthermore, they must pay everything for which they might be debtors at that time in the book of the said Guild; and not having first paid everything into the chamberlain's accounts, they may not be re-confirmed, nor practice as a broker, except as and how much it shall please His Most Illustrious Excellency.

### XVIIII. [Brokers must perform their office well by themselves].

These brokers, so elected and re-confirmed, shall always be bound and must perform and practice the craft and profession of the broker well, loyally, faithfully, and diligently, without any deceit, fraud, or malice,

### XX. Other orders not mentioned are not to be considered repealed.

Likewise, the aforementioned reformers and statute-makers, noticing and considering that many other things regarding brokers were ordered and established in said Guild at various times, did not feel it necessary to dispose of them otherwise, finding that they are well-ordered and established and should be observed. Having seen and considered everything necessary in the best possible way, they ordered and declared that all those previous rules concerning brokers are to be seen as an addition to those contained in these other orders and statutes, where they regard the above-written matters. And by these present orders, it is not intended to prejudice or repeal <note>original: "derogato"</note> any other statute or law made in the said Guild concerning brokers, except in those parts that contradict the aforementioned rules. In such cases of conflict, they repealed and do repeal them, declaring and commanding that all other rules must be observed by the brokers in every detail, under the penalties and sanctions declared in the statutes and orders regarding this matter. ## XXV. Of the steelyards and weights and other things to be kept.

### Copy of the customs law of Florence regarding the manner of handling drugs.

Likewise, to facilitate the work of merchants and prevent frauds that might be committed daily regarding the <term>duties: "ghabelle"</term>, and for the purpose of keeping the <term>customs house: "dogana"</term> as clear as possible, they have ordained that everyone who, in the future, brings or causes to be brought merchandise, <term>drugs: "drogherie"</term>, <note>In this period, "drogherie" referred to spices, medicinal compounds, and exotic dry goods</note> and salted meats <term>for transit: "per passo"</term> into the customs house of Florence, shall be required within 10 days from the day of such arrival to have an inspection made of them distinctly, item by item and with the weight as recorded for Florence. 

And once such an inspection has been made, they must have them conveyed within the said time to their houses or shops or elsewhere, wherever they wish in Florence; of which merchandise, drugs, and salted meats, they are required within four months following the said inspection to have made the <term>withdrawal: "ritracta"</term> and paid the transit duty. Otherwise, once the said time has passed, they can no longer withdraw them at that rate, but shall be obligated to pay the duty of the city or territory of Florence according to the regulations within 35 days after the four months then next following; within which time, if they do not pay it, they shall incur a penalty of one-fourth more, as is clearly set forth for other merchandise and goods. 

It is intended that the present provision also takes place and is observed for those goods, drugs, and salted meats which are already found in the said customs house for transit, for which the inspections and clearing must be done within 10 days as said above for the others; it is not intended by this that their term of four months to make the withdrawal and pay the transit duty is extended, but rather the course of the said four months is understood to continue and shall continue from the day the goods were placed there, as if such inspection and clearing had not occurred. 

And whoever shall have charge of such duties over time cannot and must not grant a withdrawal for said goods under any sought-after pretext after the said four months have passed, under penalty of 25 <term>pounds: "lire picciole"</term> <note>The "lira picciola" was a standard Florentine silver-based currency unit</note> for each withdrawal that he grants; for which penalty he shall be subject to the Conservators of the Law. And the informer, whether public or secret, shall gain one-fourth of the fine. 

And because I, Giovanni Battista of Monte Catino, <note>original: "Iohannes Baptista de Monte Catino"</note> have caused the aforesaid to be extracted from the <term>Green Book: "libro viridi"</term> of the customs laws of the Ducal city of Florence and have compared it with the original, therefore, in good faith I have signed my name, this day, November 4, 1556, in the 15th indiction [etc.].

...it is appropriate that care should still be taken regarding the holding, possessing, and selling of clean and well-sifted drugs, ensuring there is no dust nor husks, as is ordained in the law of the <term>Guild: "Arte"</term> of 1509 <margin>just as with pepper, added in the margin by a hand from 1558</margin> (1). And let it be understood that the said siftings, pepper-dust, powder, shells, and husks are and shall be prohibited as much if they are found inserted and mixed into any of the said goods and items as if they were found outside of them, separated by themselves, or brought in differently or held by anyone under any other pretense. This is specifically to the effect that all [goods], by virtue of the present [reform], always are and must be—and thus shall be brought, held, and sold in every place of the city and its countryside and district—good, clean, pure, and <term>merchantable: "merchantile"</term>, and without any deceit, fraud, or malice.

And they deliberated and commanded that no broker of the said Guild can or should make any trade, nor intervene in any way, regarding the said goods and items that are not well-cleaned or sifted as stated, nor any of the aforementioned prohibited things, in whatever place or part or manner they are mixed or by themselves; nor shall the weigher weigh them or cause them to be weighed, under the same penalties and prejudices in the said provision...

### XXXI. Concerning orders of pledges.

Regarding orders of <term>pledges: "pegni"</term> <note>Goods given as collateral for a debt</note>, the custom of the said <term>Guild: "arte"</term> shall be observed as in the past: the debtor is to be assigned a period of eight days to redeem the pledged goods. Once those eight days have passed, according to the regulations of the said Guild, the debtor must be summoned to receive a sentence for the sale of the goods, which will be granted to whoever offers the highest price. Once such a summons has been made, the sentence may be issued by the <term>Consuls: "consoli"</term> <note>The elected judicial and administrative leaders of the Guild</note>, as it shall best seem fit and pleasing to their Lordships.

Once this sentence is given, it must—at the request of the person in whose favor it was granted—be notified through the Guild's officials to the person against whom it was issued, so that the goods may be sold. The debtor is then granted a further eight days from the time of notification to be able to redeem the goods. All of this must appear in the records of the Guild.

Only after those eight days from the notification have passed, and not before, can and must the goods subject to the sentence be sold and granted to whoever offers the most via a <term>bid: "poliza"</term> <note>A written offer or ticket</note> containing a specific amount of money declared therein. To this end, the Chancellor is required to conduct a search through one of the <term>messengers: "donzelli"</term> <note>Minor officials or attendants who carried out the Guild's physical errands</note> of the Guild. 

Every messenger, upon any simple commission from the Chancellor, must immediately and diligently go among the craftsmen in the places throughout the city of Florence where it is most appropriate to sell such goods. He must show and offer them to everyone, collect the bids, and receive them sealed from whoever makes an offer, then bring them to the Guild into the hands of the Chancellor. As soon as the Chancellor has received them, he must open them all in the presence of the said messenger, and the goods shall be understood as granted and awarded in sale to the one who made the highest offer, as stated above.

The person to whom the goods remain, as described, is required on that same day or on the next non-holiday day to receive and accept them, and immediately pay the full amount of his offer into the hands of the Chancellor or the messenger at the Guild. If the buyer does not come or send for them, the Chancellor must, on that day or afterward, as best and as quickly as he can, send the messenger to demand payment. If the buyer has still not paid the money from his offer, the Chancellor can and must—using every appropriate practical remedy, bypassing all formalities and legal technicalities—compel him by every executive way and means to effectively pay the full amount in cash as stated above...

# REFORM OF 1558 XXXX-XXXXII

## XXXX. The messenger who is on duty may not depart.

Likewise, they deliberated that whichever of the aforementioned messengers <note>Italian: *donzelli*, the guild's junior administrative officers or attendants who acted as couriers and guards</note> is on duty in the guild <note>Italian: *arte*</note>, he is required and must remain continuously at said guild for the entire duration of his shift. He may not leave, except at the accustomed hours, without express license or commission from the consuls, or by their order through the chancellor. He must thus serve in all appropriate and necessary matters that occur daily within the guild.

## XXXXI. He must take care of the weights and measures.

And beyond his other obligations, he must keep and take diligent care of the steelyard <note>Italian: *stadera*, a portable balance scale with a sliding weight used for trade</note>, the scales, the weights, the measuring rod <note>Italian: *channa*, a standard unit of length used for measuring cloth or construction materials</note>, and generally all the things in said guild belonging to it or depending on it in any way, always acting with sound and pure intent <note>Italian: *sano et puro intellecto*, a legal phrase meaning he must act in good faith and with honest judgment</note>. In those matters for which either the purveyor <note>Italian: *provveditore*, the official responsible for the guild's supplies and finances</note> or the chancellor are held and obligated by virtue of their office, the messengers shall not be held liable except as and how—in the event of an accidental loss or damage (which God forbid)—it seems fitting to the consuls at that time (and obtained by a two-thirds vote) that each of them should be responsible respectively according to the quality, the case, and the quantity of the matter. Furthermore, except for the aforementioned circumstances, the messenger must always render and give a true and full account to whomever and in whatever manner the said consuls freely see fit. For whatever is found missing, as determined by the consuls as stated above, he shall be required to replace and pay for it out of his own funds to the guild.

## XXXXII. When the messenger is absent, a penalty of 1 lira.

And they willed that for every time and every day that the messenger on duty fails to be present in the aforementioned guild as stated, he shall be condemned—now as then in such a case—every time he is absent for a day, to a fine of twenty small soldi <note>Italian: *s. venti picc.* (soldi piccioli); twenty soldi equaled one lira</note>, to be withheld from his salary. Thus, time by time, the chancellor who has notice of it must record it in the book of absences <note>Italian: *libro dell'appuntature*, a logbook for tracking official attendance and penalties</note>, and then notify the consuls of said guild assembled at that time. Once their lordships have found this to be the truth, they shall declare that such a messenger has not observed the rules, and by such declaration, he shall remain fully condemned. If the said consuls are not convinced this is the case, they may acquit him, and thus he shall remain acquitted from time to time, and not otherwise. And the purveyor—

# XXXXII, XXXXIII REFORM OF 1558

Regarding this, having seen and considered—for the advancement of the orders and statutes of the said guild <term>arte: the professional guild</term> and university <note>In the 16th century, "university" (università) referred to the legal corporate body of the guild members, not an educational institution.</note>—what was necessary to be seen, considered, and observed for the best possible adherence to them, they provided, ordained, and deliberated that these shall begin to be observed (providing it pleases His Illustrious Excellency <note>A reference to Cosimo I de' Medici, Duke of Florence, whose approval was required for guild statutes.</note>), from the first day of May 1557 onward, for as long as it shall seem fit and pleasing to him in every respect. ### XXXXIII. That the chancellor must notify the articles, having received the order from the consuls.

...in the manner and form that will be ordered for them. And the **haberdashers** <note>original: "merciai"</note> alone shall be bound to the **audit of their accounts** <note>original: "tara dei conti". In this context, *tara* refers to a regulatory check or balancing of financial records to ensure compliance with guild standards.</note> just as the **apothecaries** <note>original: "spetiali"</note> from outside the city are bound, and with the same penalties in all respects. This is expressly declared: that said haberdashers and other practitioners, by reason of the payment of said oratory fee and matriculation, are not understood to be subject to the said guild regarding civil disputes among themselves, but shall be left to their ordinary **court jurisdiction** <note>original: "foro". And all those who fall under the statutes of said guild and who pay said oratory fee within the month (1), shall be understood to be free from the penalty of 25 **lire** contained in the statutes of said guild for whoever practices a trade without being matriculated. Otherwise, they shall be understood to have incurred said penalty, and shall also be obliged and compelled to pay the said oratory fee and matriculation; and the aforesaid rectors shall be bound to conduct a diligent search for them, providing a list of transgressors to the said consuls. What was previously provided and ordered regarding the branch of doctors and apothecaries from outside the city remains firm [etc.].

The aforementioned provision was **passed** <note>original: "vinta". Literally "won," referring to the successful outcome of a vote.</note> among the said four reformers on the 30th day of October 1574 by way of a vote, and a copy was sent to His Most Serene Highness.
